en: The *Jātakamālā*, an alternative title for the *Bodhisattvāvadānamālā*, composed by the noble Āryaśūra.
Oṃ, homage to all the glorious Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!

With devotion, I shall worship with this handful of flower-garlands of my own poem the wondrous deeds of the Sage in his previous births— deeds that were glorious, auspicious through their possession of excellent virtues, the abodes of fame, and enchanting beyond all praise.
Since the path to the state of a Sugata is indicated by these praiseworthy signs that serve as its marks,
even those of harsh minds will surely find serenity, and discourses on the Dharma will attain a state of being most delightful.
"Having observed that it is for the sake of the world, this effort shall be undertaken by way of scripture, the teachings of the sages, and sound reasoning;
so that, through portions of the extraordinary deeds of the Supreme Being, my own intuitive insight may attain the state of being dear to the sacred tradition."

I bow my head to that peerless one, together with his Dharma and Saṅgha, whose splendor of recognized virtues—even by those striving for their own self-interest—could never be fully grasped; he whose fame shines with unerring words as "the All-Knowing One."
The Tigress Jātaka:

Since even in previous births the Blessed One was one whose nature was supremely affectionate toward all beings without cause, and who had become the very self of all creatures, one should cultivate the highest faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Thus it is heard—this *avadāna* of a former birth of the Blessed One being proclaimed by our own gurus, who hold the Three Jewels as supreme, who have won over their teachers through the excellence of their practice, and who are supreme in the discernment of virtues:

"It is said that when this Blessed One was a Bodhisattva, he favored the world with the natural outflow of compassion—consisting of generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and so forth—which were consistent with his extraordinary vows and rendered blameless through the mastery of wisdom; and while he delighted in his own Dharma, he brought about a pure and ever-increasing way of life."

He took birth in a great brahmin family. Having undergone the sequence of purificatory rites, such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and others, and growing up, he— due to his natural intelligence, his exceptional support, his curiosity for knowledge, and his lack of indolence— before long attained mastery over the eighteen branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*) and all the arts (*kalā*) not inconsistent with the traditions of his own lineage.
He attained that state;
like Brahmā, he became the object of great honor among the knowers of Brahman, like a king among kings;
like the thousand-eyed Indra in person, he was the fulfiller of the aims of his subjects who sought knowledge, like a father.
A great abundance of gain, honor, and fame appeared for him, won over by the excellence of his fortune and virtues;

yet the Bodhisattva, whose mind was cultivated through the practice of the Dharma and who was already familiar with the life of renunciation, did not take delight in that. His intellect purified by his former conduct, he perceived the multitude of faults inherent in sensual pleasures.
Having cast off the life of a householder as if it were a state of ill health, he adorned a certain forest retreat.
There, through that state of non-attachment and through his tranquility purified by wisdom,
he seemed to rebuke the world of men, whose peace was shattered by attachment to evil deeds.
With their minds pervaded by a tranquility consisting of loving-kindness that seemed to flow forth from him,
the wild beasts roamed about like ascetics, their natures turned away from mutual hostility.
Through purity of conduct, restraint of the senses, the practice of contentment, and the quality of compassion,
he became as dear to the people of the world— even those with whom he was unacquainted— as they were to him.
Due to his state of few desires, he was unacquainted with hypocrisy; having abandoned longing for gain, fame, and pleasure, he inclined even the minds of the gods toward serenity and devotion.

Then, having heard that he had gone forth, men whose hearts were bound by his virtues abandoned their kinsmen and possessions and entered into discipleship under him, as if approaching spiritual perfection itself.
In purity of conduct, in the cultivation of the senses, in the non-forgetfulness of mindfulness, in solitude,
and likewise in the mental concentration of loving-kindness and the rest, he instructed his disciples according to their capacity.

Then, at one time, when that Great Being’s assembly of disciples had become fully perfected and greatly increased, when they had been established on this auspicious path and led onto the true road of renunciation, and while the gates to the states of woe were effectively closed and the paths to happy rebirths were made like royal highways,
he was followed by his contemporary disciple Ajita for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life, [practicing] those things conducive to yoga.
He wandered through mountain caves and forest thickets;
then, there in a mountain glen, he beheld a tigress who,
due to the exhaustion of childbirth, had fallen into a state of motionless lethargy.
With a pair of eyes emaciated by fasting and a belly exceedingly hollowed by hunger,
she looked even upon her own young children as if they were food.
She was scolding with cruel cries of "roar-roar," as if threatening enemies, those who had approached her out of thirst for milk and were free from fear due to their confidence in their mother.
But the Bodhisattva, though steadfast, seeing her, trembled through the power of compassion at the suffering of another,
like the king of mountains at an earthquake.
It is truly marvelous that those whose nature is compassion, having manifested fortitude even amidst their own great sufferings,
tremble at the slightest suffering of another.

Then that Bodhisattva, with words composed by the power of compassion, which revealed his extraordinary nature and were uttered with a hurried repetition of syllables, said to his disciple: "Child, child! Behold the worthlessness of cyclic existence; this doe, driven by hunger, disregards even the bounds of affection for her own offspring and desires to devour them."
"Alas! How exceedingly cruel is this ferocity of self-love, by which even a mother desires to devour her own children!"
Who would wish to nourish the enemy consisting of self-attachment,
by which one might set foot even upon such deeds as these?
"Therefore, let some means to counteract her suffering from hunger be sought immediately, before she destroys both her children and herself.
I too shall strive to dissuade her from this rash act.
Having promised him "So be it," he departed and became intent on searching for food for her.
Then the Bodhisattva, having dismissed that disciple with an evasive pretext, fell into reflection:
"While my entire body is present, why do I seek flesh from another?"
For his success in obtaining [the fruit] was accidental; likewise, this failure in my task would be accidental as well.

Moreover: He who does not feel joy when his body— which is soulless, subject to division, devoid of essence, painful, ungrateful, and perpetually impure— is being employed for the sake of another, is no wise man.

Out of attachment to one's own happiness, or due to a lack of power, the suffering of another is neglected. Yet, since I have no happiness while another suffers, and since I possess the power [to help], how could I remain indifferent?
If, while possessing the power to do so, I were to remain indifferent even toward an assailant engulfed in suffering,
my mind would burn as if I had committed a sin, like dry grass consumed by a great fire.
Therefore, by casting my life from this precipice into the water with this body,
I shall protect the doe from the slaughter of her son and her offspring from the deer-hunter.
Furthermore:
It is a vision for those eager for the welfare of the world; an encouragement for those of feeble resolve;
a source of joy for those skilled in renunciation; and an attraction for the minds of the virtuous. (Jm 1.26)
It causes despondency to the great armies of Māra; it inspires confidence in those who love the qualities of a Buddha;
it gives rise to shame in those intent on their own self-interest, and in those whose souls are afflicted by stinginess and greed.

It inspires faith in those who rely on the supreme vehicle, it causes wonder in those who pride themselves on their renunciation, it purifies the great path to heaven for those who delight in giving, and it brings joy to men who rejoice in such acts.
"When will the wish that arose in me—'May I indeed benefit others even with my own limbs'—bear fruit, and may supreme enlightenment also be not far off? Jm_1.29.
Moreover: It is not out of rivalry, nor from a desire for fame, nor for the sake of attaining heaven, nor for the cause of sovereignty,
nor even for my own ultimate happiness, that I have such devotion as this toward anything other than the accomplishment of the welfare of others.

Likewise, may I always possess the power to remove the suffering of the world and to bring about its happiness at the same time as this [sun], just as the sun possesses the power to dispel darkness and produce light.
Whether I have seen his virtues, or have come to remember them, or have clearly entered into a conversation with him,
may I at every turn bring about for the world benefits that are ever accompanied by happiness.
Having thus resolved to accomplish the welfare of others, he— experiencing joy even at the risk of his own life—
cast off his body, astonishing even the minds of the steadfast deities.

Then that tigress, her curiosity and indignation aroused by the sound of the Bodhisattva’s body falling, ceased her attempt to slaughter her own offspring and cast her eyes about. As soon as she saw the Bodhisattva’s lifeless body, she rushed forward suddenly and began to devour it.
Now, that disciple of his, having failed to obtain any meat, returned and, looking about for his teacher, saw the Bodhisattva’s lifeless body being devoured by that young tigress.

He beheld him; and, his surge of grief and suffering momentarily checked by the wonder at that excellence of action, as if overflowing with profound respect for the refuge of such virtues, he would shine while speaking these words to himself:
"Oh, how great is the compassion of this noble-souled one toward people afflicted by calamity! Oh, how great is his lack of attachment to his own happiness!"
Oh, how the state of the virtuous has been brought to its highest excellence! Oh, how the glory of the fame of others has been crushed!
"Oh! What supreme love, free from fear and resting upon virtue, has been displayed through this great courage!
Oh! His slender body has been forcibly made a worthy recipient of the highest honor!"

"Alas! This indignation of mine toward the misfortunes of others—who naturally gentle and the upholders of the earth—is truly remarkable. Alas! My own stubbornness has been brought to light by this excellence of valor."
Now that the world has come under the protection of this Lord, it truly need no longer grieve;
for today, the God of Love, seized with agitation at the fear of defeat, is surely intent on sighing deeply.

"In every way, let there be homage to this illustrious one, the refuge of all beings, possessed of exceedingly vast compassion, the immeasurable being, the Bodhisattva of ultimate reality, the Mahāsattva!
Then he reported that matter to his fellow religious practitioners.
Thereupon, with faces struck with wonder by that deed, his disciples, along with Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Bhujagas, and the lords of the gods, [honored him].
The earth, covered with showers of garlands, garments, ornaments, and sandalwood powder, became a ground of his bones.

Thus, since that Blessed One—even in previous births—possessed a nature of supreme, disinterested affection for all sentient beings and was the very self of all living creatures, one should cultivate the highest faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One; and those who have developed such faith should generate supreme joy toward the Buddha, the Blessed One.
One should also reflect: "In this way, our faith has found its proper object."
In that same way, the Dharma should be heard with due respect.

Thus, because it was accomplished through hundreds of difficult feats, even in the description of compassion (*karuṇā*), one must speak in this manner: "Compassion is the cause for engaging in the act of favoring others, which brings about the excellence of its own nature.
This concludes the first *Vyāghrījātaka*.
2. The Śibi-jātaka: "This True Dharma was acquired by that Blessed One for our sake through hundreds of difficult deeds"; thus, it should be heard with reverence.

Thus it is heard: This Blessed One, while formerly a bodhisattva, having through practice over immeasurable time made his accumulated meritorious deeds a part of his very nature, once became the king of the Śibis.

From his childhood onward, he delighted in attending upon his elders, was devoted to discipline, and had subjects who were likewise devoted to him. By virtue of his natural intelligence, his mind became exceedingly vast through the acquisition of many sciences; and he was endowed with energy, the power of mantras, majesty, sovereign strength, and divine fortune.
He protected his subjects like his own children.
In him, the floods of virtues conducive to the three aims of life shone forth in their full form, as if established through the union of great joy;
they did not suffer any loss of splendor due to the agitation of mutual conflict.
Like a mockery for the insolent and arrogant, like a most grievous calamity for the dull-witted,
and like wine for those of small soul, that royal fortune there was truly worthy of its name.

On account of his noble nature, his quality of compassion, and his sovereignty over wealth, that best of kings took delight in beholding the faces of supplicants— possessing an untroubled splendor— rejoicing in the fulfillment of their desires.

Then that king, out of his love for giving, caused alms-halls to be built all around the city, well-stocked with every requisite, wealth, and grain; and like a cloud at the beginning of the Kṛta age, he rained down a shower of gifts— conforming to his own majesty, fulfilling every desire, provided with all honors, enchanting, and auspicious because it was not untimely.
Food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink,
and bedding, seating, clothing, meals, perfumes, garlands, silver, gold, and so forth, to those seeking each of these.
Then, having heard of that king’s generosity and magnanimity, men dwelling in regions distinguished by various directions approached that land with hearts struck with wonder and filled with joy.
Having mentally traversed the entire world of men and found no opportunity for a request elsewhere,
those seekers approached him with joyful faces, just as wild elephants flock to a great lake.

Then that king, his eyes dilated with joy at the sight of the beggars— who were approaching from all sides with minds delighted by the hope of gain, whose natural beauty was concealed by the attire of travelers, and who appeared like friends long separated— experienced a blossoming of affection.
He welcomed the supplication as if it were pleasant news, and by giving, he conquered the petitioner with his own satisfaction.
The fragrant scent of his fame, born of his generosity, was spread abroad by the wind of the words of those who sought his aid;
it dispelled the pride of other kings, just as the scent of a scent-elephant (gandhadvipa) subdues rival elephants.

Then once, as that king was inspecting his halls of charity, he observed that because the people seeking wealth were satisfied, the arrival of supplicants had become sparse; yet, because the practice of giving had not increased, he did not find contentment.
Those seeking wealth approached him and quenched their thirst, but that prince, exuberant in generosity, did not satisfy them merely by granting their requests.
For no seeker was able to overcome his resolve for giving simply by the magnitude of his petition.
The thought occurred to him: "Extremely fortunate are those distinguished holy men to whom supplicants, with full confidence and without restraint, even beg for their own limbs.
As for me, however, my suppliants have become hesitant in their requests for mere wealth, as if they had been threatened by harsh words of rejection.
Then, [he saw] that king who had turned away from attachment even to his own limbs, so exceedingly noble...
Perceiving that thought centered on giving, the earth trembled like a wife devoted to her husband.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, on Mount Sumeru— the king of mountains, which was shaken by the trembling of the earth’s surface and illuminated by the radiance of various jewels—
was seized by the thought, "What is this? Having perceived that excessive deliberation of the king as being caused by the shaking of the earth's surface,
his heart overcome with wonder, he fell into reflection.
With a mind exultant and uplifted by his zeal for giving, what indeed was reflected upon by the king,
who had girded himself with the belt of resolve for generosity and remained firm in his determination to give away his own body?
"I shall first investigate this matter. Then,

while that king was seated upon his throne, surrounded by his assembly of ministers, and after the customary proclamation had been made— calling out, "Who among the petitioners desires what?"— and while the treasuries under the supervision of the treasury officials were being opened...

While the heaps of jewels, gold, and silver were being distributed, while bags filled with various garments were being brought forth, and while a multitude of diverse and excellent vehicles— yoked to the shoulders of various well-trained mounts— were being set in motion as a stream of supplicants began to flow, Śakra, the lord of the gods, manifested himself in the form of an aged and blind brahmin.
He appeared within the range of the king’s vision.

Then, as if welcomed and embraced by the gaze of that king—which was imbued with compassion and loving-kindness, and was steady, serene, and gentle—he was invited, "What is your need? by the king’s attendants, and approached the presence of the monarch.
Preceded by words of victory and blessing, he spoke thus to the king: "O foremost of monarchs, an old man has approached from afar seeking the sight of your eyes.
For even with a single eye, O lotus-eyed lord of the world, the course of worldly life may be maintained."

Then that Bodhisattva, experiencing a supreme festival of joy through the fulfillment of his heart’s desire, yet feeling a sense of inquiry— wondering whether what the brahmin had spoken was indeed true, or whether he himself had merely perceived it so due to the habit of conceptualization— and with a mind thirsty to hear the pleasant words of the request for his eyes, spoke to that beggar for his eyes:
"By whom were you instructed, O chief of brahmins, that you have come here to beg my eyes?
It is a common saying that 'the eye is very hard to give away'; whose confidence in me has led you to believe this?"
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, wearing the guise of a brahmin, having understood the king’s intention, said:
"I have come here to beg your eye at the instruction of Śakra, who is like Śakra himself.
Fulfill the honor shown to him and my own hope by granting me an eye."

Then that king, having reflected that by the power of the deity Śakra’s proclamation, this brahmin would surely regain his sight through this ritual, spoke to him with words clear from joy: "O brahmin, I shall fulfill for you that very desire for which you have come;
to you who long for it, I give one eye, and I shall even give you both eyes."

With your face adorned by eyes like blossomed blue lotuses, go as you please before the people who gaze upon you, wondering whether he is indeed that very person or not— tossed on the swing of doubt and filled with wonder as the thought "It is he! arises.

Then the ministers of that king, perceiving his resolve to give away his eyes, their minds distressed by agitation, alarm, and despair, said to the king: "Out of excessive joy for giving, you have failed to consider this improper act which will result in misfortune.
Be gracious, O Lord; do not, do not do this; you ought not to give away your eyes."
Do not abandon us all for the sake of this one brahmin;
enough with burning our subjects, who have been raised in happiness, with the fire of grief.
Bestow wealth that awakens prosperity, glorious jewels, milch-cows, and harnessed chariots; or grant elephants, beautiful with the playful majesty of intoxication.

"Grant houses that resound with the tinkling of anklets, possessing a splendor exceeding autumnal clouds and providing comfort in all seasons; do not give away your own eye, O sole eye of the world! Jm_2.18.
Furthermore, let this be considered, O Great King:
how indeed can the eye belonging to one person be applied to another?
Or, if this is the power of a deity, why is your own eye required?
Moreover, O King: what is the use of eyes to a poor man that witness the prosperity of others?
Therefore, O King, give wealth; do not act with such rashness.
Then the king spoke to those ministers with words that were both conciliatory and sweet:
"He who, having said 'I shall give,' then sets his mind on not giving,
fastens upon himself the loosened noose of greed."
Who could be more sinful than he who, having promised "I shall give," sets his mind otherwise through stinginess and an irresolute intellect? (Jm 2.22)
Having firmly established the hopes of those who seek aid with the promise, "I shall give," there is no atonement for speech that is harsh due to its failure to fulfill that promise.
As for the argument that his eye might exist solely through the power of the deity, let this be heard:
indeed, it is observed that effects are not accomplished by a single cause alone.
For even a god or fate must depend upon other causes.
"Therefore, you ought not to strive to create an obstacle for my resolve regarding this extraordinary act of giving.

The ministers said, "We informed [Your Majesty] that Your Majesty ought to give wealth, grain, and jewels, but not your own eyes; therefore, we do not wish to lead Your Majesty astray at an improper occasion. The king said:
"One should give exactly what is requested; that which is not desired does not please the recipient when given here in this world.
What use are waters to one being carried away by a flood? Therefore, I shall give him the object he has asked for. (Jm 2.25)

Then the chief minister, who enjoyed the king’s profoundest confidence and affection, disregarding all formal etiquette out of the force of his devotion, spoke thus to the king: "O King, do not [do this]!

That which cannot be attained by anyone through any small measure of austerity or meditative discipline, and having reached which one may obtain both fame and heaven through hundreds of great sacrifices—"
Having attained this kingship that rivals the splendor of Śakra, what have you seen that you wish to give away your eyes? Who are you, and from where does this strange custom originate?
Having found your opportunity among the gods through sacrifices, and shining everywhere with your fame,
with your feet colored by the luster of the crest-jewels of kings— what is it that you desire that you give away your very eyes?
Then the king spoke to that minister with conciliation:
"This effort is not for the sake of attaining universal sovereignty, nor heaven, nor liberation, nor fame.
This is my intent to protect the worlds; let not this trouble of his begging be in vain."

Then that king, having slowly extracted one eye—possessing a beautiful luster like a fragment of a blue lotus petal—without injury, according to the method prescribed by the physician, gave it with supreme joy to the petitioner for eyes.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, performed such a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that the king, together with his retinue, saw that eye re-established in its place.
Then, beholding the eye-seeker with one eye opened, the king, his heart filled with supreme joy, gave him even the second eye.
Thereupon, having bestowed both eyes, the king’s face was like a lotus-pool deprived of its lotuses.
The citizens felt an extraordinary joy, and the twice-born beheld him with their full vision.
Then, in the inner apartments and throughout the city of the lord of men, the earth was drenched on all sides with tears of grief;
but Śakra was filled with wonder and supreme satisfaction upon beholding the king’s unshakable resolve for perfect enlightenment.
Then, his heart overcome with wonder, this thought occurred to Śakra:
"Oh, what constancy! Oh, what courage! Oh, what desire for the welfare of beings!
Even though this deed is before my very eyes, it seems to provoke reflection."
Therefore, this wondrous being ought not to endure such suffering for long;
for I shall strive to restore his sight by demonstrating the proper means.
Now, as time passed, the king’s eye-wound gradually healed, and the grief of the women of the inner court, the citizens, and the people of the countryside subsided and became diminished.

Because of his desire for solitude, as he sat cross-legged on the bank of a garden pond— where excellent trees were most beautiful, bent down by the weight of their blossoms, where a soft, fragrant, cool, and pleasant breeze blew, and which resounded with the humming of swarms of bees— the god Śakra, lord of the deities, appeared before him. When the king asked, "Who is this?", he replied:
"I am Śakra, the lord of the gods, who has come into your presence.
The king said, "Welcome! Please command what is required."
Having spoken thus with due courtesy, he said again to the king:
"Choose a boon, O royal sage; whatever you desire, let it be told."
Then that king, because he was accustomed to giving and unpracticed in the path of the wretchedness of begging, suppressing his astonishment and pride, said to him:
"O Śakra, my wealth is abundant and my great power is effective;
yet, because of this blindness, death alone now appeals to me."
"O Indra, it is because I do not see the faces of supplicants— even though their desires have been fully satisfied and their eyes are overflowing with joy and serene faith— that death is dear to me."
Śakra said: "Enough, enough with this resolve of yours! Only such as you, O noble being, attain such things.
Moreover, I shall first question you."
Tell me truly, how is your mind now toward those beggars who have reduced you to this state? Enough of concealing it; go now and remove that [distress] from yourself. (Jm_2.35)
The king said: "Why do you persist in making me boast before this venerable one?
Moreover, O Lord of the Gods, listen:
at that time as well as now, the words of supplicants are fixed by the very nature of their request."
Just as my beloveds are like personified blessings to me, so may my single eye arise [as it was].

Then, by the power of that king’s solemn declaration (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) and the particular accumulation of his merit, immediately upon these words, one eye appeared— resembling the petal of a blue lotus, with its center as if filled with fragments of sapphire. When that wondrous eye had appeared, the king, his mind filled with joy, spoke again to Śakra:
And as for that man who begged me for one eye, having joyfully given him two eyes,
may my mind likewise become single-pointed on the festival of joy regarding even the second eye.
Then, immediately upon his speaking, a second eye appeared for that king as if in rivalry with the first;
thereupon the earth, together with its mountains, trembled, and the ocean surged beyond its shores,
while the drums of the gods resounded with deep and enchanting tones.
His body, lovely with serene grace, shone like the sun in autumn with its purity as it illumined the quarters;
and wonderful flowers, colored by swirling sandalwood powder, fell from the vault of the sky.
The gods, accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, arrived there with eyes blossoming in wonder;
a breeze of pleasing nature blew, and joy expanded within the minds of all living beings.
Uttered by hosts of beings of great supernatural power, their minds filled with joy and wonder,
auspicious words were heard on all sides praising the king’s extraordinary deeds.

"Oh, what magnanimity! Oh, what compassion! Behold the purity of this mind! Oh, how his intellect is indifferent toward its own pleasures! Homage be to you, whose fortitude and prowess are exalted! (Jm_2.42)
The world has truly attained a protector through you, who possess the beauty of a fully blossomed lotus-eye;
indeed, the accumulation of merit has at last become fruitful, for by means of Dharma, the powerful have been conquered.
Then Śakra, having cheered him with the words "Excellent! Excellent!", spoke again:
"O King, your pure intention was not unknown to us.
Thus, O monarch, these two eyes have been restored to you by me."
And these two shall possess the power to see, without obstruction, even that which is concealed by mountains for a hundred yojanas on every side.
Having spoken thus, Śakra likewise vanished.
Then the Bodhisattva, followed by ministers whose minds were filled with wonder and whose eyes were wide open and blinking very slowly,
watched by the citizens, and greeted with words of victory and blessing by the brahmins, proceeded toward the excellent city adorned with raised banners and variegated flags.

Having approached the assembly where the splendor of his rising glory was being fully displayed, he sat down; then, for the sake of honoring the ministers led by the prime minister, as well as the elders of the brahmins and the citizens and country-folk who had come to pay their respects, he taught them this Dharma concerning himself:
"Who indeed in this world would be slack in their zeal to perform with wealth what is pleasing to those who seek it?"
"Having beheld these two eyes of mine, endowed with divine power and obtained through the merit of my former gifts."
Even though it is hidden by many mountains and more than a hundred yojanas away,
I see that clearly visible object from every side as if it were standing nearby.
What means for attaining prosperity is superior to the gift born of discipline and compassion for others, by which,
having given away my human eye right here, I have obtained a superhuman, divine eye?
Having understood this, O Śibis, make wealth fruitful through gifts and enjoyment;
for this is the path in both this world and the next for one who prizes fame and whose happiness arises from it.
The essence of wealth—which is otherwise pithless and trivial—is that which is given away by one intent on the welfare of the world;
for what is being given becomes a true treasure, whereas what is not given results solely in destruction.
Thus, this True Dharma was brought forth for our sake by that Blessed One through hundreds of difficult feats; it should therefore be heard with reverence.

Furthermore, as before, the greatness of the Tathāgata and the praise of his compassion should be recounted here, as well as the demonstration of the fruits of merit: how merits accumulated with such reverence manifest even in this very life a mere blossom of one’s own power—a captivating succession of fame.
Thus ends the second Jātaka, the Śibi-jātaka.
3. The Kulmāṣapiṇḍī-jātaka.
There is no gift whatsoever—whether arising from a serene state of mind or bestowed upon an excellent recipient—that is not significant, because of the greatness of its maturation.
As it is heard in tradition: when the Blessed One was a Bodhisattva, he was indeed the sovereign of Kośala.
The splendor of his divine endowment surpassed even the excellence of those royal qualities such as energy, counsel, and sovereign power;
for his virtues shone all the more brightly when adorned by that divine fortune,
like the rays of the moon when its beauty has blossomed in autumn.

He abandoned even his arrogant enemies, while Fortune, like a passionate woman, took her pleasure with those who sought refuge in him; thus, his sovereignty over other kings was subject to his anger and his favor.
Because his very nature was rooted in righteousness, his mind never turned toward the cruelty or ill-will that harms others;
yet his affection for his servants grew so great that the Goddess of Fortune could no longer find pleasure even among his enemies.
He recollected his own birth that had just passed away.

Through that recollection, a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him, and he bestowed gifts upon ascetics, brahmins, the destitute, and beggars as a primary cause for the attainment of happiness; he continuously cultivated the restraint of ethical conduct and undertook the observance of the *poṣadha* on festival days.

And the king, desiring to establish the world in the highest good by manifesting the power of merit within his assembly and his own inner apartments, spoke with a confident heart these two verses of certain meaning:

"Service rendered to the Sugata, even if it be very slight, does not yield a meager result; for consider this greatness of the fruit of that single ball of sour gruel, which was previously heard of as being saltless, parched, rough, and coarse. (Jm 3.4)

Behold the splendor of the abundance of my fruits: this army of mine, diverse with chariots and horses and featuring intoxicated lordly elephants; this entire earth; vast wealth; devoted prosperity; noble wives; and even this lump of sour gruel. Jm_3.5 //

The ministers, the elder brahmins, and the leading citizens, though their minds were whirled by curiosity, did not dare to question him as to what the Great King had in view when he repeatedly recited these two verses. Then, because the king’s speech was constant, the queen— whose flow of affection remained entirely unimpeded— her curiosity having arisen, questioned him in the assembly when the opportunity for conversation presented itself.
"O Lord of Men, you speak with certainty as if pouring forth the joy residing in your heart;
my own heart is filled with curiosity by that which you have said."
If this person is worthy to hear it, O King, then tell me why you speak thus;
for such a secret is never proclaimed anywhere, and yet I am asking about it openly.
Then the king, gazing at the queen with an affectionate and tender look, his face blossoming with a smile, said:
"Having heard this utterance of mine without discerning its cause or purpose,
it is not only your mind that is stirred by curiosity in this matter."

Moreover, this entire circle of ministers has their minds agitated and restless with curiosity, as does the city together with its inner apartments; therefore, let it be heard by you why I speak thus.

Like one awakened from sleep, I remember my birth; I was once a laborer in this very city, possessing moral virtue yet maintaining a wretched livelihood earned through the performance of work for those exalted by wealth alone.
Thus, desiring to enter into service— a hall of humiliation, toil, and wretchedness— out of hope for protection and fear of lacking a livelihood,
I saw four ascetics seeking alms, their senses subdued and as if followed by the very splendor of mendicancy.
Having bowed with a mind softened by faith to them, I, being self-restrained, gave a mere portion of boiled grain in my own home;
for this is like the sprouting of its fruit, that the radiance from the crest-jewels of other kings is now fixed upon the dust of my feet.
Intending this very thing, O Queen, I say:
"I find satisfaction through merit and through the sight of the Worthy Ones. (Jm 3.13)
Then that queen, her eyes wide with joy and wonder, gazing at the king with great respect, said this to him:
"Such a distinguished excellence of the arising of karmic fruition as this is truly worthy of merits;
and it is fitting for the Great King, who has witnessed the fruits of merit firsthand, that you have such devotion toward meritorious deeds."
Thus, being averse to the practice of evil, like a father toward his subjects, he was intent on their proper protection and devoted to the accumulation of masses of merit;
blazing with the glory of fame and the abundance of his gifts, his commands were established upon the heads of rival kings.
Protect for a long time the earth, whose garment is the ocean lashed by the winds, according to the way of Dharma.
The king said: "How could this not be so, O Queen?
I shall strive once more to take refuge in that very path to the highest good, whose lovely signs have been clearly perceived.
For when people, having heard of the fruit of giving, offer it to others, why should I not give away what belongs to myself upon hearing of it?"
Then the king, gazing affectionately upon the queen—who blazed with splendor like a goddess—his heart filled with curiosity regarding the cause of her magnificent fortune, spoke again:
"O auspicious lady, you shine in the midst of women like the crescent moon among the stars. What deed, indeed, have you performed that results in such exceedingly sweet prosperity?"
The Goddess said: "O Lord, there is something that I too remember from my former birth.
When she was respectfully questioned by the King, saying, "Tell me, tell me now," she replied:
"I remember it as if experienced in childhood, when, being a maidservant, I [ate] a single portion of food that had been set aside."
Having respectfully offered [this] to the Sage whose outflows are exhausted, I have now awakened here from that state in which I was as if asleep.
"I remember this merit, O god among men, by which I have attained lordship over the earth together with you;
for you spoke just as the Sage did: 'Among those whose outflows are exhausted, not even the slightest thing is called "mine". (Jm 3.18)

Then that king, perceiving that the assembly had conceived great respect for meritorious deeds through the demonstration of the fruits of merit, and that their minds were serene and filled with wonder and one-pointed attention, gave this instruction: "Seeing such an extensive splendor of the ripening of even a small amount of virtue,
who indeed would not be intent on performing meritorious acts through the practice of generosity and ethical discipline?"
That man, even though he possesses sufficient wealth, is not even fit to be looked upon, for his mind is shrouded by the darkness of miserliness and he fails to attain fame through gifts.
That which must be relinquished by one who is powerless, and that which is not for the sake of anyone else— if one should abandon wealth according to what is right and thereby manifest some virtue,
who that knows the essence of virtues would resort to a path of envy in that regard?
Various qualities such as joy and others, followed by fame, arise from the merit of giving and establishing [shrines].
Generosity is indeed a great treasure that follows one and cannot be shared with thieves and the like;
generosity is the washing away of the dust of the faults of stinginess and greed from the mind,
and it is a comfortable vehicle that removes the exhaustion of the path of saṃsāra.
Generosity is a constant friend, its face ever pleasant with the provision of manifold comforts.

Whether it be the arising of great wealth, or the radiant quality of sovereign knowledge, or the excellence of physical beauty in dwelling within the city of the Thirty-three gods—whatever one desires, all that is obtained through giving. Considering this fact, who would not bestow gifts?
They say that among all riches, giving is the extraction of the essence; they say that giving is the foundation of all sovereignties.
Giving is the noble deed of glorious and virtuous people; even for those of childish intellect, the gift of sand is a true gift.
Then that assembly, having with great respect rejoiced at those persuasive words of the king, became intent upon the practice of giving and so forth.
Thus, there is no gift whatsoever—whether arising from a pure state of mind or bestowed upon an excellent recipient—that is not of small consequence, because of the greatness of its maturation.
Therefore, one who gives a gift with a clear heart to the Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit, should generate supreme joy.
"Such riches as these, and even more distinguished than these, are not far from me either.
Thus ends the third Jātaka, the Kulmāṣapiṇḍī-jātaka.
(Vaidya 20)
4. In the Śreṣṭhijātaka, virtuous men desire to give even without regard for their own loss;
by what healthy person, then, should anything not be given?

Thus it is heard: when this Blessed One was a bodhisattva, having acquired vast wealth and prosperity through the excellence of his fortune and the perfection of his exertion, he became a repository of great respect in the world due to his character of impartial conduct; being of noble lineage and possessing an exceedingly pure intellect through the mastery of various sciences, arts, and disciplines, he was honored by the king on account of the greatness of his virtues.

Having received great honor and possessing wealth common to all people due to his habit of giving, he became a merchant chief (*śreṣṭhin*). His name, exalted by his heroic generosity, was proclaimed here and there by supplicants with joyful hearts, and it pervaded the ten directions.
The petitioner’s mind was not wavering on the swing of doubt as to whether he would give or not;
for toward him, whose noble deeds were renowned, the multitude of supplicants maintained a bold intimacy born of confidence.
He did not protect his wealth for the sake of his own pleasure, nor out of rivalry, nor from being overcome by greed;
he was unable to endure the suffering of beings who sought help, and therefore he protected it only to say, "There is nothing."

Then once, at the time of that Great Being’s meal, when he had bathed and anointed his body, a Pratyekabuddha—whose fuel of all afflictions had been consumed by the fire of wisdom and who desired to increase the accumulation of that [Great Being’s] merit—came to his house seeking alms. He arrived just as a variety of foods, such as hard and soft delicacies, had been prepared by a skilled and noble cook; these were endowed with an array of excellent qualities such as color, fragrance, taste, and texture.
Having approached, he stood at the gateway,
looking a yoke’s length ahead upon the earth with a gaze that was fearless, steady, firm, and gentle;
there he remained, born of tranquility, his lotus-like fingertips resting upon his alms-bowl.
Then Māra, the Evil One, unable to endure that perfection of the Bodhisattva’s generosity, and for the sake of creating an obstacle to it,

manifested between the Venerable One and the threshold of the door a hell— many fathoms deep, with a belly as terrifying as flickering flames, most profound, hideous to behold, and filled with a fearful roar; it was crowded with many hundreds of writhing beings.
Then the Bodhisattva, seeing that a Pratyekabuddha had approached seeking alms, said to his wife: "My dear lady, give the noble one a sufficient portion of food yourself.
Having assented with "So be it," she took excellent hard and soft foods and set out.

Beholding the hell near the gateway chamber, her eyes trembling with fear and despair, she suddenly turned back. When questioned by her husband, "What is this?", she—though her throat was choked by sudden terror—somehow related it to him. Then the Bodhisattva, in great agitation, thought, "How can this noble one depart from my house without having received alms? and [acted accordingly].

Disregarding what she had said, he himself took various kinds of food and drink, intending to offer alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) to that Great Being; having approached the vicinity of the gateway, he saw that most terrifying hell in between. As the thought "What could this be? arose within him, Māra, the Evil One, emerged from the wall of his palace.
Manifesting a divine and wondrous form, he stood in the sky and, as if desiring their welfare, spoke these words: "Householder, this is the great hell named Mahāraurava.
Those who, enticed by the praise of supplicants, desire to give away their wealth through an addiction to giving—"
For many thousands of autumns, their residence shall be here, from which departure is difficult to obtain.
Wealth is the specific cause for the fulfillment of the three aims of life; when that is destroyed, by whom is Dharma not destroyed?
And having destroyed Dharma by the destruction of wealth, how indeed could one not be established in hell?
Because you committed this sin for the sake of wealth while destroying the root of the Dharma through your addiction to giving,
this mouth of Naraka-antaka has risen up to devour you, its tongue a crest of flames.
Therefore, it is well that you restrain your mind from giving; for in this way, you shall not suffer immediate downfall.
Do not become equal to these givers who are struggling and weeping piteously.
But the recipient, having ceased the removal of the gift, attains the state of a god.
Therefore, desisting from obstructing the path to heaven, take recourse in self-restraint rather than the effort of giving.

Then the Bodhisattva, realizing, "Surely this is an attempt by this evil-minded one to obstruct my giving," spoke to him with words that were firm due to his steadfastness toward sentient beings and characterized by an uninterrupted sweetness of discipline: "This Noble Path has been shown to you by one who is skillful in looking after our welfare."
And his conduct, especially toward the deities, was characterized by an exceptional skill in compassion for others.
It is proper to proceed along the path of pacification either before the arising of a fault or immediately after it;
for once a disease has undergone the effort of manifestation through the faults of its treatment, the application of medical therapy becomes futile.
And I suspect this addiction to giving of mine has passed beyond the scope of medical treatment;
for even disregarding your well-wishing, my mind does not shrink from bestowing gifts.

As for what you have said—that from giving arises both merit and the specific cause for the excellence of one's purpose—this human intellect of mine does not understand it; for how could the path of Dharma truly exist apart from giving?
Whether that cause of dharma is being deposited, or is forcibly plundered by thieves, or its form is submerged within the belly of a flood, or has become food for the fire; Jm_4.14 //
"As for what you said— that the giver goes to hell while the recipient goes to the world of the Lord of the Gods—
this zeal of mine for giving has been further increased by you, even though you were restraining me."
"May these words of yours be unfailing, and may my supplicants go to heaven;
for my giving is desired for the sake of the world's welfare, not as a means to achieve my own happiness."
Then Māra, the Evil One, once again spoke to the Bodhisattva with a steady hand, as if seeking his welfare:
"Having considered these words of mine, whether they be for your benefit or mere impetuosity, go wherever you wish."
Whether filled with happiness or with remorse, you shall remember me with great respect.

The Bodhisattva said: "Forgive me, may you be patient with me. I would rather fall into a hell of flickering, fierce flames, my head bowed low and consumed by a wreath of fire, than spend the time for honoring those seekers who have shown their friendship through their requests by treating them with contempt."

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva—relying on the power of his own good fortune and knowing the absence of any harm in giving—shook off his kinsmen and attendants who were intent solely on dissuading him; with a mind unassailed by fear and his desire for generosity ever-increasing, he proceeded through the midst of the hells.
Then, by the power of his merit, a lotus free from mud appeared there for him.
He laughed at Māra as if in contempt, with his row of tusk-like filaments that were white as jasmine.
Then the Bodhisattva, having approached the Pratyekabuddha by means of a lotus-bridge produced from the excellence of his own merit, offered him alms-food with a heart filled with faith and joy.
Then, in order to awaken the clarity of his mind, the monk flew up into the sky;
raining and blazing, he shone there with the splendor of clouds illuminated by lightning.
But Māra, his desires crushed and deprived of his splendor, was overcome with dejection;
he could not bear to look at him face to face, and so he vanished along with his hell.
What, then, has been brought forward here? Even disregarding such a transgression as this, virtuous persons desire to give;
indeed, what healthy person would not wish to give?
It should also be inferred that those possessed of courage cannot be made to go toward a wrong path even out of fear.
Thus ends the fourth Jātaka, the Story of the Merchant Guild Leader.
5. The Jātaka of the Inviolable Merchant-Prince. Virtuous men do not fall into a deficiency of generosity out of regard for the loss of wealth, nor out of a desire for prosperity. As it is heard—

It is said that when the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he was a merchant named Aviṣahya (Unassailable), who was preeminent in virtues such as renunciation, morality, noble lineage, discipline, learning, and wisdom; who bestowed wealth through his abundant prosperity; who was a supreme donor because he never ceased his charitable feasts due to his hospitality toward all guests; and who was dedicated to the welfare of the world, being invulnerable to the defects of stinginess and the like.
Because it destroys the anxiety regarding the attainment of desired objects, the sight of him was a cause of particular joy for those in need,
just as his sight had been for those previously in need.
When addressed with the fixed request, "Give me," he was unable to say, "I have nothing";
for his attachment to wealth had been deprived of any room in his heart by great compassion.
As the essence of his house was being carried away by supplicants, he experienced even greater joy;
for he understood that wealth is a source of terrible and dense misfortunes, and that it quickly causes detachment from the world without cause.
For the worldly goals of people are mostly caravans on the path to miserable rebirths because they rely on greed;
yet his goals, because they brought about the prosperity of both himself and others, truly lived up to their name.

Then, as that Great Being was completely satisfying the people who came to beg with abundant distributions of wealth— distributions that were unblemished, according to their desires, and adorned by refined etiquette— Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, his mind overcome with wonder upon hearing of such noble generosity,
sought to test the firmness of his resolve regarding giving; thus, day after day, [he caused] all kinds of wealth, grain, jewels, and household goods to [disappear].
He caused each of those things to disappear, thinking, "Perhaps he might be led to practice stinginess out of fear that his wealth would be exhausted.
However, as for the Great Being who was intent upon giving...
Just as his wealth perished like droplets of water released by the sun,
even so he drew those riches out from his house with vast gifts, as if from a burning fire.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving that the Great Being was indeed devoted solely to renunciation, and with a mind even more struck with wonder because his entire wealth and essence were being exhausted, caused all that wealth and essence to vanish in a single night, with the exception of a coil of rope and a single sickle.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the Bodhisattva woke as was his custom and beheld his own palace empty of wealth, grain, furnishings, attendants, and prosperity;
it was silent and desolate, appearing as if it had been plundered by *rākṣasa* demons and no longer pleasing to the sight.
With this reflection having arisen, he searched about and saw there only that coil of rope and the sickle.

The thought occurred to him: "If someone who lives by the fruits of his own prowess and speaks with words that are not improper has shown such affection in my house and these goods were well utilized;
yet now, due to the fault of my own misfortune, they have been wasted and scattered by someone who could not endure my prosperity—that is a tragedy!
I already knew long ago that the friendship of those possessed of wealth is fickle."
But it is the very suffering of those who seek aid that burns my heart here.

"Long accustomed to the happiness of giving and hospitality, how will those who have come to my house seeking wealth fare now that they find it empty, like thirsty men who have arrived at a dried-up lake?"

Then that Bodhisattva, through the support of his own fortitude, remained untouched by despondency or dejection; yet, because he was unaccustomed to the practice of begging even in such a state, he did not dare to ask others for anything, even those with whom he was well-acquainted, thinking, "It is so difficult to beg," and thus his compassion for the supplicants became even greater. Then that Great-souled One, out of consideration for the hospitable reception and other courtesies due to the people who came to him as beggars, took up that coil of rope and the sickle himself, and every day, with whatever small amount of wealth he obtained from the sale of grass, he honored the requests of those in need.
He did so.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, observing his lack of despondency even in the midst of extreme poverty and his inclination toward giving, was filled with wonder and great respect; appearing with a divine and marvelous form, he stood in the sky and sought to dissuade him from his generosity.
He said to the Great Being: "Householder, you have fallen into this state that causes anguish to the hearts of friends because of your excessive giving;
your wealth is not being seized by bandits, nor by water or fire, nor by kings."
Out of regard for your welfare, I tell you this in truth: restrain your passion for the vice of giving.
Even if you have reached such a state as this, if you do not give, you shall return once more to the splendor of your former prosperity.
Seeing that even with constant and frugal expenditure, acquisitions diminish over time,
and observing how anthills grow through accumulation, those who desire prosperity find that self-restraint alone is the path.
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating the greatness of the practice of giving, said to Śakra:
"O Thousand-eyed One, it is very difficult for a noble person to act ignobly, even when in extreme distress.
O Śakra, let there not be such wealth for me that, for the sake of acquiring it, I might become one whose intent is base."

Since there is a path that serves as a remedy for suffering, by which one may go even unto death through the act of begging, what man who considers himself a son of noble family would strike those who are afflicted with the dry thunderbolt of saying, "There is none"?
Therefore, what indeed would one such as I take— be it a jewel, wealth, or even sovereignty in heaven—
if by that he could not gladden the faces of suppliants, which have been turned pale by the distress of begging?

That which leads to the accumulation of the fault of stinginess, or which does not nourish the spirit of renunciation— that destruction disguised as the acquisition of possessions deserves to be bestowed only upon those like me.
Since wealth is as fickle as the dance of a lightning-flash, common to all, and a cause of manifold calamities,
what noble person would resort to stinginess regarding giving— the very source of the arising of happiness?
O Śakra, you have shown me this favor by speaking for my benefit; I am moved by compassion.
Yet, how could one restrain a mind whose joy is so well-practiced through acts of giving and which has thus strayed onto a wrong path?

Furthermore, you ought not to direct your mind toward the path that follows after resentment; for it is not possible to ascend the difficult heights of one's own inherent nature with only a small amount of strength.

Śakra said: "Householder, this course of action is for one whose wealth is sufficient, whose treasuries and granaries are full, whose various and extensive enterprises are properly conducted, whose future prospects have flourished, and who has brought sovereignty under his control in the world; it is not for one who has fallen into this present condition. Behold—[this path is] either that which is composed of the spontaneous activity of one's own intellect, or that which is favorable to fame and appropriate to one's lineage."
Having attracted prosperity through auspicious karma, he overcame the splendor of his rivals like the sun.
Having awakened his kinsman to the true state of existence through this discourse, he brought joy to his friends and relatives;
and having received honors even from the king, he felt as if embraced by the Goddess of Fortune herself, who longs for him.

Furthermore, one whose efforts are fully exerted toward giving incurs neither the censure of people regarding his own pleasures, nor does he suffer the frustration of one who, like a bird with undeveloped wings, desires to ascend into the sky but possesses only the wish to give. (Jm 5.20)
Therefore, let wealth first be acquired by resorting to self-restraint and modesty; enough with the desire to give it away!
For what indeed would not be considered ignoble in this world, were one to give away riches that are destined to perish?
The Bodhisattva said: "Enough with your persistent insistence, sir.

Even for one for whom their own interest is weightier than the welfare of others, that person should give, disregarding their own prosperity. For one does not experience such joy through great abundance as one enjoys the satisfaction born from the conquest of greed through acts of giving."
Since one does not attain heaven by wealth alone, and since one acquires meritorious fame through giving alone,
and since one does not overcome faults such as envy through that [wealth] alone— for these reasons, who would not resort to giving? (Jm 5.23)
He who desires to give even his own self out of compassion in order to protect the worlds overwhelmed by old age and death—
he who finds no taste for his own pleasures because of the sufferings of others— what purpose would there be for him in wealth that has come to you?
Moreover, O Lord of Gods, just as the accumulation of wealth is unstable, so too is the duration of life; thus,
having encountered a beggar, one should not look back at one's own prosperity.
When one chariot makes a path upon the earth, another follows it even more boldly;
yet my mind, rejecting this first path as auspicious, finds no pleasure in following a wrong road.
"And if my wealth should increase further, it will certainly captivate the minds of beggars.
Even when that happens, O Śakra, I shall give according to my means; let us not falter in our commitment to generosity."
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind thoroughly pacified, honored him with the words "Excellent! Excellent! and, looking upon him with great respect and affection, spoke:
"Even by means of deeds that rival one's own fame, people seek prosperity through base and cruel acts;
blinded by attachment to their own pleasure and disregarding the consequences, they are deceived by their own fickle minds. (Jm 5.28)
Without considering the loss of wealth, the sacrifice of your own happiness, or my deception, you—
whose mind was resolute in accomplishing the welfare of another— have manifested the greatness of your own noble qualities.
"Oh, how wonderful! The heart of this one who shines with such extraordinary magnanimity has wiped away the darkness of stinginess;
for even when his wealth was lost, his intention did not fall into the deformity of shrinking from giving. (Jm 5.30)
And it is no wonder in this regard that you, who suffer at the suffering of others, who are moved by compassion, and who desire the welfare of the world,
were not shaken by me through my gift— just as a snow-white mountain peak is not shaken by the wind.
I have kept this wealth of yours hidden in order to test you and manifest your fame;
for a gem, even if it possesses great luster, does not attain the high value of a jewel's renown unless it is otherwise [tested].
Therefore, rain down upon supplicants with gifts, filling them as a great cloud fills the lakes;
you shall not suffer the loss of wealth through my protection, and you should forgive this conduct of mine.
Having thus propitiated him, Śakra withdrew the essence of his wealth, asked for forgiveness, and vanished right there.
Thus, noble persons do not fall into a deficiency in giving out of regard for the loss of their wealth or out of hope for prosperity.
This is the fifth Jātaka, the Story of the Merchant Aviṣahya.
6. The Śaśajātaka:
Even for those great-souled beings who have entered the state of animals, an engagement in giving according to their capacity is observed.

By what person, indeed, having become human, should a gift not be given? As it is heard in tradition: in a certain region of a forest retreat, thick with lovely creepers, grasses, and trees, abounding in flowers and fruits, and [watered] by a pure-flowing river as blue as lapis lazuli—

In a place whose borders were adorned by rivers, where the surface of the earth was beautiful to behold with its soft carpet of young grass and pleasant to the touch, and which was frequented by ascetics,
the Bodhisattva became a hare. By virtue of his spiritual nature, the excellence of his body, the preeminence of his strength, and his vast vital energy, he [shone forth].
Unobserved by small animals and free from fear, he roamed there with the playful grace of a king of beasts.
Clad in his own skin as an antelope hide and wearing the bark of his own body-hair as a garment,
he shone there like a sage with a contented mind, surrounded by blades of grass and sprouts.
By his mental, vocal, and physical actions, which were purified by loving-kindness,
the deer that were his disciples had for the most part cast off their wild nature.
His companions—Udra, Śṛgāla, and Vānara—whose hearts were bound to him with an especially intense affection born from his preeminent virtues, lived there in great joy.
Like kinsmen tied together by mutual bonds of love, and like friends whose intimacy had grown through mutual affection and respect, they roamed about.
Turning away from the nature of beasts, they practiced compassion toward living beings, and through the pacification of greed, they forgot their habitual practice of theft.

Through their fame that was not inconsistent with righteousness, through their conduct that was firm in self-restraint due to their sharp discernment, and through their actions beloved by the virtuous, they became objects of wonder even for the gods.
[They remained thus] amidst a course of life that, while conforming to pleasure, obstructed virtue, and which, while conforming to virtue, obstructed pleasure.
Even a human being shines by resorting to the side of virtue; how much more so, then, one who possesses the form of an animal?
But among them there was one who was skillful, shaped like a hare, a teacher whose heavy burden was compassion for others;
his natural excellence followed the sequence of virtues, and his fame reached even the world of the gods.

(Vaidya 31) Then once, at the time of evening, that Great Being was being reverently attended by his companions who had come for the purpose of hearing the Dharma; together with them, he beheld the nearly full lunar disc, its beauty becoming increasingly radiant due to its distance from the sun, like a mirror of silver.
Beholding the moon risen on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight— devoid of its crescent and with its orb slightly turned to one side— he said to his companions:
"Like one smiling with its nearly full orb,
this moon announces to the virtuous the festival of the Poṣadha."
It is evident that tomorrow is the fifteenth day;
therefore, while you are fulfilling the Poṣadha observances, you should sustain your lives by honoring guests who arrive at the proper time with special food obtained through righteous means.
Behold!
Since unions end in separation, physical forms conclude in fall and deformity,
and life is as flickering and unstable as a flash of lightning, one must therefore practice firm heedfulness.
Therefore, strive to increase your merits through generosity and the ornament of moral conduct;
for in this world, which is a difficult terrain for those turning back from progress, merits are the supreme support.
That the moon shines, surpassing the splendor of the hosts of stars by its quality of beauty,
and that the thousand-rayed sun blazes, outstripping all luminous bodies— that is the manifestation of his exalted merit.

Ministers and kings of haughty nature, by the power of the merit of the lords of the earth, have their pride entirely subdued through the conduct of noble horses; they bear the yoke of command as if filled with joy.
Misfortune pursues those who are devoid of merit even as they strive upon the path of righteousness;
for, being rebuked by those of superior merit, she turns away from them as if out of indignation toward their adversaries.

Having desisted from that path of demerit which is bound up with suffering, instability, and ill repute, set your minds upon the pursuit of merit, which is glorious and the means for the arising of happiness.
Having accepted his instruction with the words "So be it," and having saluted and circumambulated him, they departed for their respective abodes.
Not long after those companions had gone, that Great Being fell into reflection.
They possess the power to provide hospitality by whatever means possible to a guest who has arrived; I alone am to be pitied in this matter.
These bitter sprouts of grass, severed by the tips of my teeth, cannot possibly be given to a guest; fie upon this total lack of power!
"Thus, being powerless and wretched, what purpose is there in my life? For whom such a guest as this has come to me, even my joy would turn into grief. (Jm 6.15)
Reflecting, "Now, where might this worthless little body, being cast away due to the failure of hospitality toward a guest, be of use to someone? that Great Being regained his memory: "Ah!
This blameless wealth of a body, which is capable of honoring guests, is indeed my own and is easily obtained at my command. (Jm 6.16)
Why then do I despair? I have attained this hospitality; O heart, abandon therefore this dejection and wretchedness.
I shall honor the request of this guest with my very body, now that it has come to me.
Having thus resolved, that Great Being, having attained what was like a supreme gain, remained there with a mind filled with the highest joy.
As an abundance of such reflections unfolded within his heart,
the serenity and power of the celestial dwellers were revealed.
Then, as if out of great joy, the earth, though mountainous, trembled; the ocean became her unrestrained garment;
the sounds of celestial drums spread through the sky; and the quarters of the world shone, adorned with clarity.
Clouds that were incessantly rumbling softly, laughing with lightning, and enveloped on all sides,
showered him continuously with flowers whose pollen was scattered by their mutual friction.
Carrying with it the pollen born of various trees and flowers, the wind, moving with a steady course,
joyfully honored him as if with garments of fine cloth, scattered with devotion that was indistinguishable from its own essence.

Having perceived that, while his extraordinary resolve was being proclaimed on all sides by the deities with minds full of joy and wonder, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind filled with astonishment and curiosity and desiring to test the disposition of that Great Being,
appeared on the second day as the power of his most brilliant rays overspread the midst of the sky.

When the quarters were veiled by the spreading mass of radiant heat, clothed in the net of Savitar’s flashing rays and becoming unbearable to behold; when the shadows were shrinking and the forest interiors were resounded by the increasing cries of jhillikas; when the flight of birds was interrupted and travelers had their vigor sapped by the exhaustion of the heat—Śakra, the lord of the gods, having assumed the form of a Brahmin, appeared as one who had lost his way.
With a throat distressed by hunger, thirst, fatigue, and despair, he wept aloud and cried out not far from them:
"O virtuous ones, you ought to rescue me, who am wandering alone, separated from my caravan in this dense forest, my body exhausted by hunger and weariness."

"Do not terrify me with these cries! Who would gladden me? I am alone in this wilderness, distressed by thirst for the Dharma and exhaustion; I am uncertain of the knowledge of what is and is not the path, and I am wandering somewhere due to my confusion regarding the directions. (Jm 6.23)
Then those great beings, their hearts shaken by the sound of his piteous crying, approached that place with great haste and agitation.
Beholding him looking as miserable as a traveler who has lost his way in the wilderness, they drew near and, after first offering words of courtesy, spoke to comfort him:
"Enough of this delusion of yours; you have not truly lost your way in the forest."
For you remain close to us, as if you were among your own circle of disciples.
Therefore, O gentle one, by accepting our service today and bestowing your favor upon us, you shall depart tomorrow as you desire.
Then, perceiving from Udraka’s silence that his invitation was accepted, he approached with a hurried gait due to the agitation of joy, brought seven rohita fish, and said to him:
"These seven fish—either forgotten by their enemies, or leaping onto dry land out of fear, or as if fallen asleep from exhaustion—I have caught them; eat these and dwell here."
Then the jackal, having gathered whatever food he could find, spoke respectfully with a prostration, saying:
"I have discovered here a lizard and a vessel of curd, which were abandoned by someone."
Therefore, O abode of virtue, having partaken of this out of regard for my welfare, let your dwelling be in this forest.
Having spoken thus, with a heart full of supreme joy, he presented these to him.

Then the monkey, taking mango fruits that had become soft through the quality of ripeness—extremely golden-hued as if colored by red arsenic powder, with stalks deeply reddened and gathered into clusters—spoke to him with palms joined in reverence:
"The mangoes are ripe, the water is pleasing, and the shade is cool with the happiness of meeting a virtuous friend."
"Thus it is, O best among the knowers of Brahman; having eaten this, let your dwelling be right here."
Then the hare, having approached him and performed the customary rites of hospitality, gazed at him with great respect and invited him to partake of his own body:
"There are no mung beans, no sesame seeds, and no rice for one raised in the forest like me;
let this body of mine, consecrated by fire, be used today, and dwell in this penance grove."
"Whatever wealth one possesses that serves as a means to achieve one's desires, that one employs in the festival of meeting with supplicants.
But I have no wealth greater than my body; therefore, accept this, which is my entire possession."
Śakra said:
"How could one such as I even contemplate the killing of another?
What need is there for further discussion regarding one who has shown such friendship as you?"
The hare said, "This is most fitting for a Brahmin who is near to compassion.
Therefore, may you remain right here out of regard for our favor, until I obtain some means of saving myself from somewhere.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving his intention, miraculously created a smokeless heap of embers, the color of molten gold, with flickering, slender flames and scattering showers of sparks.
Then the hare, looking all around, saw that mass of fire;
and having seen it, with a joyful mind, he said to Śakra: "I have found this means for my own benefit. Therefore, you ought to fulfill my hope for favor by making use of my body."
Behold, O Great Brahmin!
There is that which is to be given, a mind inclined toward the desire to give, and the encounter with a guest such as yourself.
(Vaidya 35)
For it is not possible to attain this easily; may it therefore become fruitful for me through my taking refuge in you.

Having thus conciliated him with respect and courtesy out of his love for guests, that Great-souled One saluted him; then, seeing that blazing fire which was like a treasure-trove, he who desired wealth suddenly ascended it with supreme joy, as a solitary swan alights upon a lotus in the water.

Seeing this, the Lord of the Gods, his mind overcome with supreme wonder, resumed his own form and, preceded by a rain of celestial flowers, honored that Great Being with words pleasing to the mind and ear.
Then, taking him up himself with both hands— which were as beautiful as lotus petals and adorned with radiant fingers and ornaments— he showed him to the Thirty-three gods.
May your honors, the gods dwelling in the abode of the thirty-three, behold this;
may you likewise rejoice in this most wonderful deed and heroic exploit of this Great Being:
"Ah, how he has today fearlessly surrendered his body, out of affection for his guest!"
Even so, those of unsteady nature are not able to cast off even a withered flower from their heads without trembling.
Where is this birth, and where is this generosity that contradicts it, as well as such acuity of mind? This is a clear repudiation of both gods and men who have little regard for merit.
"Oh, how his mind is perfumed by the practice of virtue!
Oh, how his affection for good conduct is revealed through the nobility of his actions! (Jm 6.36)

Then Śakra, observing the welfare of the world, in order to proclaim the excellence of that deed, adorned the moon-disk upon the pinnacle of the palace Vaijayanta and the gabled pavilion of the divine assembly hall Sudharmā with the mark of a hare’s image.
Even today, this very image of a hare remains complete within the moon.
Like a reflection in a mirror, he shines; he shines in heaven.
From that time forth, the moon— known as the smile of the lily pond and the ornament of the night— is celebrated by the world as "Śaśāṅka" (the Marked with a Hare).
Those crocodiles, jackals, and monkeys, having passed away from there, were reborn in the world of the gods after encountering a spiritual friend.
Thus, since even great beings who have gone into the animal realm are seen to engage in the practice of giving according to their capacity,
what person born as a human would not give?
Furthermore, one should infer from this that since even those in the animal realm are honored by the virtuous out of affection for their qualities, one must cultivate respect for virtues.
Thus ends the sixth Jātaka, the Śaśajātaka.
7. The Agastyajātaka.
"Even for those dwelling in the forest of asceticism, renunciation and heroism are ornaments, let alone for householders.

This is what has been heard: while the Blessed One was still a Bodhisattva, wandering on the path of *saṃsāra* for the sake of the welfare of the world, he was distinguished by the purity of his conduct and virtues.
A certain great Brahmin family, which was like an ornament upon the surface of the earth, graced the very sky as the moon, with its full and stainless orb in autumn, ascended it.

Having received in due order the sacraments such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and having studied the Vedas together with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*), he mastered them in their entirety.
And for an entire eon, he attained supreme abundance of wealth, as his fame for learning pervaded the world of men and his riches were accepted by donors who loved virtue;
he [honored] his kinsmen, friends, dependents, the destitute, those worthy of respect, guests, and teachers.
In that way, he gladdened the lands with his prosperity, like a great rain-cloud pouring down its bounty.
His fame, already radiant through his learning, shone even more brightly because of his heroic self-sacrifice;
it was like the orb of the moon, pure as autumn, whose splendor increases its beauty when it is full.

Then that Great-souled One, perceiving the state of household life to be crowded with the faults of attachment to evil deeds, a source of negligence, agitated by the preoccupation of acquiring and guarding wealth, a target for hundreds of arrows in the form of vices that oppose tranquility, a laborious undertaking of endless occupations, producing no satisfaction and yielding meager enjoyment; and beholding the life of renunciation— which is free from those defects, possesses happiness, is conducive to the practice of Dharma, and serves as the foundation for the undertaking of the path to liberation— [regarded] even that great abundance of wealth, though acquired without hardship and pleasing to the world’s admiration...

Casting aside [worldly life] like a blade of grass, he became devoted to the discipline and observances of the ascetic’s wandering life. Yet, even though he had gone forth, people seeking the highest good continued to approach him in that same manner—drawn by his fame, their memory of former acquaintance, their estimation of his virtues, and his conspicuous tranquility—their minds won over by the multitude of his qualities. He, however, did not highly regard that association with householders, as it disturbed the bliss of solitude and caused the obstacles of attachment and distraction.

Out of a delight in solitude, he established a hermitage, endowing it with the splendor of a sacred retreat by occupying Kārā Island—which plunges into the midst of the southern ocean, its shores dappled by playful garlands of waves as dark as fragments of sapphire driven by the force of the wind; whose ground is strewn with white sand; which is adorned with various trees whose branches are decorated with flowers, fruits, and sprouts; and whose banks border a pool of pure water.
There, Sutanu, though emaciated by asceticism, shone through his penance;
though physically thin, he was not emaciated in splendor, like the new moon in the sky.
With his senses stilled by the practice of tranquility, dwelling in the forest with a singular devotion to vows and restraints,
he was followed even by the deer and birds as "the Sage" because of his meager power of intellect and physical strength.

Then that Great-souled One, because he was accustomed to giving, even while dwelling in the forest of asceticism, honored any guests who arrived at the proper time with whatever roots and fruits were available, with pure water, and with words that were pleasant with greetings and blessings,
suited for ascetics, and full of kindness; and he sustained himself on that forest food, which remained after the guests had consumed it, taking only as much as was necessary for his own subsistence.
