Śakra, the lord of the gods, his heart captivated by the fame spread abroad through the excellence of that one’s asceticism, desired to test the steadfastness of that Great Being; thus, in that forest retreat, he gradually caused all the roots and fruits suitable for the enjoyment of ascetics to vanish.

The Bodhisattva, moreover, because his mind was intent upon meditation, through his habituation to contentment, and because he was free from infatuation—having no attachment to food or to his own body—did not take that cause of disappearance to heart. Relying on the tender leaves of trees to accomplish his need for sustenance, he remained there with a healthy mind, unthirsty and without longing for special kinds of food. For those whose selves are restrained by contentment, a livelihood is nowhere difficult to obtain.
Where, indeed, are grass, leaves, and pools of water not found?

But Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind even more struck with wonder by that state of his, and his estimation of the Bodhisattva’s virtues becoming even firmer, sought to test him. For that purpose, he stripped the entire multitude of shrubs, grasses, and trees in that forest region of their abundance of leaves, like the winds of the summer season. Then the Bodhisattva, having gathered fresh fallen leaves and subsisting on them after steaming them in water, remained there with an untroubled mind, his heart gladdened by the bliss of meditation, as if satiated by the nectar of immortality.
He lived thus:
freedom from pride is the supreme ornament of the learned; lack of envy, that of the prosperous; and contentment, that of those dwelling in the forest—such is the rule for the splendor of virtues.
Then Śakra, his wonder greatly increased by that marvelous constancy in contentment, as if filled with indignation,

assumed the form of a brahmin and appeared before the Great Being— just as he was looking about, desiring to see a guest, after he had completed his fire-sacrifice and finished his recitations— at the time for his religious observances, appearing like a guest indeed.
With a joyful mind, the Bodhisattva approached him and, preceded by kind words such as "welcome," invited him by announcing that it was time for food.

Perceiving from his silence that the invitation was accepted, that Great-souled One— his beauty enhanced by eyes and face blooming with the joy of the desire to give— welcomed him with affectionate words pleasant to the mind and ear.
He gave all of that cooked food, though obtained with great difficulty, to him, and he himself became satisfied as if by joy alone.
Having entered the meditation chamber in that very manner, he passed that day and night with that same joy and gladness.
Then, on his second, third, fourth, and even fifth day, Śakra likewise appeared before him at the time of his vow;
he too, with a mind even more joyful, honored him in that same manner.
For the desire to give among the virtuous increases through the cultivation of compassion.
He does not succumb to the wretchedness of contraction even by sufferings that end in death.

Then Śakra, his heart overcome with supreme wonder, perceiving that through the excellence of this man’s asceticism his union with the splendor of the Lord of the Thirty-three would depend upon a mere request, became seized by fear and apprehension. Assuming his own divine form of wondrous beauty, he questioned him regarding the purpose of his asceticism:
"Having abandoned dear kinsmen with tearful faces, as well as possessions and the enjoyments of happiness..."
Having cast away the goad of hope, where have you taken refuge in this affliction of asceticism?
Having disregarded the enjoyments of those born in happiness and having abandoned their kin who are overwhelmed with grief,
the wise do not enter the ascetic groves— which obstruct pleasure— unless for a significant cause.
If you think I should be told this, you ought to satisfy our curiosity;
what indeed is it that has so captivated even your intellect by the entry of its virtues?
The Bodhisattva said: "Listen, O noble one, to the cause for which I exert this effort:
Repeated birth is exceedingly painful, as are old age, calamity, disease, and deformity;
and there is the agitation of the intellect at the thought that one must die—it is for the sake of protecting the worlds from these that I stand firm."

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, his heart comforted by the thought, "He does not desire this glory that has come from us," and his mind further propitiated by those well-spoken words, honored them as fitting and invited the Bodhisattva with the granting of a boon:
(Vaidya 39)
"O Kāśyapa, since your well-spoken words here resemble those of an ascetic, I grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire."

Then the Bodhisattva, having no attachment to the pleasures of existence and enjoyment, and perceiving that longing itself is suffering, being one whose contentment had become his very nature, said to Śakra: "If you wish to grant me a boon that brings favor, then I choose this boon from you, O foremost of the gods."

May that fire of greed never enter my heart— that fire which, even after obtaining wives desired by the mind, sons, sovereignty, and vast wealth sought after, leaves the intellect scorched and never attains satisfaction.

Then Śakra, his mind even more thoroughly gladdened by that state of the Bodhisattva’s mind which was inclined toward contentment and manifested through his well-spoken words, praised the Bodhisattva again, saying, "Excellent, excellent! and invited him to choose a boon: "In this well-spoken discourse of yours, which is worthy of a sage..."
Out of affection, as if giving a return gift, I grant you another boon.
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating once more the difficulty of being free from the afflictions, taught him the Dharma again under the guise of requesting a boon:
"O Vāsava, abode of excellent virtues, if you grant me a boon, then for that reason I choose this other boon, O Lord of Gods, which is not inferior. (Jm 7.17)
Through the disparagement of their complexion, people suffer loss of wealth, fame, happiness, and even life itself;
therefore, may that fire of hatred by which beings are overwhelmed as if by an enemy remain far from me.
Having heard that, Śakra, the lord of the gods, out of wonder, praised him, saying "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke again:
"It is only fitting that fame attends those who have gone forth as if it were a devoted lover;
therefore, accept this boon from me for these well-spoken words."
Then the Bodhisattva, out of aversion toward the afflictions, expressing his reproach for association with afflicted beings under the pretext of accepting the observances of his vow, spoke thus:
"I would never even hear of a fool, nor would I look upon him, nor would I speak with him;
nor would I undergo the suffering of weariness from dwelling with him—this is the boon I choose from you."
Śakra said:
"Is it not true that one who has fallen into misfortune deserves the special compassion of the virtuous?"
Because it is the root of calamities, childishness is considered the lowest state.
Why do you, though being compassionate, not even wish to see this child who is especially worthy of compassion?
The Bodhisattva said: "It is out of necessity, O noble one;
let your honor look at this.
If it were possible by any means whatsoever to treat a fool..."
"How might one like me become effortless in the exertion toward that [liberation]? (Jm 7.23)

Thus, let it be understood that he is an unfit vessel for the application of medical treatment: he adopts a wrong course as if it were right policy, and he even desires to employ others therein; he is enraged when beneficial advice is spoken, for his manner of discipline and integrity is unaccustomed to such instruction.

Thus, when one is consumed by the delusion of pride in their own wisdom, becoming harsh with anger even toward those who speak for their benefit, and acting impulsively due to a lack of application to discipline— tell me, what means is there to offer them what is beneficial?
Thus, O best of gods, even though they were inclined toward compassion,
there was no way for them to grant even a sight of themselves to the child, who was not yet a fit recipient.
Having heard that, Śakra, greeting him with "Excellent! Excellent! and his mind gladdened by those well-spoken words, spoke again:
"There is no price whatsoever for these jewels of well-spoken verses;
out of affection, I grant you a boon here as well, like a handful of flowers."
Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating to Śakra the state of happiness found in every circumstance for a virtuous person, said:
"O Śakra, may I behold the steadfast one and hear the steadfast one; may my dwelling be with him, O Śakra.
May there be conversation with him alone—grant me this boon, O best of gods."
Śakra said: "It is indeed as if you have an excessive partiality toward the Wise One (Dhīra).
Therefore, let it be told:
what has the Wise One done for you? Speak the reason, O Kāśyapa."
For which reason you are like one lacking fortitude, longing for the sight of the steadfast.
(Vaidya 41) Then the Bodhisattva, demonstrating the greatness of this good man, said: "Listen, O noble one,
as to why my mind desires nothing but the sight of this steadfast person."
He himself walks upon the path of virtue and leads others along that same way;
even his speech is never harsh, but is always endowed with what is beneficial and free from intolerance.
"He can always be made to accept what is beneficial through discipline that is free from deceit"—thus my mind, which is partial toward virtue, bows down to you, O partisan of virtue. (Jm 7.31)

Then Śakra, having congratulated him, saying, "This is truly worthy of you," and his own faith being further increased, invited him once more to choose a boon: "Granted that everything has already been accomplished for you by your very nature of contentment, you ought nevertheless to accept a boon out of consideration for my favor."
For when one has offered a request with the intention of being helpful, with devotion, and with all one's power,
the non-acceptance of that affection is indeed a source of extreme suffering.
Then, perceiving his supreme desire to be of service, the Bodhisattva, out of a wish for his pleasure and welfare, spoke to him, manifesting the intensity of his longing for giving:
"Your food is free from the defect of depletion, and your mind is exquisite in its practice of the desire to give;
may beggars be the ornaments of my pure conduct—this excellence of boons I choose."
Śakra said: "Your Honor is indeed a mine of jewels of well-spoken words. Moreover—whatever has been requested shall all come to pass exactly so;
furthermore, I grant you another boon for these well-spoken words."
The Bodhisattva said:

"O best of all the gods, if you would grant me a boon that brings about the perfection of favor, then do not come to me again; burning with this resolve, I choose this boon which destroys all wretchedness."

Then Śakra, speaking with indignation and feeling great astonishment, said to him: "O sir, people do not seek my sight through the performance of muttered prayers, vows, and sacrifices, nor through the labors of ascetic penance."
But for what reason do you not wish this, even though I have come before you desiring to grant a boon?

The Bodhisattva said: "Enough of your display of resentment, O King of Gods. I shall console you, for this was neither a lack of courtesy on your part, nor an act of disrespect, nor a desire not to meet with me. Rather, it was because, having beheld your superhuman and wondrous form—so serene in its radiance yet blazing with splendor—"
I fear that even from your appearance, so gracious and gentle, there might arise negligence regarding my ascetic practice.
Then Śakra, having bowed down and circumambulated him, vanished on that very spot.
When the night had turned to dawn, the Bodhisattva beheld an abundance of divine food and drink brought forth by the power of Śakra;
he also saw many hundreds of Pratyekabuddhas summoned by Śakra’s invitation, as well as numerous young gods with their girdles tightly fastened, ready to serve the meal.

By means of that method of providing food and drink, the sage, while satisfying the great seers, attained a most exalted joy; and he delighted in the conduct appropriate for ascetics, as well as in meditation, the immeasurables, self-restraint, and tranquility.

Thus, even for those dwelling in the forest of asceticism, the heroic spirit of renunciation is an ornament, let alone for householders; therefore, a virtuous person should indeed adorn themselves with the heroism of renunciation.

This is also to be inferred from the context concerning the gladdening of patrons of charity, the censure of greed, hatred, delusion, and folly, the quality of association with spiritual friends, the discourse on contentment, and the majesty of the Tathāgata.
In this way, that Blessed One was a mine of the most excellent jewels of well-spoken words even in his previous births, let alone after he had attained perfect enlightenment.
Thus ends the seventh Jātaka, the Agastyajātaka.
8. The Maitrībalajātaka.
Those of great compassion, being afflicted by the suffering of others, do not regard their own happiness.
As it is heard— once, it is said, the Bodhisattva, having attained greatness through his own majesty and compassion, possessed the resolute intention to protect the world.

Increasing through an abundance of virtues conducive to the welfare of the world—such as generosity, self-restraint, observance of vows, and gentleness—there was a king named Maitrabala whose mind was friendly toward all beings.
Whatever suffering or happiness befell his subjects, that same state befell the king as well;
therefore, being skilled in protecting his subjects, he took up both the sword and the sacred scriptures.

The weapon of that king, whose edicts were worn upon the crest-ornaments of men, served as his mere ornament; for his treatise on policy, which was clearly manifested, was seen to be directed toward the welfare and prosperity of the world.
His engagement in both restraint and reward did not obstruct the Dharma,
because of his benevolent intent and skill in governance, just like a discerning father toward his children.

While he was thus protecting his subjects according to the Dharma, and while he was increasing through the methods for accumulating the requisites for enlightenment— characterized by a particularly noble progression due to his dedication to the welfare of others through truthfulness, generosity, tranquility, wisdom, and so forth— a certain time came when five *yakṣas*, leaders of *yakṣas* who were skilled in slaying enemies and capable of stealing vital energy (*ojas*), were banished from their own domain on account of some offense and arrived in that king's territory.

And having observed that realm— where all calamities had vanished, where various festivals were perpetually celebrated, which was endowed with supreme prosperity, and whose inhabitants were joyful, contented, and flourishing— the men dwelling there conceived a desire to steal away their vital energies (*ojas*).
Even though they exerted themselves with great effort in their own task,
they were simply unable to take away the vital energy of those staying within that domain.

Because of the extraordinary power of that king, wherever the thought "this is mine" arose in him, that itself became his supreme protection; therefore, they were unable to steal away his vital energies.
And when, despite making even the greatest effort, they were unable to steal the vital energy (*ojas*) of any person dwelling in that region, they looked at one another and thought:
"What indeed is this, friends?"
The extraordinary powers consisting of knowledge, austerity, and spiritual accomplishment, which are capable of resisting our influence, do not exist in them;
yet today we have all become those whose very names are rendered meaningless.

Then those yakṣas, having transformed themselves into the form of brahmins and wandering about, saw a certain cowherd tending the cattle in the forest, seated at the foot of a shady tree on a grassy plot; he was wearing sandals, bearing a garland fashioned from the blossoms of wild trees with fresh sprouts, with his staff and axe laid down to his right, alone, occupied with twisting a rope, and sitting there singing with the playful grace of a warbling song.
Approaching him, they said: "Tathathadadakākākākā!
O you who are appointed as the protector of the cattle, how is it that you do not fear wandering thus alone in this forest, which is so secluded and devoid of human traffic?
Looking at them, he replied: "Why should I be afraid?"
The yakṣas said: "Have you not heard before that the innate nature of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas is exceedingly fierce?
For even one who is accompanied by allies, and endowed with knowledge, asceticism, and auspicious rites—though the world, disregarding fear through valor, might somehow find escape from them—"
How is it that you have no fear of those Rākṣasas who devour human fat and flesh,
while you are alone in the depths of the forest, which are secluded, profound, and terrifying?
When this was said, the cowherd laughed and spoke to them: "This man is protected by a great blessing;
he cannot even be overcome by the Lord of the Gods, much less by flesh-eaters."
Because of that, I wander about without fear even in the forest as if in a house, even at night as if by day, and though alone, as if in the midst of people.
Then those yakṣas, out of an intensity of curiosity, spoke to him respectfully as if encouraging him: "Tell us, tell us first, O blessed one, what kind of this particular *svastyayana* of yours is?
Laughing, he said to them: "Listen to what kind of this most wonderful *svastyayana* of ours is."
The lord of men had a chest as broad as a slab from the Golden Mountain, the lovely beauty of his face like the stainless autumn moon,
arms long and thick like golden clubs, and the eyes and gait of a bull.
"Such is our particular means of securing well-being.
Having said this, looking at those yakṣas with indignation and amazement, he spoke again: "How wonderful!
How is it that such manifest royal power has not yet reached the path of your ears?"
Or perhaps, because of its extreme wonder, even though it was heard from you, it did not take root due to incredulity.
I suspect that the people of this land are either too dull to seek out virtues, or lack curiosity;
or perhaps they have abandoned the fame of the lord of men due to the exhaustion of their own good fortune, since they do not come to him.
"It seems you possess some remnant of good fortune that you have come here from such a desolate wilderness.
The yakṣas said, "Noble sir, tell us: by what cause does this majesty of the king exist, such that non-human beings do not dare to harm the people living within his realm?
Gopālaka replied, "This majesty of our great king has been attained through his own greatness."

Behold, O great brahmins, the power of his loving-kindness, which is as variegated as the tip of a banner; he possesses only the strength of mere outward conduct, for he knows neither anger nor does he speak harshly, and he protects the cow perfectly.
For him, dharma was his method, not the deceit of worldly policy; wealth was for the sake of honoring the virtuous.
Thus, though filled with wonders, he did not indulge in pride over the riches of the wicked.
Our lord is thus endowed with hundreds of such qualities;
therefore, calamities cannot prevail against the people living within his realm.
Moreover:
How much could I possibly say to you?
It would be more fitting for you, who are eager to hear of the king’s virtues, to enter the city itself.

For there, you will find a place where the boundaries of noble conduct are firmly established through devotion to one's own duty, which is ever-secure and well-supplied with food, flourishing and joyful, where the dress of the people is neither arrogant nor vulgar, and which is exceptionally kind toward guests and visitors.

Seeing the people whose hearts are captivated by the king’s virtues, who out of great joy practice praises based on his fame as if they were auspicious benedictions or protective charms, you will infer the full extent of the king’s qualities.
And when there is such a manifestation of high esteem for his virtues, you will certainly become direct witnesses to those qualities through your desire to see them.

(Vaidya 46) Then those yakṣas, their hearts filled with resentment because their own power had been thwarted, did not at all become softened by that discourse on his virtues, even though it was delivered with appropriate skill and sincerity.
For generally, the minds of the dull-witted are inflamed by indignation.
When a person is burned by the fame of a particular thing, it is because of that very excellence of that thing.
Observing the king’s fondness for giving, those yakṣas, desiring to do him harm, approached the king at the time of his audience and requested food.
Then the king, with a joyful mind, commanded the officials in charge: "Let the food desired by the brahmins be given immediately.
However, those yakṣas did not accept the food—even though it was served fit for a king—any more than tigers would accept green grass, saying, "We do not eat such food as this."
Having heard that, the king approached them and said, "Now, what kind of food is suitable for you? Let such food be sought out. The yakṣas replied, "The warm flesh and the blood of men."
"Such is the food and drink of the yakṣas, O Padmākṣa, you whose vows are inviolable."

Having spoken thus, they assumed their own bodies, which were terrifying and deformed, with mouths formidable with fangs, fierce reddish-brown and squinting eyes that blazed, cracked and flat misshapen noses, hair and beards tawny like flaming fire, and forms as dark as water-laden clouds.
Having gazed upon them, the king reached the conclusion: "These are surely piśācas and not humans; that is why they have no desire for our food and drink.
Then, in that lord of men, whose nature was compassionate and whose mind was pure, there arose an even greater compassion for them.

With his heart single-mindedly intent on compassion and grieving for those yakṣas, he reflected with certainty upon this matter: "For one possessed of mercy, such food and drink are exceedingly difficult to obtain;
and since they must be sought after every day, what indeed could be more painful than this? (Jm 8.18)
The exertion of one who is both merciless and powerless results solely in frustration;
yet what could be more wretched than that of one who, though capable, exerts himself through harmful practices? (Jm 8.19)
When will the sufferings of those who are devoted to such food, whose minds are devoid of compassion and inauspicious, come to an end as they daily consume their own welfare?
Therefore, how could I now, for the sake of providing such food for them, commit even a single day’s injury to another being or destruction of life?
Indeed, I do not recall ever having allowed the radiance of those who came as supplicants to be struck down by the frustration of their hopes.
To make their faces share the same dejection as lotuses withered by the cold wind.
"Let it be so; it is seen.
From my own body, I shall give flesh that is firm and plump, along with blood. For when supplicants have arrived, what course of action could be more appropriate for me than this? (Jm 8.22)
For the flesh of those who have died of their own accord becomes devoid of heat and bloodless;
indeed, these are not dear to them, for their bodies are already tormented by intense hunger.

Moreover, while I am still alive, from where else shall I obtain flesh? And having approached me, how indeed will these [beings] depart with their eyes and faces wasted by hunger and thirst, their minds even more afflicted by the frustration of their hopes and requests being rendered fruitless?
Therefore, this is the time for action here.
Like a malignant ulcer, ever-infested, foul-smelling,
and a source of pain, I undergo the weariness of treatment for this body, which is exceedingly loathsome, for the sake of its application toward the supreme task.

Having thus resolved, that Great Being, the beauty of whose eyes and face was expanded by the outburst of intense joy, revealed his own body and said to those yakṣas: "This flesh, together with its blood, has been maintained solely for the sake of the welfare of the world. If they were to receive hospitality today, that would be my great prosperity and my true success."
Then those yakṣas, although they knew the king’s intention, did not believe it because of its extreme wonder; they said to the king:
"When a petitioner has revealed the suffering within himself through the wretchedness of his request, it is the donor alone who ought to know what is appropriate for the occasion beyond this."
(Vaidya 48) Then the king, his mind filled with joy, thinking, "This is approved by them," commanded, "Let the physicians be ordered to perform the venesection.
Thereupon, the king’s ministers, perceiving his determination to give his own flesh and blood, had their hearts agitated by confusion and indignation.

Clearly, out of affection, they spoke of some such matter: "It does not behove Your Majesty, on account of excessive joy over a gift, to disregard the sequence of what is beneficial and harmful for your devoted subjects.
Nor is this unknown to Your Majesty, namely—"
"O giver of honor, whatever brings about harm to living beings is dear to the Rākṣasas;
O sinless one, it is the very nature of this race to find satisfaction in a livelihood earned by obstructing others."
O Lord, though unattached to pleasures, you endure the toil of sovereignty solely for the sake of the world's welfare;
therefore, abandon this resolve to give away your own flesh, for it is a path that leads away from your own [true] purpose.
Without a doubt, O god among men, these people do not dare to oppress a world protected by your prowess;
for, ruined by their cleverness in causing harm, they seek through policy that which is contrary to the welfare of the subjects.
The gods attain satisfaction in sacrifices through oblations of fat, marrow, and the like poured into the fire;
yet it is said that your food, though purified by hospitality, does not at all please their palates.
Granted that Your Majesty’s intellect is not to be swayed by people such as myself;
yet this attachment to your own interests causes you to fall away from the path of proper conduct toward us.
What kind of dharma-path is this for Your Majesty, that for the sake of these five, the entire world should be rendered wretched? Moreover—
"Why is there such a lack of affection toward us?

Or by whom have our flesh and blood, which were previously kept hidden while being employed for the sake of our master, been revealed, so that Your Majesty now desires to give away his own [limbs] even while these remain undiminished?
Then the king spoke to those ministers:
How could one like me say that what exists does not exist, or clearly utter the falsehood "I will not give" when entreated? (Jm 8.31)
If I, being the leader in the established order of Dharma, were to myself walk along a wrong path,
what would become of my subjects who follow the path of conduct practiced by me?
Since I am observing that living beings alone are the essence [to be extracted] from this body, I shall draw it out;
for what power would I possess to accomplish the welfare of the world if my heart were small and seized by selfishness? (Jm 8.33)
Furthermore, as for what you have said— motivated by love and great respect, and imbued with affection and confidence— "For what reason do you show such lack of affection toward us,
that Your Majesty desires to give your own [limbs] while our flesh and blood have not yet failed?"—
in this matter, I shall console you.
Indeed, my path of affection toward you is neither obstructed by your status nor difficult to fathom due to the absence of distrust; rather—
when wealth has gradually diminished or has come to an end through the course of fortune,
a friendship that flourishes with affection is truly beautiful among friends, but one who is overflowing with riches does not shine when his companions are destitute.
While my own limbs have grown large and are elevated with an abundance of flesh for the sake of those who seek my wealth, it would be a misfortune for you if your affection were directed toward me.
I could not endure the suffering even of those with whom I am unacquainted; how much less, then, of you?
For it is my own flesh that I desire to give, and these people are begging for me, not for you.
Therefore, enough of this lack of restraint regarding obstacles to the Dharma born of excessive affection for us;
indeed, such conduct toward those who seek our favor is unbecoming of your honors.
Furthermore, this matter ought first to be investigated:

How could one who wishes to give food and other necessities for his own sake be a righteous person if he were to forbid it—let alone one who follows such a rule? Or how could he be anything but unrighteous? (Jm 8.37)
Therefore, enough of this persistence of yours in this matter.
Let your minds be turned away from the wrong path in a manner worthy of being my companions, through a rational investigation.
Indeed, your honors would shine even more so with such words of approval, rather than with these agitated glances. Why?—
Every day, there are not so many supplicants for wealth that is of a single use;
yet such a person seeking wealth cannot be found even through the propitiation of the gods.

When such a person seeking [help] has arrived, while the body is perishable and a seat of unhappiness, even the path of reflection would be base; but the wretchedness of stinginess is the ultimate darkness. (Jm 8.39)

"Your honors ought not to prevent me from this," he said, thus entreating his assembly. Having summoned the physicians and caused five veins to be opened in his own body, the king spoke to those yakṣas:
"You should grant me your assistance and your highest pleasure in this act of dharma, by accepting this gift."
Having said, "So be it," they began to drink the king's blood, which was as crimson as liquid red sandalwood, with their very hands joined in hollowed palms.
As his blood was being drunk by those night-stalkers, the lord of the earth shone with a golden body,
like Mount Meru embraced by clouds that are reddened by twilight and bent down by the weight of water.
Due to the excellence of his joy, the perfection of his fortitude, and the very quality of that king’s body,
his limbs did not grow faint, his mind did not lose consciousness, and the flowing blood did not diminish.
Their thirst and fatigue having been subdued, those yakṣas said to the king, "We have had enough of this.

"Though this body—a constant source of manifold sufferings and ever ungrateful—has become for the lord of men a means for honoring supplicants, its acceptance was nevertheless performed with a heart favorable to joy. (Jm 8.43)

Then that king, his eyes and face even more radiant with the awakening of joy, took up a sharp sword whose blade was as pure blue as the petal of a blue lotus and whose hilt was beautiful, shining with the luster of jewels; having cut off his own flesh, he gave it to them.
Yet, because of his delight in giving, he repeatedly offered it even as the opportunity for it to be taken away was being lost.
His mind was unable to endure the pain of that cutting.
As he was being drawn forward by the strikes of sharp weapons and pushed back again out of affection,
his suffering became slow in its ascent toward his mind, as if languid with exhaustion.
He remained full of joy, satisfying those night-stalkers with his own flesh; by this means,
even their cruel minds were revealed to possess a newfound gentleness.

Whether out of love for the Dharma or through the power of compassion, one who sacrifices their own dear body for the sake of others can transform even minds scorched by the fire of hatred into something fresh with the golden hue of serenity.

Then those yakṣas, beholding the king intent on cutting out his own flesh, yet with a countenance as serene and unshaken as before, and undisturbed by the pains of the incision, were moved to both faith and wonder;
their hearts stirred with inquiry and joy, they exclaimed, "How marvelous! How extraordinary! Oh, what can this be? Is it real or not?"
Having suppressed their indignation toward the king, they manifested serenity of mind by means of praises and prostrations to him.
"Enough, enough, O King! Desist from this course of afflicting your own body.

We have been fully satisfied by this marvelous act of yours, which so captivates the hearts of supplicants. Having thus hurriedly and respectfully dissuaded the king, their faces bathed in tears of grace, they looked up at him with great reverence and spoke again:
It is fitting that people, out of devotion, become eloquent in proclaiming your fame; it is fitting that the Goddess of Fortune, abandoning the lotus-thicket, takes pride in seeking refuge with you.
It is evident that she has even attained the status of being presided over by Śakra, protected as she is by your own valor.
The heavens look down with longing upon the earth; alas, if they did not, they would surely be deceived.
What need is there for much? The world of men is indeed fortunate to be graced by such a person as you. Yet, it is we ourselves who are consumed here by our own joy in consenting to your exertions.
We ask you this with the hope of counteracting our own difficult task, thinking that even those who have fallen into such a state can rescue themselves by taking refuge in a person like you.
Disregarding the royal splendor that has come to you so easily and is devoted to you,
what is this most extraordinary place that you desire by means of this path?
Do you desire through this asceticism the sovereignty over all the earth, or the status of the Lord of Wealth, or even the rank of Indra, or the state of Brahmā, or perhaps final liberation?
For there is nothing more distant from this resolve than what we desire;
we must hear this, and you ought to speak it to us.

The king said: "Listen to the purpose for which this effort of mine is undertaken. Since that prosperity which is obtained with great exertion and perishes without effort does not lead to the happiness of contentment, much less to peace—therefore, I do not desire even the sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods, let alone any other."
Yet my mind does not travel the path of contentment by the mere destruction of my own suffering,
when I behold these helpless embodied beings, afflicted and distressed by the toil of intense calamities.
"By this merit, having attained omniscience and having conquered the enemies that are the afflictions,
may I rescue the world from the ocean of existence, which is turbulent with the great waves of old age, sickness, and death."

Then those yakṣas, their hair standing on end with joy and devotion, bowed to the king and said: "This deed is truly worthy of such extraordinary resolve. Therefore, we declare with firm conviction that for those like you, the fulfillment of your intentions is not far off. Granted, this entire endeavor of yours is indeed for the benefit of the world."
But you should remember that at that time we showed them the utmost regard for their own welfare.
And for the fact that we have thus troubled you out of ignorance,
failing to see even our own interest, let that too be forgiven by us.
Furthermore, you ought to grant us your command as a path of favor,
issuing it with confidence, just as one might to one's own ministers.

Then that king, perceiving that their hearts had been softened by his graciousness, said to them: "This is indeed a favor to me and not a hardship; therefore, enough of your apprehension regarding my lack of capacity in this matter. Moreover, having attained enlightenment, how could I forget such companions on the path of Dharma as these?"
I shall first bestow upon you alone a share of the nectar of the Dharma of liberation.
Observing what is dear to us, you must avoid violence like poison;
likewise, greed for the possessions of others, censurable speech, and the sin of intoxication with liquor.
Then those yakṣas, having promised him "So be it," bowed down, circumambulated him, and vanished right there.
At the very moment that Great Being resolved to give his own flesh and blood,
the earth trembled in many ways and caused the Golden Mountain to shake.
The drums situated there resounded, and the trees, from being shaken, shed their blossoms.

Driven by the wind in the sky like a cloud, it scattered everywhere around the king simultaneously: in some places spreading out like a flight of birds, and in others falling like a canopy or a woven garland.
As if wishing to restrain the lord of the earth with its surging momentum, the great ocean shone forth,
its body radiant with the vigor of its departure, its waters naturally possessing an exceedingly powerful roar.

"What is this?"—with such agitation he arrived; then the Lord of the Gods, having reflected upon the cause there, went quickly to the king's palace, which was utterly overwhelmed by grief and fear due to his apprehension of the king's demise.
But even the Tathāgata, filled with extraordinary wonder at the gracious expression on that king's face,
approached him and, moved by the power of his own serenity and joy, praised that deed with a pleasing voice.
Oh, the excellence of the conduct of the virtuous! Oh, the nobility of one who is a treasury of the practice of virtues!
Oh, how exquisite is the mind intent on benefiting others! Alas, by being entrusted to you, the earth has truly found its protector.

Having praised him thus, Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, immediately made his body free from pain and restored it to its former state using divine and human medicinal herbs capable of healing wounds instantly. Then, having been honored by the king with a sweet reception of courtesy, humility, and service, he returned to his own abode. Thus, those of great compassion, distressed by the suffering of others, pay no regard to their own happiness.

This should be said when inciting potential donors, thinking: "Who indeed would not be able to relinquish attachment even to mere wealth? It should likewise be said when praising compassion, when describing the majesty of the Tathāgata, and when encouraging the reverent hearing of the Dharma.
And as for what was said by the Blessed One, "These five monks are indeed very helpful," it was with this very intention that he spoke.
At that time, those five yakṣas were present;
to them, the Blessed One first made a distribution of the nectar of the Dharma exactly as he had promised.
Thus ends the eighth Jātaka, the Maitrībalajātaka.
9. The Story of Viśvantara:
It is not easy for those of small spiritual capacity even to rejoice in the conduct of a Bodhisattva, let alone to practice it themselves.

As it is heard: Having made the conquest of his senses his very nature, having attained the glory of victory through excellence in prowess, policy, and discipline, and having realized the true essence of the meaning of the three Vedas and the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*) by virtue of his constant attendance upon the elders, he was surrounded by devoted women who were attached to their own duties and rituals, accustomed to undisturbed happiness, and full of affection for him.

There was a king of the Śibis named Sañjaya, whose splendor of the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) was manifested by his ministers, and who maintained the proper system of the economic pursuits (*vārttā*).
The royal fortune dwelt with him, its affection bound by the arising of his virtues, just as a noble lady remains with her husband;
it was inaccessible to other monarchs, like a cave protected by a lion is to wild beasts.

Those who had always applied themselves with diligent effort to asceticism, the sciences, and the arts, attained his special esteem; their true worth being revealed through honors, they were shown the highest respect.
Immediately following that king’s passing, his son named Viśvantara—whose multitude of renowned virtues was uninterrupted—became the crown prince.
[He was none other than the Blessed One Śākyamuni at that time.
Though young, he delighted in the tranquility of the aged; though radiant with splendor, his very nature was the bliss of patience.
Though learned, he was not arrogant in his knowledge; though enriched by prosperity, he was free from pride.

When the quarters had been traversed by him and the three worlds were pervaded by his glories, there was no longer even the slightest space or inclination for the fragments of other men's fame to spread.
Unable to endure the spreading arrogance of the arising sufferings of those throughout the world, he—
showering gifts as a great archer of compassion— advanced against them with the fury of battle.

Day after day, he brought exceeding joy to the seekers who approached him by means of gifts of wealth that surpassed their desires, were given without effort, and were made enchanting through the service of kind words. And on the festival days, adorned with the tranquility of the *poṣadha* vows and observances, having bathed his head and wearing white linen garments,
he [presented] a horse that resembled a peak of the Snowy Mountains, its face graced by a flowing mane, and endowed with auspicious marks, discipline, speed, and strength.
Having mounted Gandhahastin, the renowned royal mount and best of elephants, he inspected his own almshouses situated all around the city, which served as drinking wells for those who came seeking;
and thus he experienced a particular joy.
Indeed, the splendor residing in his palace does not produce such joy for one who loves giving as that very same splendor does when it is being transferred to the multitude of supplicants.

Then, at one time, having observed this kind of engagement in giving being scattered in all directions by supplicants with joyful hearts, a certain neighboring king, reasoning that "this man can be overreached because he has fallen under the sway of his passion for giving," dispatched brahmins there for the purpose of seizing his excellent elephant.

Then those brahmins stood before Viśvantara as he was inspecting his own sacrificial halls, their eyes and faces radiant with even greater splendor due to their joy, their voices resonant with blessings of victory, and their right hands raised and extended forward. Having halted his excellent elephant there, he inquired of them with due courtesy regarding the purpose of their visit: "Command me, what is your need?"
The brahmins said:
"We have come to you as suppliants because of the virtues of this nāga, who moves with such graceful ease, and because of your own generosity and heroism."
By the gift of this elephant, which resembles the peak of Mount Kailāsa,
first cause the minds of all people to consist solely of wonder.
When this was said, the Bodhisattva, his heart being filled with joy, fell into reflection:
"After a long time indeed, I behold supplicants whose faces are brightened by noble affection;
but what possible need could these brahmins have for such a lordly elephant?"

"Clearly, this is some king’s act of stinginess, his mind agitated by greed, envy, and hatred. May that monarch not suffer the wretchedness of frustrated hope— he who, disregarding both fame and dharma, exerts himself as if for our own welfare."

Having thus resolved, that Great-souled One quickly descended from his excellent elephant and stood before them with a golden pitcher raised, saying, "Let this be accepted. Then, although he was learned in the treatises on statecraft—which, by following worldly interests, had led him away from the path of Dharma—he gave away the lordly elephant out of devotion to righteousness; he did not waver because of his aversion to policy.

Having given away that lordly elephant, adorned with beautiful ornaments of golden mesh like an autumnal mass of clouds wreathed in lightning, the prince attained supreme joy; yet the city was agitated by its partiality for the side of policy.

(Vaidya 57) Then, upon hearing of the gift of the lordly elephant, the Śibis— the elder Brahmins, ministers, warriors, and leading citizens— were stirred by a surge of anger and agitation; raising a great clamor, they approached King Sañjaya with a mixture of haste, indignation, and fury.
With their formal constraints now greatly relaxed, they said: "Your Majesty, why is this royal fortune being plundered thus left unheeded?
Your Majesty ought not to overlook such a growing calamity to your own kingdom.
When asked by the King with agitation, "What is this?", they spoke again as follows: "Why does Your Majesty not know?"
Having attended upon his face, which is fragrant with ichor and celebrated by the songs of intoxicated bees,
the wind wipes away the pride of rival elephants without the suffering of exertion.

"Since your enemies, their strength and power overcome by his splendor, are like those whose pride has fallen asleep, this elephant—which is your victory incarnate—has been given away by Viśvantara; it is being taken to another land."

"O King, cows, gold, garments, and food are the forms of gifts to be given to the twice-born; but that for which the glory of victory is certain—namely, a preeminent elephant—that indeed should be given. This is the supreme valor of giving. (Jm 9.14)
"How will the royal fortune seek him out as he travels by this wrong path?
O King, it is not right for you to neglect this matter; otherwise, before long, he will bring joy to your enemies."

Having heard that, the king—out of affection for his son, though somewhat displeased with them, yet out of regard for what was required—said "So be it" with an air of agitation; and then, seeking to conciliate them, he spoke to the Śibis: "I am aware of Viśvantara’s addiction to the practice of giving and his disregard for the rules of statecraft, but this is not the proper course for one appointed to the burden of sovereignty."
"Who can take back this elephant of his, which he has given away as if it were vomit?
Nevertheless, I shall act in such a way that Viśvantara will know the proper measure in giving.
Therefore, enough of this agitation of yours."
The Śibis said: "O Great King, Viśvantara cannot indeed be managed in this matter by mere threats.
Sañjaya replied: "What else can I possibly do here?
For one who has turned away from the pursuit of faults, his engagement in virtues is being treated as a vice."
What could be the ransom for that elephant—his imprisonment or even the execution of his own son?
"Therefore, enough of this agitation of yours;
I myself shall restrain Viśvantara from this."
Then the Śibis, their indignation aroused, said to the king:
"O lord of men, who would approve of the execution, imprisonment, or flogging of your son?
For he is righteous by nature; because of his compassion and gentleness, he is not one to endure the agitation of the burden of sovereignty."
Those who have attained renown through their splendor and are skilled in pursuing the three aims of life resort to the lion throne;
however, this man, out of devotion to dharma and indifferent to his own eyes, is fit only to dwell in a forest of asceticism.
The faults of the evil policies of kings bear fruit among those who depend upon them;
yet even so, these are tolerable for them, for they are seen as obstacles to the roots [of their own power], but not for the kings themselves.
What need is there for further words here? This is the firm resolve of the Śibis, who cannot endure your misfortune:
let the prince go to Mount Vaṅka, frequented by the Siddhas, in order to increase his ascetic power.

Then that king, being addressed so harshly by those people who—out of affection, devotion, and confidence, and desiring his welfare while perceiving the danger of this misconduct—spoke thus, became dejected with shame and bowed his face due to the provocation of his subjects; his heart overwhelmed with anxiety over the separation from his son, he sighed with distress and said to the Śibis: "If this is your persistence, then let even a single day and night be endured for him."

"When night has turned to dawn, Viśvantara will carry out what you desire. Having thus accepted their entreaty with the words "So be it," the king spoke to his chamberlain: "Go and report this news to Viśvantara.

He, having promised "So be it," approached Viśvantara—who had gone to his own quarters—with a face drenched by tears of grief; overcome by the force of sorrow and suffering, he wept aloud and fell at his feet.

When Viśvantara asked with concern, "Is all well with the royal family?", the chamberlain, sinking down and faltering, replied to him with words that were indistinct and broken: "All is well with the royal family.

Then, when questioned again by Viśvantara, "Why are you so distressed?", the chamberlain, his throat choked by a surge of tears, spoke slowly with syllables stumbling and wavering due to his breath, saying:
"Disregarding even the King’s command, those who are discourteous..."
"O King, the Śibis, being enraged, are banishing you from the kingdom."
Viśvantara said: "What connection is there between me and the fact that the Śibis, being angry, are banishing me?
I do not delight in the path of misconduct, and I loathe negligence."
"Where are my Śibis angry, since I do not see any misdeed?"
The steward said:
"O giver of honor, while your contentment remained bright with dispassion in the face of such extreme generosity, the minds of the supplicants became agitated by greed;
yet when you gave away that lordly elephant, it was anger that robbed the Śibis of their fortitude."
"Thus the impetuous Śibis have transgressed their own bounds because of you;
go indeed by that same path by which they have been sent forth into exile."

Then the Bodhisattva, manifesting his affection for those who beg—rooted in the practice of compassion—as well as the excellence of his supreme fortitude, said: "The Śibis are indeed fickle by nature, as if ignorant of my own character.
What need is there to speak of external objects? I would give even my own eyes or my head."
For it is for the sake of this world that I bear this physical form; what need have I for clothing?
"He whose mind desires to honor even with his own limbs the words of those who seek alms—yet would not give them out of fear—is a mere conjecture; it is the manifestation of a fool's caprice."
"Let all the Śibis kill me or banish me as they wish; however, I shall certainly not fail to give [the horse]. I am going now to the forest of asceticism."
Then the Bodhisattva spoke to his wife, whose face was distressed by the hearing of unpleasant news: "Has your ladyship heard the resolution of the Śibis?
Madri replied, "I have heard it, O Lord.
Viśvantara said:
"Whatever wealth you have acquired from us,
O faultless-eyed one, and whatever ancestral wealth belongs to you— place all that in storage."
Madrī said, "O Lord, where shall I place this?
Viśvantara replied,
"One should always give gifts, accompanied by honor and respect, to those who possess virtuous character."
For thus it is: wealth that is well-stored is both indestructible and follows one [into the next life].
"You should do what is pleasing to your parents-in-law and provide for your two sons;
practice only dharma and heedfulness, but do not grieve over my separation. (Jm 9.30)
Having heard this, Madrī, though her heart was deeply distressed, disregarded the wretchedness of grief for the sake of preventing her husband's despondency and spoke thus:
"O Great King, it is not right that you should go to the forest alone;
therefore, O Kṣatriya, I too shall go where you will go."
With you revolving around my limbs, death itself is a festival for me;
yet more painful than death would it be if I were to live without you.
Indeed, O King, it does not even appear to me that dwelling in the forest is a hardship. For instance:

the penance groves are more delightful than pleasure gardens, being free from wicked people, possessing rivers and trees untouched by others, echoing with the songs of various birds, teeming with deer, and featuring grassy lawns as enchanting as floors of beryl.
Moreover, O King, beholding these two princes adorned with ornaments and bearing garlands, playing among the forest thickets, you will no longer remember the kingdom.
The ever-new beauties of the forest, fashioned by the seasonal efforts of nature,
and the river groves filled with water will delight you in the woods.
There was the wonderful singing and musical instruments of the birds longing for pleasure,
and the dances of the peacocks as instructed by their teacher, intoxication.
And the sweet, unblemished song of the female bees,
performed as a concert in the forests, will gladden your heart.
The gentle splashing sounds of the waters stumbling over moving stones, and the soft warbling of the river-brides,
like the tinkling of ornaments, will delight your mind in the forest.
Thus being entreated by his beloved wife, his mind yearning for the departure to the forest, he began to give a great gift out of regard for those who came as supplicants.
Then, having learned of this undertaking regarding Viśvaṃtara’s exile, a tumultuous sound of lamentation broke out within the royal palace.

Overwhelmed by the force of grief and suffering, the crowd of supplicants, as if possessed by a fainting fit or like one intoxicated or insane, lamented in many ways. "That the earth, the nurse of all beings, feels no shame when men raise their axes to cut down a shade-tree that yields sweet fruit—clearly this demonstrates her lack of consciousness. (Jm 9.40)
If there were no one to prevent those who wish to destroy a watering place with cool, pure, and sweet water,
then alas, the guardians of the world would be either useless in their proclamation or merely a name heard from scripture, or perhaps long departed.
"Alas, unrighteousness is awake, while righteousness is either asleep or dead, since King Viśvantara is being expelled from his own kingdom! (Jm 9.42)
Who is so skilled in causing misfortune that he is cruel enough to prepare for our execution— though we are innocent and our conduct is not harsh toward those who beg?

Then the Bodhisattva, having bestowed upon supplicants according to their merit everything—including treasuries filled with hundreds of thousands of jewels, gold, and silver; storehouses containing various accumulations of wealth and grain;

and female and male servants, vehicles, mounts, garments, and furnishings—prostrated at the feet of his parents, whose fortitude was overcome by grief and sorrow, and, accompanied by his wife and son, ascended his excellent chariot amidst the sound of auspicious proclamations and the cries of lamentation from the great multitude of people.
He departed from the excellent city;

having with great effort turned back the crowd of followers who followed out of affection and whose faces were drenched with tears of grief, he himself took up the reins of the chariot and set out toward Mount Vaṅka.
Having passed beyond the vicinity of the excellent city, which was adorned with lovely garden groves, he—his mind undaunted—gradually reached the forest.

There the shade of the trees was sparse, the movement of people was severed, the quarters were filled with the sight of herds of animals roaming about, and the woods resounded with the cries of jhillī birds.
Then, certain Brahmins who had arrived there by chance begged him for the horses that drew his chariot.
While traveling on a journey of many yojanas, though he was without companions and accompanied by his wife,
he— out of joy at the gift— gave four horses to the brahmins, regardless of his future needs.

Then, as the Bodhisattva himself desired to take up the position of charioteer and was tightening his girdle with even greater firmness, four young yakṣas, appearing in the form of red deer, took up the chariot-pole themselves upon their shoulders like well-trained, noble horses.
Seeing them, the Bodhisattva said to Madrī, whose eyes were wide with joy and wonder:
"Behold the extraordinary power of these forests, which are honored by the presence of those whose wealth is asceticism."
Wherein such affection for guests was thus firmly rooted even among the noble deer.
Madrī said:
"I consider this superhuman power to be yours alone;
for even when the practice of virtue has taken root, it is not equally present in all virtuous people."
The beauty of the reflection of the stars in the waters is distinguished by the blooming of night-lotuses;
thus, the moon’s rays, as if drawn forth by curiosity, become the cause for this splendor here.
Thus, as the two of them traveled along the road, speaking pleasant words to one another out of mutual affection, another brahmin approached and requested the Bodhisattva’s excellent chariot.
Then, unattached to his own comfort and regarding the petitioner as a dear kinsman,
he fulfilled the brahmin’s desire with the chariot.

Then the Bodhisattva, with a joyful mind, descended from the chariot and, having entrusted his kinsmen [to their care], gave the excellent chariot to the brahmin; taking the prince Jālin in his arms, he set out on the road on foot.
And Madrī, her mind undisturbed, followed behind him, taking the maiden Kṛṣṇājinā in her arms. The trees, their branches bent low with heart-pleasing fruits, seemed as if they were inviting him.
Beholding him through the power of their merit, the disciples bowed down like those who are well-disciplined.
And right there, wherever he desired water, lakes appeared, their lotuses stirred by the shoulders of swans and bright yellow-orange with the pollen of their filaments.
The clouds assumed the beauty of canopies, a pleasant and fragrant breeze blew,
and the Yakṣas, unable to endure the distress of his fatigue, cleared the path before him.

Thus the Bodhisattva, like one who has entered a pleasure garden, experiencing the joy of wandering on foot and without tasting the flavor of weariness from the road, saw Vanka Mountain in the very distance together with his sons and wife; there he beheld a dense thicket of various beautiful, glossy, and excellent trees adorned with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, resounding with the many kinds of cries and songs of birds intoxicated with joy.
Having entered that penance grove— adorned by flocks of peacocks engaged in their dance, frequented by many herds of deer, as if surrounded by a moat of pure blue water from the river,

and filled with the pleasant breeze reddened by floral pollen— the forest-dweller, shown the way, entered a secluded dwelling there, beautiful to behold and pleasant in all seasons, which had been personally constructed by Viśvakarman at the command of Śakra.
He dwelt in the middle of a leaf-hut;
in that forest, being attended by his beloved and hearing the effortless, sweet prattle of his son,
he practiced austerities for more than half a year, having forgotten all anxieties regarding his kingdom as if he were staying in a pleasure garden.

Then, on one occasion, while the princess had gone out for the sake of roots and fruits, and while the prince remained in the hermitage to look after his two sons, a certain Brahmin arrived— his feet and shanks made rough by the dust of the road, his eyes and face withered by fatigue, and his water-pot suspended from his shoulder over a wooden staff— in order to bring a servant for his wife.
Having entrusted his firm message [to the messenger], he arrived at that place.

Then the Bodhisattva, seeing after a long time that a person seeking his aid had arrived, felt a surge of joy in his heart; with a gracious expression appearing on his face and eyes, he went out to meet him, preceded by kind words such as "Welcome," and having led him into the hermitage and offered him the honors due to a guest, he asked the purpose of his visit.
Then that brahmin, his fortitude and shame cast aside through affection for his wife, being ready to accept the gift, spoke these necessary words:
"Since there is light and the path is level, this world travels by that way and not by a difficult one;
yet in this world, which is mostly shrouded in the darkness of envy, others do not carry me across to the state of friendship."

"Your fame and glory, born from the heroism of your giving, have reached the end of all that is to be traversed. Therefore, I have come to you as a petitioner; grant me those two sons of yours to be my attendants."
When this was said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
who had practiced the joy of giving and was untrained in refusal,
boldly replied, "I give," even regarding his two beloved sons.

"May there be well-being! Why do you now remain seated? When the Brahmin had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva—the Great Being—replied, his heart held fast by the force of affection for his two sons whose eyes were overwhelmed with the despair arising from hearing the discourse on the gift. He said:
"I have given these two to you; however, their mother has gone to the forest for the sake of roots and fruits, and she will return this evening. (Jm 9.56)
"Having seen and smelled these two sons of mine, who are adorned and decorated with garlands, you shall lead them away tomorrow after they have rested here for one night."
The Brahmin said: "Enough of this insistence from your honor.
For it is established that the name 'vāmā' (crooked) applied to women is merely figurative.
Moreover, there might be an obstacle to your giving; for that reason, I do not find staying here agreeable."
The Bodhisattva said: "Enough with this fear of an obstacle to giving;
she is my partner in the practice of Dharma, or do as it pleases your honor."
Moreover, Great Brahmin,
due to their delicacy, their youth, and their lack of skill in service,
what kind of satisfaction as slaves could these two possibly provide for you?
Seeing them in such a state, the grandfather, King Śibi, said: "Truly, I shall give you whatever wealth you desire as the ransom for these two."
Therefore, it is right that you take these two to their destination;
for in this way, you will be united with great wealth and merit.
(The Brāhmaṇa said:
"I shall not be able to approach the king, who is as difficult to assail as a venomous serpent, by means of an unpleasant gift.
The king might snatch these two from me, or he might inflict punishment upon me."
Since I shall take these two as attendants for the brahmin woman.

Then the Bodhisattva, having spoken thus according to his desire— though his purpose was not yet fully accomplished— and having instructed his two sons with affection, inclined his water-pot toward the outstretched hand of the Brahmin in order to accept their service and compliance;
by force of his effort, the water fell from the pot.
But with his own eyes, which were as copper-red as lotus petals, he himself—

Then that brahmin, his mind agitated by the confusion of excessive joy over his gain, spoke a blessing in hurried words due to the urgency of carrying off the Bodhisattva’s daughter; he then began to drive the two princes out of the hermitage with the harsh command, "Depart!
Thereupon, the two princes, their hearts pained by the unbearable weight of the suffering of separation, bowed down to their father and, with eyes choked by tears, said:
"Mother has gone out, father, and you wish to give us [to others].
Let us first see her as well; then you may give us away."

Then that brahmin, reflecting that perhaps their mother might arrive before long, or that remorse might arise in her due to her affection for her son, bound their hands together like a cluster of lotuses.
Threatening them with a creeper, he dragged the two princes—who were struggling toward their father with faces turned away and who were naturally delicate—along with him.
Then the maiden Kṛṣṇājinā, due to the onset of such unprecedented suffering, wept aloud and said to her father:
"O father, this merciless brahmin is beating me with a creeper."
And this man is clearly not a brahmin, for it is said that brahmins are indeed righteous.
"This is surely a yakṣa in the guise of a brahmin who carries us away to devour us.
O father, why do you disregard us as we are being led away by this piśāca?"
Then Prince Jālī, lamenting for his mother, said:
"This is not such a great sorrow to me that this twice-born man kills me;
rather, it is because I do not see my mother today that it rends me asunder."
Surely my poor mother will weep for a long time in the empty penance grove out of grief for her son, like a female cātaka bird whose young has been killed.
"Having gathered much root and fruit from the forest for our sake,
how indeed will my mother fare upon seeing the hermitage empty?"
"Father, these horses, elephants, and chariots—half of this should be given to Mother; by that she will dispel her grief. (Jm 9.70)
"O venerable one, by my word, you must prevent our mother from grieving in every way;
for, dear father, it is difficult indeed to behold her again."
"Come, Kṛṣṇā, we shall die; what indeed is the use of life for us two?
We have been given away by the king to a Brahmin seeking wealth. (Jm 9.72)
Having spoken thus, they departed.

Then the Bodhisattva, though his mind was unshaken by that most piteous lamentation of his children, felt his heart consumed by an inextinguishable fire of grief, thinking, "Who now, having given, would feel regret? and he was overcome by a swoon from the onset of poison.
With his mind thus completely overwhelmed, he sat down right there;

and having regained consciousness through the fanning of a cool breeze, he gazed upon the hermitage—which was silent as if empty of his son—and with a throat choked by sobs and stammering, he spoke these words to himself:
"Striking at my very heart, which bears the name of my son, in my very presence..."
"How could he not have suspected this? Shame on that shameless brahmin! (Jm 9.73)
"Feet shod only with cloth slippers and unable to endure fatigue due to their delicacy, how will they travel the road? And he has become his servant. (Jm 9.74)
Who today will provide rest for those withered by the fatigue of the road? Or, when they are overcome by the suffering of hunger and thirst, whom will they approach to beg?
If even for me this is such suffering as I strive to maintain my composure,
what must be the condition of those two sons of mine, who have grown up in happiness?
"Alas! The fire of separation from my son is indeed consuming my mind;
yet, remembering the duty of the virtuous, who would indulge in such remorse?"

Then Madrī, her mind distressed by inauspicious omens foreboding the arrival of some unpleasant event, though desiring to return as quickly as possible with the roots and fruits she had gathered, found her path obstructed by predatory beasts. Not seeing her two sons at the usual place where they would meet her or in their playground, she fell deeply under the sway of grief. Then, filled with agitation born of apprehension for the undesired, her eyes darting about in search of her children—
Perceiving that their call was unanswered and that they were no longer being cared for, she lamented, overcome with grief.
That forest which formerly appeared to me as if filled with a social gathering, resounding with the playful chatter of my children,
now that those two are out of sight, seems to me like a desolate wilderness, devoid of refuge.
Could it be that those two princes have fallen asleep from the fatigue of their play, or perhaps they have perished in the dense forest? Or,
being displeased by my long absence, they may have hidden themselves somewhere out of childishness?
Why do even these birds not cry out, they who were witnesses to his slaughter?
Was he perhaps swept away by the exceedingly swift river, its anger unrestrained by the breaking of its waves?
"Could my thoughts now have been vain and false? Could it be that all is well with the prince and his son?"
"May the ripening of even those omens that portend misfortune occur within my own body!
Why indeed does this heart of mine seem to dissolve, as if shrouded by the darkness of dejection that has driven away all joy?
My limbs seem to fall apart."
"The quarters of the sky seem agitated,
and this forest, its splendor ruined, seems to be reeling. Then,
having entered the hermitage and set aside the roots and fruits in a secluded spot, she approached her husband with due ceremony and asked, "Where are the two children?"

Then the Bodhisattva, knowing the weakness of his mother’s heart due to affection and the difficulty of speaking what is unpleasant, was unable to say anything to her. For it is exceedingly difficult for one who is compassionate to approach a person worthy of kindness with the fire of announcing unpleasant news, which burns the mind.

Then Madrī, concluding, "Clearly some misfortune has befallen my two sons, since he remains thus silent, merely persisting in his grief and dejection," looked all around the hermitage with a distracted mind; not seeing her two children and finding that he did not address her, she spoke again with a voice choked with tears:
"I do not see the boys, and you do not speak to me."
I am indeed destroyed, for a wretched woman like me does not speak what is unpleasant.
Having spoken thus, her heart overwhelmed by the fire of grief, she fell down like a creeper whose roots have been severed.
As she was falling, the Bodhisattva caught her, brought her to a bed of grass, and having sprinkled her with cool water, he spoke to comfort her once her breath had returned:
"Madri, I did not tell you of my sorrow all at once."
For steadfastness is not possible in a mind weakened by affection.
"A brahmin, afflicted by the sufferings of old age and poverty, approached me;
I gave my two sons to him, so take heart and do not grieve."
Look at me, Madri; O Queen, do not lament for my two sons.
Do not strike my heart, which is already pierced by the arrows of grief for my sons, as if with a further blow.
"How could I not give even my life when asked?
Therefore, noble lady, rejoice in this gift of my son."

Having heard that, Madrī—her heart tormented by the fear of her sons' destruction, yet her grief and exhaustion diminished by hearing news of her sons' survival—wiped her eyes and, looking up at her husband with wonder so as to prevent his despondency, said to him:
"It is a marvel! What need is there for much?"
Surely even the gods, though their minds were filled with wonder and speechlessness,
found that envy had no scope within your heart.
For thus, with the sounds of divine drums spreading in all directions and their echoes extending everywhere,
the sky itself became filled with clearly articulated words and syllables, as if out of devotion to weaving your own fame.
The earth, with its mountain-kings for breasts, trembled violently as if from intoxication;
and the sky, by means of golden flowers falling from heaven, became as if illuminated by lightning.
Therefore, enough with this wretchedness of grief; give [your wealth] and gladden your heart.
Become a watering place for the world, and be once again a giver, O noble one!

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having become reflective as to what this might be upon seeing Mount Sumeru— the king of mountains, which shines with the radiance of various jewels— tremble due to the shaking of the earth's surface, learned from the world-protectors, whose eyes were wide with wonder, that the cause of the earthquake was Viśvantara’s gift of his children; his mind reeling with joy and amazement at the break of dawn, he [approached].

Assuming the form of a brahmin, he approached Viśvantara like one seeking a favor. Having been received with the hospitality due to a guest, he was invited by the Bodhisattva, who asked, "What is your need? and then requested his wife;
for among the virtuous, the practice of giving never reaches exhaustion, just as water in great lakes does not dry up.
Therefore, O one who resembles a god, I entreat you to grant me this wife whom you are worthy to possess.
Without any dejection, the Bodhisattva promised him, saying, "So be it. Then, taking Madrī with his left hand and his water-pot with his right,
he poured the water from the tip of his hand upon her, while the fire of grief fell upon the mind of the god of love.
Madrī was provoked to anger, yet she did not weep, for she understood his natural disposition;
though overwhelmed by the burden of unprecedented sorrow, she stood gazing at him as if she were a painted image.
Seeing this, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his heart overcome with supreme wonder, spoke in praise of that Great Being:
"Oh, how vast is the difference between the true and the false Dharma!"
What power do those of unrefined self have even to believe in this deed?
While still not free from passion, he gave away his son and wife—who were exceedingly dear to him—without attachment; what indeed is this loftiness?
Without doubt, as your fame is scattered in all directions by those who delight in recounting your virtues,
the glories of others will vanish, just as other lights disappear before the brilliance of the sun.
The Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Bhujagas, as well as the Tridaśas together with Vāsava, rejoice in this superhuman deed of yours.
Having said this, Śakra resumed his own blazing form and, announcing himself, "I am Śakra," he spoke to the Bodhisattva:
"I give this wife Madrī to you alone;
for the moonlight cannot remain apart from the cool-rayed moon."
Therefore, do not grieve over the separation from your two sons, nor fall into distress over the loss of your kingdom;
for your father has returned together with them and will make the kingdom secure once more, now that it has found its protector in you.
Having spoken thus, Śakra vanished on the spot.
And through the power of Śakra, that brahmin brought the two sons of the Bodhisattva right to the realm of Śibi.
Then the Śibis and Sañjaya, the king of Śibi, [beheld] that most piteous and most difficult deed of the Bodhisattva.

Upon hearing this, their hearts were deeply moved; they redeemed the two sons of the Bodhisattva from the hands of the brahmin, and having appeased him and brought the children back, they established Viśvantara once again in his kingdom.
Thus, since the conduct of the Bodhisattva is so exceedingly marvelous, one should neither show contempt nor harbor resentment toward those superior beings who are intent upon that same path.
This should be applied to the praise of the Tathāgata and to listening to the Dharma with reverence.
Thus ends the ninth Jātaka, the Story of Viśvantara.
10. The Yajña-jātaka:
Those whose intentions are virtuous do not comply with the deceptions of evil; therefore, one should strive for purity of intention.
As it is heard in tradition—

It is said that the Bodhisattva protected the earth, which had come to him by succession of inheritance, with its single umbrella, free from thorns and rivals, with all neighboring kings bowed down by the power of his own merit, and devoid of disturbances such as those caused by his own or foreign armies. That lord of the earth, having conquered the enemies of the senses, enjoyed the blameless fruits [of sovereignty] without attachment.
With his entire being dedicated to the welfare of his subjects, he became like a sage, having the sole task of maintaining the sacred law.
For he understood that the nature of the world is primarily characterized by imitation of the conduct of its leaders;
therefore, desiring to bring about the highest good among his subjects, he applied himself especially to the ordinances of Dharma.
He gave wealth, adopted the practice of virtuous conduct, cultivated patience, and strove for the welfare of the world;
with a gentle appearance and a benevolent intent toward the benefit of his subjects, he shone like Dharma incarnate.

Then once, although that realm was protected by his arms, due to the deficiency in the karma of sentient beings and because they had fallen under the power of negligence, a state of distress caused by drought broke out here and there among the sons of the gods who were in charge of the rain. Then the king, having reached the firm conclusion that "this calamity has clearly arisen either from my own transgression of dharma or from that of my subjects," [reflected thus].

Because his resolute intention for the welfare of his subjects was firmly rooted, he could not endure their suffering; thus, he questioned the elderly Brahmins headed by the domestic priest, as well as his ministers of counsel—all of whom were esteemed for their knowledge of the true nature of Dharma—regarding the means to alleviate it.

Then, deeming the sacrificial ritual prescribed by the Vedas—which is terrifying due to its commencement involving the slaughter of hundreds of various living beings—to be the cause of abundant rain, they described that rite to him.

But that king, having learned the facts of the matter, because of his compassionate nature, did not inwardly welcome their words regarding the slaughter of living beings prescribed for sacrifice. Out of deference to their decorum, he did not address them with harsh words of refusal, but instead set aside their discourse by shifting to another topic.

Yet they, finding an opportunity through the introduction of a discussion on dharma, and being unaware of his disposition concealed beneath his profound gravity, again urged the king toward the undertaking of the sacrifice.
Those duties of kings which are fixed for the acquisition of the earth and its protection—
time never passes them by for you, just as their proper sequence leads to dharma and happiness.

How can your mind be possessed by such negligence and sloth regarding this bridge to the world of the gods called sacrifice— [you] who are skilled in the pursuit of the three aims of life and who have taken up the bow for the sake of the welfare of your subjects? (Jm 10.5)

O destroyer of enemies, this very time is yours to gather through sacrifices those supreme blessings that blaze with fame— blessings which are highly esteemed by kings as if they were their own commands, and which are themselves manifest success.
Granted that you are always consecrated for sacrifice through your devotion to giving and your observance of religious vows, nevertheless,
it would be fitting for you to discharge your debt to the gods by means of rituals established in the Vedas.
"For when the deities are well-pleased by a successful sacrifice, they reward all beings with rain;
therefore, favor this sacrificial rite which brings benefit to your subjects and brings glory to yourself."

A thought arose in him: "Alas, how poorly situated is this person who loves the Dharma and possesses faith, yet whose intellect is so fragile that it is led away by the convictions of others and lacks investigation!
For indeed—those very ones who are esteemed as the refuge of the worlds have themselves come to regard even violence as dharma.
Alas, people turn toward the narrow straits of the miserable states of existence, following the evil paths prescribed by them."
For what possible connection can there be between the slaughter of an animal and the dharma of dwelling in the world of the gods or pleasing the deities?
