"It is said that an animal being slaughtered goes to heaven by the power of mantras; therefore, its slaughter attains the status of dharma. This too is false, for who among those others will receive [the merit] in the next world? (Jm 10.11)
With a mind that has not turned away from unwholesome conduct and whose resolve is not rooted in virtuous deeds,
by what cause shall this beast go to heaven, even when sacrificed in a ritual, if it lacks refuge in its own past merit? (Jm_10.12)
If one slain in a sacrifice were to go to the third heaven, then surely the twice-born would themselves become sacrificial animals;
since this rule is not observed anywhere, who indeed will accept their word?
Having abandoned the auspicious nectar, held by excellent celestial nymphs, which possesses incomparable fragrance, miraculous power, flavor, and vitality,
the denizens of heaven will instead find joy in the slaughter of a pitiable beast for the sake of its fat and other such things.

Having determined that this was the opportune moment, the king, as if eager for the commencement of a sacrifice, accepted their words and said to them: "I am indeed well-protected and favored, since your honors are thus intent upon my welfare. Therefore, I desire to perform a thousand human sacrifices."
"Let the ministers, according to their respective offices, seek out and procure the necessary materials for that purpose.
Let a site suitable for the construction of a sacrificial hall be examined, as well as an auspicious lunar day, *karana*, *muhurta*, and conjunction of constellations favorable thereto.

Then the domestic priest said to him: "O Great King, first bathe for the sake of accomplishing your desired object, at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) upon the completion of a single sacrifice."
"Now, the undertaking of the northern [sacrifices] will be carried out in due order;
for if thousands of human victims were seized all at once, they would clearly cause distress to the subjects.
When the Brahmins said, "This is so," the king spoke to them: "Enough of your apprehension regarding the provocation of the subjects."
"For I shall make such arrangements that my subjects will not fall into distress.
Then the king, having assembled the people of the city and the countryside, said to them: "I desire to sacrifice with a thousand human sacrifices (*puruṣamedha*).
Yet, I do not wish to appoint any man who is unwilling or innocent to the state of being a sacrificial victim."

"Therefore, from this day forward, whenever I see any among you who has transgressed the boundaries of moral conduct, who disregards my command, and who is a defiler of his own family and a thorn in the side of the land— I shall seize him for the sake of a sacrificial victim. Let this be known to you all."
Then their most eminent members, with palms joined in reverence, said to him:
"O God among men, all your actions are directed toward the welfare of your subjects; what purpose, then, is served by this act of insulting them?"
Even Brahmā ought to approve of your conduct; in this matter, you yourself are the supreme authority for what is right.
Whatever is dear to Your Majesty is dear to us as well;
indeed, nothing other than what is dear and beneficial to us is seen as dear to you.

Having thus accepted the words of the city-dwellers, the king dispatched trusted ministers throughout the countryside and the cities to apprehend wicked people with great public display and ostentation. And every day, he caused proclamations to be made everywhere: "The king, the giver of safety, grants fearlessness to the virtuous man whose wealth is his steadfast and pure character."
Desiring to perform a sacrifice with thousands of human-beasts for the sake of the welfare of his subjects, he [dealt] with those who delighted in lawlessness.
Therefore, whoever from this time forward, out of adherence to the praise of lawlessness, shall disregard even the king’s command— which is honored by neighboring princes—
shall himself, through his own actions, be made into a sacrificial animal after being devoured.
With his body bound to the sacrificial post, miserable with despair and wasting away, he will be seen by the people.
Then, the people dwelling in that region, observing the king’s intense preoccupation with searching for men of immoral conduct for the sake of sacrificial animals,

hearing daily that most terrifying proclamation, and seeing royal officers intent on seizing wicked folk arriving from all sides, abandoned their attachment to immorality and became devoted to undertaking the restraint of virtuous conduct.

Averse to the pursuit of enmity, favorably disposed toward one another with love and respect, with strife and disputes stilled, following the instructions of their elders, skilled in sharing, hospitable to guests, and praising humility and modesty, they lived as if in the Kṛta Yuga;
[all this was] through fear of death, concern for the next world, family pride, and the preservation of their reputation.
And because of his exceedingly pure nature, that man, adorned with the stainless ornament of virtuous conduct, became possessed of a modesty that was its opposite.
The more the people became devoted to the Dharma, the more the guards specifically sought out those of immoral conduct; consequently, no one deviated from the Dharma.
Then, having heard this news concerning the events in his own country, the king— adorned with a special joy—
gratified his spies with extensive gifts for bringing such pleasant tidings and commanded his ministers.
"My higher resolve was to protect my subjects, and they have now become worthy of my veneration;
furthermore, this wealth has been intended for sacrifice, for I am desirous of performing a rite according to that very intention."
"May whoever desires wealth as fuel for their happiness obtain it to their heart's content from my presence;
thus may this poverty that afflicts our realm be rendered homeless. (Jm 10.23)
While I stand firm in my resolve to protect the people, and while the means for this task are augmented by an abundance of allies,
this suffering of the populace— kindling my indignation— seems to blaze ever more intensely within my heart.

Then those ministers of the king, accepting his words with great assent, had alms-halls constructed in all the villages, cities, and market towns, as well as at rest-places along the roads; and according to the king's command, they daily satisfied the needy with the distribution of desired wealth.
Thus, that people abandoned poverty and simultaneously attained riches from the lord of the earth.
Adorned with various colorful garments and ornaments, he became like the splendor of a widespread festival.
The king’s fame, accumulated through the praises of joyful people, spread throughout the quarters;
its extent increased like the pollen born from the filaments of lotuses on a lake, where its expansion is augmented by gentle ripples.
Thus, as all the people turned toward virtuous conduct through the king’s reliance on the qualities of sound policy,
calamities— whose power was utterly overwhelmed by the increase of merit— went to their destruction without lingering.
The seasons became pleasant due to their lack of irregularity, devoted to righteousness like new kings;
and the earth bore various crops, possessing lotus-filled, stainless, and blue reservoirs of water.
Powerful diseases did not afflict the people; medicinal herbs possessed their most potent qualities;
the wind blew regularly according to the seasons; and the planets moved along auspicious paths.
No fear arose from the armies of enemies, nor from one another, nor from divine calamities;
among the people who were intent on the dharma of self-restraint and remained tranquil, it was as if a golden age had arrived there.
Now, when the king had thus pacified the sufferings of the needy through this sacrifice of Dharma along with all its calamities;

when the earth was delightful to behold due to its prosperity and crowded with joyful people; and when fame was spreading everywhere among the subjects who were occupied in reciting benedictions for the monarch—a certain chief minister, his mind won over by royal favor, spoke thus to the king:
—This is indeed well said:
"Because they constantly observe the superior, inferior, and middling tasks [of others], the intellects of the lords move ever upward, surpassing all other intellects. (Jm 10.31)

Thus it was: for by means of this sacrifice of Dharma—which was free from the blameworthy fault of slaughtering animals—the King accomplished the welfare of his subjects in both worlds, brought calamities to an end, and [removed] the sufferings of poverty for those established in virtuous conduct.
What need is there to say more? Fortunate indeed are those subjects!
The black antelope skin spread upon his body was like the expansive splendor of the moon; yet,
due to the constraints of his consecration, his natural gracefulness of movement did not become sluggish,
nor did the beauty of the arrangement of hair on his umbrella-like head diminish.
By your renunciations, even the wonder that rests upon the fame of one who has performed a hundred sacrifices has been surpassed.
O knower of policy, for the world that is generally attached to violence, wretched, and desirous of rewards, sacrifice is merely a means;
but for one whose entire conduct is faultless and captivating, sacrifice is but an ornament of fame. (Jm_10.33)
"Oh, how great is the fortune of these subjects, for you have become their protector!
Indeed, it is evident that even among subjects, a father would not be such a guardian."
Another said:

"When wealth arises, people give what is called charity, being under the sway of hope; and even in the matter of moral conduct, they are intent on social standing and have conceived a longing for heaven."
But this engagement of theirs, which proceeds with such skill in the service of others' affairs, is not observed among the ignorant, nor among those devoid of the application of goodness.
Thus, those with virtuous intentions do not succumb to the deceptions of evil; therefore, one should strive for purity of intention.
Thus, the exertion for the welfare of subjects brings about prosperity, fame, and happiness;
therefore, it is not right for kings to act by disregarding it. (Jm 10.36)

The same should be said regarding the censure of kings. Since the practice of Dharma brings about the welfare of subjects, it should be inferred that one who desires welfare must follow the Dharma. Furthermore, it should be stated that the slaughter of animals never leads to prosperity, whereas giving, self-restraint, and self-control do lead to prosperity; therefore, one who seeks such prosperity must be devoted to giving and the like.
"In this way, even in his previous births, the Blessed One’s mind was intent upon acting for the welfare of the world"—this should also be stated in the praise of the Tathāgata.
Thus ends the tenth Jātaka, the Sacrifice.
(Vaidya 77)
11. The Śakra-jātaka:
Even in times of adversity, neither sovereignty nor prosperity causes the great-souled ones to slacken their compassion for sentient beings.
As it is heard in tradition:

It is said that once, a Bodhisattva— who had practiced meritorious deeds for no small length of time, who had made generosity, self-restraint, and self-control his very nature, and whose extraordinary activity was fixed upon the welfare of others— became Śakra, the lord of the gods.
The splendor of the lord of the immortals shone with exceeding brilliance by virtue of his reliance on him,
like the light of the moon clinging to a palace whose walls were fresh with plaster and newly anointed.
For her sake, the sons of Diti impetuously rushed forward and struck with their chests the mace-like tusks of the elephants of the quarters;
yet Lakṣmī, though she had come to him through the bliss of the fullness of his good fortune, did not make his heart stained by pride.

The hosts of Daityas, unable to endure his abundant fame— which pervaded all the worlds— earned through the perfect protection of heaven and earth, nor that most wonderful prosperity, marched forth with a vast army consisting of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry, which was more terrifying than the swelling pride of a world-age, possessed a roar as formidable as the agitated ocean, and was difficult to behold due to its various blazing weapons and armor.
They approached him with their army for battle;
yet, although he was righteous by nature, that arrogance of the enemy, the fear of his people which is distasteful as it interrupts play,
his own majesty established on the path of policy, and his gradual advance— all these caused his heart to turn toward the onset of war.

Then that Great Being, having mounted a magnificent golden chariot yoked to a thousand excellent horses— its beautiful banner adorned with the insignia of the robes of an Arhat raised aloft, its body brilliantly blazing and illuminated by the radiance of various jewels and gems, its two sides graced by various sharp, flaming weapons arranged in distinct rows, and draped with white woolen cloth— proceeded with a vast celestial army consisting of a diverse array of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Surrounded by his retinue, he then advanced to meet that army of asuras right upon the shore of the ocean.
Thereupon, a battle commenced there, shattering the courage of the timid, in which the armor of the combatants was shattered by the clashing of their mutual weapons.
"Stay! Not thus! Look here; where now will you escape from me?
Strike! You shall not remain!"—thus did they strike one another down.
Then, as that tumultuous battle with flashing weapons commenced,
the surface of the sky seemed to burst asunder from the sounds of kettledrums and the shouts of warriors.
While elephants, formidable like mountains shaken by the winds at the end of an eon, rushed at one another with fury aroused by the scent of the ichor of rut; (Jm_11.7)
Chariots with banners flickering like lightning spread in every direction, emitting sharp sounds like the clouds of a portentous storm.
As the banners, umbrellas, weapons, armor,
and crowns of the heroic gods and dānavas were being cast down by their sharp, mutually directed arrows, [the battle raged].
Then, scorched by the weapons and arrows of the Asuras, the army of the Lord of the Gods fled in fear;
yet the Lord of the Gods alone stood firm in battle, holding back the force of his enemies with his chariot.
Beholding the surging Asura army— attacking with excessive joy, with loud shouts, roars, and lion-like bellows—

and perceiving his own forces intent on flight, Mātali, the charioteer of the Lord of the Gods, concluded that the time for retreat had arrived and turned back the chariot of the Sovereign of the Devas.
Then Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, saw on the way of the impact as the chariot was springing upward toward the tips of the poles, the nests of Garuḍas in the Śālmali trees.
As soon as he saw them, his heart being seized with compassion, he spoke to Mātali, the charioteer:
"The bird-nests, crowded with fledglings whose wings have not yet grown, are sheltered in the Śālmali trees."
"Drive my chariot in such a way that these [trees] do not fall, crushed by the chariot-pole."
Mātali said: "O noble sir, these hosts of Daityas are now attacking us.
Śakra said: "What of it? Avoid these nests of Garuḍas properly."
Then Mātali spoke to him again:
"O lotus-eyed one, by turning this chariot back, there would be safety only for the birds;
for this army of our enemies, having finally found its opportunity against the gods, is indeed charging at us."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, revealing his own superior inner resolve and his extraordinary compassion for that particular being, said:

"Therefore, turn back the chariot; death by the blows of the terrible mace sent by the lord of the Daityas is better for me than life with my fame consumed by the cry of 'fie'—life after killing these beings whose faces are dejected with fear."
Then Mātali, having assented with "So be it," brought back his chariot yoked with a thousand horses for him.
But his enemies, having witnessed his heroic feats in battle, saw that the chariot had turned back.
Fleeing in fear and stumbling, they prostrated themselves like dark clouds driven by the wind.
When his own army was broken and he was retreating, he blocked the path of the enemy host;
though alone, because of his inconceivable prowess, he alone caused the pride and arrogance of the foe to shrink.
Then, seeing that the asura host was broken, the army of the lord of the gods also retreated;
for there was no longer any affection among the enemies of the gods who were fleeing in fear, since they were intent on turning back.
Then, being honored by the gods with feelings of both joy and shame, the Lord of the Suras,
his beautiful body radiant with the splendor of victory, slowly departed from the field of battle for the city, where his inner apartments were filled with longing.
Thus, that very battle became his victory.
Therefore it is said:
"The base man, devoid of compassion, commits evil; but the man of middling intellect, possessing compassion, does so only when overtaken by calamity."
But even at the risk of losing his life, a virtuous person is no more able to overstep his own conduct than the ocean is able to overstep its shore.
Thus, having even sacrificed his own life, the Blessed One protected sentient beings throughout the long night of saṃsāra;
it is therefore not fitting for a wise person to harbor malice toward them, let alone act wrongly. A noble person should be devoted to compassion toward all living beings.
For it is said, "Dharma indeed protects the one who practices Dharma"—this principle should also be inferred here.
Likewise, [he spoke] on the praise of the Tathāgata and on listening to the Dharma with reverence.
Thus ends the eleventh Jātaka, the Śakra-jātaka.
(Vaidya 80)
12. The Brāhmaṇa Jātaka:
Out of self-respect alone, virtuous men do not transgress the bounds of proper conduct.
As it is heard—

It is said that a Bodhisattva took birth in a great Brahmin family that was irreproachable in its lineage and conduct, renowned for its adherence to its own dharma, and praised for its disciplined behavior.

Having undergone the sequence of purificatory rites in due order— beginning with the ceremonies for conception, the quickening of the male fetus, the parting of the hair, and the birth ceremony— he resided with a teacher who was endowed with learning, noble birth, and proper conduct, for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
His proficiency in hearing, grasping, and retaining [the teachings], his constant devotion inherited from his lineage as established in his own family,
and his state of being adorned with tranquility even in early youth, made his guru’s face bright with love and grace toward him.
For the mantras of subjugation are always unimpeded qualities;
they succeed even for those tormented by the fire of hatred, let alone for those with healthy minds.
Then his teacher, for the purpose of testing the character of all his students, frequently described during the intervals between their recitations the sufferings of his own poverty:
"Poverty is a state where one has no one to cry out for help even among one's own kin, where there is no joy even at a festival,
which is sluggish in the hope of receiving gifts, and where every desire is fruitless."

The state of being destitute of wealth is a source of humiliation, a ground for exhaustion, utterly devoid of happiness, and exceedingly weak; it is always like a calamity, full of lamentation, and truly most dreadful.

Then those disciples of his, like well-bred horses urged on by a whip, were moved with a sense of urgency born from their affection for their teacher, and they brought back an even greater and more abundant amount of alms-food.
He said to them: "Enough of this exertion on your parts;
the offerings of alms-food do not destroy the emaciation caused by anyone's poverty."
"However, since you cannot endure our suffering, it would be more appropriate for you to exert this very effort toward the acquisition of wealth. Why?
Because food destroys hunger, water quenches thirst, spells destroy poison, and medicine destroys disease; but wealth, when properly acquired through a lineage, destroys the misery of poverty."

The disciples said: "What shall we do, for we are unfortunate that our exertion of power is so limited? Moreover, O Preceptor, even if wealth were obtained by us through begging, we would not be able to endure this suffering of poverty in such a manner."
"For the acquisition of wealth by Brahmins consists of the meager means of receiving gifts;
yet this person here is a non-giver. Thus, having no other recourse, we are ruined. (Jm_12.7)
The teacher said: "There are other means of acquiring wealth observed in the scriptures;
however, our capacities having been drained by old age, we are unfit for their practice. The students replied: "O Preceptor, our prowess has not yet been impaired by old age."
Therefore, if you consider those means prescribed by the scriptures to be capable of being practiced,
then let it be said:
we shall proceed until we have discharged our debt for the labor of your instruction.
The teacher said: "Even for the young, such means of acquiring wealth are indeed difficult to accomplish when the heart is lax in its resolve.
However, if you have such persistence in this matter, then listen well to one excellent method for the acquisition of wealth."

In times of distress, theft is permitted for the twice-born; and the ultimate form of distress in this world is indeed poverty. Therefore, the property of others may be taken by those who are not wicked; furthermore, all of this belongs to the Brahmins as their own.

Granted, those such as you certainly possess the power to seize wealth even by force; however, this is not the proper course, for one's own reputation must be protected. Therefore, one must certainly exercise self-restraint in empty places.
Thus, with their reins cast loose, those students—except for the Bodhisattva—accepted his words as "excellent," even though they were improper, taking them to be reasonable.
For he, being naturally virtuous, could not bring himself to approve of it;
yet, because they had set out as if on a necessary task, he suddenly spoke to restrain them.

With his face bowed down by shame, the Bodhisattva sighed softly and remained silent. Then the teacher, observing that the Bodhisattva neither approved of nor rejected that ritual, and having conceived a high regard for the Great Being's virtues, wondered: "Could it be that he is thus because of a lack of resolve or a lack of affection?"

Having arisen with the doubt, "Is it that theft is not committed against me, or is it because of the perception of unrighteousness?", he spoke to the Bodhisattva in order to clarify its true nature: "O Great Brahmin, these twice-born ones, unable to endure my misfortune, have taken refuge in the path of heroic men."
But you, dull-witted from a lack of resolve, surely do not suffer on account of our misfortune.
"Even though my own suffering has been fully revealed by me in detail and without concealment through these words,
how is it that you remain as if nothing were wrong, with a mind so unperturbed and free from dejection? (Jm 12.12)

Then the Bodhisattva, filled with agitation, saluted his preceptor and said: "May all evil be stilled! It is certainly not because of a lack of affection or a hard heart that I remain thus, unpained by the great sufferings of my teacher;
rather, it is because of the impossibility of the course of action shown by the preceptor."
For it is not possible to commit a sin anywhere while remaining unseen. Why? Because secrecy is impossible;
there is no such thing as secrecy for one who performs an evil deed in this world.
For indeed, invisible beings surely see human beings.
Seeing those sages who have perfected their souls and whose divine eyes are opened, a fool, devoid of shame, proceeds toward evil.
I, however, do not see anything anywhere that is empty;
even that wherein I do not see another, is it not indeed non-empty by my very self?
Whether a misdeed be seen by another or committed by oneself,
that which is seen by oneself is the more clearly seen.
Because his mind is preoccupied with his own affairs, one may or may not observe the conduct of another;
however, one who has focused his entire mind on passion certainly knows when he himself is committing evil.
"For this reason, I am established in this way.
Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that his preceptor’s mind was thoroughly pacified, spoke again:
"My mind has not yet reached a firm certainty in this matter; you too might be deceiving me for the sake of wealth."
Having understood this, who indeed would disregard the distinction between virtue and vice, and reduce the suppression of virtue to the price of wealth?
I indeed declare my own intention:
it is better to take up a skull-bowl and wear discolored robes than to behold the prosperity of an enemy's house.
Having cast aside all shame at the violation of dharma, his mind was set even upon seizing the position of the Lord of the Gods.
Then his teacher, his heart overwhelmed with joy and wonder, rose from his seat, embraced him, and said:

"Excellent, excellent, my son! Excellent, excellent, great brahmin! This is worthy of you, a wise man adorned with such tranquility. For when fools encounter even the slightest circumstance, they abandon the path of their own duty."
But the virtuous, whose wealth consists of austerity, sacred learning, and knowledge, do not undergo transformation even in the face of supreme hardship.
By you, this peerless and stainless family has been adorned, just as the sky is graced by the autumnal moon;
your learning, renowned for its virtuous conduct, has become meaningful, and my own labor has borne fruit through the resulting happiness.
Thus, because virtuous persons do not transgress the boundary of proper conduct solely out of self-respect (*ātma-lajjā*), one should become noble through the power of moral shame (*hrī*).

This [principle] is to be applied to such sūtras as those stating: "In this way, the noble disciple, being endowed with the moat of moral shame, abandons the unwholesome and cultivates the wholesome," and so forth; as well as to those discourses concerning the praise of moral shame and the sovereignty over the world.
Thus ends the twelfth Jātaka, the Brāhmaṇa-jātaka.
13. The Unmādayantī-jātaka.

Even for those afflicted by intense suffering, there arises a refusal to follow the base path through the support of one's own fortitude. As it is heard: once, the Bodhisattva—who was striving for the welfare of the world with his preeminent virtues such as truthfulness, generosity, tranquility, and wisdom—became the king of the Śibis, like the Dharma itself personified as discipline.
Like a father toward his subjects, he was intent on doing them good;
being restrained from the practice of vice and established in the nobility of virtue by that king as if by a father, the people rejoiced in both worlds.
His policy of governance, equal in its power toward both his own kin and the common people, followed the path of righteousness;
by closing off the unrighteous way for the populace, it became like a flight of stairs leading to heaven.
Perceiving that the welfare of the world was rooted in the Dharma, that protector of the human realm, whose sole purpose was that end,
devoted himself with his whole being to the path of righteousness and could not tolerate its suppression by others.

Now, that king had a daughter, the chief of the citizens, who was like the goddess Śrī incarnate, or like Rati herself, one of the foremost of the Apsarases; endowed with the highest perfection of beauty and grace, she was most beautiful to behold and esteemed as a jewel among women—
indeed, for people not yet free from passion, she remained within the range of their vision only so long as her form could be perceived by the eyes.
For that long, he was unable to shift his gaze, which was bound by her beauty and virtues.
And for this reason, her kinsmen gave her the name Unmādayantī. Then her father sent word to the king: "O King, a jewel among women has appeared in your realm;
therefore, Your Majesty is the authority regarding whether she shall be accepted or dismissed."
Then the king commanded the brahmins who were experts in the marks of women: "May your honors examine her; is she suitable for us or not?
Thereupon, her father led those brahmins into his own residence and said to Umādayantī, "My dear girl, serve the brahmins yourself.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," she began to serve the brahmins in due order.
Then those brahmins,
their eyes fixed motionlessly upon gazing at her face, had their fortitude carried away by the god of love.
Deprived of mastery over their eyes and minds, they were as if robbed of their senses by intoxication.
And when they were no longer able to remain steady and composed through their power of discernment, much less to eat,
that householder withdrew his daughter from their sight and, serving the brahmins himself, dismissed them.

Then this thought occurred to them: "Truly, this exquisite beauty of this girl is like a magical illusion, so utterly captivating that it is not even fit for the king to behold her, much less to take her as his wife. For if his heart were surely infatuated by this splendor of form, his enthusiasm for the pursuit of Dharma and worldly affairs would surely slacken; and through the neglect of royal duties, he would bring suffering to the path of the welfare and happiness of his subjects."
These would lead to his ruin;
for she, by her mere appearance, could create an obstacle to the spiritual attainments even of sages,
let alone that of a young king established in pleasure, upon whom the rain of glances from those imbued with passion falls.
Therefore, perceiving that this was the appropriate time, they approached the king according to the occasion and reported: "Your Majesty, we have seen that maiden;
she possesses only a certain beauty of form, but it is devoid of splendor due to the presence of inauspicious marks.
Therefore, Your Majesty ought not even to look upon her."
How much more so, then, to reduce her to the status of a wife? For a woman who brings reproach upon two families eclipses both their fame and prosperity,
just as a cloudy night with a moon submerged destroys both the beauty and the distinction between heaven and earth.
Having heard this matter, the king thought, "She indeed possesses inauspicious marks and is not suitable for my family," and his desire for her ceased.
But perceiving the king's lack of interest, the householder gave that girl to Abhipāraga, a minister of that very king.

Then once, that king, his mind eager to behold the Kaumudī festival—which had come in due course and whose splendor was fixed upon his excellent city—mounted his preeminent chariot. The city’s streets, marketplaces, and inner courtyards were sprinkled and swept; various banners and flags were raised on high; the ground in every direction was made white and variegated with offerings of flowers; dancing, singing, laughter, rhythmic movement, and instrumental music were underway; and it was filled with the pervasive, sweet fragrance of flowers, incense, aromatic powders, garlands, perfumes, bathing unguents, and ointments.
Wandering through that preeminent city, where various beautiful wares were spread out for sale and the royal highways were crowded with citizens and country folk who were contented,

well-fed, and dressed in most brilliant attire, he approached the residence of that minister. Then, having been rejected by the king because she was considered to bear inauspicious marks and thus likely to cause madness, Unmādayantī— her indignation aroused, yet her physical beauty manifest as if she were lightning amidst the peaks of a cloud— approached out of curiosity to see the king.
She remained there, illuminating the palace roof.
[The king thought: "May he now have the power to maintain himself with unshaken fortitude and mindfulness by not looking at these inauspicious signs.
Then, the king's gaze, which had been extended out of curiosity to behold the splendor of the excellent city, suddenly fell upon her as she stood directly before him.
Then that king—

though his eyes were captivated by the physical charms and graceful gestures of the beauties of the inner apartments— remained undisturbed due to his devotion to the path of Dharma and was diligent even in the conquest of his senses.
Though possessed of the quality of vast fortitude and modesty, and though his eyes were usually averse to gazing at another's young woman, he—
his wonder stirred by passion— beheld that woman for a long time with unblinking eyes.
"Is this perhaps Kaumudī herself, the presiding deity of this palace;
or is she a celestial woman or a daughter of the Daityas? For this is no human form."
Even as the king was thus reflecting, his eyes unsated by the sight of her, the chariot passed beyond that place and no longer conformed to his desires.

Then the king, as if with a vacant heart yet with a mind one-pointedly fixed upon her, returned to his own palace; his fortitude shaken by the god of love, he questioned the charioteer Sunanda in private:
"Whose house is that which you see, surrounded by white walls?"
Who was it that shone there, like lightning in a white cloud?
The charioteer said: "There is a chief minister of the King named Abhipāraga;
his house is that very one, and his wife is the daughter of Kirīṭavat, named Unmādayantī.

Upon hearing this, the king’s heart became despondent because she was another's wife; with eyes motionless from anxiety, he sighed long and hot, and with his mind fixed upon her, spoke softly to himself:

Oh, how the name of this girl of pure smiles has been made beautiful with syllables that are pleasing and true to its meaning! For indeed, it has made me as if intoxicated by the thought, "She who intoxicates. (Jm 13.12)
I wish to forget her, yet I seem to see her with my mind;
for my heart remains fixed upon her, as if she were there by her own power.
"Since another man has taken my wife, I too have become so lacking in self-control;
therefore, like one driven mad, I am today abandoned by sleep as if by shame."

As my mind was rendered motionless by passion at the sight of her body’s graceful movements, smiles, and glances, the *nālikā*— suddenly resounding with the bold sound announcing the sequence of other duties— pierced my heart with resentment.

Thus, that king, his fortitude shaken by the power of passion, though striving to compose himself, became pale and emaciated; intent on brooding, sighing, and yawning, the symptoms of love became manifest even as they were being suppressed by his great self-command. Through his face, with its fixed gaze of anxiety, and through his physical wasting, the transformation of the monarch’s mind became clearly apparent.

Then a minister, whose mind was skilled in discerning gestures and outward appearances and who had reached the further shore of political wisdom, having learned the king's situation along with its causes, and fearing for his safety out of affection while recognizing the overwhelming power of passion, approached the king in private after receiving permission and addressed him thus: [The minister said: "Sire, this matter is grave. It is not fitting for you to act rashly. For one who acts without due deliberation may later repent, like the man who killed the crow. The king asked, "How was that? The minister replied: "Sire, it is told: There was once a certain man who lived in a village. He had a single crow as a pet, which he cherished more than his own children. One day, as he was traveling along the road, he saw a large herd of elephants being led by their keepers. A female elephant, seeing the man from afar, called out to her mate with a loud cry. Hearing her call, the male elephant, driven by passion, rushed toward the man at full speed. Seeing the elephant charging, the man fled in terror. As he ran, the crow, perched on his shoulder, also flew away. But the man, turning back to look, saw the female elephant following him. Fearing she would seize him, he climbed up onto the crow's back. The crow, terrified of the elephant, flew up into the sky. The man, clinging to the crow's back, cried out in fear, 'Fly, fly! The crow, though urged to fly, remained motionless in the air. When the man asked why he did not fly, the crow said, 'If I fly now, I shall surely die; therefore, I do not fly. But if I do not fly, I shall certainly die; therefore, I will fly. The man, hearing this, thought, 'This bird knows what is right,' and so he remained silent. The crow then flew down and alighted upon the branch of a tree. The man, seeing the elephant close behind, jumped down and fled. The crow, seeing the man flee, flew up again and perched upon the elephant's head. The elephant, unable to endure the crow's touch, turned back and went away. The man, having escaped the danger of the elephant, returned to his home safe and sound. The king said, "What then? The minister replied: "Sire, that man, having escaped the danger of the elephant, later repented, saying, 'Alas! I have lost my crow, who was dearer to me than my life. The king said, "And what of that? The minister replied: "Sire, just so it is with you. You have abandoned your kingdom and your life for the sake of a woman. This is not fitting for one such as you. Therefore, Sire, you should abandon this improper course and return to your own city. The king said, "I shall do as you say. Thus, having been granted permission, the minister informed the king of the secret plan. The king, having heard it, reflected: "This is indeed a great favor to me. And so, having resolved to carry out the plan, he departed for his own city. Thus ends the story of the crow. The minister then said to the king: "Sire, this is how it happened. The crow, seeing the man flee, flew up again and perched upon the elephant's head. The elephant, unable to endure the crow's touch, turned back and went away. The man, having escaped the danger of the elephant, returned to his home safe and sound. The king said, "What then? The minister replied: "Sire, that man, having escaped the danger of the elephant, later repented, saying, 'Alas! I have lost my crow, who was dearer to me than my life. The king said, "And what of that? The minister replied: "Sire, just so it is with you. You have abandoned your kingdom and your life for the sake of a woman. This is not fitting for one such as you. Therefore, Sire, you should abandon this improper course and return to your own city. The king said, "I shall do as you say. Thus, having been granted permission, the minister informed the king of the secret plan. The king, having heard it, reflected: "This is indeed a great favor to me. And so, having resolved to carry out the plan, he departed for his own city. Thus ends the story of the crow. The minister then said to the king: "Sire, this is how it happened. Therefore, you should not act rashly. For one who acts without due deliberation may later repent, like the man who killed the crow. The king asked, "How was that? The minister replied: "Sire, it is told: There was once a certain man who lived in a village
"O lotus-eyed one, today as you were worshipping the gods in person, O lord of men, a yakṣa approached me and said:
'Why do you not know that the heart of the king is fixed upon Unmādayantī? (Jātaka-mālā 13.17)
Having spoken thus, he who possessed discernment suddenly vanished; this is what I have understood.
If that is indeed so, O Lord, why is there such a lack of affection toward us, this silence of yours?
"Therefore, O Lord, for the sake of showing me favor, you ought to accept her.

Then the king, his face bowed with shame at this refusal, though overcome by passion, remained firm in his composure because of his long-practiced sense of righteousness, and replied to him in clear words of rejection:
"This is not so. Why?"
"May I fall from my merit and not become an immortal; may people also know of this sin of mine.
For through separation from her, my mind, burning like fire, will consume me as fire once consumes dry grass."
Whatever action brings harm to both worlds—both in this life and in the next—that very same action the ignorant pursue for its cause; the wise do not pursue it for that same cause. (Jm_13.20)
Abhipāraga said: "Enough of your fear regarding a transgression of dharma in this matter.
By assisting in the act of giving, there will be only dharma for you;
whereas by obstructing the gift, adharma would accrue to you for refusing to accept it from me."
Furthermore, I see no opportunity here for Your Majesty’s reputation to suffer. Why?
Who else but the two of us could possibly know this?
Therefore, do not harbor suspicion in your mind out of fear of public scandal. (Jm 13.22)
"And this would be a favor to me, not a hardship. Why?
For what obstacle could there be to a mind that is undisturbed by the satisfaction earned from acting for the sake of one's master?
Therefore, O Lord, fulfill your desire at will; enough with your fear of causing me pain. (Jm 13.23)
The king said: "May evil be averted!
Clearly, out of excessive affection for me, you did not consider this;
just as in the case of giving away everything, providing assistance is not a means for achieving dharma."
She is the wife of that friend who, out of excessive affection for my sake, did not even regard his own life; he is a kinsman superior to all others, and she is my friend.
Therefore, it is improper for you to deceive me at this sacred ford.
Furthermore, as for your thought that "no one else will know of this," how could such an act be free from sin?
For how could one who commits evil, even while remaining unseen, prosper, as if having consumed poison?
Those of pure vision—the gods dwelling in heaven and men who are practitioners of yoga—do not fail to see him.
Furthermore,
who would believe this— that she is not dear to you, or that you would immediately meet with ruin upon abandoning her? (Jm 13.27)
Abhipāraga said:
"Together with my wife and son, I am your slave; you are my master and my deity."
"Since she is a slave, O Lord, what transgression of dharma is there for you?"
"And as for what you have said, 'She is dear to me'—what of it?
She is my beloved, O granter of desires; therefore, I wish to give her to you.
For by giving what is dear, a person obtains in the next world dear things that are most delightful."
"Therefore, let Your Majesty accept her.
The king said, "Do not say so! This is improper. Why?"
I would indeed rather enter a sharpened weapon or a fire of blazing flames than, having attained prosperity through righteousness, ever strike back at that very source again.
Abhipāraga said: "If Your Majesty does not wish to accept her because she is my wife, then I shall ordain for her the vow of a courtesan, which is contrary to the requests of all people;
then Your Majesty may accept her.
The king said: "Are you mad?"
If you abandon a wife who is not at fault because of intoxication, you shall incur punishment;
having become an object of reproach, you will be consumed by fire both in this world and in the next.
"Therefore, enough of this persistence in what should not be done;
be one who is intent upon the right method.
Abhiprārapāraga said:
If I should suffer any loss of dharma, such as public censure or the ruin of my happiness,
I shall meet each of those with the very heart's joy I have gained through your welfare, receiving it upon my breast.
"O Great Lord of the Earth, I see no one else in this world superior to you as an Āhavanīya fire;
therefore, accept that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which brings me joy and increases my merit, just as a priest accepts his fee."
The king said: "Granted, this exertion of yours in acting for my sake has disregarded the sequence of your own welfare and harm due to your excessive affection for me.
For that very reason, however, I ought not to neglect you especially. Indeed, you must not be one who is fearless of public censure. Behold:"
He who disregards the censure of the world, who is indifferent to dharma or to rewards from others— people do not place their trust in him, and he is surely abandoned even by prosperity. (Jm_13.34)
Therefore, I tell you this: let not the transgression of dharma for the sake of your life appeal to you;
it is a certain and great fault, whereas its benefit is uncertain and meager.
Furthermore:
"The virtuous do not seek their own happiness by casting others into the sufferings of blame and the like.
Therefore, without oppressing others even in the slightest, I shall remain established in dharma and undertake the burden of my own welfare. (Jm 13.36)

Abhipāraga said: "As I am acting here for the sake of my master out of devotion, what possible opportunity for unrighteousness could there be for me, or for Your Majesty who would accept her as she is being given?
For if the Śibis, along with the merchants and the country-folk, were to ask, 'What unrighteousness is there in this?', they would surely say, 'Let Your Majesty accept her.'"
The king said: "Truly, your mind is inclined toward acting for my sake.
But this must be considered here: among the Śibis, including the merchants and the country folk, between you and me, who is the greatest knower of Dharma?
Then Abhipāraga, with great agitation, said to the king:

O Lord, because you have exerted yourself in serving the elders, possess mastery over sacred learning, and have keen intelligence, the essential truth regarding the excellence of the sciences of the three aims of life resides in you as much as it does in Bṛhaspati.
The king said: "In that case, you ought not to deceive me in this matter. Why? Because the welfare and the harm of the world depend upon the conduct of kings.
Therefore, having reflected upon the devotion of my subjects, I shall delight only in the path of the righteous, which is worthy of fame."
Just as cows follow the bull’s movement— whether it be slow or swift—
without hesitation, following his lead, so do subjects follow the conduct of a king, free from the fear of the goad and without obstruction.
Please consider this as well:
even if I were unable to protect myself, [I would still act].
What indeed is the condition of these people who long for protection from me?
Thus, observing the welfare of my subjects, as well as my own stainless duty and fame, I do not wish to follow the sway of my mind; for I am the leader of my subjects, like a bull.
Then the minister Abhipāraga, his mind gladdened by that state of the king, bowed to the monarch with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus:
"Oh, what a perfection of supreme fortune for these subjects, O God among Men, that you yourself are their protector!
For such a devotion to Dharma, indifferent even to pleasure, is indeed to be sought only among those dwelling in the groves of asceticism."
"O Great King, this title 'Great' truly shines forth only in you; for in those devoid of virtue, the attribution of virtues is indeed a statement of words even harsher than an insult. (Jm 13.43)
What cause for wonder or agitation is there in this for me regarding you,
since you are a mine of virtues, just as the ocean is a source of jewels?

Thus, even for those afflicted by intense suffering, there arises an aversion to the base path through the support of one's own fortitude and because of the well-practiced perception of Dharma; therefore, one should apply oneself to the practice of fortitude and Dharma.
Thus ends the thirteenth Jātaka, the Unmādayantī-jātaka.
14. The Supāraga-jātaka:
Even the mere utterance of truthful words based on the Dharma dispels adversity, let alone its fruit; therefore, one should follow the Dharma.
As it is heard—there was once a Great Being who, while still a Bodhisattva, was a navigator of ships possessed of supreme skill and intelligence.

For this is the natural law of Bodhisattvas: due to their innate wisdom, whatever exceptional treatise they wish to investigate or whatever specialized art they seek, in each and every one of those fields they become even more preeminent in their intelligence.
Of the world.

Now, that Great-souled One, because he understood the course of the luminaries, was unconfused regarding the divisions of the directions; he was thoroughly conversant with the signs of fixed and adventitious portents; he was skilled in the sequence of proper and improper times; and he had clearly identified the regions of the ocean by means of such marks as fish, water-colors, terrestrial formations, birds, and mountains.

Possessed of mindfulness, having conquered sloth and sleep, enduring the hardships of cold, heat, rain, and so forth, vigilant, and steadfast, he was a guide who led merchants to their desired destinations because of his skill in acquiring and transporting goods;
since he had reached the ultimate perfection of his journey, his name became Supāraga (One Who Has Reached the Further Shore).
And the city inhabited by him was known as Supāraga;
it is now known as Sūpāraga.

Because he was considered auspicious, even in his old age, sea-faring merchants desiring success on their voyages would board their ships after first honoring him with supplications and respectful offerings.
Then once, some merchants from Bharukaccha, desiring success on their journey to the Land of Gold, arrived at the port of Supāraga and requested that Great Being to board their ship.
He said to them:
"My vision is being withdrawn by the command of old age, and my memory has been thinned by the onset of exhaustion."
When even my own bodily functions have failed in their vigor, what assistance could possibly be expected from me?
The merchants said: "This condition of your bodies is known to us. Even though you are unable to endure physical exertion, we do not wish to trouble you by assigning you labor. What then?
This ship has attained auspiciousness through the dust that has been honored by taking refuge in the lotuses of your feet."
Thinking that you might travel safely even across this vast and difficult ocean, we have come to you.
Then that Great Being, out of compassion for them, ascended that vessel even though his body was weakened by old age.
Upon his boarding, all those merchants became joyful in mind, thinking, "Surely our supreme success in the voyage is certain.

And in due course, they entered [the sea], which was frequented by various schools of fish, filled with the restless clamor of water, and where the waves were tossed about by the playful force of the wind.

The great ocean, with its bottom difficult to reach and its waters immeasurable, had its surface adorned with various kinds of jewels and precious gems, was variegated with garlands of foam like clusters of flowers, and contained the dwellings of the asuras and the serpents.

Then they entered the midst of the fathomless ocean, its waters as deep blue as a heap of sapphires, appearing as if the sky had melted away from the heat of the sun's rays, with no trace of a shoreline visible on any side.

When they had arrived there at the time of evening, as the sun’s power of its circle of rays grew soft, a great and most terrifying portent appeared: in an instant, the ocean became fierce, its entire body of water freed from stillness, with waves breaking and foam scattered about, and a formidable roar produced by the lashing of violent winds.
With vast masses of water and land tossed by cataclysmic winds and whirling with terrifying speed,
the ocean assumed a fierce form, like the earth trembling at the end of an eon.
Clouds, with flickering tongues flashing like streaks of lightning and resembling many-headed blue serpents,
veiled the path of the sun, resounding with continuous and terrifying peals of thunder.
The sun, its web of rays shrouded by dense clouds, gradually ascended toward the setting;
the darkness, having gained full scope at the end of the day, seemed to reach a state of solid density on all sides.
In the great ocean, whose circle of waves was drenched by showers of arrows, the boat seemed to leap up in fury;
trembling excessively as if terrified, it caused their hearts to despair.

Terrified, silenced by despair, yet firm and agitated by the search for a remedy, they were intent on supplicating their own deities; thus, according to their dispositions, they revealed their various natures and qualities.

Then those seafarers, being tossed about by a ship that was subject to the force of the speed of the waters stirred by the power of the wind, did not see any shore at all even after many days, nor did they see any signs of the ocean as they had desired.

However, due to unprecedented signs of the ocean, their despondency increased, and they fell into a state of agitation caused by fear and despair. Then the Bodhisattva Supāraga, steadying them, said: "It is no wonder that those who have plunged into the midst of the great ocean should suffer the affliction of sudden, calamitous disturbances. Therefore, enough with your persistence in despair. Why so?"
Despair is not the method for remedying misfortune; therefore, enough with embracing dejection.
For those skilled in taking action through fortitude cross over hardships without difficulty.
Therefore, casting aside despondency and wretchedness, devote yourselves to action with the opportunity for duty;
for the splendor of a wise man, kindled by fortitude, is the grasping hand that seizes the attainment of all goals.
"Thus, may you all remain attentive to your duty!

Having been thus encouraged by that Great Being, those seafarers, their minds steadied and their thoughts eager to see the shore, looked out over the ocean and beheld human forms rising and sinking, appearing as if they were not clad in silver armor.

Having carefully observed their forms and characteristics, they reported with amazement to Supāraga: "Indeed, an unprecedented sign is perceived here in this great ocean. These are surely Daitya warriors with faces like silver masks, possessing terrible eyes and misshapen snouts resembling hooves.
Through their constant emerging, diving, and quivering, some appear as if they are enjoying a sport in the waters of the sea. (Jm 14.12)
Supāraga said: "These are neither humans nor non-humans;
they are indeed fish. Therefore, you need not fear them. However—"
"We are very far removed even from the two cities; this is the ocean Khuramālī. Therefore, strive to turn back."
Driven by a mass of water carrying a fierce current and by a western wind that swept everything away, those merchants were unable to turn back their ship.
Then, as they gradually plunged forward, they beheld another ocean, illuminated by the luster of silver and white with masses of non-blue foam; filled with wonder, they said to Supāraga:
(Vaidya 95)
What is this great ocean, appearing as if covered by waters submerged in its own foam, or as if clad in white silk garments;
bearing the rays of the moon like liquid, it spreads forth on all sides like a smile?
Supāraga said: "Alas!
One is indeed plunging into something very far away.
This ocean, known as the Ocean of Milk, is actually [the ocean] Dadhimālya."
It is not fitting to go further than this, if it is possible to turn back.
The merchants said, "Indeed, it is not even possible to delay the ship, much less turn it back, because the vessel travels with extreme speed and because the wind is adverse.

Then, having crossed that ocean as well, those merchants, filled with wonder and curiosity upon beholding another ocean whose rows of moving waves were colored by the radiance of gold and whose waters were tawny like the flames of fire,
questioned Supāraga:

With its rising waters, which are not dark blue but rather colored as if by the splendor of the morning sun, this great ocean shines like a blazing, massive fire; who indeed could fail to recognize it? Jm_14.16.
Supāraga said:
"This ocean that appears here is renowned as Agnimālī.
It would indeed be most excellent if we were to turn back from this place."
Thus that Great Being, out of his far-reaching foresight, explained to them the mere name of that lord of rivers, but did not speak of the cause for the water's discoloration.

Then those seafarers, having crossed even that ocean, beheld another sea whose waters were illuminated by the luster of *puṣparāga* and *indranīla* gems, and which had the color of a grove of ripened *kuśa* grass; filled with curiosity, they questioned Supāraga.
"What ocean is this that shines forth, its waters having the color of withered kuśa grass leaves,
appearing as if strewn with flowers by the variegated clusters of foam and by the breaking waves tossed by the force of the wind?"
Supāraga said: "O caravan leaders, let an effort be made toward turning back;
indeed, it is not possible to go further from here. This Kuśamālin ocean is like an elephant beyond the reach of the goad."
Carrying away its irresistible waters by force, it robs us of our delight.

(Vaidya 96) Then those merchants, unable to turn back even with the greatest effort, crossed that ocean as well and, beholding another ocean whose waters were green from the mingled radiance of bamboo-dye and beryl,
asked Supāraga:
"Carrying waters with the green luster of emeralds, as if bearing the fresh beauty of a meadow,
and adorned with foam as white as the glow of night-lotuses— who is this ocean that is now being beheld?"

Then that Great Being, his heart burning with grief at the calamity that had befallen the merchants, sighed long and hot and spoke slowly: "You have come too far; it will be difficult to turn back from this. This ocean, like the very edge of the world, is a barrier even for Nala’s garland."

Having heard that, those merchants, their minds overwhelmed by despair and the vigor of their limbs failing, sat right there, intent solely on sighing. And when they had crossed even that ocean, at the time of evening, as the maker of day— with its circle of rays lingering— was desirous of entering the ocean, [they saw] as if from the surging sea, or like thunderbolts falling, [the following:]

They heard a tumultuous and most terrifying sound, like that of bamboo groves enveloped in fire as they crackle apart— a sound that tore at the ears and the heart, resembling the roar of the ocean. Upon hearing it, overcome by terror and with their hearts trembling, they rose up suddenly and, looking about in every direction, beheld that great mass of water falling like a precipice or a vast chasm.

Upon seeing him, they were overwhelmed by supreme fear and despondency; approaching Supāraga, they said: "This sound of the Lord of Rivers, as if piercing our ears and churning our hearts, is heard even from afar like that of one who is enraged."
This entire body of water falls as if into the terrifying abyss of the ocean;
what is this sea, and what do you consider to be the further course of action here?
Then that Great Being, filled with agitation, cried out, "Alas! Alas! and looking toward the ocean, said:
"That which, once reached, one does not return from—like the gaping mouth of Death—is this inauspicious Mare’s Mouth (vaḍavāmukha) that you have approached. (Jm_14.23)

Having heard that, those merchants, realizing "we have reached the Mare’s Mouth," abandoned all hope for life; their minds overwhelmed by the fear of death, some wept aloud, some lamented, and others cried out;
some, their senses bewildered by terror, did not know what to do.
In particular, some bowed down to the Lord of the Gods with minds struck by distress;
others sought refuge with the Ādityas, Rudras, Maruts, and Vasus, while still others fled to the ocean.
Others muttered various mantras, while others prostrated before the goddess according to the prescribed rites;
some, approaching Supāraga and mimicking his various actions, lamented piteously.

This is the time for you— the one who constantly dispels the fear of those fallen into calamity, who are endowed with the virtue of compassion for others, and who possess such extraordinary power— to apply it for their sake.
O steadfast one, turn your mind toward protecting us who are afflicted, helpless, and have come to you for refuge;
for this ocean, out of anger, desires to swallow us as if we were a morsel with its submarine fire.
"It is not right for you to neglect this person who is perishing in the midst of a flood of water;
the great ocean does not overstep your command, so let this lack of peace in him be restrained."

Then that Great Being, his heart oppressed by great compassion, addressed those merchants as he established them in order, saying: "A remedy for this also occurs to me; I shall employ it. Therefore, for a moment, please remain steadfast."
Then those merchants, their courage bolstered by the hope that "there is indeed a remedy for this as well," remained silent with their minds fixed intently upon it.

Then the Bodhisattva Supāraga, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ship, and with a heart of total devotion, bowed to the Tathāgatas and addressed those seafarers.
"May the honorable merchants and the various deities who dwell in the ocean and the sky listen!
I call to mind from what time I have known myself and from when I attained wisdom; ever since, I do not recall having intended to harm any living being anywhere."
By this word of truth and by the power of my merit,
may the ship turn back safely without reaching the Mare’s Mouth.
Then, by the power of that Great Being’s *satyādhiṣṭhāna* and the splendor of his merit, the wind, together with the force of the water, turned back and caused the ship to return.

Beholding the ship turned back, those merchants, their minds overflowing with supreme wonder and joy, announced to Supāraga, "The ship has returned," preceded by prostrations and respectful offerings.
Then that Great Being said to those merchants, "May you be steady;
let the cool things be quickly loaded.
Thus commanded by him, those officials, their strength and enthusiasm aroused by joy, did exactly so.
Then, bringing joy to the people and laughter to them, with its broad, white, cool, and beautiful wings spread,
that ship situated upon the ocean shone like a female royal swan in a cloudless sky.
When that ship had ceased its movement and was proceeding at will with the grace of a celestial chariot, propelled by favorable waters and winds,

Supāraga spoke to those merchants as the quarters of the sky— whose twilight makeup had not yet grown too dark, over which the canopy of night was spreading, and whose ornaments of stars were just beginning to be discerned— showed the path of the sun with but a slight remnant of light, and the office of night had commenced.
"O caravan leaders, let sand and stones be loaded onto the vessel from the oceans seen by Nalamāli and the others, as much as it can bear;
in this way, this ship will be filled with a crushing weight so that its sides do not give way."
"These sands and stones are considered auspicious; they will certainly lead to the attainment of wealth for you.

Then those seafarers, having taken [the gems] from the spots pointed out by the deities—whose minds were moved by love and great respect for Supāraga—loaded their ship with jewels such as lapis lazuli, mistaking them for mere sand and stones.
In that very single night, the ship arrived at Bharukaccha; then at dawn, with their vessels filled with silver, sapphire, beryl, and gold,
they reached the shore of their own country and, overflowing with joy, honored him with affection.
Thus, even a truthful word based on righteousness dispels calamity, let alone its fruit; therefore, one should follow the path of righteousness.
This should also be stated in the praise of relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): "In this way, those who rely on spiritual friends attain the highest good.
Thus ends the fourteenth *jātaka*, the Supāraga-jātaka.
15. The Matsya-jātaka:
For those possessed of virtuous conduct, auspicious intentions succeed even in this very life, let alone in the next; therefore, one should strive for the purification of moral discipline.
Thus it is heard:

once, it is said, the Bodhisattva was the lord of the fish in a certain lake that was not very large, its beautiful waters adorned with white, red, and blue lotuses; it was graced by pairs of swans, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and ruddy geese, and its banks were strewn with the flowers of trees growing along the shore.

And because he had practiced the conduct for the benefit of others throughout many previous births, even while remaining there [in that state], he was engaged in the activity of bestowing welfare and happiness upon others.
For through the power of habitual practice, both auspicious and inauspicious actions become second nature to men;
thus, such deeds are performed effortlessly in another birth, as if in a dream.

With a heart fixed upon those fish as if they were his own beloved offspring, the Great Being bestowed the highest favor upon them through the sequence of giving, kind speech, purposeful conduct, and so forth. Restraining their habit of mutual injury and increasing their mutual affection,
he caused them to forget their nature as fish through his application of skillful means and knowledge of expedients.
Being thus properly protected by him, the school of fish attained supreme growth,
like a city freed from calamities by a king who acts with justice.
Then, at one time, due to the deficiency in the merit of sentient beings and the negligence of the sons of gods appointed over the rains, the rain did not fall properly.
Consequently, as the rain fell improperly, that lake was no longer filled as before with fresh water as yellowish-white as blooming *kadamba* flowers.
Gradually, when the season of summer arrived, by the rays of the sun—which possessed exceedingly intense brilliance and seemed to move with a gait languid from exhaustion—the world was scorched.
And that lake, as if being drunk up day after day by the earth followed by flames, and by the wind longing for refreshment as if driven by thirst, became a mere puddle;
for in the heat of summer, the sun blazes like a shower of flames and the wind blows fiercely.
The earth was not cool, as if afflicted by fever, and the waters seemed to dry up as if out of wrath.

Then the Bodhisattva, seeing the school of fish— already being scrutinized even by flocks of crows, let alone by the flocks of birds wandering along the water's edge— overcome by despair and dejection, and reduced to mere gasping,
was moved by compassion and fell into reflection.
"Alas, this terrible calamity has befallen the fish!
Every day the water diminishes as if competing with their own lifespans;
yet even now, the arrival of the clouds is still seen to be far off."
There is no way to retreat, nor is there any other leader who might lead us;
meanwhile, our enemies, drawn by our misfortune, are closing in upon us.
"Without a doubt, because this remainder of water is being exhausted,
they will be devoured by my enemies while I look on."
Reflecting on what might be appropriate for this occasion, that Great Being perceived that the sole resort for those in distress was the power of an act of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
His heart being deeply moved by compassion, he sighed long and hot, looked up toward the sky, and said:
"I do not recall ever intentionally committing the slaughter of a living being, even when in the midst of extreme hardship."
By this truth, may the King of the Gods cause the lakes to be filled with water and let it rain.

Then, through the power of that Great Being’s accumulation of merit and his resolve of truth, and by the influence of the gods, nāgas, and yakṣas who were propitiated by him, unseasonable clouds appeared on all sides with their forms hanging down in the water; they possessed deep and sweet sounds, and their vast blue peaks were adorned with streaks of lightning. As if yawning, with their mountain-arms of peaks spreading outward, they seemed to embrace one another.
Black clouds appeared,
as if measuring out the directions with their extent and spreading darkness with their peaks;
the black clouds shone upon the surface of the sky like the shadows of mountains reflected in a mirror.

Those masses of clouds shone forth with their continuous, low rumbling, as if being praised by joyful peacocks with their variegated dances and closely joined cries, like the deep laughter of a wise man.
Like pearls already released, the streams discharged by them fell; the dust was stilled, and a fragrant scent wafted from the earth as it was scattered by the wind from the clouds.
Although the power of the sun’s rays had increased through contact with the summer heat, it vanished;
the waters, their mid-reaches agitated by rows of foam, flowed toward the lowlands. (Jm 15.12)
Repeatedly coloring the horizons with her golden-yellow splendors,
the creeper-like lightning, finding joy in the sound of the clouds as if they were musical instruments, performed a dance as it were.

Then, as the lake was being filled by pale streams of water flowing out from all sides, as the flocks of birds, including the crows, fled at the very moment the raindrops fell, and as the schools of fish were delighted, having regained hope for life, the Bodhisattva—
his heart drawn toward them with affection yet apprehensive that the rain might cease— addressed the rain-cloud again and again:
Roar, O Parjanya, with a deep and steady sound, and dispel the joy of the crows,
raining down waters that are like jewels and possess the brilliant luster of flashing, clinging lightning.
Having heard this, Śakra, the lord of the gods, his mind filled with great wonder, approached him in person and, seeking to honor him, said:
"O Great-souled Lord of Fishes, this is indeed the power of your own extraordinary truth;
for these clouds, like overflowing jars, pour down rain with their lovely thunder."
This is indeed a great lapse of negligence on my part,
that I do not undertake the application of service for those like you, whose minds are intent upon striving for the sake of the world in their duties.
"Do not harbor such anxiety regarding what follows this; for I am the one yoked to the burden of carrying out the duties of the virtuous.
Moreover, by virtue of your presence here, this land shall never again be subject to such suffering."
Having thus propitiated him with affectionate words, he vanished on the spot;
and that lake attained a supreme abundance of water.
Thus, for those possessed of virtuous conduct, auspicious intentions flourish even in this very world, let alone in the next; therefore, one should strive for the purification of virtue.
Thus ends the fifteenth Jātaka, the Matsyajātaka.
16. The Vartakāpītakajātaka.
Even fire cannot venture to transgress speech that has been permeated by truth; therefore, one should apply oneself to truthful speech.
As it is heard: once, it is said, the Bodhisattva was a young quail in a certain forest retreat.
Having recently emerged from the eggshell, with his tender wings yet to be fully developed and his major and minor limbs still indistinct due to extreme weakness,
he lived together with many brothers in a nest constructed by the efforts of his parents, concealed within a thicket of grass and sheltered by shrubs and creepers.
Even in that state, because his perception of the Dharma was unimpaired, he did not wish to consume living beings offered by his parents;
rather, he sustained himself only on what his parents brought him, such as grass seeds and banyan fruits.
Due to that coarse and meager diet, his body did not attain nourishment.
Nor did its wings grow properly.
However, the other young quails, consuming the food as it was brought to them, became strong and their wings grew.
For this is the natural law: namely—

One who is free from anxiety regarding dharma and adharma prospers in happiness, eating whatever comes; but one who seeks a strictly righteous livelihood, being selective in what he eats, suffers in this world.

Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One in two verses: "A life well-lived by the shameless, by the crow-like one of impure deeds, by the impetuous and arrogant—such a life is indeed thoroughly defiled. (Jm 16.2)
But for one who possesses a sense of shame, who is ever seeking purity, who remains withdrawn and modest, and who lives by a pure livelihood— it is difficult indeed to live in this world.
These two verses are recited in the Ārya-Sthavirīya Nikāya.

While they were situated in this manner, not far from them there appeared a great forest fire— terrifying with its continuous roar, swelling masses of smoke, and scattering garlands of flames with flickering sparks— a source of terror to the forest-dwellers and a calamity for the thickets of the woods.
With its arms of flames whirled and scattered by the wind, variegated by its diverse dances,
and with its hair of smoke disheveled as it leaped about, the fire roared, robbing them of their fortitude.
Like grass in the forest fleeing in fear, trembling from being lashed by a fierce wind,
that fire— advancing as if in a rage with its mass of flickering sparks— consumed them.
With its flocks of birds bewildered and fleeing in fear, with terrified deer wandering in every direction,
and submerged in a mass of smoke with the sharp crackling of fire, that forest shrieked out as if in intense agony.

Gradually, as if being fanned by a sharp wind, that fire, following the thickets of grass, approached their nest. Then those young quails, emitting distressed and discordant cries of fear, suddenly flew up together, regardless of one another. But because of his extreme weakness and because his wings had not yet grown, the Bodhisattva made no effort to fly away.

But that Great Being, fully aware of his own power and remaining entirely unperturbed, spoke with courtesy to the fire as it approached him impetuously: "O Fire, my wings have not yet grown, and my name and conduct are still unestablished; moreover, because of your haste, my parents have already flown away.
There is nothing here worthy of you as a guest, so it is right for you, O Fire, to turn back from me."
When these words had been spoken by that Great Being, whose speech was permeated with truth— even though that fire was being fanned by the wind in a thicket of dry, clinging grass—
it was immediately extinguished upon encountering his speech, as if it had reached a river with swelling waters.
Even today, that celebrated region in the Himalayas, though assailed by a forest fire with flames driven high by the wind, attains peace;
its flames curl back slowly and subside like a many-headed serpent charmed by a mantra.
"What, then, has been brought forth here? It is said in reply:

"Just as the ocean, with its hood-like waves in motion, cannot transgress the shore; or as Satyakāma cannot violate the instruction ordained by the Lord of Sages; so too, because even Fire is unable to overstep the command of those whose very nature is truth, one should therefore never abandon the truth. (Jm 16.10)
Thus, since even fire cannot withstand transgressing speech that has been purified by truthful words, one should apply oneself to truthful speech;
this should also be spoken in praise of the Tathāgata.
Thus ends the sixteenth Jātaka, the Story of the Quail’s Chicks.
17. The Kumbha-jātaka:
"The virtuous restrain others from the most grievous act of drinking intoxicants—which is beset by manifold defects—let alone themselves."

As it is heard: Once, the Bodhisattva— whose mind was thoroughly cultivated by an excellence of compassion and who was devoted to bringing about the welfare and happiness of others— manifesting a meritorious path through generosity, self-control, restraint, and other virtues, became Śakra, the lord of the gods.

Although he was one who obtained at will even the most excellent divine pleasures of the senses, because he was under the sway of compassion, he did not allow his mind to become slack in its exertion for the sake of the world’s welfare. Generally, people do not remain awake even to their own benefit due to the intoxication of wealth; but he, though possessing the splendor of the lord of the gods, was free from intoxication and remained vigilant even for the sake of others.
Toward beings afflicted by manifold and intense calamities, he felt affection as if toward kinsmen;
and because he relied upon fortitude and knowledge of their true nature, he did not forget his practice for the sake of others.

Then, on one occasion, that Great Being, surveying the world of men with an eye that was naturally vast, imbued with compassion, and tender with loving-kindness, beheld a king named Sarvamitra who, due to the fault of association with unwholesome friends, was becoming addicted to the consumption of intoxicants along with his citizens and countryfolk.
Observing therein his failure to perceive the faults and the great evils of drinking intoxicants, that Great Being, his heart oppressed by intense compassion, fell into reflection:
"Alas, what a calamity has befallen the world!
For they drink this beverage which is sweet at first, being too faint-hearted to perceive its defects."
It surely carries one away from the highest good, like a pleasant but wrong path.
What, then, would be appropriate for this occasion? Very well; it has been seen that people are by their very nature destined to imitate the actions of one who is preeminent.
In this matter, the king alone must be treated, for in this world, both good and evil originate from him.

Having thus resolved, that Great Being assumed a majestic Brahmin form with the color of molten gold, bearing a mass of matted locks tied up and not coarse, and clad in bark garments and deerskin; and having fashioned a moderately large jar on his left side filled with wine, he appeared in the sky before King Sarvamitra as he sat in his assembly, at a moment when conversations concerning wine, spirits, rum, *śīdhu*, *maireya*, and honey were underway.
And being honored by that people, who rose up with palms joined in reverence, overcome by wonder and great respect, he spoke aloud with a deep voice like a water-laden cloud:
"Who wishes to buy this jar, which laughs with a garland of flowers reaching to its neck, and whose mouth is made into an ear-ornament? (Jm_17.5)

"Who among you desires to purchase this jar, which is as if adorned with a spreading garland of flowers by the playful movement of the wind, and which is overflowing with an arrangement of young sprouts?"
Then the king, his curiosity aroused by wonder, looking upon him with great respect and joining his palms in reverence, said:
"In brilliance you are like the newly risen sun, and in beauty you appear like the moon; in your physical form, you are perceived as one of the foremost among sages.
Therefore, you ought to tell me how you are known in the world, for our esteem for you is extraordinary because of your virtues."
Śakra said:
"Later you shall know who I am; for now, strive to purchase this jar, provided that you have no fear of the suffering of the next world or of the onset of intense calamity in this very life."
The king said: "Truly unprecedented is this commencement of sale by your honor! To praise the virtues and to conceal the defects—such is the well-known method of selling goods in the world."
