"This practice is indeed suited for those like you who fear untruth;
for the virtuous do not wish to abandon truth even in the midst of hardship."
Therefore tell me, O illustrious one: whose full jar is this?
Or what may be obtained from us even by those such as you in exchange?
Śakra said: "Listen, O Great King:
this vessel is not filled with water fallen from a cloud, nor with the water of sacred fords, nor with fragrant lotus-pollen, nor with honey, nor even with a special kind of clarified butter."
But hear now the power of that man for whom the jar of evil is full— whose complexion is like the rays of the moon amidst a cloudless sky, causing the night-lotuses to bloom. (Vaidya 106) Jm_17.12 //
Having drunk which, one wanders about independently due to being overwhelmed by the defects of intoxication;
though not falling even into dangerous places, one falls down with diminished power and memory;
and devoid of any discrimination between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, one would taste this or that indiscriminately.
"Purchase this lowest of jars, which has reached the marketplace completely full."
Deprived of mastery over his own mind, he wanders about with his intellect clouded by that [ignorance],
acting like a dull-witted bull to provoke the laughter of his enemies; and by means of that very ignorance, he might even dance in the midst of an assembly, using his own face as a drum.
"This [woman], devoid of beauty and placed within a jar, is for sale to you."
Having drunk [the wine], he abandons even his natural modesty,
like a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) freed from the distress of restraint regarding clothing;
he should walk with composure along paths crowded with townspeople.
She approached while they were looking on and was placed here in this jar.
Having drunk which,
they sleep unconscious even upon the royal roads, their faces smeared with vomited food and being licked by dogs without hesitation.
That which was thrown into this jar is beautiful as a purchase.
That by which a woman, through the power of wine, might even bind her parents to a tree,
and would no longer count her husband as anything but the Lord of Wealth— that very thing has been placed and hidden within this jar.

Having drunk this, the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, their senses clouded by intoxication and forgetting their kinship, crushed one another with maces; that madness-inducing potion has been placed here in this jar.
"This very thing, which brings about the destruction of wealthy families that have flourished ever higher and served as the abode of fortune— now it has been placed here for sale within this jar."

With his speech indistinct due to incessant weeping, staying still, or laughing, and with eyes heavy and dull as if under the influence of a planetary spirit, he has certainly become an abode of humiliation; that which is thus impaired in intellect is what is contained here in this jar. (Vaidya 107) Jm_17.20 //

Even those who are advanced in years, when their minds are agitated and they are timid in resorting to the path of their own welfare, speak much with unexamined conclusions; this very thing has come to pass in the case of the jar by way of purchase.
"Because of whose fault the former gods, becoming heedless after Lakṣmī robbed the King of the Gods,
fell into the ocean seeking protection— choose this full jar of hers."
One who, appearing confident, might speak even untruth as truth; one who, appearing joyful, might perform even what should not be done as if it were a duty;
by whose quality one would perceive the good as evil and the evil as good—such a person, like the very embodiment of a curse, has been placed here in this jar.

Purchase that science of madness, the foundation of vice, the manifest misfortune and mother of sins; that established path of the Kali age, a terrible darkness of the mind, which is non-dual in its success.

O King, take from here that [woman] by whom one whose mind is utterly robbed might even slay his father or his innocent mother, or a mendicant who disregards the pursuit of pleasure— taking her according to the method of purchase.
"O King, this liquor, renowned in the world as *sura* and possessing the brilliance of the gods (*surābha*), is of such a kind.
Let him who has no partiality toward virtues make an effort to purchase it. (Jm 17.26)

Who indeed would even venture to look upon that by indulging in which those addicted to evil conduct fall into the terrifying abysses of hell, or into the states of animals, hungry ghosts, and poverty? (Jm 17.27)
Even the slight ripening that results from drinking intoxicants destroys the moral conduct and right view of those who have entered the human realm;
by it, one dwells further in the Avīci hell, which is as fierce as a blazing fire, as well as in the world of the ancestors and among the lowly animals.
"It closes the eyes of virtue, forcibly destroys fame, casts away shame, and defiles the intellect;
since that which, once drunk, destroys all such qualities—O King, how can you possibly drink wine today? (Jm 17.29)

Then the king, having been made to understand the evils of drinking intoxicants through those heart-captivating and reasoned words of Śakra’s, and having turned away from his desire for the indulgence in liquor, said to Śakra:

"Whether it be a father, affectionate due to the qualities of discipline and devotion; or a teacher, who ought to speak what is right; or a sage, wise in conduct and its opposite—it is exactly as you have spoken out of a desire for my welfare. I shall strive to honor this deed of yours according to the prescribed rites."
And first of all, may your honor deign to accept this reward for your well-spoken words:
I give you five excellent villages, five hundred female slaves, five hundred cows, and these ten chariots yoked with fine horses; for you are my teacher, as you have spoken what is beneficial.
"Or rather, whatever else must be done by me, your majesty ought to favor me once again with a command.
Śakra said:
"I have no need for excellent villages or the like; come to me, O King, as the lord of the gods."
But one who speaks for one's benefit should be honored by the acceptance of his words with a mind that follows them.
For this is the path to fame and prosperity, and to every kind of happiness in the world beyond;
therefore, casting aside addiction to intoxicants, take refuge in the Dharma and follow my instruction.
Having spoken thus, Śakra vanished on the spot.
And that king, together with his citizens and countryfolk, desisted from the drinking of intoxicants.
Therefore, since the drinking of intoxicants is beset by many evils and is exceedingly wretched, the virtuous restrain others from it even more than they do themselves.
"In this way, that Blessed One was a benefactor to the world even in his previous births"—this should also be stated in the *Tathāgatavarṇa*.
Thus ends the seventeenth birth-story, the *Kumbhajātaka*.
(Vaidya 110)
18. The Story of the Sonless Man (*Aputrajātaka*).
Householder life is a confinement that opposes virtue and tranquility; thus, those who desire such things do not find it pleasing.
As it is heard—

It is said that once, a Bodhisattva was born into a certain merchant family that was endowed with praiseworthy conduct and character, sought after for alliances by those of noble birth, a watering place for ascetics and brahmins, no different from a treasury or granary to friends and kinsmen,
accessible to the poor and beggars, a refuge for artisans, and one who received the favor and honor of the king’s fortune.
He was born into a family esteemed by the world.

In the course of time, having grown up and applied himself with diligence to the branches of knowledge esteemed by the world, he attained direct insight into them; and in the various arts based on manifold conceptual distinctions, he became like a member of his own family to the world through a body lovely to the eyes of men and through a worldly wisdom that was not in conflict with the Dharma.
It revolved within their hearts;
for one does not hold a kinsman in high regard merely because he is a kinsman, nor is a stranger viewed otherwise than as a stranger simply because he is a stranger. (Jm 18.1)
But by discerning virtues and faults, the world becomes an object of either great respect or contempt for its own kin or for strangers alike.

However, because that Great Being had already become familiar with the life of renunciation, and having recognized that the state of a householder is followed by the suffering of seeking [wealth] and is contrary to the Dharma,
while the groves of asceticism bring about happiness, his mind did not cling to the pleasures of home.

His heart agitated by the passing of his parents, he distributed that wealth of his household, numbering many hundreds of thousands, among friends, kinsmen, the poor, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, according to their merit,
and went forth into homelessness. Wandering in due course through villages, towns, market-towns, kingdoms, and royal capitals, he arrived at a certain city and dwelt on a particular forest slope.

Through the cultivation of the virtues of meditative concentration, he possessed a natural clarity of the senses that was uncontrived, a speech that delighted the hearts of the learned, indicated his wisdom, and was free from arrogance; it was devoid of the wretchedness and misery of craving for gain, vigorous in its discipline, and possessed the excellence of appropriately sweet and courteous conduct; and it was skilled in discerning the distinction between dharma and adharma, as well as being burdened with the observances of the life of a renunciant.
He became distinguished there by his conduct, which was beloved by the virtuous;
and as the curious people learned the sequence of his noble birth and renunciation, he became even more highly esteemed by the world.
For virtues attain greater acceptability when they are accompanied by noble lineage, beauty, and character.
Just as the sprouts of the moon's rays [shine] by virtue of the excellence of their source.

Then, having learned of his arrival there, a friend of his father approached him; out of great respect for his virtues, and after first inquiring after his welfare, he introduced himself, declared his friendship with the prince’s father, and in the course of conversation, spoke to him with affection: "Indeed, the Venerable One has acted with a certain rashness by renouncing the world at this age, without regard for his family lineage."
"When this Dharma is practiced by those possessing right conduct, whether in a palace or in a forest,
why do you abandon your glorious palaces and set your mind upon the wilderness? (Jm_18.5)
Subsisting on alms obtained through the favor of others, disregarded by the wicked as if they were chaff,
wearing tattered rags, deprived of kinsmen and friends, his body cast away upon the ground at the edge of the forest.
How is it that you have fallen under the power of grief, as if embracing poverty personified?
For even your enemies, beholding this condition of yours, would surely have their eyes clouded with tears.
Therefore come, for this ancestral home of yours is surely one whose essential meaning has been heard by you;
dwelling here, you may fulfill both your duty and the desire of a virtuous son.
Indeed, there is this common saying of the world: "Even for a servant working for another, one's own home is pleasant like a watering-trough;
how much more so for those who have attained happiness, whose prosperity blazes with glory! (Jm 18.9)

Then the Bodhisattva, his mind permeated by the nectar-like flavor of the bliss of solitude, his heart inclined toward it, having attained a state of excellence, felt as much discomfort at the invitation to enjoy sensual pleasures—as one would at talk of food when already satiated—and said: "Because it arises from affection, these words of yours may indeed involve little blame; yet—"
But never form the notion that there is happiness within the prison of the household.
The life of a householder is a great state of unease for one, whether wealthy or poor,
due to the exhaustion of guarding what one has and the toil of acquiring what one lacks.
Where there is truly no happiness for either the wealthy or the poor,
the delusion of finding pleasure therein is the arising of the fruit of evil alone.
As for what you have said—that this Dharma can be practiced even by a householder—surely that is so.
However, it seems to me exceedingly difficult because of the confinement of obstacles to the Dharma and the great amount of toil involved in household life.
Please consider this.
There is no home for one who does not covet, nor for one who does not speak falsehoods,
nor for one who has laid down the rod of punishment, nor for one who does no harm to others.

Thus, this person whose heart is bound to the pleasures of the home and whose mind is intent on their means—if he pursues the Dharma, there is no home; but if he is intent on the home, how can he have the Dharma? For the path of Dharma has the singular essence of tranquility, whereas the success of the household comes through the course of exertion.

Thus, since it is corrupted by its opposition to the Dharma, what self-possessed person would resort to the life of a householder? For those who disregard the Dharma out of a desire for pleasure, there is no certainty in the attainment of the arising of happiness.
"Certainly, there will be defeat of one's reputation, remorse in the mind, and a miserable rebirth;
thus, those who do not know the right path do not resort to that which opposes the Dharma, even if it appears to be an easy means, for it leads to ruin."

Moreover, it seems to me that this belief—that living as a householder is happiness—is something to be accepted only through faith; for it is characterized by the inevitable suffering of acquiring and protecting wealth, and is the sole target for slaughter, imprisonment, and calamity.
Even for a king, there is no satisfaction with riches, just as the ocean is never filled by showers of rain.

How, from where, or when could there be happiness here, unless it is approached through the pursuit of conceptual construction? Even in the engagement with sense objects, there is a conceit of happiness due to delusion, like the scratching of an itch on a wound.
Indeed, I say this as a general rule: for the most part, one falls into intoxication through prosperity at home, into pride through noble lineage, and into arrogance through power;
through suffering one feels anger, and through calamity, wretchedness—so when, then, would there ever be an opportunity for tranquility?

Therefore, indeed, I entreat you, my lord: [this world] is an abode for the serpents of intoxication, pride, and delusion, and it is the destruction of the blissful happiness that delights in tranquility.
Who indeed would resort to this abode that faces immediate dissolution and is a repository of many intense sufferings?
But how could the mind find such serenity even in the triple heaven as it does in a forest— secluded and full of bliss— wherein dwell people who are content?
Therefore, even one who earns his livelihood through the favor of others dwells happily at the edge of the forests, clothed in rags;
yet a self-possessed man does not desire happiness mixed with unrighteousness, just as a wise man avoids food mixed with poison.
Having understood this through those heart-touching words of his father’s friend, he showed great respect toward that Great Being by means of a particularly distinguished application of hospitality.
Thus, those who desire their own welfare abandon the life of a householder, which is crowded with obstacles to moral conduct and tranquility;
for they have found the true taste of solitude.
"They do not turn back toward sensual pleasures"—this should also be cited when discussing the virtues of seclusion.
Thus ends the eighteenth Jātaka, the Aputra-jātaka.
(Vaidya 114)
19. The Bisaja Jātaka.
To those who have tasted the flavor of the bliss of solitude, sensual pleasures are as disagreeable as mockery and as painful as injury.
As it is heard in tradition:
It is said that a Bodhisattva took birth in a certain great Brahmin family, renowned for its virtues and glory, and free from any reproach regarding its conduct.
He had six younger brothers who, possessing corresponding virtues, were always in harmony with him due to their affection, high esteem, and shared qualities;
and there was also a seventh sister.
Having exerted himself in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the Upavedas, he attained fame for his learning and was honored in the world like a deity.

With supreme devotion, he attended upon his parents; and like a teacher or a father, he disciplined those brothers in the sciences. Skilled in both worldly conduct and spiritual discipline, he lived at home. In the course of time, his heart was deeply moved by the death of his parents. Having performed their funeral rites, and after some days filled with grief had passed, he assembled those brothers and said to them:
This is the inevitable course for the world, utterly bitter with sorrow:
that even after dwelling together for a very long time, one is separated by death.
Therefore, I wish to go forth by the auspicious and praiseworthy path,
before the enemy Death strikes me while I am still attached to the household life.
Since I am addressing all of you:
there exists in this brahmin family a certain measure of wealth acquired through righteous means;
it is possible to subsist upon this.

Therefore, all of you must dwell properly within the home, being oriented toward mutual affection and respect, maintaining unremitting care for moral conduct and social customs, devoted to the study of the Vedas, affectionate toward friends, guests, and kinsmen, and dedicated to righteousness;
you should always praise discipline and be intent upon the practice of self-study.
The householder’s life must be properly maintained by those who delight in giving.

"In this way, there shall be for you the full attainment of fame, of dharma, and of wealth which is the foundation of happiness; and even the next world will be easy to enter. Therefore, dwell in your home with vigilance."

Then his brothers, their minds distressed by the fear of separation at the mention of his renunciation, their faces clouded by tears of grief, bowed to him and said: "It does not behove your honor to further wound this unhealed sore of our hearts, already pierced by the dart of sorrow from the loss of our father, with the caustic application of another misfortune."
"Even now our hearts, wounded by the arrow of grief for our father, have not yet healed. Therefore, O steadfast one, properly restrain this resolve; do not pour salt upon our wounds."
Now, if you consider attachment to home to be unbearable, or the happiness of dwelling in the forest to be the path to the highest good,
why do you wish to go to the forest alone, abandoning us who are without a protector at home?
"Whatever is the destination of your honor shall be ours as well; we too shall go forth into the religious life.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Because they have not practiced discernment and follow after the passion for sensual desires,
people for the most part regard the life of renunciation as if it were a precipice."
"Thus, although I knew the distinction between dwelling in a home and dwelling in the forest, I restrained you and did not urge you toward the life of renunciation.
Therefore, if this is pleasing to you, let us go forth.

Then all seven brothers, with their sister as the eighth, abandoned their abundant household wealth and the circle of friends, kinsmen, and relatives who stood before them with tearful faces, and went forth into the ascetic life of renunciation.
With his heart devoted to them, he was accompanied by one companion, as well as a female and a male slave who had followed him into the religious life;

they took refuge at a certain great forest retreat by a vast lake of pure blue water, which, with its blooming lotus groves, seemed to be ablaze, and with its clusters of full-blown white lilies, seemed to be laughing, while swarms of bees hummed incessantly there.
In separate leaf-huts, situated apart and embraced by shady trees in a secluded and pleasant place, they dwelt devoted to vows and observances with minds intent on meditation.
Every fifth day, they approached the presence of the Bodhisattva for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.

And he delivered to them various discourses on the Dharma, which were directed toward the instruction of meditation; which revealed the peril of sensual desires; which were intended to stir spiritual urgency; which abounded in praise for the joy of solitude; which censured faults such as hypocrisy, flattery, and indolence; and which set forth the path of tranquility and serene faith.
And that maidservant, under the influence of great respect and affection, attended to them in exactly that manner.

Having extracted lotus stalks from that lake and arranged them in portions upon large lotus leaves on a clean stretch of the bank, she would announce the time by the sound of clashing wood and then depart.
Thereafter, when those sages had completed their rites of recitation and fire-offerings, each one approached her in order of seniority and took his respective portion of the lotus stalks.
Taking their respective portions in due order and consuming them according to the prescribed rules within their individual leaf-huts, they dwelt with minds intent on meditation.
Thus engaged, they did not see one another except at the time for hearing the Dharma.

Having heard of their blameless conduct, observance of moral discipline, and habitual practice, as well as their delight in solitude and their inclination of mind toward meditation, Śakra, the lord of the gods, [approached] for the purpose of testing them.
He approached them;

and observing their inclination toward meditation, their lack of involvement in evil deeds, their absence of longing, and their state of abiding in the delight of tranquility, he— conceiving an even firmer expectation of their virtues— became attentive in mind for the purpose of testing them.
Dwelling at the edge of the forest without anxiety, devoted solely to tranquility,
he inspires in the hearts of the virtuous a high regard for his qualities.
Then, having gathered and washed lotus stalks as pale and tender as the tusks of a young elephant, and having arranged them upon lotus leaves with the luster of emerald green—

adorned with offerings of lotus petals and filaments— and having signaled the time for those sages by the sound of clashing wood, Śakra, the lord of the gods, withdrew after that maidservant had departed in order to test the Bodhisattva.
At that very moment, he caused the lotus stalk to disappear;
for when suffering arises and pleasure is obscured,
the exertion of the steadfast is perceived as if it were flashing forth.

Then the Bodhisattva, having arrived at the first lotus-division, observed that the lotus leaf in that division was devoid of its lotus portion and that the offerings had been thrown into disorder; thinking, "My share of the lotus has been taken by someone," his mind became fixed on this realization, and with the agitation and impetuosity of his heart subsided, he turned back from that very spot, entered his leaf-hut, and began the practice of meditation as was appropriate.
To avoid causing distress to the other sages, he did not inform them of that matter.

However, his other brothers, thinking, "Surely he has taken his share," each took their own allotted portions of lotus stalks in due order, enjoyed them in their respective leaf-huts, and remained absorbed in meditation.
In this manner, on the second, third, fourth, and fifth days as well, Śakra presented him with that portion of lotus stalks.
And the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise remained with a mind free from agitation and perfectly tranquil;
for to the virtuous, it is the agitation of the mind alone that is considered death, not the exhaustion of life.
Therefore, the wise do not allow their minds to be disturbed even for the sake of their own lives.

Then, at the time of afternoon, those sages, having approached the leaf-hut of the Bodhisattva as was appropriate for the purpose of hearing the Dharma, beheld him with a body exceedingly emaciated, his cheeks and eyes sunken, the beauty of his face faded, and the profundity of his voice diminished;

yet, though he was wasted away, his qualities of fortitude and tranquility remained undiminished, and he was as pleasant to behold as the new moon. Approaching him, they proceeded with due formalities.

Filled with agitation, they asked him, "What is this? and inquired about the cause of his emaciation. To them, the Bodhisattva related the matter exactly as it had occurred. Then those ascetics, unable to conceive of such misconduct and deeply moved by the suffering he had endured, cried out, "Alas! Alas! and stood there with their faces bowed down in shame.
And because the scope of their knowledge and movement was obstructed by Śakra’s power, they could reach no certainty as to how this had come about.
Then the Bodhisattva’s younger brother, demonstrating his own agitation and his own purity, made this extraordinary oath:
"May he obtain a home adorned with the signs of prosperity and a wife who delights the mind!"
And may he who took away your lotus stalks, O Brahmin, attain completeness through sons and grandsons.
Another said:
"Wearing garlands, wreaths, sandalwood paste, and fine silks, and adorned with ornaments touched by his daughter— "
Let him cultivate an intense longing for sensual pleasures—he who, O foremost of birds, stole your lotus stalks.
Another said:

"Let that householder who finds wealth through his reliance on agriculture rejoice in the playful prattle of his children and take delight in his home, even as he grows old— let him be the one who has plucked lotus stalks for you even once."
Another said:
"May he who, while being honored by kings whose gestures were humble toward their servants and whose crest-jewels were bowed low,
protected the entire earth, take away your lotus stalks out of greed for royal service."
Another said:
"Let him be the royal chaplain of the lord of men, endowed with the power of mantras and other rites for securing well-being;
let him receive honor from the king, he who indeed carried away your lotus stalks."
Another said:

"Let the people of the countryside assemble and honor that teacher who has properly studied the Vedas with great veneration for his asceticism; let them not honor him for whom you have greed for lotus stalks rather than for his virtues."
The companion said:
"Having obtained from the lord of men a prosperous and excellent village containing four hundred households, let him go to enjoy it;
let that man who has not yet overcome passion meet his death—he who could not conquer even greed for lotus stalks."
The slave said:
"Let that village headman remain in the midst of his companions, being entertained with the songs and dances of women."
Do not, for the sake of your own self, incur calamities from the king today like the one who sought lotus stalks.
The sister said: "Let the king—
who stole even the lotus stalks from one such as you— take her, who shines with beauty and form, as his wife, making her the foremost among thousands of women."
The maidservant said:
"Alone, having bypassed virtuous men, let her set her affection upon the enjoyment of delicious things;
carrying the joy obtained through honor, she saw the lotus stalks, but not your dharma."
Then, the yakṣas, elephants, and monkeys dwelling in that forest, who had gathered there for the purpose of hearing the Dharma, heard that story and were overcome with great shame and agitation.
Thereupon, the yakṣa, in order to demonstrate his own purity, made this oath before them:
"May he be the resident monk at the Mahāvihāra and the overseer of new construction works at Kacaṅgalā!"
May he who stumbled even upon you for the sake of a lotus stalk create a passage of light through the days.
The elephant said:

"O best of sages, may he who stole your lotus stalks suffer imprisonment in the midst of men from this lovely forest by means of six hundred firm snares, and may he endure the pains born of being dragged by sharp goads."
The monkey said:
"May he who wears flower garlands and has his throat rubbed with lead, when struck by a staff, go to the mouth of a serpent!"
And he who, out of greed, stole your lotus stalks shall dwell in his home bound by a cross-strap.
Then the Bodhisattva addressed them all with words that were free from attachment and indicative of peace and profundity:

"Let him who says 'it is lost'—yet for whom nothing is lost—having attained his desired pleasures, meet his death while remaining attached to the household life; such is the doubt held by those among you. (Jm 19.24)

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, his astonishment and great respect aroused by that extraordinary oath which indicated their aversion to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, approached those seers in his own blazing form and spoke as if with indignation: "O sirs, let me not say this;
for sleep does not come to the minds of those who seek happiness and whose hearts are yearning for its attainment."
Why do you thus disparage those desires which people seek to obtain through the hardships of asceticism?
The Bodhisattva said: "O noble one, sensual pleasures have endless disadvantages.
Listen briefly, however, to that which the sages perceive and for which they do not praise sensual pleasures:
through sensual pleasures, the world incurs bondage and death, as well as grief, exhaustion, fear, and manifold suffering."
And for the sake of sensual pleasure alone, kings, impetuous in their destruction of righteousness, fall into hell in the world beyond.
That friendships suddenly turn bitter, that they proceed by a path stained with the deceit of political intrigue,
and that they suffer separation from fame and encounter miseries both here and in the hereafter— surely the cause of all this is desire.

"Thus, O Śakra, sages do not resort to those sensual desires which lead to the ruin of the low, the mediocre, and the superior— both in this world and the next— just as one avoids angry serpents who seek their own gratification."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having rejoiced at those words of his as being well-spoken, and his mind being gladdened by the majesty of those sages, confessed his own transgression to them:
"The manifestation of the abundance of one's virtues is that which is perceived through examination."
"I have deposited these lotus stalks with you for the sake of testing you. (Jm 19.29)
By good fortune, this world has been graced by sages of truthful renown;
O you of steadfast conduct, this purity of yours is as pure as these lotus stalks.
Having said this, he offered those lotus stalks to the Bodhisattva.
Then the Bodhisattva rebuked him for that impudent impropriety with words that were both majestic and composed:
"We are neither kinsmen nor companions; we are not your actors, nor are we jesters."
O King of the Gods, relying upon what indeed do you approach the sages in this manner, as if on a path of sport?
When this was said, Śakra, the lord of the gods, hurriedly casting aside his earrings and crown, his face radiant as lightning, bowed deeply with great reverence and asked for forgiveness:
"This rashness of mine was committed for a stated purpose and without selfish motive;
may you, like a father or a teacher, forgive it."
This is the nature of those whose eyes of wisdom are closed: they stumble even on level ground.
Therefore, you should not harbor this thought in your mind that those who possess self-mastery ought to be held accountable for it.
Having thus asked for forgiveness, Śakra vanished on the spot.
Therefore, for those who know the taste of the bliss of seclusion, sensual desires are as disagreeable as a mockery or an injury.
And the Blessed One explained this Jātaka as follows:
At that time, Śāradvatīputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Pūrṇa, Aniruddha, and Ānanda were my brothers.
The sister became Utpalavarṇā, the maidservant became Kubjottarā,
the householder Citra became the servant, and Sātāgiri was then the Yakṣa.
The nāga was Pārileya, the monkey was Madhudāta, and Kālodāyin was Śakra; thus ends the Jātaka story beginning with "Let it be upheld."
Thus ends the nineteenth Jātaka, the Bisajātakam.
20. The Śreṣṭhijātakam.
The attribution of non-existent virtues acts as a goad to spur on the virtuous; therefore, one should strive to cultivate true qualities.

As it is heard in tradition: the Bodhisattva, it is said, was well-versed in learning, lineage, and discipline; he possessed a great, noble, and subtle intellect; he delighted in impartial conduct; and through the study of many treatises, his eloquence was clearly manifested.

Through the continuous flow of his compassion, his abundant wealth spread in all directions; because of his great generosity and vast riches, he was esteemed as a "Jewel of a Householder" (*gṛhapati-ratna*) and became the chief merchant (*śreṣṭhin*) of a certain king.
By nature he was righteous, adorned with the virtues of learning and other such qualities.
He generally became the sole object of the world's great esteem.

Then, on one occasion, when that Great Being had gone to the royal palace for some business, his mother-in-law came to his house to see her daughter. Having been shown the hospitality due to a guest, she questioned her own daughter—the Bodhisattva’s wife—in private during the course of their conversation, after first inquiring about her welfare: "My dear, does your husband not treat you with contempt?"
"Does he know the virtue of service?
Or does he not cause distress through his harsh character?
With her face bowed down in shame, she spoke slowly, modestly, and with diffidence: "Such is he, in terms of his conduct, virtuous qualities, and manner of behavior."
"Even one who has gone forth is difficult to find; who now could such a person be?

Then her mother, because her hearing and memory were impaired by old age, did not properly comprehend those words being spoken by her daughter—words whose syllables were faltering due to her embarrassment;
however, from the mention of "one who has gone forth," she reached the conclusion: "My son-in-law has become a renunciant."
She wept aloud, mourning her own daughter, and under the sway of the force of her grief, she became intent on lamentation:
"Of what nature was his conduct regarding moral virtue and good qualities, that he should renounce his own people who were so devoted to him and go forth into homelessness?
Or what indeed is the use of his renunciation?"
How indeed could the mind of that youth— who was handsome, delicate, accustomed to comfort,
and beloved by the king— be inclined toward dwelling in the forest?
Having received no unpleasantness from his own kin, nor having encountered the deformity brought on by old age,
how could he suddenly abandon his home— which overflowed with wealth— without any physical ailment?
How could such a lack of compassion and rashness toward one's own kin have been adopted by the wise Vinayābharaṇa, who was devoted to the Dharma and compassionate toward others? (Jm_20.4)
Honoring ascetics, brahmins, friends, dependents, his own kin, and the wretched,
and possessing the wealth of pure conduct— what would he not obtain in his home that he might desire in the forest?
Abandoning his blameless and devoted wife who shares his religious duties, does he,
intent on the dharma of an ascetic, not perceive this transgression of the path of righteousness?

"Alas, fie upon the wicked course of fate! For if the mind of those who thus abandon their devoted subjects does not enter the path of compassion, then perhaps not even a fraction of dharma is accomplished."

Then his wife, the Bodhisattva’s consort, her heart distressed by that sincere and piteous lamentation of her mother concerning her husband’s renunciation, was agitated by her feminine nature; with a face clouded by despondency and confusion, she forgot the context of the conversation due to the shock of being struck by grief and suffering, and cried out, "My husband has gone forth! My mother has come to this house for my sake because she heard such unpleasant news!"
Having reached this certainty, the young woman, weeping aloud with lamentation, fell into a swoon.
Hearing this, the household members and the circle of attendants wailed out of the force of their grief and suffering.

Upon hearing that, the neighbors, friends, kinsmen, and circles of relatives, as well as the Brahmins and householders who followed the householder out of affection, and most of the citizens, came to his house.
Because he generally shared the same experience of pleasure and pain as the world,
the world likewise, as if following his example, came to share the same experience of pleasure and pain.

Then the Bodhisattva, having approached his own residence from the royal palace, perceiving the sound of lamentation within his quarters and the gathering of a great multitude of people, commanded his own man:
"Find out what this is. Having learned the circumstances, he approached him and reported the matter to him:
"Having abandoned his vast palace, the noble one has indeed gone forth into the religious life"—
hearing this from somewhere, people have come here out of sheer affection.
(Vaidya 123) Then that Great Being, whose disposition was pure by nature, feeling as if rebuked by those words, was overcome with shame and agitation and fell into reflection:
"Ah, how noble is the people's estimation of me!"
If, having obtained this praiseworthy reputation for my virtues from the people,
I were to turn back toward home, what manliness would there be in me?

"Thus, there would be a well-known devotion to faults and a disposition made bitter by contempt for virtues; because of this, I would incur insignificance among virtuous people—what kind of life would such a person have? (Jm 20.11)
Therefore, I honor this person’s esteem by means of my virtuous deeds;
abandoning my home, which is filled with the afflictions of the unreal, through the virtue of my love for the penance grove.
Having reflected thus, that Great Being turned back from that very spot and had the king’s doorkeeper summoned, saying, "The merchant wishes to see Your Majesty again.
Having been granted permission, he entered and approached the king with the appropriate formalities.
When questioned by the king, "What is this?", he replied, "I wish to go forth into the religious life."
"Therefore, O Lord, you ought to grant me your permission.
Then the king, with a heart agitated by haste and moved by affection, said to him:
"While I, who am distinguished as a kinsman and a friend, am still here, for what sorrow do you depart for the forest?"
That which it would not be within my power to take away, whether by wealth, by policy, or by the excellence of my strength.
If you need wealth, take riches from me; if you suffer from anything, I shall prevent it. Having abandoned me and your kinsmen who entreat you, for what other reason do you depart for the forest?

Thus addressed by the king with affection and great respect, that Great-souled One spoke to him with conciliation: "How could there be suffering for those who have taken refuge in your arms, or any wretchedness regarding the acquisition of wealth? Therefore, I do not go to the forest out of sorrow; rather, learn the purpose for which I am departing."
"O King, I am known as one who has taken up the initiatory rite (*dīkṣā*), by reason of the great multitude whose faces are clouded by the stormy rain of tears of grief.
Therefore, I wish to dwell in solitary forests; I have become worthy of trust regarding the attainment of my virtuous qualities. (Jm_20.16)
The king said: "It does not behove you to abandon us on account of mere public rumor.
For those such as yourself, the excellence of your virtues is neither gratified by the fulfillment of public gossip, nor is it offended by its non-fulfillment.
Those various worldly tales wander about unrestrained, woven together merely by the fancies of one's own will."
Even he who merely harbors such thoughts in his heart would be an object of ridicule; how much more so the one who actually attempts it?
The Bodhisattva said: "Do not say so, Great King!
For a virtuous popular saying is certainly not to be disregarded.
Let Your Majesty behold:"

O King, when a man of human nature attains the reputation of being a man of virtuous character, he should not fall short of that standard; for even out of a sense of shame, such a man of integrity should bear that burden.
For one who is perceived as such, whether by way of esteem or by the cultivation of virtues, shines forth with distinction through the establishment of fame; otherwise, he would be like a dry well.

The body of fame of men, pulverized by the falling reports of their virtues— which have increased through falsehood, are agitated by the onset of critical inquiry, and are collapsing— is unable to grow again with ease.
"O King, you ought not to restrain me as I avoid those possessions which are the cause of conflict— possessions that are like black snakes with their hoods raised in anger."
This conduct of yours toward your servants is indeed appropriate, being joined with affection and an understanding of their devotion;
but what use have I, a renunciant, for wealth or for the burden of maintaining possessions?
Having thus entreated the king, that Great-souled One, having received his permission, set out from that very place for the forest.
Then his friends, kinsmen, and dependents approached him; with eyes overflowing with tears of grief, they embraced his feet and sought to dissuade him.
Some, preceded by the joining of their palms in reverence, stood blocking his path.

Others, with embraces, conciliatory gestures, and entreaties, sought to lead him back toward his home; others, out of affection, spoke to him with words harsh from the reproach of his reckless conduct;
and still others displayed compassion by appealing to his regard for friends and kinsmen.
Others endeavored to make him accept the view that the householder’s life alone is most meritorious, binding it with scriptural citations and logical arguments.

They strove to turn him back by describing the hardships of dwelling in the forest of asceticism, by urging the completion of remaining duties, by entreating him, by recounting doubts regarding the fruits of the next world, and by various other such discourses.

Beholding those friends—whose faces were turned away from the refuge of the religious life, whose expressions were firm in their attempt to prevent his departure for the forest, yet whose faces were moistened with tears—the prince thought clearly to himself: [The prince thought: "Clearly... (The remainder of the verse follows).
When a friend has become negligent, those who have pledged themselves as friends ought to apply what is right and beneficial, even if it is harsh;
for this is the well-established path of duty for the virtuous, especially when that which is applied is both pleasing and beneficial.

"The home is better than the forest; how indeed has this taken root in their healthy minds, that they fearlessly restrain me from taking refuge in the forest as if I were about to fall into sinful attachment? (Jm 20.24)
A man who is dead, or about to die, or who has fallen away from the Dharma—such a one should be wept for.
With what kind of understanding do these people weep for me, who am still alive and desirous of dwelling in the forest?
But separation from me is the cause of this grief; why do they not dwell in the forest together with me?
If their homes are more pleasing than I am, what regard indeed can there be for the shedding of tears?
But now, perhaps it is affection for his own kin that prevents them from granting him permission to practice asceticism;
how was it that he did not possess such power even when those armies were arrayed in battle formations here and there?
His noble deeds have been witnessed during times of calamity, and he is perceived as if his compassion were incarnate through the shedding of tears;
yet, even when its roots are firmly established, the nature of friendship turns to deceit here in the absence of constant devotion.
Their voices faltering as they spoke words of restraint, their eyes filled with tears,
and their heads bowed in prostration— these act like the pride of one who is equal toward them.
Likewise, he ought to show them affection and even commend their resolve to follow him into the religious life;
let this conduct not be like that of actors, which causes shame in the minds of the virtuous.
Even for one who is utterly devoid of merit, there will inevitably be two or three friends even when fallen into calamity;
yet, for one exalted by virtues, a single companion is exceedingly difficult to find when setting out for the forest.

Those who formerly used to take the lead for me in battles amidst the perils of rutting elephants do not follow me now to the forest; am I still the same person, and are these my companions still the same?
I do not recall any fault in these men that could cause the decay of affection, which is the very source of its destruction;
such is my state toward my friends, and may it result from this in some way as a cause for well-being.

Or rather, this is my own state of being devoid of qualities, that they do not follow me today to the forest; for whose mind is it possible to sever, since minds are bound by the qualities? (Jm 20.34)
Or those who do not see even the manifest faults of the household as virtues, nor the virtues of the penance grove—
how could I otherwise conceive of those whose eyes of wisdom are closed? (Jm_20.35)
"They do not venture to abandon desires, which are the cause of suffering both in this world and the next;
yet they now abandon the penance grove, which is the opposite of those, and even me. Fie upon this delusion! (Jm 20.36)
"By whom these friends of mine have been deceived, and by whom all the worlds find no peace—
I, possessing true power acquired in the forest of asceticism, shall forcibly destroy those very faults."
Having thus reflected and reached a firm resolve, he cast aside the affectionate gestures of his friends with words made sweet by conciliation, and clearly departed for the forest of asceticism.
Thus, the attribution of non-existent qualities acts as a goad to spur the virtuous on; therefore, one should strive to cultivate those qualities.
For a virtuous person who is regarded for their qualities as a "monk" or a "lay follower" must indeed adorn themselves with those very qualities that justify such a status.
Likewise, it should be inferred that companions for the practice of the Dharma are difficult to find.
Thus ends the twentieth Jātaka, the Story of the Merchant.
21. The Cūḍḍabodhi Jātaka:
By subduing anger, one pacifies enemies.
Otherwise, however, it only causes increase.

As it is heard in tradition: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was born into a certain great Brahmin family that had attained extreme renown through the greatness of its practice of virtues, possessed specific qualities of prosperity, was honored by kings, and was esteemed as a deity.

Born into this world, he grew up with the passage of time; having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and through the practice of the qualities of sacred learning (*śruta*), he soon became known as Prakāśa among circles of the wise.
For fame unfolds among the learned only within the assemblies of the wise.
Just as gems are to those who know them, or as heroes are in battles.

Then that Great Being, because he had cultivated the life of renunciation in previous births, because the perception of the Dharma was well-practiced by him, and because his mind was purified by wisdom, found no delight in the household life. Desiring his own true welfare, he abandoned sensual pleasures—like food mixed with poison—on account of their abundance of strife, dispute, intoxication, and enmity; on account of their being shared with kings, thieves, water, fire, and unpleasant heirs; on account of their failure to produce satisfaction; and on account of their being the abode of manifold faults. Having thus abandoned them, he shorn the beauty of his hair and beard, donned discolored saffron robes, and cast off the finery and ornaments of the householder’s dress.
She had taken refuge in the splendor of the discipline of renunciation.

And his wife, overcome by her passion for him, having let down her hair and abandoned the wearing of ornaments and finery, her body adorned only by the beauty of her own natural form and virtues, and her limbs clothed in saffron robes, followed him into the religious life.

Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving her determination to follow him to the forest of asceticism and considering that the delicacy of a woman was unsuited to dwelling in such a forest of penance, said to her: "My dear lady, you have demonstrated this nature of your devotion to me."
Therefore, enough of this resolve of yours to follow after me.
It would be more appropriate for you to dwell together with those other female renunciants wherever they reside;
for forest retreats are indeed difficult to inhabit. Behold—
Ascetics, devoid of fixed dwellings, reside in cremation grounds, empty houses, mountains, and forests teeming with predatory beasts, wherever the sun goes to its setting.
Constantly devoted to meditation and solitary practice, and having turned their hearts away from even the sight of women, set your mind on returning; what purpose is there for you in this wandering?
Having firmly resolved to follow him, her eyes choked with tears, she replied in this manner:
"If I had felt the inclination for weariness regarding the festival of following you,
why would I have undertaken this suffering, which is so disagreeable to you?"
"Since I am truly unable to live apart from you, you ought to forgive this transgression of my command. (Jm_21.5)

When she did not wish to turn back even though addressed thus two or three times, the Bodhisattva’s mind became indifferent toward her. Followed by her like a cakravāka bird by its mate, he wandered through villages, towns, and market-towns; and once, having finished his meal, he—

In a certain secluded and glorious forest grove, adorned with a dense thicket of various trees and providing deep shade, where the dust of flowers was scattered upon the ground by the sunbeams that fell like moonlight here and there as if to do him a favor, he performed the rite of meditation; then, having arisen from his meditative absorption at the time of evening, he sewed together robes made of rags from dust heaps.

She too, having gone forth as a renunciant, dwelt not far from him, beautifying the foot of a tree; shining like a goddess by the power of her own physical form, she meditated according to the method of mental attention taught by him.

Now, the king of that region [beheld] the trees whose splendor was intensified by the new shoots produced by the spring season, and which were filled with the humming of swarms of wandering bees and female honey-bees.
Wandering through the groves—where the flocks of intoxicated cuckoos warbled their "ki-lā-ki-lā" cries; where the waters of the lovely ponds were adorned with blooming lotuses and water-lilies;

and where pleasant breezes were scented by the fragrance of various flowers in full bloom—he arrived at that place, which was radiant with clusters of diverse blossoms as if they were the very canopies fashioned by the Goddess of Spring.
The male cuckoos and peacocks were vocal, and the reservoirs of water were filled with lotuses.
The sight of forests where the young grass is tender from recent growth, filled with the humming of intoxicated bees, and serving as the playground of the god of love, truly brings joy to the mind.
Then that king, having approached the Bodhisattva with courtesy and exchanged greetings of welcome, sat down to one side.

Beholding that female ascetic, whose appearance was exceedingly captivating, his heart was utterly captivated by the beauty of her form. Concluding that she must surely be his lawful wife, he—owing to his fickle nature—reflected upon a means to carry her away.

Though his fortitude was diminished by the god of love, he— aware of the power of the ascetics' curse, which has the fire of wrath for its fuel and the radiance of sacred learning for its flame— did not succumb to the impetuosity of contempt toward him.

The thought occurred to him: "Having understood the power of his asceticism, it is possible to proceed with that [plan] here, but not otherwise. If this man’s mind is clearly characterized by passion for her, then there is no power of asceticism in him;
however, if he were free from passion or had little regard for her..."

"Therefore, the greatness arising from the power of asceticism must be evident in this man," the king reflected. Desiring to test the power of his penance, he spoke to the Bodhisattva like one seeking his welfare: "O renunciant, in this world filled with many rogues and reckless men, it is not fitting for your honor to remain thus in these cryless forests."

To wander together with this worthy companion in the practice of the Dharma; for if someone were to offend her, they would surely make even you an object of reproach. Behold, some person might thus treat you—who are solitary and emaciated by asceticism—with contempt, along with the Dharma itself.
If someone were to forcibly seize this [woman] from you, what else indeed could you do there than grieve?
For the onset of anger leads the mind astray and is the destroyer of both dharma and fame;
therefore, let her dwell only among the common folk. What need have ascetics for the proximity of women?
The Bodhisattva said: "The Great King has spoken rightly. Nevertheless, hear what I would undertake given these circumstances:
should there be anyone here who acts contrary to me, whether out of arrogance or through lack of discernment."
It is evident that he shall not escape from me while I am alive, just as dust cannot escape from a torrent of wealth.

Then that king, possessing intense passion for her, thought, "This one is devoid of the power of asceticism," and having thus despised the Great Being, he became free from any apprehension of harm to him.
Overcome by sensual desire, he commanded the men in charge of the women's quarters: "Go, bring this female renunciant into the inner apartments.

Upon hearing this, that female renunciant—like a forest doe pursued by a predatory beast, her face distressed with fear and despair, her eyes choked with tears, and her throat faltering—lamented under the sway of various pangs of affliction.
For the world overcome by suffering, the lord of the earth is the refuge, like a father;
yet for one who would be overcome by such misconduct, whom indeed should he call upon for help?

Alas! The world-protectors have either fallen from their office, or they do not exist, or they have come under the power of death; for they do not strive to protect the distressed. I believe that even Dharma is now a mere matter of scriptural sound.
What use have I for the gods, since the Blessed One remains thus silent despite my ill fortune?
Even an enemy must be protected by us when he is being mistreated by evil-minded men.
"May this mountain, whose form is now to be remembered, be struck by the thunderbolt of a curse saying 'it shall perish'!
Even though he has come to such a state, he remains silent; yet I, unfortunate as I am, still live on.

O sinful one, am I not even more worthy of compassion? For have I not fallen into such a calamity? Is this not the path of those whose wealth is asceticism—their activity being rooted in compassion toward the afflicted?
I suspect that even now that same thought remains in your mind, for I have not desisted though I am being turned away;
since I desired my own pleasure even through what was unpleasant to you, how can this [act of yours] be right for me?

Thus, while that woman was solely intent on piteous lamentation, wailing, and weeping, those men commanded by the king placed her upon a vehicle and departed for the inner apartments even as the Great Being looked on.
The Bodhisattva, too, having repelled the force of his anger through the power of analytical reflection, continued to sew his rag-robes just as before, unperturbed and with a tranquil mind.
Then the king said to him:
That powerful roar was uttered by you with words fallen from indignation and rage;
yet, even while seeing that beautiful-faced woman being carried away, you remained with your composure lost to helplessness.
Therefore, show either the wrath of your own arms or the splendor accumulated through reliance on asceticism;
for one who is ignorant of his own measure and whose vow is in vain does not shine when overstepping his bounds.
The Bodhisattva said: "Know me, O Great King, as one whose promise is never in vain.
He who acted contrary to me here, even though he struggled, was not released by me."
But since I have forcibly brought him to peace, my vow has indeed been fulfilled according to its true meaning.

Then that king, having conceived a high regard for the ascetic virtues of the Bodhisattva through that tranquility which manifested his extraordinary fortitude, fell into reflection: "This Brahmin must have had another intention, which we did not understand; thus we acted rashly. Having thus come to this realization, he spoke to the Bodhisattva:
"Who else was there who acted so contrary to you, yet escaped from you unscathed even while struggling?"
Like rising dust being brought to rest by a rain-cloud, who has been pacified here by you?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Listen, O Great King: that which is not seen when one has been born, but is clearly seen when one is unborn—such anger, which afflicts its own support, arose within me and was not released."
That anger which brings joy to those who wish ill upon men when it arises— such anger was not yet released from me, that delighter of my enemies.
O King, when that which causes one to fail to perceive the true meaning arises, I have quelled that blinding anger.
That anger, which, when overcome by it, causes one to abandon virtue and fall away even from wealth already attained—
bring that very anger, which resembles a fierce and deformed planet and is ever throbbing, to its end within yourself.
Just as fire arises from wood when it is being rubbed together, yet leads to the very destruction of that same wood,
so too does anger, when provoked by false conceptualizations, lead to the ruin of a man.
He who does not quell his anger— the fierce heart-fever that expands like a blazing fire—
is shorn of his reputation as being "light," just as the moonlight, the friend of the night-lotus, fades at dawn.
He who, without considering the misfortunes of others, regards anger alone as his enemy,
will surely see his fame blossom like the splendor of the orb of the newly risen moon. (Jm_21.28)
This is another great fault of anger:
even if adorned with the qualities of ornaments, one does not shine when the beauty of one's complexion is consumed by the fire of wrath;
and with the dart of anger lodged in the heart, one suffers even while lying upon a costly bed.
Forgetting his own side of patience and spiritual attainment, he surely proceeds along that wrong path out of anger;
by which he is deprived of fame and the success of his aims, just as the moon of the dark fortnight is deprived of its own splendor.
Driven by anger, he falls into the abyss of misconduct even when restrained by his friends;
generally, such a person becomes dull-witted in enmity, his intellect incapable of discerning between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
And because of anger, one who has made evil deeds his own nature grieves in states of woe for hundreds of years;
beyond this, what could even enemies do, though their fury be aroused by intense malice?
This anger is an internal enemy; thus it is known to me. What man would tolerate the spread of its arrogance?
"Therefore, my anger is not released even though it throbs within my heart;
for who indeed would neglect an enemy that brings such calamity? (Jm_21.34)
Then the king, his mind gladdened by that wonderful quality of tranquility and by those heart-captivating words, said:
"This manner of speech is worthy of your tranquility; but what is the use of saying more? Those who have not seen you have been deceived."
Having praised him in this manner, she approached and fell at his feet; she confessed her transgression,
and having asked forgiveness from that female renunciant, she dismissed her.
He even offered himself as an attendant to the Bodhisattva;
thus, by subduing anger, he pacifies his enemies,
whereas otherwise he would only increase them.
Thus, one should exert effort in the subduing of anger;
in this way, hostilities are pacified through non-hostility,
and through self-restraint, enmity does not accumulate.

And this should be stated in those sūtras connected with the praise of forbearance, such as "thus one who is free from anger acts for the benefit of both," as well as in the discourse on the faults of anger and in the majesty of the Tathāgata.
Thus ends the twenty-first Jātaka, the Cūḍābodhi-jātaka.
22. The Haṃsa-jātaka:
Even for those who have fallen into an unfortunate rebirth, the conduct of the virtuous is impossible for base persons to emulate.
How much more so for those established in a happy rebirth!

As it is heard: once, in the great lake Mānasa, there was a king of swans named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was the leader of a vast flock of swans numbering many hundreds of thousands; he was indeed a Bodhisattva.

At that time, there was a commander-in-chief named Sumukha—an elder named Āryānanda—who possessed an intellect skilled in discerning right and wrong policy; whose power of memory reached far into the past; who was a praiseworthy ornament to his noble lineage; adorned with dexterity, courtesy, and humility; a hero in steadfast, pure conduct, character, and behavior; patient in hardship, vigilant, and expert in both battle and the transport of supplies; and one whose face was brightened by devotion to his lord.
With their power blazing even more intensely due to their mutual reliance on the quality of affection— like two preeminent disciples of a master,

or like an eldest son and his father— they properly established that flock of swans in matters conducive to the welfare and prosperity of both worlds; thus, they aroused the utmost wonder in the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and ascetics who witnessed it.
Those two were the sole means for that flock of swans to sustain their bodies for the sake of their welfare,
just as the two wings of a bird traveling through the sky are the sole means for it to sustain its body.
Thus, being favored by those two, that flock of swans attained supreme growth through the expansion of both dharma and wealth, like the world itself;
and by that flock of swans with the sound of their tinkling anklets, that lake assumed a state of supreme beauty.
The lake shone as if with a moving forest of white lotuses.
With swans spreading out in some places and gathered unevenly in others,
it stole the splendor of the sky variegated by scattered fragments of clouds.

Then, the hosts of accomplished sages (*siddha*), knowledge-holders (*vidyādhara*), and deities, their minds struck with wonder by the power of the extraordinary virtues of both that lord of swans and the general Sarvasattvahitasumukha,
delighted themselves here and there with stories centered upon their fame.
[He possessed] a glorious body resembling refined gold, and speech with distinct words and syllables.
Born of the Dharma, both discipline and policy are here in the singular form of swans.
Their fame, spread in all directions by those who proclaimed their virtues without envy,
attained a state of high esteem among kings, as it circulated like a gift in their assemblies.
At that time, there was a certain king named Brahmadatta in Vārāṇasī.

Having repeatedly heard in the assembly the account of the preeminent virtues of the lord of the geese and his commander-in-chief—being praised by trustworthy ministers, brahmins, and elders—his curiosity to see them grew ever stronger; [he summoned] those whose intellects were skilled through the study of many treatises.
He said to his ministers: "O sirs, let some clever-minded person consider whether there might be some means by which those two excellent swans might at least come within the range of our sight.
Then those ministers, having deliberated according to the path of policy through the power of their respective intellects, spoke to the king:
"O King, the hope for happiness draws living beings hither and thither;
for it is the report of the excellence of the qualities that cause happiness which brings them here."
Therefore, Your Majesty ought to have a lake constructed here in some forest region, possessing the most excellent beauty of qualities such as those two lakes are said to have,
and issue a daily proclamation granting safety to all birds. Perhaps,
by hearing of this extraordinary excellence of qualities which causes both curiosity and happiness, they might be drawn here.
"Behold, Your Majesty:
generally, O King, happiness that has already been attained is not esteemed;
yet, because it is out of sight, the mind is captivated by happiness that is merely pleasant to hear."
Then that king, saying "So be it," after a short time had a great lake constructed not too far from the city park;

its wealth of qualities rivaled Lake Mānasa, its pure waters were most enchanting, and it was filled with clusters of lotuses, blue lilies, night-blooming water-lilies, white lotuses, fragrant lilies, and red lotuses.
The riverbanks were lined with trees covered in blossoms and radiant with trembling new shoots,
as if they had sprouted there for the sake of beholding him.
It was crowded with bees that wandered about, agitated and enticed by the lotuses which seemed to laugh as they trembled from the movement of the waves.
In some places, with various white water-lilies emerging as if to carry away the moonlight,
they appeared like fragments of lunar radiance partitioned by the shadows of trees.
In some places, the edges of the shore were adorned by the pollen of lotuses and water-lilies scattered by the fingers of the waves, as if with golden threads.
In various places, it displayed an expansive beauty as if composed of offerings, with variegated petals of lotuses and water-lilies, complete with their filaments.
Adorned by schools of fish darting about as if in the sky, their variegated forms clearly visible due to the water being serene and still.
In some places, with the ichor of elephants appearing like broken strings of pearls,
it bore the appearance of carrying spray from waves scattered by their impact against the rocks.
In some places it seemed as if it were inhabited by the bathing of Vidyadhara maidens, by the sprinkling of ichor from elephants, and by the pollen of flowers.
It was like a common mirror for the stars, the wives of the moon;
it was crowded with joyful birds and resounded with their songs.

Having thus caused such a lake to be constructed and having given it to the entire flock of birds for their unobstructed enjoyment and happiness, he caused a proclamation of the grant of safety to be made every day for the sake of inspiring confidence in all the birds:
"This lake, its waters covered with the petals of lotuses and water-lilies,"
Out of affection, the king gives to the birds a gift accompanied by the assurance of safety.
Then, at one time, when the darkness of the clouds had been withdrawn like a curtain, and the quarters of the sky—rendered beautiful by the qualities of autumn—had become capable of being beheld;

when the lakes, charming with their clear waters, were adorned by the splendor of blooming lotus groves; when the moon, as if possessing an ever-increasing mass of rays, had attained the height of its loveliness and youth; and when the earth was wearing the ornaments of an abundance of various crops, [the season] had set in.

Wandering in succession through the quarters of the sky, which were bright with autumn, from Lake Mānasa where young swans gathered, a certain pair of swans from that very flock arrived within the territory of that king.
There, [they found] a place resounding with the clamor of flocks of birds, filled with swarms of restless bees, and active with the movement of rows of waves.

He beheld that lake, its fragrance of the pollen of lotuses and water-lilies scattered on all sides by gentle, cool, and pleasant breezes; it seemed to blaze with its blossoming lotuses and to laugh with its blooming night-lilies.
And as he gazed upon that exceedingly enchanting splendor of the lake, even for a pair of swans accustomed to Lake Mānasa, the thought arose: "Oh, would that the flock of swans too might come here!"
Generally, when people obtain common happiness, their memory first turns toward their friends in accordance with their affection. (Jm 22.18)

Then, after that pair of swans had sported there as they pleased, the rainy season set in; and as the masses of clouds— resembling the hosts of Daityas with their flashing weapons of lightning and their forms of dense, yet intermittent darkness— advanced,
they were as beautiful as a full plumage of peacock feathers and seemed to celebrate the victory of the clouds with their continuous cries of *kekā*.

While the flocks of peacocks began their dances, the small parrots became vocal, and the winds— fragranced with the scent of *kadamba*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, and *ketakī* flowers, cool and pleasant like the sighs of the forest— began to blow; while the young female cranes appeared like rows of teeth belonging to the clouds, and the birds warbled softly out of eagerness for departure.
While the flocks of swans were distracted by their departure, that pair of swans returned to Lake Mānasa itself.

Having approached the presence of the lord of swans, and while stories concerning various regions and directions were being related, he described the extraordinary qualities of that lake: "Your Majesty, to the south of the Himavat, in Vārāṇasī, there is a ruler of men named Brahmadatta."
He gave to the birds a great lake of most wonderful beauty and indescribable excellence of quality and loveliness, to be enjoyed at their own will and pleasure;
and safety was proclaimed there every day. And the birds sported there as if in their own homes, free from fear and apprehension.
"Therefore, it is fitting that Your Majesty should go there once the rains have passed.
Upon hearing this, all those swans became eager for a sight of him.
Then the Bodhisattva beheld his commander-in-chief, Sumukha, with a face displaying a gentle expression and a steady gaze.
"And how do you see it? he asked.
Then Sumukha, having prostrated before him, said: "I see that Your Majesty's going there is not appropriate.
Why? Because these forms are indeed alluring, captivating, and like bait."
And nothing of ours here is lost;
for human hearts are generally fragile in their compassion and deceitful, concealing their sharp wickedness behind words of artificial and sweet courtesy.
Let my lord observe this.
"Generally, beasts and birds have their hearts set on the female;
but some humans, on the contrary, possess skill in the opposite."
It is said that what is sweet by name is followed by consequences and leads to ruin;
for even merchants incur expenses with the hope of achieving a profit.
Therefore, O King, trust is never appropriate on account of such [a reason];
even for the sake of a task, a course of action that involves risk and ruin is not beneficial.

"If, however, you must certainly go there, then having gone and experienced the essence of the splendor of that lake's qualities, I see that it will not be possible for us to wander there for long, nor will our minds be inclined toward making it our dwelling.
Then, when the night was adorned by the pure moon, the constellations, and the stars, in that autumn, the Bodhisattva—

His curiosity greatly increased by the sight of the lake at Vārāṇasī, he was repeatedly entreated by the flock of swans to visit it; thus, out of consideration for those swans, surrounded by a great multitude of swans headed by Sumukha, he went there like the moon accompanied by an autumnal mass of clouds.
Upon merely seeing the splendor of that lake, the various arrangements of their beautiful forms became equal in quality as they took refuge there, filled with joy, agitation, and wonder.
Because that lake surpassed even Lake Mānasa through its various extraordinary states,
the minds of those whose hearts were fixed upon it did not for long remain in Lake Mānasa.

There, having heard that proclamation of safety and perceiving the freedom of that flock of birds as well as the splendor of that lake, their hearts were filled with joy; experiencing it as if it were a pleasure excursion to a garden, they attained the highest perfection of delight.
Then, the men appointed over that lake reported the arrival of those swans to the king, describing their qualities and forms exactly as they were.

"Your Majesty, it is reported that those two excellent swans are indeed such: with wings as bright and beautiful as gold, with the splendor of their faces and feet more radiant than refined gold, of even greater stature, with well-proportioned bodies, and accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of swans, they have arrived as if to grace Your Majesty’s lake.
Thereupon, the king, having sought out a fowler whose skill in the art of bird-catching was renowned and celebrated, respectfully commanded him to capture them.
Having promised "So be it," he thoroughly ascertained the range and dwelling places of those two swans, and there, in various locations, he laid down firm and well-concealed snares.
Then, as those swans wandered about with minds exultant with joy, free from fear due to their confidence and no longer apprehensive of danger, that lord of swans had his foot caught in a snare.
This occurred through subtle methods of gaining trust, while they had forgotten the suspicion of any calamity.
Indeed, misplaced confidence causes transformation, for it is the source of the removal of heedfulness.
Then the Bodhisattva, thinking, "May such a calamity not befall anyone else," revealed the perilous nature of the lake by means of a particular cry.

Thereupon, those swans— distressed in heart due to the capture of their leader, uttering confused and piteous cries of fear, and disregarding one another like soldiers whose chief warrior has been slain— flew up into the sky.
But Sumukha, the commander of the swan army, did not move from the presence of the lord of the swans;
for minds bound by affection do not consider even their own destruction.
For these birds, the wretchedness, suffering, and distress caused by the misfortune of a friend are more painful than the loss of life itself.
Then the Bodhisattva said to him:
"Go, go indeed, Sumukha; there is no need for delay here.
For what opportunity is there for you to provide assistance when I am in such a state?"
Sumukha said:
"Death is not certain for one staying here, nor does it cease for one who departs; there is no state of being free from old age and death.
And since I have constantly attended upon you in times of happiness, O giver of honor, how could I abandon you now that you have fallen into calamity?"
"O Lord of Birds, as you abandon me for the sake of merely preserving the thread of your own life,
what shelter will there be for me from the downpour of reproaches?"
"O Great King, this is not the dharma that I should abandon you in times of distress;
O Lord of Birds, whatever destiny awaits you, that is what pleases me."
The Bodhisattva said:
"What other destination can there be for one bound by a snare than the great kitchen?"
How can that be acceptable to you, who are liberated and possessed of a healthy mind?
Do you see any purpose in this, whether for me, for yourself,
or for your remaining kinsmen, now that the lives of both have come to an end?
And where no object is perceived, as if in darkness, whether it be equal or unequal— by abandoning your life in such a place, what purpose would you illuminate?
Sumukha said:
"O best of those who fall [from heaven], why do you not consider the purpose within dharma?
For dharma, when properly cultivated, brings about the highest goal."
Thus, perceiving the Dharma and seeing that worldly benefit arises from the Dharma, O giver of honor, through my devotion to you I do not desire life itself.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Truly, this is the law of the virtuous: that a friend should not abandon a companion in adversity even for the sake of his own life, remaining mindful of righteousness."
"Since you have honored Dharma and shown devotion to me, grant this final request of mine; go now, with my permission."
Moreover, since this matter has come to such a pass, O one endowed with wisdom, whatever remains deficient for my friends should be most fully provided by you.
While the two of them were thus conversing about the quality of their mutual affection,
the hunter appeared before them like Death itself descending in person.
Then those two excellent swans, seeing the Niṣāda approaching, became silent.

And he, seeing that flock of swans fleeing, concluded with certainty, "Surely someone here has been caught," and as he searched through the places where snares were set, he saw those two excellent swans.
His mind struck with wonder at their beauty, and thinking they were trapped, he untied the snares that had ensnared them.

Then, seeing one bound while the other remained unbound and composed as he watched him, his heart filled with even greater wonder, he approached Sumukha and said: "This bird, its prowess restrained by a great snare,
would not have reached the sky had I not come near."
But you, moreover, are unhurt, healthy, strong, and possessed of a chariot with well-fastened wings;
why is it that even though I have arrived, you do not flee through the sky with such speed?

Having heard that, Sumukha spoke in human speech with a voice whose articulation of syllables and words was distinct, and which was powerful with the qualities of natural description, fortitude, and vigor: "The reason why I do not go, though I am capable, is this."
"This bird has fallen into the distress of the snare."
"This one is bound by you with a great noose at his foot;
but I am bound in my heart by his virtues, which are far more firm."
Then that Niṣāda, his mind filled with supreme wonder and the hair on his body standing on end, spoke again to Sumukha:
"The other swans have fled in all directions out of fear of me;
yet you do not abandon him. Who indeed is this one to you, O twice-born?"
Sumukha said:
"The king is my friend, dear to me as my own life; he is the giver of happiness and is now in a state of peril.
Therefore, I cannot bring myself to abandon him, even for the sake of protecting my own life."
Then Sumukha, perceiving that the hunter’s mind was overcome with favor and wonder, spoke to him again:
"O good man, may this conversation of ours result in happiness;
and by releasing us today, may you attain merit and renown."
The Niṣāda said:
