"I do not wish you any suffering, nor have you been bound by me.
Therefore, go as you please and see your kinsmen; bring them joy."
Sumukha said:
"If you do not wish for my suffering, then grant my request;
if you are satisfied with one, then let him go and take me instead."
"Know that we are equal in height and girth, and alike in age;
this is the price for him, not for you to suffer a loss of profit."
Therefore, my dear friend, look upon me; let your greed be directed toward me.
Let your honor bind me first, and afterwards release the lord of birds.
That alone shall be your gain, my request will have been fulfilled,
and there will likewise be joy for the flock of swans and friendship with him.
"Behold now, O sirs, the lordly swan liberated and joyfully received by the flocks of swans,
shining in the clear sky like the moon released from the lord of the Daityas. (Jm_22.51)

Then that Niṣāda, although his heart was hardened by habitual cruelty, had his mind won over by those words of the deer—words which were indifferent to life itself, which praised devotion to their master, which were powerful with the virtue of gratitude, and adorned with fortitude and sweetness. Overcome by wonder and reverence, he joined his palms in salutation and spoke to Sumukha: "Excellent, excellent, O noble one!"
This dharma which you have demonstrated here— by sacrificing your life for the sake of your master— is a marvel among both humans and gods.
Therefore, O King, honoring you, I release this for you;
for who would do what is displeasing to one whose life is dearer than your own?
Having spoken thus, that Niṣāda, disregarding the command of the prince and honoring the king of swans, released Sumukha from the snares.
Then the commander-in-chief Sumukha, his heart filled with supreme joy at the liberation of the king of swans, looked upon the Niṣāda with affectionate tenderness and said:
"Just as I am delighted today by you, O gladdener of friends, through the release of the lord of swans."
In this way, O auspicious Nanda, you shall spend many thousands of autumns with your circle of friends and kinsmen.
Therefore, let this labor of yours not be in vain; taking me and the lord of the flock of swans, place us securely upon the glass and show us to the king within the inner apartments.
Without doubt, that king, his mind filled with joy upon seeing you and the swan-king along with your followers,
will grant you seeds of grain in such abundance as has never been seen before, increasing your delight.

Then, due to his persistence, the Niṣāda thought, "Let the king see this most wonderful sight," and having bound those two chief swans with a cord while they were still alive, he presented them to the king,
saying: "O giver of honor, you ought to behold this marvelous gift."
"This very lord of swans has been brought here by me together with his army."

Then the king, his mind filled with joy and wonder upon seeing those two principal swans—blazing with splendor like two heaps of gold and possessing enchanting forms—said to that Niṣāda: "How did these two birds, now secure and released, come into your hands while wandering on the ground? Tell me the details."
When this was said, that Niṣāda bowed to the king and said:
"Many extremely cruel snares have been set by me in the sporting grounds of birds, in ponds, and in lakes."
Then, moving about with confidence and free from fear, this best of swans was caught by the foot in a concealed snare.
While I was still unbound, he approached me and made this request:
"Having made myself the price, let me ransom the life of the king of swans."
He uttered human speech with clearly articulated and sweet syllables,
making even his request for the sacrifice of his own life a display of resolute resolve.
By his well-composed speech and by his conduct, which was steadfast in its devotion to his master's interests,
I became so pleased that I released his lord along with me, despite his cruelty.
Then this lord of birds, his mind gladdened by my release, spoke many kind words and urged me, saying, "It was for your sake that I undertook this"; may my labor indeed not have been in vain.
Thus, this certain being of exceedingly virtuous character and the form of a noble bird has,
in an instant, produced tenderness even in my heart,
as he recalls how he performed the liberation of the lord of birds for my sake.
Accompanied by his sovereign, he himself has come here to your inner apartments.

Having heard that, the king, with a mind full of joy and wonder, assigned for the king of swans a golden throne worthy of a monarch's seat— a throne resplendent with the luster of various jewels upon its beautiful feet, delightful with the arrangement of the finest coverings, possessing the grandeur of a glorious and comfortable resting place, and provided with a footstool.
And for Sumukha, he provided a cane seat worthy of the chief minister’s presence.
Then the Bodhisattva, thinking, "Now is the time to exchange greetings," addressed the king with a voice as sweet as the tinkling of anklets:
O you who are worthy of well-being, is all well with this body of yours, which is the abode of splendor and beauty?
And is your Dharma-body unblemished, as it were, breathing forth through these abundant utterances?

Furthermore, though consecrated to the protection of your subjects, you increase the splendor of your own fame and the world’s affection— which brings about their welfare— by engaging in the timely bestowal of favor and the infliction of punishment.

Moreover, do you examine the welfare of your subjects through ministers who are pure, unattached to their offices, loyal, and skillful in action; and in this regard, are you not indeed one whose insight is never obscured?
Even when entreated by neighboring kings whose majesty had been curbed by your policy and prowess,
you maintained the splendor of compassionate conduct, yet never succumbed to the sleep of negligence born of misplaced trust.

O Hero among Men, your deeds—consistent with dharma, happiness, and purpose, and beloved by the virtuous—are spread throughout the quarters like fame achieved through success; they are countered by your enemies only with sighs of wretchedness.
Then, with the clarity of his senses manifesting through joy, the king replied to him: "O swan, today all is well for me,
and it shall remain so forever, since this long-desired meeting with the virtuous has been attained."
When you had fallen under the power of the noose, did he not perhaps, his impetuosity destroyed by great joy, cause you pain by striking you with his staff?
For thus, when misfortune befalls these wretched birds,
their intellect, agitated by excessive joy, falls directly into sin.
The Bodhisattva said:
"O Great King, even in such a calamity, there was safety."
And he did not behave toward us in any way like an enemy.
Seeing Sumukha standing there, though unbound, as if bound because of his affection for him, he spoke with conciliation alone, filled with curiosity and wonder:
Then, his mind won over by his sincere and pleasant words,
he released me from the snare, honoring me with his courtesy.
Therefore, this beneficial purpose intended by Sumukha—
that we should come here— will also result in the arising of happiness for him.
The king said:
"Welcome to you both, who have come here as desired;
I am exceedingly delighted by this festival of beholding you."
And today this hunter shall meet with a great purpose;
having done what is pleasing to both parties, he deserves a great reward in return.
Having spoken thus, the king honored that Niṣāda with a magnificent distribution of wealth and spoke again to the king of the swans:
"Since you two have come to your own abode, let this restrictive vow toward me be relinquished.
Tell me what purpose you have and how it may be served; for all my riches are at your disposal."

The satisfaction that a friend brings to one established in prosperity through words of affection spoken without hesitation—that kind of satisfaction he does not obtain from wealth; therefore, among friends, affection is the greatest benefit.

Then King Sumukha, his heart filled with curiosity to converse with him, looked at Sumukha with wonder and said: "Among people with whom one has no deep acquaintance, one does not readily attain the boldness of intimacy; yet, your words—composed of syllables imbued with courtesy and overflowing with the weight of polite formality—are not lacking."
Since you ought to grant us success even through mere conversation,
you will thereby fulfill our hope for intimacy and increase the affection within our hearts.
When this had been said, the swan-commander Sumukha, having bowed with humility, spoke to him:
"This festival of conversation with you, who are like Mahendra himself, is a great joy."
When such friendship has been demonstrated, whose loftiest desire would it not be fulfilled?
While the lord of men was conversing with the lord of birds, who was charming in his friendliness,
it was indeed an act of audacity for a servant to interrupt their discourse and speak out of turn.
This is not the path for one born into the discipline; knowing this to be so, how could I accept it?
Therefore, O Great King, that I remain silent should be forgiven by you, if indeed it is to be forgiven.

When this was said, the king, his face filled with joy and wonder, spoke to Sumukha in a conciliatory manner: "It is fitting that the report of your virtues delights the world; it is fitting that you have been made a friend by the Lord of the Swans. For such humility and excellence of conduct as these are never borne by those whose hearts and souls are unrefined."
Therefore, so that this affection now begun may not be severed for us, let there be such confidence in me as well; for the association of the noble is enduring.
Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving the king’s supreme desire for affection and his favorable disposition arising from love, spoke to him in order to win him over:
"That which is the duty toward a supreme friend has been performed by you toward us; for even in this new acquaintance, you have acted in accordance with your own greatness."
And who indeed, O Great King, would not hold it in their heart,
this method of honor which has been shown by you toward us?
"O giver of honor, what purpose or what need of mine do you perceive that you look upon me?
It is certain that your practice of being a kind host toward those who possess virtue has proceeded from the excellence of long-standing habit."
This is not surprising in you, who have conquered your self and undertaken the vows of a king for the sake of the welfare of your subjects; for,
like a sage devoted to austerity and meditative concentration, all virtues abide in you by your very nature.
Thus, virtues made fortunate by praise are pleasant, yet prosperity does not dwell in the difficult terrains of faults.
Having understood this nature of virtue and fault, what conscious person would stray from the path of their own welfare?

A king does not attain that region through military prowess, nor by the power of his treasury, nor by the excellence of his policy; rather, he reaches it without toil or expense, solely through the nobility of his virtues.
Even the glory of the Lord of the Gods observes virtues; it approaches only those exalted by virtue with humility.
From virtues alone do fame and majesty arise; thus, greatness of power rests upon virtues.

Qualities possessing a splendor exceeding that of the moon’s light truly pacify the minds of enemies— minds that may be hardened by the rise of indignation and pride, and fixed in long-standing enmity and malice.
Therefore, O protector of the earth, while thus ruling the world whose arrogant kings are bowed down by your majesty,
awaken the world’s affection for virtue through your qualities such as modesty, which possess no small splendor.
The welfare of the subjects is the king’s most important duty; for there is indeed another path that leads to prosperity in both worlds.
This shall come to pass when the king is devoted to righteousness, for the people follow the conduct of their ruler.
"Rule the earth with righteousness; therefore, let the Lord of the Thirty-three gods also grant you protection.
Yet, even from the thought of being dependent upon you, the suffering of my own kin seems to drag me away."

Then that king, having fully rejoiced at those words of his, dismissed the two leaders of the geese along with his assembly, preceded by the employment of honors and kind speech. Then the Bodhisattva, having flown up into the expanse of the sky—which was as dark-blue as a stainless sword-blade and possessed the serene beauty of autumn—was followed as if by a reflection by Sumukha, the commander of the geese; and upon merely seeing him, he approached the flock of geese.
He caused [the king] to be filled with supreme joy.
And in due time, that swan, devoted to compassion for others, approached the king and spoke of the Dharma, while being honored by that monarch who was bowed low in humility.

Thus, even for those who have fallen into miserable states, their conduct is not something that base persons can emulate, let alone for those dwelling in happy realms. In this way, virtuous speech brings benefit to both [the speaker and the listener]; therefore, this should also be applied in the praise of virtuous speech and in the description of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Thus, for those who possess virtuous friends, their aims are accomplished even in times of hardship. Furthermore, in the demonstration of the former association with the Elder Āryānanda,
it is shown that this Elder has practiced his conduct together with the Bodhisattva, and thus possesses long-cultivated affection and great respect for him.
Thus ends the twenty-second Jātaka, the Haṃsa-jātaka.
23. The Mahābodhi-jātaka:

Even when treated with disrespect, the compassion of virtuous persons toward those who have previously benefited them does not slacken, owing to their gratitude and their habitual nature of forbearance.
It is thus heard: when the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he was a wandering mendicant named Mahābodhi.

Even while still in the state of a householder, he had thoroughly mastered the sequence of his studies and possessed an inquisitive intellect regarding the fields of knowledge esteemed by the world, as well as various [other branches].

Moreover, due to his proficiency in the arts, his dedication to the welfare of the world through his life as a renunciant, and his particularly keen attention to the treatises on Dharma, he attained the status of a master (*ācārya*) in them.

Because of his accumulated merit, the majesty of his knowledge, his worldly wisdom, and the excellence of his conduct, wherever he went, there he was honored by the learned and those dear to the learned— by kings, brahmins, householders, and followers of other sects.
And he became one to be approached and cultivated by those who had gone forth into the religious life.
For virtues, having attained brilliance through their reliance on merit, become dear by the excellence of their practice;
even from enemies, they receive special honors for the sake of preserving their own reputation.
Then that Great Being, wandering for the sake of benefiting the world through villages, towns, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals, arrived within the domain of a certain king.

Having learned of his arrival from afar, the king—whose renown for his vast learning and virtues had spread far and wide—became joyful at heart and had a residence constructed for him in a delightful section of his own garden grove.
Having ushered him in with honors such as rising to meet him, he welcomed him into his own realm and honored him according to the rites of service and attendance, like a disciple honoring a teacher.
For one who delights in virtue, a guest endowed with virtue and possessed of abundant qualities, having arrived at his home out of affection, is a source of supreme celebration.
The Bodhisattva, too, daily favored him by instructing him in the path to the highest good through righteous discourses that gladdened both his ears and his heart.

For those who are compassionate toward others and devoted to the Dharma desire to speak what is beneficial even to those who have not seen their devotion; how much more so, then, in the case of a person who is like a pure vessel, seeking their own welfare and eager for the quality of affection?

Then the ministers of that king, who had received the recognition of the learned and had attained high honor as members of the assembly, could not endure the abundance of the Bodhisattva’s virtues— the honor toward which increased daily— because their intellects were corrupted by envy.
Having demonstrated the power of his ability to win over the world through the fame arising from the excellence of his own virtues,
he surely kindles the fire of indignation in his rivals who are honored here for their own merits of composition.

Being unable to overcome him by force in discussions of the scriptures and unable to endure his devotion to the Dharma, they gradually incited the king against the Bodhisattva, saying: "Your Majesty ought not to place your trust in this wandering mendicant.
Evidently, having perceived Your Majesty’s love for virtue and your inclination toward the Dharma, he has become one whose smooth, sweet, and artful words deceive you in times of calamity."
This was not the subtle employment of spies by some hostile king seeking to incite a rebellion;
rather, having assumed the guise of one whose very nature is righteousness (*dharmātman*), he instructs Your Majesty exclusively in the practice of compassion and humility.

Furthermore, through a pretense of compassion, he encourages those on Your Majesty’s side—those who obstruct wealth and pleasure, who act outside the duties of a Kṣatriya, and who are prone to immediate transgressions—by means of consoling them with the adoption of "righteous" practices. He also maintains friendly relations with the envoys of other kings.
"Moreover, he is not ignorant of the treatises on statecraft;
therefore, our hearts are apprehensive regarding him.

Then, as that king was being told repeatedly by many people that [the Bodhisattva] was harmful though appearing beneficial, his affection and respect for the Bodhisattva—which had previously been expansive—became otherwise, its flow constricted by suspicion.
A thought occurred to him:

"Even if there were someone who possessed the composure of a mere mortal, yet remained unchanging in the midst of the terrifying roar of the thunderbolt of treacherous slander falling like a bolt of lightning— " *Jātaka-mālā* 23.5.
Then that king, his affection and high esteem having diminished due to the loss of intimacy, was no longer as inclined as before toward the practice of honoring the Great Being.
The Bodhisattva, however, because of his pure nature, reflected in his mind that kings are occupied with many affairs.

Perceiving that the king’s heart had become alienated from him upon observing the slackening of their disciplined conduct among those in his presence, he took up his mendicant’s equipment—the triple staff, water-pot, and so forth—and prepared to depart.
It came to pass;

having heard that, the king—out of the lingering affection he still felt, and out of courtesy and deference—approached him and, displaying great agitation as if wishing to turn him back, said to him: "Why do you intend to depart so suddenly, abandoning us? Why is your mind so set upon going?"
"Have you perhaps seen some careless lapse on our part that might give rise to suspicion?"
Then the Bodhisattva said to him: "This exertion of mine to depart is not without cause, nor is it due merely to a harshness caused by a lack of hospitality."
But because you have turned away from the Dharma through deceit, I am departing from here.

Then, pointing out his beloved dog who had arrived there with its mouth wide open, barking impetuously, he spoke again: "And here, O Great King, let this superhuman witness be observed. For formerly, this dog was skilled in flattering words, following after you because of my devotion."
But now, because he does not know how to conceal his facial expressions, he betrays his true state through his words.
"Surely he has heard something from you regarding me that was harsh and destructive to his devotion;
therefore, he has certainly persisted in this way as a servant's duty out of a desire to please you."

Then the king, his face bowed with shame because of that refusal, and his mind won over by the Bodhisattva’s skill of intellect, was moved to a sense of spiritual urgency; thinking, "This is not the time to persist in deceit," he bowed to the Bodhisattva and said: "Was this story, which has some bearing upon you, introduced by the bold ones in our assembly? And it was overlooked by me due to the pressure of business; therefore, please forgive it, and stay—do not go."
The Bodhisattva said: "Indeed, Great King, it is not because of a lack of hospitality or because I am driven by impatience that I am departing.
Rather, Great King, this is not the time for me to remain; therefore I do not stay. May your majesty observe this."
If I myself were to go to this ceremony of honor— which, due to its mediocre nature,
possesses inferior splendor— whether out of attachment, necessity, or the force of dullness, I would surely be met with the gesture of the "half-moon" (a sign of dismissal).
Since this course of action is the one prescribed by destiny here, I shall depart without my heart being tormented by displeasure;
for among the virtuous, former favors do not become equalized when struck down by even a single instance of contempt.
But one who is not of a kindly nature should not be attended upon, like a dry well by one seeking water;
for even if success in one's purpose is achieved through effort from such a person, it will be turbid and meager.
Tranquil indeed is the form to be approached, resembling a great lake of pure water in autumn;
this is the path clearly established in the world for one who seeks happiness and turns away from the afflictions.

He who turns his back even when one is intent on devotion, or who is distressed by the very sight of one who has turned away, or who is indolent in remembering past favors— he is a man in human form whose true nature remains to be discerned.
Non-cultivation, excessive cultivation, and the pressure of begging all burn away loving-kindness;
since this remnant of affection must be protected from the faults of dwelling together, I shall depart for now.
The king said: "If your honor's mind is firmly resolved that you must certainly go, then it behoves you to favor us by coming here once again;
for affection should indeed be preserved even through non-attendance."
The Bodhisattva said: "Great King, the world is beset by many obstacles and many adversaries; therefore, it is not possible to promise with certainty that I shall come.
However, if the full set of reasons for my coming should exist, perhaps we might see you again.
Having thus entreated the king, that Great-souled One, having received the king’s permission and honors, departed from that realm.

His heart agitated by that intimacy with householders, he retired to a certain forest hermitage. Dwelling there with his mind intent on meditation, he soon attained the four dhyānas and the five superknowledges (abhijñās).
As he tasted the flavor of the bliss of tranquility equally, a memory followed by compassion toward that king arose within him: "What indeed is the current state of that king?"
Then he saw him being enticed by those ministers toward their respective dogmatic views.
One minister, employing difficult-to-discern arguments and illustrations, drew him toward the doctrine of non-causality (*ahetuvāda*), asking:
"What is the cause for the configuration, color, arrangement, softness, and so forth, of the lotus stalk, petals, filaments, and pericarp?"
Who paints the feathers of birds? This world is likewise fixed by its own inherent nature.
Another described to him a cause consisting of a Lord, according to his own intellectual preference:
"All this cannot be without a cause; there exists here a certain infinite One upon whom everything depends."
By means of specific restrictions according to his own will, he creates this diverse world and again brings it to equilibrium.
"All this happiness and suffering is produced by past karma;
there is no efficacy in present effort"—thus another sought to dissuade him, saying:
"How indeed could one act in such a way [as to produce] various, immeasurable, and infinite states that exist at different times and have distinct bases?"
But all this is caused by karma performed in the past; for even one who is skillful in the exertion for happiness encounters suffering.
Furthermore, others, through discourses on the doctrine of annihilationism, deceived him regarding his attachment to sensual enjoyments:

"Just as logs of wood—possessing various colors, qualities, and forms—are not made of karma and yet do come into being, and once destroyed they never arise again; even so is this world. Thus, one should be devoted solely to pleasure. (Jm 23.20)

Furthermore, regarding matters of statecraft and political intrigue as observed in the science of governance—though they are stained by cruelty and contrary to dharma—he instructed him: "This is the duty of a king:
while men have taken refuge under him like birds in shady trees, he should seek to augment his own fame through deeds of gratitude;
he should not seek wealth for the sake of mere personal enjoyment, but rather, when it comes to their service, they should be employed like sacrificial animals at a sacrifice."
Thus those ministers sought to lead the king along various wrong paths of dogmatic views.

Then the Bodhisattva, observing that the king was heading toward the precipice of dogmatic views due to the influence of association with wicked people and because his intellect was led by the convictions of others, felt a heart moved by compassion for him and reflected upon a means to turn him back.
Through the practice of virtue, the good keep their deeds in their hearts;
whereas an injury done to them falls away from them like water from a lotus leaf.

Then the Bodhisattva, having determined that this was the appropriate course of action, manifested a large monkey within his own hermitage; by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), he stripped off its skin and made the rest disappear.
Wearing that great manufactured monkey-skin, he appeared at the gate of the king’s palace.

Having been announced by the gatekeepers, he entered the royal assembly in due order—a gathering that was guarded at its perimeter by armed men, crowded with ministers, twice-born brahmins, warriors, envoys, and leading citizens; where the people were dressed in modest, dignified, and noble attire; whose main gates were presided over by door-keepers bearing swords and staffs; and where the sovereign sat upon his lion-throne amidst an atmosphere free from agitation.

Being honored by the king with the reception of guests through the rites of going forth to meet him and so on, and having been offered greetings, hospitality, and the provision of a seat, he was questioned by the king out of curiosity regarding the acquisition of the monkey skin: "By whom was this monkey skin brought to the Noble One, thereby endowing himself with such great favor?"
The Bodhisattva said: "O Great King, this was obtained by me alone; it was not brought by anyone else.
For while sitting or lying down upon the earth—which is naturally hard and covered with nothing more than *kuśa* grass—one whose body is tormented cannot perform the practice of the Dharma with ease.
Moreover, I saw this great monkey in my hermitage."
The thought occurred to me: "Ah, this hide of this monkey is indeed a suitable means for my practice of Dharma!

Seated upon it, or even while sleeping, one can perform the ordinances of one's own duty, free from longing even for royal beds spread with the most exquisite coverlets. Thus, I took hold of this hide of his.

"And he has been pacified. Upon hearing this, the king, out of consideration for courtesy and disciplined decorum, did not say anything in reply to the Bodhisattva; however, with a heart full of shame, he became somewhat downcast.

Then those ministers, who had already harbored resentment in their hearts toward that Great Being, their faces blossoming with joy now that they had found an opportunity to speak, looked up at the king and, pointing out the Bodhisattva, said: "Oh, how the Blessed One’s mind is singularly devoted to the flavor of the Dharma!
Oh, what fortitude!"
Oh, how great is the power of virtuous resolve!
It is truly marvelous that as soon as he reached the hermitage, a great monkey named Mahān was subdued by this man alone, his body emaciated by asceticism.
May there be success in his ascetic practice in every way!
Then the Bodhisattva, remaining entirely unperturbed, replied to them: "It is not fitting for your honors to censure us thus, regardless of the beauty of your own doctrine.
For this is not the proper way to manifest the fame of the wise.
Your honors should rather consider this:"
He who censures others with words that destroy his own doctrine truly desires the infamy of another as if by his own self-destruction.
Having thus rebuked those ministers in general, that Great-souled One, desiring to rebuke them individually once more, addressed that proponent of causelessness and said:
"You proclaim that the world is produced by inherent nature (*svābhāvika*); yet if you despise that very principle, why do you blame us?
When a monkey met its death through inherent nature, what sin did I commit, such that it was well-slain by me? (Jm 23.24)
"If there is sin for me from his killing, then it is established that this is indeed due to a cause.
Therefore, either abandon this doctrine of causelessness, or say here what is not consistent with your own position."
If the arrangement of the lotus stalks and such were indeed causeless, then surely they would exist at all times;
however, that [arrangement] is produced by water and so forth from the seed, for it occurs when those [causes] are present, and not when they are absent.
Moreover, venerable sir, consider this carefully: by asserting that "there is no cause," would you not be abandoning your own thesis along with its very reason?
Moreover, even if he were to become indolent in adducing reasons, what would be gained for him by a mere thesis alone?
He who, having failed to observe a cause in a certain instance, proclaims on that very basis the absence of all causes— has he not,
by perceiving the essence of causality through direct perception, become its hater, his speech corrupted by contradiction?
If no cause is perceived anywhere, how can you say that it is firmly non-existent?
For even that which exists is not seen due to other causes, such as the stainless orb of the sun at the end of the day.
"Indeed,
sir, you pursue desired objects for the sake of pleasure, yet you do not wish to enjoy those things that conflict with them;
you perform service to the king, yet you say there is no reason for doing so."
If you thus perceive all things as being without cause,
then since the killing of the monkey would be established as causeless, why do you reproach me?
Thus that Great Being, having rendered that proponent of causelessness speechless with clear arguments, addressed that proponent of God as the cause:
"Even you, O Venerable One, ought not to revile us;
for you hold God to be the cause of everything. Behold—"
"If the Lord indeed ordains everything, then surely that monkey was slain by Him alone;
why then do you harbor such ill-will toward me, pouring the faults of another upon me?"
Alternatively, since that slaughter of the monkey heroes was not carried out by him out of compassion, how can you proclaim that the Lord is the cause of the world? Jm_23.33 //
Moreover, O good sir, for one who perceives that everything is created by Īśvara,
what hope is there for grace from Īśvara through praises, prostrations, and the like?
Whatever he does himself, O self-existent one, that is his own karma.
Furthermore, if the sacrifice was performed by you, then he is not its agent;
for he who performs an act through his own power is the true doer.
If the Lord commits all these evil deeds,
then what benefit could possibly be seen in placing one's devotion in Him?
If he does not perform those [deeds] out of fear of unrighteousness,
it is improper for him to say that everything is created by Īśvara.
And his status as lord must arise either from his own nature or from another;
if it were from his own nature, he was not a lord previously.
Furthermore, that which is caused to be done by another would be mere servitude;
yet even so, for what reason would there be no sovereignty for anyone?
Even so, having proceeded thus out of devotion and passion, disregarding what is proper and improper—
if the Lord alone is intended by you to be the cause of this entire world,
then surely you ought not to have imposed upon me the execution of the king of monkeys ordained by that All-pervading One.

Thus that Great Being, having reduced that proponent of God as the cause to a state of silence as it were by means of well-articulated reasons, addressed that proponent of past karma with skillful courtesy and said: "It does not become you to revile us."
For you have the conceit that "all this is indeed the result of my past karma. And because of that, I say to you:
if everything were solely due to the power of past actions, then this monkey would certainly have been well-slain by me.
For when this [body] has been consumed by the forest fire of previously committed karma, what fault of mine is there here for which you reproach me?
If there is sin for me in killing the monkey, then it was not caused by my previous karma;
and if it is held that karma is caused solely by karma, then no one at all will attain liberation.
If there were happiness for one situated among the causes of suffering, or suffering for one amidst the means of attaining happiness,
then it could be inferred that pleasure and pain certainly proceed solely from the single cause of past actions.
Furthermore, since pleasure and pain are not seen to arise from past karma alone, that [past karma] cannot be their sole cause;
for if new karma were non-existent, how could there be old karma? (Jm 23.44)
If you believe that everything is thus created by past karma,
then why is the killing of the monkey attributed to me?

Thus that Great-souled One, having instructed that proponent of annihilationism as if in a vow of silence through irrefutable arguments, spoke to him with a smile: "Venerable sir, what is this excessive zeal of yours in censuring us?
If you consider annihilation to be the truth, then if there is no other world, what sin is to be avoided, and why this delusion of great respect for what is auspicious?"
In this situation, one who acts according to his own will would be wise; for if things proceed thus, this monkey will surely be well-slain.
Out of fear of public gossip, he avoided what was unwholesome by resorting to the path of virtue; yet,
through actions that contradicted his own words, he did not even transcend public censure.
"And yet, out of fear of public censure, he does not attain the happiness that comes from following his own established path.
Thus, this delusion of fruitless speech is indeed the ultimate mark of the lowest among fools.
Furthermore, as for what you have said:
"Pieces of wood, though possessing various colors, qualities, and forms, do not consist of karma, yet they do exist;
once destroyed, they never arise again. This world is just like that—what indeed could be the cause here? [Jm_23.49]
Even so, if you still cherish the doctrine of annihilationism, then why indeed should one who kills a monkey or a human be censured? (Jm 23.50)

Thus, having rendered that proponent of annihilationism speechless through a sequence of replies so clearly brilliant, the Great Being spoke to that minister, who was skilled in the science of governance: "Why do you also revile us in this way,
if you consider the course of action seen in the treatises on statecraft to be just?"
For in that case, whatever is desired—whether good or bad—must be performed for the sake of wealth;
or else, having extracted oneself from wealth, one will practice dharma.
Therefore I say this to you:
when one's purpose has been achieved, virtuous conduct toward even affectionate kinsmen need not be observed.
Now that this monkey has been killed by me for its skin, what blame can there be, even according to the principles seen in the scriptures?

Since such an act has been seen to be censurable and to result in suffering due to its separation from compassion, by what means can you justify entering into that system where this [act] is permitted? Jm_23.53.
Where such is the splendor of this policy, what kind of delusion could there be for its opposite?
Alas! By the audacious, having disregarded the world, unrighteousness is elevated by means of the paths of sacred treatises.
Or perhaps this which you desire is indeed unseen [in the world], yet it is taught in the scripture by a path clearly set forth.
Following the method established in the scripture, I am not to be censured for the killing of the monkey.

Thus that Great-souled One, having forcibly overcome those ministers— who were accustomed to boldness and had won over the assembly— and having perceived that the entire assembly, including the king, was deeply moved, spoke to the king for the purpose of removing their distressing thought regarding the killing of the monkey: "Indeed, O Great King, I have not killed any living creature, nor even a monkey."
This is a method of transformation;
for this skin of a monkey, which has been created by me, was taken specifically for the purpose of introducing this very sequence of stories.
Therefore, enough of regarding me otherwise.

Having spoken thus, he withdrew that miraculous manifestation and, perceiving that the king and his assembly were inspired with supreme faith, said: "Who, seeing the accomplishment of all things through causes, being independent, knowing the world beyond,
firm in his vows, and compassionate, would kill a living being?"
Behold, O Great King:
how could one who speaks according to reason accept that which an advocate of causelessness, one with a dependent view, an atheist,
or a follower of the kṣatriya code might do for the sake of a mere fragment of fame?
O best of men, whether auspicious or inauspicious, view is the cause for the undertaking of corresponding actions;
for, having conceptualized various things through their views, they manifest them by means of those very words and deeds.
Therefore, right view should be cultivated by you, while wrong view—which rains down calamity—must be abandoned;
this sequence is to be attained by one who relies on the virtuous and keeps far away from the wicked.
Unrestrained, yet wearing the garb of those who are restrained, these Rākṣasa-like mendicants roam at will upon the earth;
indeed, like serpents whose very glance is poison, they utterly consume the foolish folk with their evil views.
The specific characteristic of those [heretics] there is that they are howled at with harsh cries such as the doctrine of causelessness, like jackals;
therefore, a wise person should not serve them, but should instead exert himself for their sake when he has the power to do so.
Moreover, even one whose fame has grown in the world should never form a friendship for any purpose with an unworthy person;
for even the moon, when afflicted by the onset of a winter storm, suffers a loss of its splendor.

By avoiding those who shun virtue and by serving those who are wise in the pursuit of virtue, cause your own fame to blaze forth; thus, you shall produce in the people the dissolution of passion for faults and an affection for virtues.
And while you practice the Dharma, this world of men shall for the most part become well-disposed through good conduct and established upon the path to heaven.
Since this world must be protected by you in this way, exert yourself and follow this Dharma, which is a path made beautiful by discipline.
Purify your conduct and acquire the fame of a donor; maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all people as you do toward your own kin.
Protect the earth righteously for a long time with vigilance; in this way, you shall attain happiness in the third heaven and renown.
For a king who protects his subjects— who are primarily engaged in agriculture and intent on cattle-rearing, like trees laden with flowers and fruit—
and who receive taxes from them, is indeed endowed with all medicinal herbs.

That king who does not protect the merchants and the citizens— who rely on the buying and selling of various goods and who benefit the royal treasury through the payment of taxes— comes into conflict with the abundance of his own coffers.
A king who, through negligence, treats with contempt an army that has never shown fault in battle, whose prowess has been witnessed, and whose skill in weaponry is renowned,
will certainly be opposed by the Goddess of Victory in war.

In the same way, O Lord of Men, by proceeding along a path defiled by contempt toward virtuous men— who possess the qualities of moral conduct, learning, and yoga, and whose greatness and virtues are manifest— one is excluded from the joys of heaven.
He who gathers fruit from a tree before its time destroys the seed and finds no flavor;
likewise, a king who extracts taxes in an unrighteous manner ruins the country and does not rejoice because of it.
Just as a great tree endowed with all its virtues yields fruit through the process of ripening,
even so does a land protected by a king provide a ruler with the attainment of dharma, wealth, and happiness.
Bind to their hearts your beneficial ministers who perceive subtle matters, as well as your pure friends and your own people,
by means of speech that is pleasing to them, and by wealth bestowed with due honor.

Therefore, always placing Dharma at the forefront, with a mind intent on securing the welfare of your subjects, protect the worlds by means of a system of punishment free from passion and hatred; in so doing, you shall protect both yourself and the worlds.

Thus, that Great Being, having diverted the king from the evil path created by false views and having established him upon the true path along with his retinue, rose up from that very spot into the expanse of the sky.
While being honored by those people who bowed down with great reverence and joined palms, he returned to that very same forest hermitage.

Thus, even for virtuous men who have been treated with disrespect, compassion for those to whom they previously rendered service does not slacken, owing to their gratitude and their natural disposition toward forbearance.
Thus, one should not forget what was done previously merely because of a lack of hospitality.

Likewise, it should also be stated in the praise of the Buddha that even while the Blessed One had not yet attained full enlightenment, he subdued the arguments of opponents and performed the discipline of sentient beings.
Similarly, this should also be applied in the censure of wrong views, as wrong view is not to be relied upon because it is incapable of withstanding inquiry.
By the opposite [method], there is the praise of right view.
Thus ends the twenty-third Jātaka, the Mahābodhi-jātaka.
(Vaidya 162)

24. The Mahākapi-jātaka: The virtuous do not suffer as much from their own pain as they do from the loss of the side of wholesome qualities on the part of those who wrong them. As it is heard in tradition:

It is said that the Bodhisattva was on the glorious slope of the Himalayas—a place whose surface was adorned with various mineral ores as if they were beautiful and variegated unguents; where the splendor of the dense forest seemed to wear an upper garment made of blue silk; where the edges of its slopes were decorated with natural formations of many colors and shapes, appearing like artistic designs created with great effort; where numerous springs flowed forth; which was filled with deep caverns and waterfalls; and which resounded with the most vibrant humming of bees.

In that place, where various trees bearing flowers and fruits were being fanned by a pleasant breeze and which served as a playground for the *vidyādharas*, there lived a large-bodied monkey wandering alone.

Even in such a state, compassion did not abandon him—though he was one whose sense of dharma was undiminished, who was grateful, noble in nature, and endowed with great fortitude—as if out of the power of affection.
"The earth, along with its forests, its best of mountains, and its oceans, has gone to destruction hundreds of times."
At the time of the end of the eon, neither water, fire, nor wind can overcome the great compassion of a Bodhisattva.

Then that Great Being, like an ascetic subsisting on nothing more than forest roots, leaves, and fruits, dwelt in that forest region out of compassion for the living beings who fell within his range of vision, according to various prescribed methods.

Now, a certain man, having set out to search for a lost cow, wandered about in all directions; having lost his way and being confused as to the cardinal points, he arrived at that place while roaming about, his body withered by hunger, thirst, heat, and fatigue, and burning within from the fire of despondency as if from the excessive weight of despair. In one part of it—
Seated at the foot of a tree, he saw several *tindukī* fruits, tawny with ripeness, fallen by the force of their maturity.
Having tasted them, and considering them most delicious because of his extreme emaciation from hunger, his energy redoubled as he sought their source.
Looking all around, he beheld a *tindukī* tree growing on the edge of a precipice, its top branches bent down and tawny with ripe fruit.

Drawn by his thirst for that fruit, he climbed that mountain slope and ascended a fruit-bearing branch of that *tinduka* tree which overhung the precipice; out of greed for the fruit, he approached its tip.

Then, due to the excessive weight of the man and because of its own frailty, that branch of the great tree bent down and suddenly fell with a loud crashing sound, as if its root had been severed by an axe.
Together with her, he fell like into a well into a great mountain fastness surrounded on all sides by rocky walls;
yet, due to the mass of leaves and the depth of the water, not a single limb of his was injured.
Having emerged from that water and crawling about in every direction, he saw no way of escape anywhere.

Thinking, "I must die here before long without remedy," his hope for life was dissolving; with a wretched face drenched in tears of grief, pierced by the sharp dart of despondency, his heart fainting, he lamented in various ways under the power of his affliction.
In this wilderness, difficult to traverse and devoid of the presence of people,
who other than Death could have seen me fallen here, even though searching with great effort?
Deprived of kinsmen and friends, made a solitary drinking-trough for swarms of mosquitoes,
and submerged face-down in a precipice— like a deer, who will rescue me?

Alas, this intermediate night— variegated with gardens, groves, celestial palaces, and rivers, its sky resplendent with stars scattered like jewels— overcomes my world with a dense darkness like that of a night in the dark fortnight.
Thus that man, lamenting various things and subsisting on that water and those *tinduka* fruits which had fallen along with him, dwelt there for several days.
Then that great monkey, wandering through that forest in search of food, arrived at that spot as if being summoned by the top branches of that *tinduka* tree, which were trembling in the wind.
Having climbed it and looking down at the precipice, he saw that man struggling there, his eyes and face emaciated by hunger, his limbs pale, thin, and miserable, and full of longing.
Moved by compassion for his distress, the great monkey set aside his search for food and, questioning that man persistently, spoke these human words:
"You are wandering here in this precipice inaccessible to humans;
you ought to tell me clearly who you are and from where you come."
Then that man, bowing down to the great monkey out of distress and gazing up at him with palms joined in reverence, said:
"O noble one, I am a human being who has become lost while wandering in the forest; seeking fruit from this tree, I have fallen into this calamity."
"O Lord, for me who am bereft of friends and kinsmen and have encountered this great calamity, please become my refuge as well, you who are the leader of the monkey hosts."
Hearing this, that Great Being was overcome with supreme compassion:

"One fallen into calamity, deprived of kinsmen and friends, looking up wretchedly with palms joined—such a person inspires even enemies with pity, but he truly moves those who already possess compassion. (Jm 24.9)

Then the Bodhisattva, feeling compassion for him, consoled him with affectionate words that were difficult to find at such a time: "Do not grieve, thinking, 'My prowess has been shattered by the precipice,' or 'I am without kin.'"
Whatever duty toward a kinsman there may be for you here, I shall perform it all; enough with fear.
Thus, having comforted that man, the Great Being brought him *tinduka* fruits and other fruits, and prepared elsewhere a rock suitable for his extraction—one as heavy as a man’s load.

Then, having ascertained the measure of his own strength and being certain in mind that "I am able to lift him out of this abyss," he descended into the precipice; urged on by compassion, he spoke to that man.
"Come, climb onto my back and hold fast to me,
while I extract you and your essence from my own body."
For this is considered by the virtuous to be the essence of this pithless body:
that it is employed by the wise for the sake of benefiting others.
Having agreed, saying "So be it," and having bowed to him, he mounted [the elephant].
Then, once mounted by that man, though oppressed by the excessive weight, he—
his fortitude unshaken due to his excellence of character— carried him away despite the extreme suffering.
Having lifted him up, filled with supreme joy yet walking with a faltering gait due to exhaustion,
he made the surface of a rock, dark as a rain-cloud, his bed for the sake of rest.
Then the Bodhisattva, because of his pure nature and because he had already received assistance from that man, felt no apprehension of harm from him; with full confidence, he said to him:

"In this forest region where predatory beasts and wild animals enter unimpeded, along this path on all sides, someone might suddenly strike me down while I am asleep from exhaustion—thereby destroying both my own welfare and the benefit of your own prosperity."
Therefore, may you cast your gaze in all directions and provide protection for both me and yourself;
for my body is utterly overcome by exhaustion, and I wish to sleep for just a moment.
Then he, arrogant in his false discipline, promised him, saying: "May you sleep as you please for the sake of a pleasant awakening;
I shall remain here to protect you."
Then, when that Great Being had fallen under the power of sleep due to the exhaustion of his labor, the man fell into an inauspicious reflection:
"With roots obtained only through excessive effort, or with wild fruits found by chance—
how can there even be sustenance for one whose body is so utterly wasted, let alone nourishment?"
And how shall I cross this wilderness so difficult to traverse, being devoid of strength?
Yet this flesh of his is sufficient for me to cross over this treacherous wilderness.
"Even though he has rendered assistance, he is surely to be eaten; for such is his natural disposition.
Moreover, this is indeed a duty well-known in times of calamity; therefore, he should be made into provisions for the journey."
"As long as he remains fast asleep in the comfort of his confidence, I am able to slay him;
for even a lion, upon encountering him while he is facing toward battle, might suffer defeat."

Having resolved that this was no time for delay, that evil-minded one— his intellect deluded by the fault of greed, ungrateful, having lost his sense of dharma, and whose compassionate and gentle nature had perished— raised a massive boulder and hurled it at the head of that great monkey, despite being utterly weak himself due to his excessive passion for what ought not to be done.
Then that stone, released by him who was agitated by weakness yet impelled by excessive zeal for his task,
served as a departure from sleep for the monkey, leading instead to a state of extreme slumber.
With her entire body she did not strike our heads, nor did she crush them;
but piercing them with only a portion of one corner, she fell upon the surface like a thunderbolt.
His head unhurt by the blow from the rock, the Bodhisattva leaped up with speed and looked around,
wondering, "By whom have I been struck? He saw no one else, but beheld only him [the hunter] with a face cast down in shame.
His radiance was drained by shame; he was lacking in confidence, his complexion shattered by despondency and wretchedness;
with his throat parched from the onset of terror, he was drenched in sweat and unable even to look up.
Then that great monkey, having resolved in his mind that this was indeed the man's own doing, disregarded the pain of his own injury;
moved by a sense of agitation and compassion born of that extremely difficult deed performed by the man regardless of his own welfare, he abandoned the faults of anger and impetuosity.
With eyes full of tears, looking at the man and lamenting him, he said:
"O noble one, such a deed as this has been performed by you while being a human being; how indeed was it resolved upon, and how was it even undertaken? (Jm_24.25)
It behoves you, whose valor is renowned for its skill in warding off attacks, to restrain this supreme being who has approached us, enraged by my offense.
"I have performed a difficult task"—such was the pride that arose in me;
it has been cast away by you, O you of wicked mind who perform what is most difficult to do.
As if brought back from the other world, as if rescued from the jaws of death, and as if lifted from one precipice only to fall into another, you have indeed fallen elsewhere.
"Alas, fie upon this wicked and most cruel ignorance,
which casts the world— pitiable in its longing for happiness— into sufferings!"
I have cast myself into a miserable state; the fire of grief has been hurled upon me;
the fortune of my reputation has been eclipsed, and my virtue and friendship have been opposed.
Having gone there, you have become the mark of reproach and your trustworthiness has been destroyed;
what possible accomplishment of purpose did you expect by acting thus?
This pain does not distress me as much as this very mind here consumes me;
for I have become the instrument of your sin, and I am not able to remove that transgression.
"Follow me closely by my side with your body visible, for you are indeed highly suspicious;
I shall lead you along the path to the edge of the village from this dense forest so full of many terrors."
For if someone were to encounter you in the forest—alone, with a wasted body, and ignorant of the way—it might happen that, by distressing you, they would render my own efforts futile. (Jm 24.34)
Thus that Great Being, grieving for that man, led him to the edge of the inhabited land, established him there, and having pointed out the path, spoke to him again:
"You have reached the edge of the inhabited land; O beloved, leave behind this forest edge with its fearsome wilderness and difficult terrain; go forth safely!
Strive to avoid evil deeds, for the time of their ripening inevitably brings suffering."
Thus, having instructed that man out of compassion as if he were a disciple, the Great Ape returned to that very part of the forest.

Then that man, having committed that most grievous sin, his mind set ablaze by the fire of remorse, was transformed in appearance by a great disease of leprosy; his skin became variegated with spots, and his limbs were wet with the oozing from bursting sores.

His body immediately became utterly foul-smelling. Whichever place he went to, people there, beholding him— whose appearance was so loathsome and distorted that he seemed beyond belief as a human being, and whose voice was broken and wretched— thought, "This is surely a demon in person."
Raising clods of earth and sticks, and using harsh words of abuse, they drove him away.

Then, a certain king, while wandering on a hunt, beheld him roaming like a ghost in the forest—wearing tattered, soiled garments, his loincloth barely concealed, and appearing most wretched; filled with both awe and curiosity, he questioned him:
His body was disfigured by leprosy, his skin mottled with white spots;
he was pale, emaciated, and wretched, with hair as coarse as dust.
"Who are you? Are you a preta, or a piśāca, or a personified pāpmā, or a pūtana? Or which one of the many types of consumption (yakṣman) are you, this mass of manifold diseases?"
With a piteous voice, bowing deeply before him, he said: "I am a human being, O Great King, not a non-human.
When thus questioned by the king as to how he had come to such a state, he revealed his own evil conduct and spoke to him:
This is merely the flower that has now appeared as a result of that betrayal of a friend;
clearly, there will be another fruit yet to come that is even more painful.
Therefore, you ought to regard malice toward friends as you would toward an enemy;
look upon your affectionate kinsmen with genuine affection.

Adopting the conduct of an enemy toward friends, those whose minds are defiled by faults such as greed and who betray their friends meet with such a state even in this very life; therefore, the destiny of those betrayers of friends is to be inferred from what follows hereafter.
But he whose heart is gentle with affection toward his friends obtains from them fame, a state of trust, and the joy of being helpful;
he gains the quality of humility, gladness of mind, invincibility, and through his merits, the abode of the thirty gods.

O King, having understood this regarding the power and success achieved through the association with friends in both good and evil courses of action, follow the path trodden by the virtuous; for prosperity follows those who travel upon it.
Thus, the virtuous do not suffer as much from their own suffering as they do from the loss of the side of wholesome qualities for those who have wronged them;
this is what should be said regarding the majesty of the Tathāgata,
as well as in the context of listening to the Dharma with reverence, the discourse on patience, non-betrayal of friends, and the demonstration of the peril of evil deeds.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth Jātaka, the Mahākapi-jātaka. 25. The Śarabha-jātaka.
Those of great compassion feel pity even for one who seeks to kill them when fallen into distress; they do not neglect him.
As it is heard—once, it is said, the Bodhisattva was dwelling in a certain region of a wilderness forest, which was devoid of human sound and inhabited by various species of wild animals.

In a place thick with trees, shrubs, and grasses whose roots were submerged in dense undergrowth, where the boundary lines of paths were not marked by the feet of travelers, vehicles, or beasts of burden, and where the ground was made uneven by watercourses, anthills, and chasms, there lived a *śarabha* deer, endowed with strength, speed, beauty, and courage, possessing a body of firm and solid build.

Through the practice of compassion, his mind was free from malice toward sentient beings; subsisting on mere grass, leaves, and water, his intellect delighted in dwelling in the forest out of respect for the virtue of contentment. Like a yogi desiring solitude, he graced that forest region—though possessing the form of a deer, he had the wise mind of a human and, like an ascetic, was compassionate toward all living creatures. With a mind satisfied by even the tips of blades of grass, he roamed in that secluded grove like a yogi.

Then once, a certain king, the sovereign of that realm, mounted upon an excellent horse, his hand occupied with a strung bow and arrows, desiring to test his own skill in weaponry against wild beasts, pursued the deer with great speed out of passion. With his superior-speeding steed, he reached that region while his body of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry remained far behind. Having seen the Great Being from afar, his resolve to kill him arose; drawing a sharpened arrow, he urged his excellent horse toward where that Great-souled One was.

Then the Bodhisattva, seeing the king rushing toward him on his excellent horse and armed with weapons, although capable of resisting, leaped away with supreme speed because he had desisted from any impulse of violence;
pursued by that horse, he galloped on, leaping over a great chasm encountered along the path as if it were a mere cow's footprint.
Then the excellent horse, pursuing that śarabha along that very path with the utmost speed, reached that chasm; but his mind being resolved not to leap over it, he suddenly came to a halt.
Then the king, dismounted from the back of the horse and still armed, fell into the great abyss like a Daitya warrior into the ocean.
With his eyes fixed upon that śarabha, he did not notice the precipice;
then, his seat having shifted due to the fault of misplaced confidence, he fell as the speed of his swift horses came to a halt.

Then the Bodhisattva, because the sound of the horse's hooves had ceased, gave rise to the thought, "Could it be that the King has indeed turned back? Turning his face toward the rear and looking back, he saw that horse standing at the edge of the precipice without a rider.
The thought occurred to him: "That king has certainly fallen here into this precipice;

for here there is no tree root with dense shade to provide shelter for the sake of rest, nor is there any lake with clear water as blue as the petals of a blue lotus fit for immersion, nor is there any way to let down my excellent horse anywhere in this forest wilderness frequented by predatory beasts."
Either he has rested or he has engaged in hunting;
moreover, there is not even a thicket of grass here where he could have hidden himself.
Therefore, it is evident that the king must have fallen into a pit.

Then that Great-souled One, having reached his resolution, conceived the highest compassion even for that executioner: "Today, by this army— resplendent with banners and ornaments of variegated colors, with shining armor and weapons, crowded with chariots, horses, foot-soldiers, and elephants, and filled with the diverse sounds of musical instruments— " *Jātaka-mālā* 25.4.
Accompanied by a retinue, shaded by a beautiful parasol, and graced by the splendor of shimmering fly-whisks and necklaces,
he attained the pleasures of royalty and was honored by the multitudes of people with palms joined in reverence, like the Lord of the Gods.
This very day he has fallen into a great abyss, his limbs shattered by the force of the fall;
overcome by fainting or consumed by grief, alas, he has encountered this terrible suffering.

The minds of the lowly do not suffer from sorrows as much as the hearts of the noble do when calamities arrive; for the latter, having never experienced suffering before, are of such extreme delicacy that their minds seem as if marked by scars.

And this man would not be able to cross over by himself from here; yet, reflecting that even though his life-force remained, it was not right to neglect him, that Great Being, his heart drawn by compassion, approached the edge of the precipice. There he saw him, the splendor of whose armor had been crushed by contact with the dust, whose turban, garments, and mail were in disarray, and whose heart was being tormented by the pains arising from the impact of the fall, having fallen into a state of utter despair.
Seeing the lord of men writhing there, his eyes overflowing with tears,
he forgot the notion of him being an enemy under the power of compassion and came to share in the commonality of that suffering.
And he spoke to him, manifesting the natural disposition of virtuous people characterized by humility,
consoling him with clear words, gentle speech, and charming courtesy befitting the refined.
"O Great King, I hope you are not distressed, having fallen into this abyss;
I hope your limbs are not wounded here, and that your pains are subsiding."
"O best of men, though I am no human being, I am a deer dwelling within your domain;
since I have grown old on your grass and water, you ought to place your trust in me."
"Do not lose heart because of this fall from the precipice; I am capable of rescuing you from here.
If you think I am to be trusted, then command me what I should do while I return."
Then that king, his heart captivated by wonder at those extraordinary words of his, feeling a sense of shame arising within him, fell into this reflection:
"What kind of compassion can he have for me, when I am his avowed enemy? And what is this offense of mine against him, who is innocent?"
"Alas! I have been repulsed by a deed that is both sweet and sharp;
I am merely a deer or a cow, while he is some being in the form of a śarabha."
Having decided, "Therefore, he deserves the honor of accepting my affection," he said to him:
"This body of mine, covered by this armor, is not severely wounded;
moreover, the pains caused by the impact of the fall are indeed endurable for me."
"I am not so afflicted by the hardships of falling from a precipice as I am by this stumbling toward you, whose heart is virtuous. (Jm 25.16)
And as for the fact that you were seen by me in the forest as a deer due to the perception of your form—
do not take that to heart, for it was because I did not recognize your true nature.

Then Śarabha, perceiving that the king’s extraction was approved by that speech indicative of his pleasure, and having made himself capable of lifting him by a discipline heavy with human strength, and knowing the measure of his own power, resolved in his mind to lift the monarch; he descended from that precipice, approached him with humility, and said:
"Please endure for this moment the touch of my body out of regard for the task at hand,
while I, through the pursuit of my own welfare, turn your face toward joy and serene confidence. (Jm 25.18)
"Then let the Great King mount my back, and may he be firmly seated upon me. Having assented with "So be it," the king mounted him as one would mount a horse.
Then, with his forequarters raised high, the king was carried by him.
Rising up with the impetuosity of a supreme being, he shone in the sky like a gargoyle upon an archway.
Then, having rescued that king from his distress and brought him back on horseback, he joyfully showed him the way to his own city and turned his face toward the forest retreat.
Then that king, his heart won over by that humble and sweet service of his out of gratitude, embraced Śarabha and said:
"Śarabha, these very lives of mine are yours, let alone that over which I have sovereignty.
Therefore, you ought to see this city of mine; if it pleases you, let your dwelling be there."
In this forest, crowded with hunters and full of danger, where there is the suffering of afflictions such as cold, heat, and rain,
it would surely be improper for me to go alone toward home, leaving you behind.
"Come, let us go.
Then the Bodhisattva, pleasing him with a modest and sweet demeanor, replied:
"O best of men, such conduct as this is indeed appropriate for those like you who are fond of virtue."
For through the practice of yoga, the virtues of a virtuous person indeed become his very nature.

Since you consider me, who am accustomed to the forest, to be worthy of favor by providing me with shelter in your palace, that is enough; for the happiness of men is of one kind, while that of deer is of another, suited to their own nature.
"O hero, if you truly desire to do what is pleasing to me, then renounce this vow of a hunter;
for compassion alone is fitting toward these pitiable deer, who are dull-witted and born as animals."
Understand that all beings have an equal desire for the basis of happiness and the removal of suffering;
therefore, that which you would not wish for yourself, you ought not to inflict upon others. (Jm 25.26)

Having recognized that the loss of reputation, the censure of virtuous people, and the suffering born of sin all arise from evil, uproot that evil as you would an enemy faction; it is not fitting for you to neglect it, as if it were a disease.

Since it is by relying on those very merits that you have attained this kingship, esteemed by the world and the abode of Fortune, you should cause those merits to increase further; for one must never diminish the side of those who have rendered assistance.

Accumulate merits— the means to fame and happiness— through abundant gifts made auspicious by being given at the proper time, through virtuous conduct, through the resolve to associate with holy men, and by achieving the realization of a mind that regards all beings as oneself.

Thus that Great Being, having firmly assisted the king in matters concerning the life hereafter and having his words accepted by him, entered that very edge of the forest while being gazed upon with great respect by the king. Therefore, it should be stated in the description of compassion that those of great mercy feel pity even for one who seeks to kill them when he is in distress, and do not neglect him; likewise, this applies to the majesty of the Tathāgata and to listening to the Dharma with reverence.
This should also be applied when discussing patience (*kṣānti*) as a demonstration of the pacification of enmity through the absence of enmity.
Thus, even among those of great soul who have gone to the animal realm, a compassionate disposition is seen even toward their own slayers.

What person, having become human or having taken the vow of renunciation, could find it fitting to be devoid of compassion for sentient beings? Therefore, a noble one should be compassionate toward living creatures.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth Jātaka, the Śarabha-jātaka.
26. The Ruru-jātaka.
To the virtuous, the suffering of others alone is suffering;
for they cannot endure that, but not their own suffering.
As it is heard in tradition:

It is said that the Bodhisattva [dwelt] in a forest thick with *sāla*, *bakula*, *piyāla*, *hintāla*, *tamāla*, *naktamāla*, *vidula*, and *nicula* trees; dense with groves of *śiṃśapā*, *tiniśa*, *śamī*, *palāśa*, *śāka*, *kuśa*, bamboo, and reeds; filled with *kadamba*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, *khadira*, and *kuṭaja* trees; where many tree branches were shrouded by the spreading tendrils of various creepers;
and frequented by deer such as the *ruru*, *pṛṣata*, *sṛmara*, *camara*, elephant, *gavaya*, buffalo, *hariṇa*, *nyaṅku*, boar, *dvīpin*, hyena, tiger, wolf, lion, and bear.
In a vast wilderness region of forest, devoid of human traffic, there was a deer with a body brilliant with the color of refined gold and soft fur;
its variegated limbs were illuminated by spots of various beautiful colors resembling ruby, sapphire, emerald, and beryl;
it had large, clear, and glossy deep-blue eyes, and its horns, hooves, and the regions of its face possessed a smooth luster as if made of jewels.
Possessing a form of supreme beauty, he became a ruru deer moving on foot like a walking treasury of jewels.

Knowing the extreme desirability of his own body and the meager compassion of people, he took delight in dense forest thickets where there was no human traffic; and because of his keen discernment, he avoided in every place the mechanical traps, snares, nets, pitfalls, sticky resins, wooden stakes, and baited food prepared by hunters.

Protecting them properly and awakening the following herd of deer, he exercised sovereignty over them like a teacher and like a father. "Where indeed is one not honored among people who seek their own welfare, when they possess the perfection of form and knowledge, refined by excellence in action? (Jm_26.1)

Then, on one occasion, while that Great-souled One had taken up residence in that dense forest, he heard the cry of a man being carried away by a nearby river filled with fresh water and flowing with great force:
"Run to me with speed, you who are compassionate toward the wretched, to rescue this miserable man who is being swept away by the surging flood of the river's current— helpless and without a boat!"
"It is not possible to linger here with my arms rendered powerless by the defect of exhaustion, nor can a firm footing be found anywhere; therefore, this is the time for me to rush forward."

Then the Bodhisattva, as if struck in his very heart by that sound of his piteous crying, uttered a loud human voice—repeated, clearly articulated, and pressed forth with effort—to dispel fear, despondency, wretchedness, and fatigue, words practiced for hundreds of lifetimes: "Do not fear! Do not fear!
And as he spoke, he emerged from that dense forest thicket.
And from afar he saw that man being carried along by the flood of water like a desired gift being brought to him; thereupon,
having resolved to rescue him, he disregarded the danger to his own life.
He plunged into that river of fearsome current, terrifying it as a hero terrifies an enemy army.
Then, blocking his path with his body, he said to him, "Take refuge in me!
Overcome by terror and his limbs failing from exhaustion, the other climbed right onto his back.
Though being swept away by that man and tossed about by the current of the river,
he— his great heroism unshaken due to his exalted nature of being— reached the bank that was favorable to his mind.
Then, having brought that man to the shore and dispelled his exhaustion and suffering with a surge of supreme joy,
and having removed his cold with his own body heat, he showed him the way and dismissed him, saying, "Go."

Then that man, his heart won over by that wonderful readiness to help— so difficult for affectionate kinsmen and friends to find— and his wonder and great respect aroused by the beauty of his form, bowed to him and spoke these kind words:
"Whether as a friend or a kinsman, you have shown me a love accumulated since childhood."
"This deed which you have performed for my sake is not sufficient."
If these very life-breaths of mine, which belong to you, were to be employed for your sake even in the slightest degree, that would be a supreme favor to me.
Therefore, by granting me your command,
you should bestow your favor upon me in whatever matter you perceive me to be capable of fulfilling.
Then the Bodhisattva, wishing to please him, replied:
"Gratitude toward the virtuous is not a matter of outward display; for that disposition is established in them by their very nature.
Yet, seeing the world overcome by moral corruption, even gratitude is today counted among virtues."
Therefore, as I tell you, remembering that this has been accomplished by you, this matter must not be disclosed to anyone, such as by saying, "I have been rescued by such a distinguished being.
For this form of mine is a source of material things and is exceedingly alluring.
Behold:
human hearts are generally characterized by scant compassion and are restless due to abundant fickleness.
Therefore, you ought to protect both your own virtues and me.
For indeed, malice toward friends never leads to prosperity.
And being addressed thus, do not let your heart become embittered by resentment or affection;
for we are but deer, unpracticed in the deceitful arts of human social etiquette. Moreover, that has been done by those skilled in deception, who are experts in false humility.
By which even a person disciplined by his own nature is looked upon with suspicion.
"I desire that this which is being accomplished by you be made dear to me.
Having promised "So be it," and having bowed down and circumambulated that Great Being, he returned to his own home.
Now at that time, a queen of a certain king there possessed dreams that came true.
Whatever extraordinary dream she saw came to pass exactly so;
once, having fallen under the power of sleep for some reason, she beheld at the time of dawn a dream that was like a collection of all kinds of jewels.
She saw him blazing with splendor, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by his retinue including the king Ruru, teaching the Dharma in human speech with clearly articulated syllables and phrasing;
and with her heart struck by wonder, she awoke along with the sound of the drum that heralds her husband’s awakening.
And having approached the king at the appropriate moment, she— having received the honor of his welcome and affection,
her beauty enhanced by eyes wide with wonder, and the loveliness of her cheeks trembling with joy—
beheld the king with that report of her marvelous dream as if it were a gift.
Having respectfully reported that extraordinary dream to the king, he spoke again:
"Therefore, Your Majesty, let an effort be made at once to capture that deer;
let the inner apartments be illuminated by that jewel-deer, as the sky is by the starry deer."

Then that king, having gained conviction from that dream-vision and having accepted her words, out of a desire to please her and out of greed to obtain the jewel-deer, commanded his entire host of hunters to search for that deer. And every day he caused a proclamation to be made in the excellent city:—

"The king bestows upon him who points out that deer— a creature with a golden complexion, its body variegated as if with hundreds of jewels, renowned in the scriptures and seen by some— the finest village, ten beautiful women, and radiant garments. (Jm 26.16)
Then that man, having heard that proclamation again and again—
his mind exhausted by the constant reckoning of the sufferings of poverty, remembering the great benefit of that ruru deer,
and being pulled by that greed he had felt— reflected upon this and that with a wavering heart.
What indeed shall I do?
Shall I look toward virtue or the abundance of wealth?
Shall I maintain my past obligations or attend to the management of my household?
Shall I manifest the next world,
or shall I follow this worldly course?
Shall I pursue prosperity, or rather the prosperity that is beloved by the virtuous?
"I see both the present and the future.

Then, his mind agitated by greed, it occurred to him: "It is possible for one who has acquired vast wealth and prosperity, who is intent on honoring his own kin, friends, guests, and loved ones, and who experiences happiness, to also accomplish the welfare of the next world."
With his mind thus resolved, having forgotten that service rendered by the ruru deer, he approached the king and said: "O King, I know that excellent deer and its dwelling place.
Therefore, command me: to whom shall I show it?
Hearing this, the king, with a delighted heart, said, "My good man, show him to me," and then prepared himself for the hunt.
Assuming a disguise and surrounded by a vast army, he departed from the excellent city and, with the path being shown by that man, arrived at the riverbank.
