Having encircled that dense forest with his entire host, the king— bearing a bow and wearing a leather hand-guard, surrounded by resolute and trusted men, and with the path being shown by that very same man— entered deep into that dense forest.
Then that man, seeing the ruru deer standing there with full confidence, pointed him out to the king, saying: "Here he is, O King, this excellent deer!
Let Your Majesty behold him and exert yourself."
As he raised his arm out of eagerness to see the deer,
his hand fell from his forearm as if it had been severed by a sword.
For when such objects are encountered, having been prepared by specific ritual actions,
those deeds— having gained momentum through the weakening of opposing factors— attain their fruit immediately.
Then, his eyes drawn by curiosity to behold the ruru deer, the king cast them along the path shown by him;
and then, in that forest dark as a fresh cloud, [he saw] a body blazing with the splendor of a treasury of jewels.
He beheld that Ruru, vast in his virtues, like a fire whose roar has been stilled, extinguished by a cloud.
Then the king, his mind captivated by the beauty of that form, out of an intense desire to seize it,
drew his bow with the string bitten by the arrow and ascended it with the intent to split it asunder.

Then the Bodhisattva, hearing the clamor of the people on all sides, became certain in his mind that he was clearly surrounded; yet, perceiving that the king had mounted his horse with the intent to shoot him, and realizing that this was not the time to flee, he addressed the king in human speech with clear words and syllables:
"Wait a moment, O Great King; do not strike me, O bull among men.
You ought to satisfy this curiosity of mine for a while."
"In this dense forest, devoid of human traffic, who indeed informed you that 'this deer is here'? Jm_26.23.

Then that king, his heart deeply moved by that extraordinary human utterance, pointed out that man to him with the tip of an arrow, saying, "This is the one who showed us this most wonderful thing. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, recognizing that man, spoke reproachfully: "Alas!
This proverb is indeed true: 'One who has fallen into the flood of water..."
It is better to uproot a person of ungrateful mind than even a piece of wood.
Such is the recompense for that great exertion;
how is it that even he has not perceived this removal of his own welfare?

Then the king, his curiosity aroused as he wondered, "What indeed is it that he loathes so? and filled with agitation, said to the ruru deer: "Having heard these words of yours—profound in their undisclosed meaning and censured without apparent cause—my mind trembles, as it were. (Jm 26.26)
O preeminent among deer, tell me this: with reference to whom do you speak? Is it a human, a non-human, a bird, or indeed a deer?
The Bodhisattva said:
"O King, this was not merely an expression of contempt, for having understood that this deed was worthy of censure,
I spoke these harsh words so that he might resolve never to do it again."
For who indeed would pour caustic acid upon a wound, or utter harsh words when others have stumbled?
Yet even toward a beloved son, a physician applies treatment because of the power of the disease.

"O best of men, this fear has come upon me because my vehicle was seized by compassion as it was being swept away by the carrying current; indeed, association with the wicked does not lead to prosperity."
Then the king, looking at that man with a sharp, harsh gaze of reproach, said: "Is it true, you wretch, that in the past you were rescued when you had fallen into such a plight?
Then that man, overcome by fear, despair, perspiration, pallor, and dejection, said "It is true" with a voice faint from shame.
Thereupon the king, reviling him with "Shame on you!", fixed an arrow to his bow and said: "Wait a moment, sir!"
If even by such exertion his heart has not been softened,
what is the use of this lowest of men living on, bearing the banner of infamy among those of equal appearance?

Having said this, he clenched his fist and drew his bow for the purpose of killing him. Then the Bodhisattva, his heart overcome by great compassion, stood between them and said to the king: "Enough, enough, Great King! Do not kill one who has already been killed, since this man has already undergone the contemptible deception of the enemy that is greed."
He is destroyed here by the loss of his reputation, and certainly in the next world as well by the destruction of his merit.
Thus do human beings, their minds consumed by the arising of unbearable suffering, fall into calamities;
they are enticed by the hope for an abundance of rewards, like foolish moths lured by the beauty of a lamp.
Therefore, show mercy here and do not be angry; if there is anything at all desired by him, bestow it upon him, for his daring is never in vain, as my head remains bowed toward your command.

(Vaidya 180) Then the king, his mind filled with supreme wonder at that spontaneous compassion shown even toward his wrongdoer and at his earnest desire to repay that kindness, was moved to faith; looking up at the noble ruru deer with great respect, he said:
"Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one!"
Since you possess such compassion even when faced with manifest and violent injury,
you are a human by virtue of your qualities, while we are merely humans in appearance.

"Since this fool is worthy of your compassion and is the cause for our meeting with a virtuous person, I shall grant him his desired object; he may move about as he pleases within this kingdom of yours."
Ruru said, "I have accepted this fruitful favor from the Great King.
Therefore, give me your command so that we may serve you here for whatever purpose brings us together.
Then the king, having placed Ruru upon his excellent chariot like a preceptor, led him into the noble city with great honor.

Having honored him as a guest and seated him upon a great throne, the king— encircled by his courtiers and accompanied by the ladies of the inner apartments— urged him on and, gazing at him with a gentle expression of affection and high esteem, inquired about the Dharma: "Regarding the Dharma, the intellects of men have proceeded in many different ways."
But you must explain how it is that you possess such certainty regarding the Dharma.
Then the Bodhisattva taught the Dharma to that king and his assembly with words that were clear, sweet, and composed of variegated syllables:
"O King, I consider compassion toward sentient beings to be the Dharma in brief; it consists of various practices, such as the cessation of violence, theft, and other such acts. (Jm 26.38)
Behold, O Great King:

if one were to have compassion for others as one does for oneself, or for one's own kin as for a stranger, whose mind would ever be inauspicious through an inclination toward unrighteousness? (Jm_26.39)
But through the loss of compassion, a person undergoes the utmost transformation,
manifesting through the stirrings of mind, speech, and body toward his own kin just as he does toward a stranger.
One who seeks the Dharma should not abandon compassion, which brings about the arising of desired fruits;
for it gives birth to virtues, just as a good rain produces crops.
A mind overcome by compassion does not become impetuous toward harming others; when it is pure, neither speech nor body ever undergoes distortion.
Thus, his delight in the welfare of others increases, following after joy.
He produces virtues such as generosity and patience that are consistent with his reputation.
The compassionate person, through tranquility, does not cause agitation in others; being full of mercy, he becomes trustworthy to all the world like a kinsman.
Agitation caused by impetuosity does not prevail in a heart made steadfast by compassion;
for the fire of anger does not blaze in a mind cooled by the water of mercy.
In brief, the Buddhas perceive the Dharma through compassion with steadfastness.
What virtue indeed is beloved by the virtuous that has not been followed by compassion?
Therefore, having brought compassion to its highest excellence toward all people, as toward a son or even oneself—
Captivating the minds of all people with your virtuous conduct, manifest your sovereignty.
Then that king, having fully rejoiced at those words of his, together with his courtiers and the people of the realm, became devoted to the Dharma;
and he granted safety to all beasts and birds.
Thus, for the virtuous, the suffering of others is indeed their own suffering.
For they do not tolerate even their own suffering;
this should also be stated in the description of compassion,
and it may likewise be applied in the praise of the greatness of the virtuous and the censure of the wicked.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth Jātaka, the Ruru Deer Jātaka.
27. The Jātaka of the Great Monkey:
Those who follow the path of virtuous conduct win over even the minds of their enemies.

It is thus heard: the Bodhisattva, it is said, was once in the glorious lap of the Himalayas, in a region of land embraced by many excellent medicinal herbs possessing various qualities of taste, potency, and post-digestive effect, and strewn with hundreds of trees whose branches, leaves, shoots, and fruits were arranged in diverse patterns.
In that place, where crystal-clear streams flowed like pure pieces of rock crystal and which resounded with the cries of various flocks of birds, he became the leader of a troop of monkeys.

Even in such a state, envy, malice, and cruelty—though opposed by his practice of renunciation and compassion—did not overcome him, just as adversaries cannot prevail over one who cultivates their opposites.
There, he beheld a great banyan tree that, like a mountain peak, seemed to scrape the very heavens, appearing like a sovereign lord.

He took up residence, relying upon that forest whose branches were shrouded in deep darkness like a mass of clouds due to their dense foliage, and whose boughs were bent down by extraordinary fruits that were larger than palm nuts, supremely delicious, and possessed of charming color and fragrance;
for even among those who have fallen to the state of animals, the residue of merit surely serves as a basis for happiness.
It was like the remaining wealth of friends who have departed for a foreign land, which must be preserved for the sake of what remains to be done.
Now, one branch of that lord of the forest was bent down toward a river flowing nearby.
Then, because of his far-sightedness, the Bodhisattva instructed that troop of monkeys: "As long as this banyan branch remains unfruitful, none of you shall consume fruit from any other source.
Later, on that branch, there grew a single fruit—small due to its youth and covered by a leaf-cup made by ants—which those monkeys did not see.
Growing gradually in that manner, endowed with color, fragrance, flavor, and softness, it became loose in its binding through the process of ripening and fell into that river.
Carried along by the current of the river in due course, it became entangled near a fishing basket belonging to a certain king who was enjoying water-sports in that river together with his harem.
It was there, mingled with the scents of the women’s bathing powders, garlands, perfumes, and unguents.
He surpassed [all others] with his own pervasive excellence, which was pleasing to the sense of smell.
Intoxicated by that fragrance, those women, their eyes narrowed by long-drawn sighs,
cast their glances in all directions with restless curiosity.

But those women, their eyes extremely restless as they were drawn by curiosity, beheld that banyan fruit— which was larger in size than a fully ripe palm fruit— clinging to the side of the basket; and with their eyes fixed upon it, they became filled with wonder, "What is this?", together with the king.
Then the king, having had that fruit brought, tasted it himself after it had been examined by trustworthy physicians; he was struck with wonder at its extraordinary flavor,
as if by a marvelous quality inherent in its preparation.
Filled with wonder at her unprecedented complexion and fragrance,
he experienced an even greater transformation of astonishment through his intense passion for her taste.

Then, although that king was accustomed to food of delicious flavor, he fell under the sway of his passion for that particular taste and thought to himself: "Who indeed eats these fruits—who eats the true fruits of sovereignty?
For even without the toil of kingship, this man here has such food as this."

With his mind intent on searching for its source, he reflected with his own intellect: "Clearly, this excellent tree is not far from here and is situated on the bank of a river; for such is its fruit—possessing unimpaired color, fragrance, and flavor, and being uninjured and unwithered due to its long-time contact with water. Therefore, its origin can certainly be discovered. Having reached this conclusion, he was drawn by a thirst for its taste.
Having ceased his water-sports and properly given instructions for the security of his excellent city, he followed that river, surrounded by a great army equipped for the expedition;
and in due course, clearing away the dense forest thickets teeming with beasts of prey, he experienced various kinds of flavors.
Beholding the forest interiors with their unartificial and lovely splendor, and terrifying the wild elephants and deer with the resounding blasts of his kettledrums,
he approached the vicinity of that lord of trees— a place inaccessible to human beings—
which, though near a mountain, appeared like a mountain itself, heavy with water like a mass of clouds.
From afar, the king beheld that lord of trees, who appeared like a sovereign emperor gazed upon by all other trees.

As if welcomed by an exceedingly sweet, pervasive, and most enchanting fragrance more fragrant than that of a fully ripened mango fruit, he reached the certainty that "this is that very tree," and having approached it, he beheld its branches crowded with hundreds of monkeys busily occupied with consuming its fruit.
Then the king, his mind filled with rage toward those monkeys who were depriving him of his desired object, cried out: "Kill them! Kill them!"
"Destroy them! Annihilate all these wretched monkeys! he commanded his own men with harsh words.

Then those royal officers, their hands busy with strung bows and arrows, shouting threats against the monkeys, and others with clods of earth, sticks, and weapons raised, rushed toward that lord of the forest, desiring to besiege it as if it were a hostile fortress.

Then the Bodhisattva, beholding that tumultuous royal army— which, like the ocean waters lashed by the force of the wind, was filled with the unrestrained clamor of shouting men— and seeing the excellent tree being scattered on all sides as if by a rain of thunderbolts, while the host of monkeys looked up with distorted and dejected faces, intent only on wailing piteously in fear under a rain of arrows, clods, sticks, and weapons, his heart was overcome by great compassion; he cast off all despondency, wretchedness, and terror.
Having comforted that troop of monkeys and resolved his mind upon their rescue, he climbed to the summit of that tree and desired to leap across to the nearby mountain slope.
Then, although that mountain slope was reachable only by many successive bounds, that Great Being, through the excellence of his own prowess, leaped up to it like a bird.
That distance could not be traversed by other monkeys even by both methods of leaping;
yet the swift one crossed it with such speed that it seemed like a mere trifle in a single bound.
His resolve, nourished by compassion, attained proficiency through valor;
and he exerted a special effort for him, yet through the intensity of his mental application, he surpassed that effort.

Having climbed to a higher region of the mountain, he firmly bound his feet with a large, thickly grown, strong rattan vine that was greater in length than the distance between them and possessed firm roots;
then he leaped once more toward that lord of the forest.
However, because of the great distance of the interval and his preoccupation with binding his feet, that Great Being somehow managed to reach the topmost branch of that tree with both hands.
Then, firmly grasping a branch and stretching out that cane-staff with effort, he commanded his troop by means of a signal: "Therefore, descend quickly from this tree."
Then those monkeys, finding a path of escape due to their agitation with fear, fled away with extremely swift steps, free from any apprehension of being attacked by him; yet,

though his body was incessantly assailed by the feet of those monkeys who were frantic with fear, it was deprived of its own flesh, but his mind— by virtue of its extraordinary fortitude— was not at all.

Seeing this, the king and those royal officers were struck with the utmost astonishment and wonder at such a perfection of valor and intelligence, as well as at his selflessness and compassion for others.
It would produce a sense of wonder even when merely heard; how much more so when being seen directly?

Then the king commanded those men: "This lord of monkeys is clearly exhausted from having his body wounded by the trampling feet of the monkey troops fleeing in terror, and from standing for a long time on a single leg; he will not be able to withdraw himself from here by his own power.
Therefore, quickly spread a cloth canopy beneath him, and let this banyan branch, which is entangled with creepers, be cut off simultaneously with two arrows."
They did so.
Then the king, having gently lowered him from the canopy, laid him upon a soft bed as his mind was overwhelmed by a fainting fit born of the pain of his wounds and exhaustion.

Having anointed his wounds with ghee and other substances suitable for immediately soothing fresh injuries, and finding him refreshed and his fatigue diminished, the king approached him with curiosity, wonder, and great respect.
After first inquiring about his welfare, he said:
"Having gone there yourself and, disregarding your own life, having devoured these monkeys, you have rescued them; who indeed are you to them, or who are they to you? (Jm 27.13)
O foremost of monkeys, if we are worthy to hear this, then please tell it;
for the minds of those whose bonds of affection are slight do not readily incline toward such an act.
Then the Bodhisattva, honoring the king’s readiness to assist him, made his self-offering in a fitting manner:
"The burden of sovereignty has been placed upon me by these men, who are skillful in carrying out my commands.
With a heart bound to them as if they were my own sons, I have set out to bear that very burden."

"O Great King, this kinship between me and these men has been established for a long time; and my friendship, consisting of our common birth, arose from being born as kinsmen and through the connection of living together."
Having heard that, the king was struck with great wonder and spoke to him again:
"The ministers and others are for the sake of the sovereign; the lord of the earth does not exist for their sake."
Why, then, did you sacrifice yourself for the sake of your own servant?
The Bodhisattva said: "It is true, Great King, that such is the conduct of royal policy; however, it appears to me to be difficult to follow."
It is exceedingly difficult to endure even the unbearable, intense suffering of a stranger;
how much more so for a person whose mind is intent on devotion and who has attained the status of a beloved kinsman.
And seeing this distress, suffering, and wretchedness of the monkeys increasing before me— an obstacle to the opportunity for reflecting on my own affairs— sorrow suddenly rushed upon me.
Seeing bows being bent, with blazing arrows flying forth from their bowstrings that resounded with a terrifying sound,
I disregarded them and out of haste went from this tree to this mountain.

Then, being dragged away by my own kinsmen whose minds were overcome with the fear peculiar to the Vaiśeṣikas, I fastened a cane-stick— whose length was measured and which had firm roots— to my two feet.
I leaped once more from that mountain in order to rescue my companions to this tree;
then, with both hands, I grasped its foremost branch as it was extended toward me, like an outstretched hand.
"By means of that creeper with its outstretched limbs and by the trunk of this tree with its hand-like branches,
these members of my own herd have relied upon me and reached safety, free from fear of being attacked by lions."
Then that king, observing the Great Being even in that state to be born of joy, and bearing the utmost wonder, spoke to him again:
"Disregarding his own happiness, he has brought upon himself the calamity of another's misfortune."
Having thus attributed this to yourself, what benefit have you obtained?
The Bodhisattva said:
"O King, though my body is wounded, my mind has attained supreme well-being;
for I have turned back the suffering of those over whom I have long exercised sovereignty."
Just as heroes, having conquered their arrogant enemies in battle, bear the beauty of the marks of their valor upon their limbs like ornaments, so do I bear this pain with joy.
Today I have attained freedom from my debt for this succession of pleasures, obtained through my sovereignty by those of equal birth, preceded by prostrations and honors and offered with devotion.
Therefore, this conjunction of sufferings—this separation from friends or this ruin of happiness—does not distress me;
for by this very process, death has arrived as a great festival.

From the quality of gratitude comes the repayment of past favors, self-satisfaction, the pacification of distress, stainless fame, honor from kings, fearlessness even toward death, and being accepted among the virtuous.
"O tree that is the abode of excellent virtues, it is by attaining these very qualities that I have fallen into this calamity;
for a king devoid of compassion toward those who seek his protection encounters the opposites of these virtues."

For one who is devoid of virtues, whose reputation has perished, and who has made his home of the arising of faults— what other destination could there be for him than the fires of hell, teeming with flames?
O you of renowned power, I have thus shown you the influence of these virtues and faults;
therefore, govern the kingdom according to Dharma, for Fortune is indeed characterized by a fickle affection like that of a woman.

Like a father, the king should strive with beneficial and agreeable means to employ for his own welfare all those who are dependent upon him: the draft animals, the army, the provincial subjects, the ministers, the citizens, the destitute, the ascetics, and the twice-born.
Thus indeed shall there be for you the prosperity of dharma, wealth, and fame, leading to happiness both in this world and the next;
O King of Men, rule as a royal sage through this royal splendor acquired by compassion for your subjects.
Having thus instructed the king like a disciple with great effort and many words of counsel,
he abandoned his body— its functions withdrawn by the onset of illness— and went to the third heaven.
Thus, those who follow virtuous conduct win over even the minds of their enemies;
therefore, one who desires to win over the world must follow virtuous conduct.
Furthermore, it should also be stated in the praise of the Tathāgata: "Sentient beings are not capable of accomplishing even their own welfare as the Blessed One accomplished the welfare of others."
Regarding the respectful hearing of the Dharma, the praise of compassion, and the instruction of kings:
in this way, a king should be filled with compassion toward his subjects;
this should also be applied to the discourse on gratitude.
"In this way, the virtuous become grateful.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh Jātaka, the Mahākapi-jātaka.
28. The Birth Story of Kṣānti: For those who have made forbearance their very nature and possess great discernment, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be endured.
Thus it is heard:

the Bodhisattva, perceiving that [the world] was afflicted by manifold faults and calamities, was not conducive to tranquility because it prioritized wealth and sensual desire; it was a place where the dust of defects such as passion, hatred, delusion, resentment, agitation, intoxication, pride, and envy descended and settled;
it was a site for the abandonment of the virtue of shame and a stronghold for the grasping at greed and what is false; and because it was crowded with evil deeds, there was little room for [virtue].

Having understood the nature of dharma, and perceiving that the life of a householder involves the abandonment of possessions and sense objects as well as the pleasure found in solitude from their faults,
he became an ascetic whose mind was disciplined by virtue, learning, tranquility, and self-restraint.

Because his undertaking was never faltering and because he spoke in praise of patience, the world— having passed over his actual name and lineage and following its own judgment— came to know him simply as "Kṣāntivādin" (the Preacher of Patience).
The abundance of sovereignty, knowledge, and ascetic power, as well as attachment to the arts once they have been mastered,
and the various transformations of body, speech, and gesture, produce another name for men.

Knowing the power of the virtue of patience, and desiring to adorn the world with that very strength of his own, he spoke discourses on patience incessantly; therefore, he became known as Kṣāntivādin.
His great patience, which was his very nature, remained unshaken by the injuries of others;
and specific discourses concerning that [patience] spread the fame of that Sage far and wide.

Then that Great-souled One, by his mere presence, brought to a state of auspiciousness a forest region that was secluded and delightful, where flowers and fruits were easily obtained in all seasons, which possessed clear reservoirs of water adorned with lotuses and water-lilies, and which was beautiful with the charm of a pleasure garden; for wherever virtuous men adorned with excellent qualities reside,
that very place becomes a sacred ford, charming and auspicious— a true grove of penance.

Honored there and approached by the various deities dwelling in that place, as well as by a crowd of people who were seekers of the highest good and lovers of virtue, he bestowed the greatest favor upon that assembly of people through righteous discourses connected with patience, which gladden both the ear and the heart.

Then once, due to the influence of the summer season, the king of that region— his mind longing for the most desirable water-sports— went together with his harem to that forest region, which served as a dwelling place for the excellence of garden virtues.
He [beheld] that forest, possessing a beauty as delightful as the Nandana grove, filled with the beauties of the harem.
Moving with playful grace, he seemed to adorn himself with a charming and magnificent deportment.
In the regions of celestial palaces, in vine-covered bowers, among trees laughing with blossoms,
and in waters where lotuses had opened, he took delight in the extraordinary natural graces of his wives.

Seeing some women being massaged with garlands, perfumes, baths, and ointments, their beauty enhanced by the grace of playful smiles and the humming of bees agitated by the fragrance of their delightful scents, he was moved to a smile.

Just as those women found no satisfaction with flowers— despite their ear-ornaments of fresh beauty and their hair adorned with abundant garlands— likewise the King found no such satisfaction with their charms.
The king beheld the rows of women’s eyes, which, like bees, were clinging to the palaces, lingering over the lotus-pools, and hovering among the flowering trees.
Even the cries of the cuckoos bold with passion, the dances of the peacocks,
and the songs of the bees did not delight there, eclipsed by the chatter, dancing, and singing of the women.
With their plumage spread and their cries raised by the drums sounding like the thundering of clouds,
the peacocks performed service for the king, as if bowing through the excellence of their own sweet notes.

There, having experienced to his heart's content the pleasures of sporting in the gardens and groves within the inner apartments, he fell under the power of sleep while reclining on a costly couch in a magnificent part of the palace, due to the exhaustion from his indulgence in play and the embrace of intoxication. Then those women, perceiving that the king had entered a state of repose, their hearts drawn toward the beauty of the forest and insatiable in their longing to behold it, [proceeded to do so].
Gathering together according to their mutual affection, they spread out in every direction with soft chatter mingled with the confused tinkling of their ornaments;
they were accompanied by parasols, fly-whisks, seats, and other items held by female attendants, all adorned with variegated golden inlays.
Followed by the emblems of sovereignty, the women moved about unrestrainedly according to their own natures.

Having reached them, they disregarded the efforts of the female attendants and, out of greed, seized for themselves by their own prowess the forms of the trees— the beautiful flowers and the tender shoots.

Although they already possessed abundant flower-ornaments and garlands, they did not pass by the shrubs delightful with blossoms and the trees with swaying shoots found along the path without plucking them out of longing.
Then those royal women, their hearts captivated by the loveliness of the forest, wandered through that grove and arrived at the hermitage of Kṣāntivādin.

Because they were well-acquainted with the greatness of the power of that sage’s asceticism, and because he was difficult to approach due to his status as a favorite of the king, the women in charge of the ladies did not venture to restrain them. Drawn, as it were, by the splendor of the hermitage, which was made even more delightful by human artifice, those women entered the hermitage grounds.

There they beheld that best of sages, seated at the foot of a tree in the bound posture (baddhāsana), his appearance serene with tranquility, difficult to approach due to his extreme profundity, and as if blazing with the splendor of asceticism; through his devotion to meditation, he possessed the beauty of unshaken sensory restraint even amidst the proximity of noble objects of sense, appearing like the auspicious Dharma itself, a holy sight to behold.

Then those royal women, their very beings overcome by the splendor of his asceticism, cast off all coquetry, dalliance, and haughtiness at the mere sight of him; approaching him with humble composure, they sat around him in attendance.

He, for his part, having first offered kind words such as a welcome, performed the hospitable rites that delight guests; and then, through discourses illustrated by examples—designed for easy comprehension by women and introduced by their own inquiries—he extended to them the hospitality of the Dharma.
Having obtained this irreproachable human birth, with its full integrity and keen faculties,
he who— being subject to inevitable death— does not perform wholesome deeds while indulging in negligence, is deceived day after day.
No one, whether by lineage, beauty, the qualities of youth, excellence of strength, or the acquisition of wealth,
attains happiness in the next world unless they are refined by virtues such as generosity and moral conduct.
For even one who is destitute of noble birth and the like, if he is free from desire for evil and possesses virtues such as generosity and moral conduct,
he will certainly be pursued by happiness in the next world, just as the ocean is filled by the waters of the rivers at the coming of the rainy season.

Whether it be of one’s lineage, physical form, the quality of youth, excellence of strength, or the height of wealth—here too, the practice of ornamentation is merely respect for these qualities; yet the golden garland is indeed an indicator of prosperity.
Trees are adorned with flowers; clouds hanging with water are adorned by streaks of lightning;
lakes are adorned by lotuses and by intoxicated bees; and embodied beings are adorned by virtues that have been attained to an exceptional degree.

This diversity among people—distinguished as inferior, middling, or superior by way of health, lifespan, wealth, beauty, and birth—is certainly not due to their own nature nor does it depend on anything else; rather, it is threefold, arising from karma.

Having thus understood that the condition of the world is fixed, and that life is unstable and prone to destruction, abandon all evils with a mind intent on the succession of wholesome deeds; for this is the path to fame and happiness.
But mental malice proceeds like a fire that utterly consumes the welfare of both oneself and others;
therefore, a person who fears sin should avoid it with effort by resorting to its opposite.
Just as even a blazing fire, upon reaching a great river whose waters touch its banks,
attains a state of peaceful extinction, so too does one who possesses a mind radiant with patience find tranquility when relying on patience, which is capable of enduring both worlds.
Thus, through patience, one avoids evil because its causes are overcome;
and for this reason, by the power of relying on loving-kindness, one does not give rise to enmity.
Because of this, he becomes beloved and worthy of honor, and partakes in happiness;
then, at the end, by virtue of his reliance on merit, he goes to heaven as if to his own home.
Moreover, ladies, this so-called "patience" is renowned as the excellence of a pure nature; it is the supreme increase of merit and fame.
It is a purity produced by contact with iron [in the crucible], and through various floods of virtues, it is the highest prosperity.

The firm resolve of the virtuous, who are always unacquainted with obstructing others, is pleasing to the mind; patience, which produces beautiful qualities and is known through compassion, brings about the welfare of the world.

For those rich in austerity who are endowed with power, patience is the foremost excellence of strength; it is an ornament, a stream of water for the forest fire of malice, and the pacification of misfortune both in this world and the next.
Upon the armor of patience worn by virtuous people, the arrows of the wicked's words are blunted;
for the most part, they turn into flowers of praise and become components of the garlands of their fame.
They say that patience destroys the illusion that is the opposite of the Dharma, and likewise brings about the liberation that is true happiness;
therefore, who would not exert effort in patience, which is capable of bringing about absolute welfare?
Thus that Great-souled One offered them the hospitality of the Dharma.

Then the king, having awakened from his slumber and fatigue, his eyes still heavy with the remnants of intoxication, asked the bed-chamber attendants with a frown, "Where are the queens? Having learned from the attendants that they were adorning the forest glades and beholding their splendor, he [proceeded there].

That king, his mind eager to behold the unrestrained laughter, conversation, and playful movements of the women in confidence, rose from his bed and wandered through that grove, followed by the attendants of the inner apartments who carried umbrellas, fans, upper garments, and swords, and who held cane staves along with chamberlains.
Following there a path strewn with various clusters of flowers and sprouts, fashioned by the modesty of young women and variegated by the hue of betel-juice, he approached that hermitage.

But as soon as the king saw that eminent sage Kṣāntivādin surrounded by a host of deities, he fell into a state of supreme rage due to the fault of his lingering resentment from former enmity, because his memory was clouded by intoxication, and because his mind was overcome by envy.

And due to a deficiency in the power of discernment, his excellence in the practice of discipline was lost; overcome by agitation and evil, he was afflicted with perspiration, discoloration, and trembling; his eyes were narrowed, squinted, rolling, fixed, and deeply copper-red;
the beauty of his luster and charm had faded; and he rubbed his two hands, which bore finger-ornaments, so that his golden bracelets swayed.
Insulting that most excellent sage, he spoke these various words: "Ho there!
Who is this who, having humiliated our splendor, looks upon our inner apartments while disguised in the garb of a muni? He behaves like a hunter!"
Hearing this, the eunuchs, filled with agitation and alarm, said to the king, "Your Majesty, do not say such a thing!

This sage named Kṣāntivādin has cultivated his soul through vows, observances, and austerities accumulated over a long time. However, because his own resolute intention was impaired, the king did not accept their words and said, "Alas, how tragic!"
For a long time now, this world has been thus deceived by him through his hypocritical crookedness, assuming the guise of an ascetic like a jar filled with water.

"Therefore, I shall now reveal his deceitful nature, which is concealed by the garb of an ascetic and nourished by trickery," he said; then, seizing a sword from the hand of the female door-keeper, he approached that excellent sage with the firm resolve to kill him as if he were an enemy.
Then those queens, seeing the king—whose gentle demeanor was completely eclipsed by rage—upon learning of his arrival through their attendants, [beheld him].
With hearts expanded with joy, their eyes trembling with agitation and haste, they rose and saluted that best of sages;
then, with hands folded like buds in respectful greeting, they approached the king like autumn lotus ponds with a single cluster of lotus-buds rising from them.
Such was the grace of their conduct, their playful charm, and their refined modesty.
He could not pacify his mind, which was ablaze with the fire of anger.

But those goddesses, having regained their full range of vital strength, beheld the king as he rushed forward with weapon in hand, his movements harsh with the agitation of fury, his gaze turned and fixed upon that best of seers; shielding him, they said: "O King, do not, indeed, commit such a rash act!"
Thinking, "This Blessed One is a teacher of forbearance," the king, however, out of a malicious disposition, concluded that they had surely been won over by him; thus falling into even greater anger,
he rebuked their bold familiarity with harsh, sidelong glances, his brows knit and his eyes sharp with the onset of indignation.
Looking at the women's attendants with a wrathful gaze, his earrings and the branches of his crown shaking as he nodded his head, he looked toward those women and said:
"He speaks of forbearance, yet he does not actually practice it."
For indeed, he has not yet endured the thirst for contact with women.
His speech is one thing, his bodily movements quite another, and his mind, harboring evil intent, is yet another;
who is this man of unrestrained soul sitting so calmly in the penance grove, his intellect clouded by the ostentation of hypocritical vows?

Then those queens, their affection repelled by that king whose heart was hardened by the fury of his rage, and perceiving both the cruelty and the intractability of that monarch, found their minds overcome by despondency and dejection; being driven away by hand gestures from the women’s quarters by officials agitated by fear and despair.
With their faces bowed in shame, they departed from that place while lamenting for the best of sages:

"Who knows what kind of display of transformation the King’s wrath might unleash upon this self-controlled ascetic—renowned for his virtues and free from fault—even though he acted for our sake? By what path might it go forth?"
A king might indeed equally destroy the livelihood of the lord of the earth, his acquired fame, this body of the sage which is a body of austerity, these elephants of ours, and our very minds.
When those queens had thus departed, intent only on lamenting and sighing, the king, threatening that eminent ṛṣi, drew his sword in the grip of rage and began to cut him down himself.
Observing that great being—who remained unchangingly firm, unperturbed, and composed in his movements even as he was being approached—he spoke to him with even greater fury:
"Just as you have been brought to this extreme state by your adherence to the life of a mendicant ascetic..."
Assuming a display of hypocrisy, he even looks at me like a sage.

Then the Bodhisattva, his fortitude unshaken by his long-standing cultivation of patience, beheld for a moment that king— who, through his treatment of such disrespect, displayed deformed gestures of rage and agitation, whose splendor of disciplined conduct had perished, and who had forgotten the path of his own welfare and harm— and filled with wonder, he felt compassion and, wishing to console him, spoke these certain words:
Even this conjunction of dishonor, born from the fault of my own misfortune, is seen in the world; therefore, I have no anxiety over it.
But my grief is this: that toward you, who have approached me with such propriety, I cannot perform even in speech the conduct due to you as is fitting.
Moreover, O Great King,
for those like you who act for the benefit of the world and seek to restrain those who have entered upon an evil course,
it is not appropriate to act with haste; rather, the path of reflection should also be followed, for that is the proper way.
Even that which is improper may appear as proper, and even that which is improper may appear otherwise;
the true nature of an action is not perceived immediately without careful reflection upon the specific causes.
Having deliberated upon a task and understood it according to reality, and having undertaken it through righteousness and the path of policy,
a king who accomplishes the great goals of dharma, artha, and kama for his people does not suffer loss because of those very actions.

Therefore, O Mind, having restrained this excessive fickleness, you ought to practice only such actions as bring renown; for transgressions in conduct that were never seen before cause even those of distinguished character to fall into disrepute.

O Lord of the Earth, how can you yourself resolve upon that which destroys the succession of welfare, which is censured by the noble, and which you would not tolerate if it were committed by another in a penance grove protected by the prowess of your own arm?

If women, along with the guards of the inner apartments, were to come to my hermitage by chance, what transgression would there be for us in that? For you have been brought to such a state of agitation only through anger.
Even if this were indeed my fault, O King, forbearance would still befit you;
for forbearance is the supreme ornament of one who possesses power, as it indicates the purity of one’s devotion to virtue.

The various splendors of the jewel on his crest are no less able to adorn the king than the blue earrings with their shimmering luster upon his cheeks; therefore, you ought not to despise her, thinking she is unworthy.

Abandon intolerance, which is ever incapable of providing refuge; you ought to protect forbearance as if it were forbearance itself. For the conduct of lords of the earth, when directed toward those rich in asceticism, is tender with great respect.
Although he was thus being entreated by that best of sages, the king— his mind corrupted by dishonesty and suspecting him otherwise— spoke again:
"If you do not wear the disguise of an ascetic, or if you remain steadfast in your own vows of discipline;..."
Why do you seek freedom from fear from me, who am occupied with the teaching and exposition of forbearance?
The Bodhisattva said: "Listen, O Great King, to the purpose of this my effort:
'The king has slain an innocent man who had gone forth as a renunciant'—let not such a reputation, marred by scandalous talk, accrue to you because of me. (Jm 28.49)
"It is a fixed rule for all living beings that they must die;
therefore, I have no fear of this, as I observe my own conduct."
"Lest there be any harm to the Dharma that results in future happiness,
I have spoken thus to you regarding forbearance, which is capable of leading to the highest good."
Because it is a mine of virtues and a warder-off of faults,
and out of affection for this extraordinary gift, I forgive you.
Then that king, disregarding even those sweet and truthful words of the sage as if they were mere flowers of speech, spoke with malice to that best of ṛṣis:

"We shall now see your devotion to forbearance. Having said this, for the sake of warding him off, he severed with a sharp sword the right hand of the sage—which had been slightly extended and raised with its long, slender fingers outstretched—just as one might sever a lotus from its stalk.
Yet, even when his hand was severed, there was no suffering for him who was firm in his vow of patience;
he felt no pain as he contemplated the approaching agony of the one who cut him, who himself was accustomed to comfort.

Then the Bodhisattva, thinking, "Alas! This man has transgressed the bounds of his own welfare and has become an unworthy recipient of my affection," remained silent, grieving for him as a physician might for a patient who has rejected his treatment. Then the king, threatening him, spoke again:
"If you do not desist in this way, your body shall meet its destruction."
Abandon this hypocritical vow, which is a deception devised by a wicked mind.
The Bodhisattva, perceiving that he was incapable of being dissuaded and recognizing the intensity of his persistence, said nothing to him.
Then the king likewise cut off the second arm of that Great Being at the shoulder, as well as his ears, nose, and feet.
Even as these sharp weapons fell upon his body, that best of sages felt neither grief nor anger.
He had mastered the mechanism of his own body and was renowned among the people for his patient and compliant conduct.
Even as his limbs were being severed, the mind of that virtuous man remained firm with unbroken patience;
due to his union with joy, he felt no pain, yet seeing the king fallen from righteousness, he experienced deep sorrow.
For those of great discernment whose nature is compassion,
arisen suffering does not afflict them as much as it afflicts others upon whom it has fallen.
Having performed that terrible deed, O King, he was immediately overtaken by a fever as if by fire;
emerging from the edge of the grove, he suddenly entered the gaping earth.

When that king had sunk down, amidst the great clamor arising from the royal palace— which was rent by terrifying sounds and filled with flames of fire— and while it was agitated and thrown into turmoil on all sides, the ministers of that king,

knowing the power and majesty of that sage’s asceticism and considering the sinking of the king into the surface of the earth to have been caused by him, [remembered] that this best of sages in former times...

Thinking, "Because of the king's fault, this entire countryside is being consumed by fire," they became filled with fear and apprehension; approaching that best of sages, bowing down to him, and seeking his forgiveness with palms joined in reverence, they addressed him:
"By which king, through delusion and extreme recklessness, have you been reduced to this state?"
May he alone become the fuel for the fire of your curse; do not consume his city.
"You ought not to burn here women, children, the elderly, the sick, Brahmins, the wretched, and the innocent.
Therefore, O partisan of virtue, it is right that you protect both the territory of that king and your own dharma."

Then the Bodhisattva, comforting them, said: "Do not fear, venerable sirs! Even he who, while I was dwelling in the forest, cut off my hands, feet, ears, and nose with a sword—though I had committed no offense against him—" *Jātaka-mālā* 28.61.
How could even one such as I think of causing him suffering?
May this king live long, and may no evil come upon him.
Who could possibly feel anger toward one who is afflicted by the suffering of death and disease, who is enslaved by greed and hatred,
who is consumed by evil deeds, and who is thus to be pitied?
If this sequence were attainable, then this sin would ripen upon me alone;
for those accustomed to happiness, even a brief succession of suffering becomes unbearable and sharp.
"Since that king, burning away his own welfare in this manner, cannot be saved by me, why should I abandon my own incapacity and harbor resentment toward the king? Jm_28.65.
Even without a king, the suffering of death and so forth must be experienced by everyone who is born;
therefore, one should not tolerate birth itself in this world. If that [birth] does not exist, what suffering could there be, and from where?
Throughout many and countless eons, this little body has perished in manifold ways across successive births;
how could I abandon my endurance for its destruction, as if discarding a heap of jewels for the sake of a blade of grass?

"Dwelling in the forest, having taken the vow of a renunciant, proclaiming forgiveness and soon to die, why should I indulge in intolerance? Therefore, do not fear; may it be well with you, depart! (Jm 28.68)
Thus that best of sages, having instructed them and duly initiated them into the state of good disciples,
ascended from the earth to heaven with unshakable fortitude, supported by patience.

Thus, it should be said, introducing the Sage, in the praise of the virtues of patience: "For those who have made patience their very nature and whose discernment is great, there is nothing that cannot be endured.

And in demonstrating the faults of fickleness and impatience, or in the discourse on the perils of sensual desire, it should be said, introducing the King: "In this way, by indulging in misconduct for the sake of sensual desires, they become partakers of downfall. And likewise, in demonstrating the impermanence of worldly prosperity.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth Jātaka, the Story of Kṣānti.
29. The Brahmajātakam:
Those who have fallen into the calamity of wrong views are especially to be pitied by the virtuous, for wrong views are the most grievous of faults.
As it is heard— this Blessed One, the Bodhisattva, by the power of the ripening of wholesome karma accumulated through the practice of meditative concentration, obtained birth in the Brahma-world.

Although he possessed that great Brahma-happiness attained through the excellence of meditation, because of his long-standing familiarity with compassion in previous lives, his mind was never at all disinterested in the activity of working for the benefit of others.
The world falls into the utmost state of negligence even through the pleasures of the senses;
yet, for the virtuous, the desire for the welfare of others is never set aside, even by the joys of meditative absorption.

Then once, that Great Being, surveying the realm of desire— which is the very abode of compassion, yet afflicted by hundreds of various sufferings and calamities, and agitated by malice, violence, and sensual passion— beheld the King of Videha named Aṅgadinna. Due to the fault of association with evil friends and the habituation to improper mental attention,
he was wandering in the thicket of false views.
"There is no world beyond;
how then could there be the ripening of good and evil deeds? Having reached this certainty, his zeal for the practice of the Dharma was extinguished;

he turned away from the performance of virtuous deeds such as generosity and moral discipline; his mind became firmly rooted in contempt for those who follow the Dharma, and his intellect grew harsh with lack of faith toward the treatises on the Dharma.
With a mind intent on jesting, he became lax in his respectful conduct and reverence toward stories of the next world, and devoted himself to sensual pleasures among ascetics and brahmins; yet,
he maintained a firmly rooted conviction that virtuous and non-virtuous actions certainly result in happiness and suffering in the hereafter.
Having cast off evil, one who has a virtuous refuge strives for what is auspicious; however, one who lacks faith proceeds according to their own whims.

Then that Great-souled One, the divine seer, his compassion aroused by the king’s immersion in that calamity of false views— which leads to states of woe and is a source of ruin for the world— descended from the Brahma-world before the king, whose mind was unattached to the pleasures of the senses as he sat in a secluded, glorious celestial chariot, blazing with light.

Then that king, beholding him blazing like a mass of fire, shining like a cluster of lightning flashes, and resplendent with supreme brilliance like the rays of the sun, his mind overwhelmed by that splendor, rose up in haste with palms joined in reverence; gazing at him with great respect, he spoke as follows:
O you whose feet are like lotuses, even the sky embraces your feet as if it were the earth;
bearing a radiance like that of the sun, you shine with a form that delights the eyes—who are you?
The Bodhisattva said:
"Having conquered passion and hatred by the power of mental concentration, as if defeating two arrogant and preeminent teachers in battle," (Vaidya 201)
O protector of the earth, know me to be one among those divine seers who have attained the world of Brahmā.

When this was said, the king, preceded by welcoming and other kind words, offered him water for his feet, the guest-offering, and due hospitality; then, gazing at him with wonder, he said: "O Great Sage, the power of your supernatural success is indeed marvelous!
You walk upon the walls of the palace as if you were walking on the very ground, without being obstructed."
O you whose brilliance is enriched by flashes like lightning, tell me: by what means has this supernatural power of yours been attained?
The Bodhisattva said:

"O King, such is the attainment of this fruit resulting from meditation and stainless, excellent morality, as well as the restraint of the senses, which has been made habitual throughout other births."
The king said: "Is it truly so that this other world exists?
Brahmā said: "Yes;
there is, O Great King, another world."

The king said: "But how, O noble one, could even we believe this? The Bodhisattva replied: "This is evident, O Great King; it is graspable through the means of valid cognition such as direct perception, it follows the sequence demonstrated by authoritative persons, and it is accessible through the process of investigation. Let Your Majesty observe."

The sky, adorned with the moon, the sun, and the stars, and the various manifold realms of animals—this world beyond is visible before your eyes; let not your mind become dulled by doubt regarding this.
And there are those here and there who remember their past births due to their application to meditation and the clarity of their memory;
for this reason as well, the world beyond is to be inferred. Indeed, have I not myself provided the witness for this?
Since the establishment of consciousness occurs only through a preceding consciousness, know from this as well that there is another world;
for the initial consciousness of one who has entered the womb is immediately preceded by the consciousness of a previous birth.
They say that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the awakening to the objects of knowledge; therefore, there exists an object for the intellect regarding birth and so forth.
Since this [awakening] does not pertain to this world due to the absence of eyes and other [senses], that which is established as beyond this is the other world.
Since a diversity of character and other qualities is observed among living beings that transcends their paternal nature,
and since nothing that is not accidental can be established as such, it follows that this [diversity] consists of the practice of a previous birth.
Even when the power of the intellect is deficient and the sense organs are of a dull nature,
that which is born immediately undertakes the effort to suckle at the breast without any instruction.
This demonstrates that he had exerted effort in [the practice of] those things suitable for food during his previous existences;
for the perfection of practice makes the collection of skills proficient in those various tasks.
In this regard, if you have this doubt due to a lack of conviction regarding the next world—
"Granted that the contraction and expansion of lotuses may be established as the activity of another existence;
but if that is not accepted, then why do you exert yourself in suckling at the breast, which is born of the toil of a previous birth?"— Jm_29.14.
And that suspicion is not to be followed, because we observe both regularity and irregularity, and because effort is either impossible or possible [in each case].
For a temporal regularity is observed in the opening and closing of the lotus, but not in the effort to suckle at the breast.
Furthermore, there is no effort on the part of the lotus, whereas it is observed in the infant; thus, the power of the sun is the cause of the lotus's blooming.

Thus, O Great King, by one who investigates correctly, it is possible to have faith that "the next world exists. Then, because his intellect was intent on embracing false views and because he had accumulated evil karma, the king—displeased upon hearing this discourse on the next world—said: "O Great Seer, if there is no other world, then this is merely a scare tactic for the foolish; or if you think that this must be accepted by me..."
"Therefore, grant us here five hundred gold coins; I shall give those thousand to you in another life."
Then the Bodhisattva, following a logical sequence, replied to his audacious, habitual, and shameless speech— which was like an outpouring of the poison of false views and contrary to proper conduct:
"Even in this world, those who seek the acquisition of wealth do not bestow their wealth upon a wicked person."
For that which has been bestowed upon one who is gluttonous, unskilled, or lazy comes to an end right there.

But when they see one who is modest, born of tranquility, and skilled in worldly affairs—even in private—they entrust their debts to such a person; for the transfer of wealth to one of that kind brings about prosperity.
"O King, let it be understood that the sequence of repayment in the lending of debts for the sake of the next world is indeed of such a kind;
however, in your case, whose conduct is corrupted by false views, there is no way for the lending of wealth to proceed."
Who, then, would urge you on from that state— you who have been cast into hell by your own terrible deeds arising from the fault of false views,
who are senseless and tormented by pain for the sake of a thousand gold pieces?
There, the ladies of the quarters do not shine with the rays of the moon and sun, their veils of darkness having been withdrawn;
nor is the sky seen adorned with clusters of stars, like a lake filled with blossomed white lotuses.
In that other world where nihilists dwell, there is thick darkness and a freezing wind;
who that possesses self-mastery would enter it out of a desire for wealth, when it causes pain even by rending the notion that "it exists"?
In the darkness of poverty, like a thick storm of dense smoke, some wander for a long time within the belly of hell;
distressed by the dragging of their own tattered rags, they cry out in pain as they stumble against one another.
In another hell with blazing embers, they are repeatedly crushed into powder;
thus they run in all directions, desiring to escape from it, yet they find neither the end of their misfortune nor the end of their lifespan.

Like carpenters fashioning the limbs of others, the fierce wardens of Yama, having restrained them, pare them down with sharp-edged weapons; finding their joy in it, they work upon those still moist with flesh as if upon pieces of wood.
With all their skin flayed away, some are tormented by pain, stripped of flesh until only bone remains;
yet, held fast by their own evil deeds, they do not meet their destruction, while others likewise are being cut into pieces.
With their mouths filled with glowing, large bits, they long pull the chariots while circling upon iron grounds that are ablaze with steady fires,
kept under control by goads and hooks tawny with flame.
Even when their bodies are crushed by the collision of the Saṃghāta mountains,
or even when their forms are ground to dust by being trampled underfoot,
they do not die despite that great and unmitigated suffering, so long as their evil karma has not reached its exhaustion.
Some, being ground down for five hundred years upon iron mortars blazing with fire by means of great, flaming iron pestles, do not give up their lives.
On other trees, which resemble coral yet are heated and rough with sharp, glowing iron thorns,
they are split open while being dragged upward and downward by the cruel, non-human servants of Yama, who utter harsh cries.

Others, their strength exhausted by the power of mantras, experience the fruit of their own conduct upon great heaps of glowing embers that resemble molten gold, while they are unable even to move or cry out.
Some, their tongues stretched out by hundreds of sharp spikes upon a ground blazing with garlands of flames,
shriek aloud, their bodies overcome by intense agony; and at that time, they are made to realize the world beyond.
Some are bound with flaming iron bands, while others are boiled in iron cauldrons;
some have their limbs mangled by rains of sharp weapons, and others are stripped of skin and flesh by swarms of wild beasts.
Some, exhausted by the touch of fire, enter the sharp, caustic water of the Vaitaraṇī;
there their flesh is dissolved away, yet their lives are sustained by their own evil deeds.
Like those whose minds are afflicted by the exhaustion of burning who approach a lake,
those who have approached the impure corpse experience incomparable suffering there, their bodies with bones shattered by hundreds of worms.
Others, enveloped by fire and with bodies ablaze, experience the suffering of burning for a long time;
though surrounded by flames as bright as glowing iron, they do not turn to ashes, for their own past deeds sustain them.
Some are sawn apart with flaming saws; others are cut with sharp razors; some, their heads crushed by the force of mallets, shriek in the agony of grief;
and others, their bodies pierced by broad spikes, are roasted in smokeless fire.
Others, crying out in agony, are made to drink molten iron that has the color of blazing fire.
Others, having been pounced upon by powerful brindled dogs with sharp teeth,
their bodies stripped of flesh and their forms emaciated, fall down crying out in piteous lamentation.
Thus, driven by your own actions, you will experience such terrible suffering in the hells.
Who indeed would then ask you for a debt, when you are afflicted by grief and your mind is overwhelmed by exhaustion and despair?

Then, who indeed would beg you for a debt as you wander helplessly, driven by the force of boiling, amidst iron cauldrons crowded with the corpses of wicked men and difficult to approach due to the blazing fire?
And when your body is bound to glowing iron stakes, or upon the surface of the earth tawny with smokeless fire,
as your frame is being consumed and you are weeping piteously— who indeed would then beg a debt from you?
Who would then beg for a debt from you, who have met with such defeat, who are experiencing great sufferings,
and who are unable even to give a reply?

Who else in another world would be fit to beg wealth from you, when you are being torn apart by the cold wind, when your prowess has failed even though you ought to roar, and when you cry out in intense agony as you are being ripped asunder?

Who would provoke you with requests for wealth in the next world, while you are being tormented by the men of Yama, or writhing in a blazing fire, with your flesh and blood being devoured by dogs and crows?
Constantly tormented by slaughter, mutilation, beating, cleaving, burning, carving, grinding, splitting, and various forms of execution, how will you then repay my debt?
Then that king,
having heard that most terrifying discourse on hell, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; his attachment to false views abandoned and his conviction in the next world established,
he bowed to that excellent seer and said:
Having heard of such torment among men, my mind seems to flee from fear;
yet how shall I not encounter that [suffering] myself? The fire of anxiety burns me once again.
"For my mind was ruined by false views, and I traveled along an evil path, lacking foresight.
Therefore, O Sage, you are my destination of the righteous; you are my ultimate resort and my refuge."
"Just as this darkness has been dispelled by you for me, like the rising sun driving away the gloom,
even so, O Sage, explain the path to me, so that by following it I may not fall into an evil rebirth from here."

Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that his mind was agitated, his view had become upright, and he had become a fit vessel for the practice of the Dharma, instructed him out of compassion— like a father toward a son or a teacher toward a disciple— with the conduct of a true disciple:
"Just as kings of old displayed love for virtue through their own duties toward ascetics and brahmins,
and showed mercy toward their subjects, so too is one who is capable of fame on the path to the third heaven."
Conquering this most difficult-to-overcome unrighteousness and crossing over the state of miserliness so hard to surmount,
approach the city of the Lord of Heaven, blazing with its golden gateways and radiant with an abundance of jewels.

May your mind find firm delight in that doctrine which is esteemed by the virtuous and familiarized through the vision of the non-existent; and abandon that determination of what is unrighteous which has been proclaimed by people who please only the foolish.
For now, O King, by you— who are virtuous through right vision and desirous of departing with noble conduct—
as soon as the harshness of qualities was destroyed within your mind, at that very moment the state established upon the path became yours.
Therefore, acquire wealth through the cultivation of virtues, and practice auspicious compassion toward the world for the sake of your own welfare;
maintain firm restraint of the senses through moral conduct, for by this means no misfortune shall befall you in the next world.
O King, by means of the radiant splendor of his own merit, and through his pleasing command which was pure among the virtuous,
he— who was devoted to his own purpose— removed the suffering of the world and took away its distress with his fame, bringing about what was beneficial and conducive to the welfare of all beings.
In this matter, you are the charioteer with a noble mind; your own body is the chariot, with the virtues as its horses;
it has non-cruelty as its axle, self-restraint and generosity as its wheels, and is yoked to the impulse of a meritorious intention.
With the horses of his senses restrained by the excellence of the reins of mindfulness, with the goad of intelligence, and the weapons of extensive learning;
with modesty as its equipment, humility as its beautiful pole, patience as its yoke, skill as its movement, and steadfastness as its stability.

By restraining false speech, he was silent when not speaking; his voice was pleasant, slow, and deep. Because he did not violate his vows, he never broke his commitments; and by avoiding crookedness through unwholesome actions, he was upright.

O King, traveling by means of this vehicle— whose banner is glory, whose retinue is compassion, whose lofty standard is tranquility, and which shines with the light of non-delusion— you shall never go to hell for the sake of the welfare of yourself and others.
Thus that Great Being, having dispelled the darkness of the king’s false vision with the radiant rays of his words and having revealed to him the path to a happy rebirth, vanished on the spot.

Then the king, having understood the true nature of the affairs of the next world and having attained a mind of right view, became devoted to generosity, self-restraint, and discipline, together with his ministers, citizens, and countryfolk.
Therefore, those who have fallen into the calamity of wrong views are especially to be pitied by the virtuous, for false views are the most minute of faults.
In this way, it should also be understood that hearing the true Dharma fulfills perfected faith;

likewise, it should be understood that hearing the Dharma from another becomes a condition for the arising of right view. Furthermore, when virtuous people encounter abuse, they repel it by teaching what is beneficial rather than through harshness because of their cultivation of forbearance; thus, this should be stated both in the praise of the virtuous and in the description of the excellence of forbearance.
Since it is through spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) alone that one thus quickly becomes oriented toward the highest good, this should also be stated in the discourse on spiritual urgency.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth *jātaka*, the Brahmajātakam.
30. The Story of the Elephant:
The virtuous regard even suffering that results in the welfare of others as a great gain.
Thus it is heard:

Once, it is said, the Bodhisattva dwelt in a certain elephant forest—a place whose ground was covered with various creepers, trees, and grasses, and which seemed adorned by young, excellent trees whose peaks were marked with flowers, fruits, and sprouts; a place inhabited by those whose hearts were bound to the beauty of the woods and who remained there without longing for anything else.

There, in a wilderness surrounded on all sides by a vast forest devoid of trees and shrubs, where the presence of people was hidden, and which was supported by mountain plateaus serving as refuges for forest-dwellers and possessed of deep and expansive reservoirs of water, there lived a solitary elephant of massive body.
There, he subsisted on tree leaves, lotus stalks, and water.
Like an ascetic, he took delight in contentment and tranquility.
Then, on one occasion, as that Great Being was wandering along the edge of that forest, he heard the sound of people coming from that wilderness.
A thought arose in him: "What indeed could this be?
There is certainly no road leading to another region through this area."
"Having thus crossed such a vast wilderness, even hunting is not appropriate, let alone capturing our own herd with such great exertion and exhaustion.
Clearly, these [deer] have either strayed from the path, or their guide is deluded;
or perhaps they have been driven out by an angry king or by some wicked person."
For thus, devoid of mental vigor and with its joy, exultation, and flow destroyed,
the sound is heard as one consisting solely of the power of affliction, like that of weeping people.
"I shall find out about this," thought that Great Being; drawn on by compassion, he proceeded toward the direction from which the sound of people's cries arose.
Hearing that sound of lamentation, which was increasingly distinct and harsh with the wretchedness of despair, that Noble One, his mind agitated by pity, went toward it with even greater speed.

Having emerged from that dense forest, because that region was devoid of trees and shrubs, he looked out from afar and saw about seven hundred men, slowed by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, approaching that forest in pursuit of it. Those men also beheld the Great Being coming toward them like a moving peak of the Snowy Mountains, resembling a mass of clouds in autumn driven by the force of the wind.

And having seen him, though overcome by despair and dejection and seized by fear in their minds, thinking, "Alas, we are now lost," they did not exert themselves to flee, for their energy was exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue.
Overcome by despair and distressed by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion,
they did not even attempt to escape, despite the danger.

Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that they were terrified, approached them and, comforting them with his hand—its broad palm being raised, smooth, and a deep coppery red—spoke with compassion: "Do not fear! Do not fear! You have no cause for fear from me. Having thus reassured them, he asked: "Who are you, honored sirs, and by what means have you come to this state?"
"Whose forms have become discolored and emaciated by contact with the dust and rays of the sun,
and who are afflicted by grief and exhaustion— who are you, and from where have you come here? (Jm 30.5)

Then those men, their hearts restored by his human speech and by his readiness to offer protection, bowed down to him and said: "O lord of elephants, we were cast here by the tempestuous wind of the king's wrath,
while our kinsmen looked on, wretched with grief."
Surely some remnant of our good fortune remains, for Fortune has turned her face toward us,
since we have been seen by you, who are distinguished among friends and kinsmen.
And we know that we have crossed over this calamity because of the festival of seeing you;
for who indeed, having seen one such as you even in a dream, would not emerge from misfortune?
Then that excellent elephant said to them: "How many are these venerable ones?
The men replied:
"O you of lovely limbs, these one thousand men have been cast away here by the lord of the earth."
Many who had not yet experienced suffering were then destroyed by being overwhelmed with hunger, thirst, and grief.
These seven hundred men, with the elephant as their leader, remain as the survivors;
for those who were sinking into the jaws of death, you have arrived like a personified source of consolation.
Upon hearing this, tears flowed from that Great Being due to his long-standing habit of compassion.
Mourning for them, he spoke these words with certainty: "Alas! How painful it is!
The king’s intellect is indeed devoid of pity, utterly shameless, and untroubled by the world beyond."
"Alas! By royal splendor, as flickering as lightning, the senses of those who have been captivated fail to perceive their own welfare."
I think he does not perceive death standing before him, nor does he hear of the terrible end of his evil deeds;
alas, how most wretched are those kings who, due to their dullness of reflection, are incapable of speaking the truth!
Alas, fie upon this cruelty toward living beings for the sake of a single body—perishable, diseased, and subject to destruction! Oh, what delusion! (Vaidya 211) Jm_30.13 //

Then, as that lord of elephants gazed upon those men with eyes tender with compassion, a thought arose in him: "How will these people, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, their bodies utterly weakened, traverse this wilderness many yojanas in extent— devoid of water and shade, lacking wholesome food?"
Moreover, what is there even in this Nāgavana forest by which their sustenance might last for even a single day without hardship?
Furthermore, these [beings] would be able to cross this wilderness only by taking my flesh as provisions and carrying water in my intestines like leather bags; it cannot be done otherwise.
Therefore, I shall offer this body, which is the abode of hundreds of various diseases.
This is a raft for crossing over the calamity of those who are overwhelmed by suffering.
Human birth is capable of attaining the happiness of heaven and liberation, yet it is difficult for them to obtain; let it not thus come to ruin.
This is my own domain, and these guests have come to me according to dharma;
moreover, as they have fallen into calamity and are bereft of kinsmen, they are especially worthy of my compassion.

At long last, this vast collection of misfortunes known as the body— having long been a vessel for many diseases, a constant state of affliction, and a locus of manifold exhaustion— shall now be employed for the sake of the welfare of others.

Then others, their bodies afflicted by the suffering of hunger, thirst, fatigue, and heat, bowed down to him with palms joined and eyes filled with tears; out of their distress, they begged for water with gestures of their hands:
"You are our kinsman to us who are friendless; you are our refuge and our protection.
O illustrious one, as you know [the way], so you ought to save us."

Thus some spoke to him with compassion; others, however, being of more resolute mind, asked him for a body of water or a river of cool water, or if there were water from a mountain spring, in order to cross the difficult wilderness and find a path. "Is there a reservoir here, or a river of cool water, or perhaps water from a cascade? they asked.
O Lord of the Nāgas, tell us whether it was a shady tree or a patch of green grass.
"Since you consider it possible to cross this wilderness, out of compassion, please point out the way to that region. (Jm_30.20)
"For many days indeed have we wandered here in this wilderness;
therefore, O Master, you ought to deliver us.
Then that Great Being, his heart being deeply moved by their piteous entreaties, [showed them] the way by which that wilderness could be crossed.

Then, pointing out a mountain plateau to them with his hand—upraised and thick like the coils of a noble serpent—he said: "Beneath this mountain plateau lies a great lake of pure water adorned with lotuses and lilies;
go by this path."
And there, having dispelled your exhaustion from heat and thirst, you will see the body of that very elephant which fell from this mountain plateau not far from here.
Taking its flesh as provisions for the journey and gathering water with its intestines as if with leather bags, you must proceed in this very direction.
In this way, you shall cross this wilderness with little difficulty.

Thus that Great Being, having first comforted those men and sent them forth from there, ascended that mountain peak by another path even more swiftly; then, with the intent of rescuing that multitude of people, he firmly cultivated this aspiration, desiring to release his own body from there:
This effort of mine is not for the sake of attaining a happy rebirth, nor for the sovereign glory of a king with a single umbrella,
nor for heaven whose sole essence is the excellence of pleasure, nor even for the splendor of Brahma, nor indeed for the bliss of liberation.
Whatever merit I may possess from thus desiring to uplift people submerged in this wilderness,
may I, by that merit, become a savior for the world as it wanders through the wilderness of saṃsāra.

Having thus resolved, that Great-souled One, out of joy and disregarding the suffering of death from the impact of the fall, cast his own body from that mountain slope toward its intended destination.
Then, as he fell, he shone like an autumn cloud, or like the moon with its orb overturned as it descends the western mountain;
and his snowy upper garment was blown away by the fierce force of the wind from Garuḍa’s wings, like a peak of that mountain.
Then, shaking the earth and the mountains, as well as Māra’s mind which was possessed by arrogance,
it fell to the ground with a sound like a crashing thunderbolt, causing the forest creepers and the forest deities to bow down.
