Without a doubt, at that time, the gods dwelling in that forest, their minds expanded with wonder, cast their arms— whose fingers were raised like sprouts and whose hairs stood on end with joy— into the sky. (Jm 30.25)
Others continuously strewed fragrant flowers dyed with sandalwood powder;
others adorned him with upper garments and ornaments that were not woven from thread but were resplendent with patterns of gold.

Others worshipped him with hymns composed of devotion, with uplifted lotus-buds of palms joined in reverence, and with prostrations made by bowing their heads so that their beautiful crests touched the ground.
Then some fanned him with a breeze that drew along the pollen of fragrant flowers and formed garlands of ripples;
others, meanwhile, spread a canopy over him in the sky with dense clouds.
Driven by devotion, some caused the heavens to resound with the sounds of divine drums to honor him;
others then adorned the trees there with flowers, fruits, and sprouts that had blossomed out of season.
The quarters of the sky assumed an autumnal splendor, and the rays of the sun appeared as if they had grown even taller;
the ocean, its waves trembling with curiosity, seemed to rise up in joy to go forth to meet him.

Then those men, having reached that lake in due course, their thirst and fatigue for the Dharma being dispelled, beheld not far from where that Great Being had spoken a body of an elephant that had recently died.
The thought occurred to them: "Aha! How similar this elephant is to that lord of elephants!
Could he be the brother of that great tusker, or perhaps a kinsman, or one of his sons?"
Indeed, even when crushed, the form of this very [mountain] shines with the splendor of a white mountain.
Like the beauty of a white water-lily, or like moonlight gathered into a mass,
this is truly his very shadow resting upon the surface of the mirror.

Then, as some there observed more closely, the thought occurred to them: "As we see it, this very same elephant, possessing a preeminent beauty that rivals Indra himself, has indeed fallen from this mountain slope out of a desire to rescue us, who are without kin or friends and have fallen into calamity."
"That sound which was like a thunderclap, as if making the earth tremble—
it is clearly the sound of him falling that we have heard."
This body is indeed that very same one—white as a lotus stalk, with hair as bright as moonbeams and variegated with fine spots;
these feet with their white nails resemble tortoises; and this bow is that very same one, sweetly curved like a bamboo reed.
This very same head of mine, adorned with a beautiful mane, its broad face expanded by the fragrant wind, its lofty crest marked by the auspicious goad, and its great neck—this is it. (Jm 30.35)

This very trunk, with its long fingers like lotuses, indicates the path by which we must go; it bears this pair of tusks, honey-colored yet reddened by the dust of the riverbank, a mark of its own pride.
"Alas, this is truly a marvel of most extraordinary form!

Toward us—who have never before seen his lineage, character, or devotion; who are wounded by misfortunes and unheard of even by fortune—how can such friendship exist? What kind of friend or kinsman could he possibly have?"
In every way, let there be homage to this highly fortunate one,
who assists those like us who are overwhelmed by calamity and distressed by fear and grief.
I think this is some manifestation of an elephant, which seems to uphold the conduct of those who desire to cross over.
Where was he trained in this extreme gentleness, and who indeed was his teacher in the forest?
For people do not find delight in the beauty of form without virtues; that which they say is now clearly seen here.
"Aha! By this excellence of his extraordinary nature, his inherent nobility has been demonstrated as it truly is.
Even though he is dead, this man—like the beauty of the Snowy Mountain—is surely satisfied within himself and seems to laugh with his very body."

Therefore, who now would be able to consume the flesh of this one— who possesses such exceptional affection for his dear kinsmen and friends, who is so well-disposed toward providing assistance, who has set out to benefit us even with his own life, and who is of such exceedingly virtuous conduct?
It is indeed fitting that we discharge our debt to him by honoring him with a funeral rite preceded by the proper ritual of worship.
Then, observing them— their hearts inclined toward the persistence of grief due to the calamity that had befallen their kinsman, their eyes filled with tears, and their throats choked with emotion—
others of more steadfast mind, looking toward another matter at hand, said: "Indeed, this excellent elephant would not have been thus honored or treated with such hospitality by us."

We see that he is worthy of being honored by us through the fulfillment of his wishes; for this most beloved guest, who is a kinsman to those with whom he has no prior acquaintance, has looked only to our rescue and has thus sacrificed his very body.
However, it is proper to follow his intention;
for otherwise, would not this effort of his indeed be in vain?
"Indeed, he has offered all his possessions as hospitality out of affection;
who then would render this act of honor futile by refusing to accept it? (Jm 30.43)
Since we have received her words as if from a guru,
we ought to perform this act of hospitality for her own sake and for our own well-being.
And once this calamity has been overcome, whether by all together or individually, worship shall again be performed for this noble Naga, exactly as was done for their deceased kinsman.
Then those men, out of a desire to escape the wilderness and keeping in mind the intention of that lord of elephants, did not reject his words;
they took the flesh of that Great Being and, using his intestines like water-skins, carried the water by the path he had shown them.
They emerged safely from that wilderness in every direction.
Thus, virtuous people highly esteem even suffering that results in a favorable future outcome as if it were a gain; this is what should be said in praise of virtuous persons.

This should also be stated in the description of the Tathāgata, in the description of listening to the Dharma with reverence, and in the description of accomplishing a noble nature (*bhadraprakṛti*): "In this way, a noble nature practiced in previous lives continues into subsequent births.

This should also be stated in the demonstration of the quality of familiarity with renunciation: "In this way, through familiarity with the giving away of material things, one also abandons self-attachment without difficulty."

And as for what was said by the Blessed One when the time of his final nirvāṇa had arrived, in the presence of divine flowers, musical instruments, and the like: "Indeed, Ānanda, the Tathāgata is not thereby honored"—this should be understood in this way:
worship is performed through the fulfillment of such an intention, and not merely by the offering of perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
Thus ends the thirtieth Jātaka, the Story of the Elephant.
31. The Sutasoma Jātaka:
Since association with the virtuous brings about welfare in whatever way it may come about, one who seeks welfare should take refuge in the company of good people.

Thus it is heard: this Blessed One, while formerly a bodhisattva, took birth in the illustrious royal lineage of the Kauravyas— a family whose fame was radiant, which was devoted to the cultivation of virtues, in which affection for the subjects had become second nature, and where proud vassals were humbled by its majesty.
His father gave his son, who was garlanded by the rays of a hundred virtues and possessed a moon-like pleasing appearance, the name Sutasoma.

Like the moon in the bright fortnight, with his beauty and charm increasing day by day, he gradually attained proficiency in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the Upavedas; and having mastered the sequence of the arts, including those that follow them, as well as worldly accomplishments, he became a man of vision.
He became the very abode of the world’s love and high esteem; through his readiness to provide proper assistance, his ever-increasing respect, and his commitment to protection,
he was like a kinsman to virtues— virtues such as moral conduct, learning, generosity, compassion, self-restraint, majesty, forbearance, wisdom, fortitude, and humility.
Of freedom from arrogance, modesty, loveliness, fame, courtesy, intelligence, strength, and purity.
And he became the refuge for those various individuals who were like ornaments adorned with youth,
pure, noble, and captivating, just as the moon is the resort of its digits.

Therefore, because of his capacity to protect the world and his noble and auspicious nature, the king invested him with the splendor of the position of crown prince. Furthermore, due to his wisdom, he was exceedingly fond of righteous and well-spoken words;
thus, he honored him with extraordinary marks of respect, and anyone who approached him did so with such eloquent sayings.

Then once, that Great-souled One beheld the delightful splendors of the spring season: the beauty of fresh sprouts produced by the power of the month of flowers; the charming smiles of blossoming blossoms; the surface of the earth covered with carpets of spread-out young green grass; the clear blue waters strewn with petals of lotuses and water-lilies;

the regions resounded by the songs of swarms of wandering bees and female honey-bees; the areas filled with groups of unrestrained cuckoos and peacocks; and the gentle, fragrant, cool, and pleasant breezes.
Wandering through city parks that evoke serenity of mind, he went out to a certain pleasure grove for the sake of diversion, surrounded by a not inconsiderable body of troops.
There, in that forest resounding with the calls of male cuckoos, adorned with enchanting gardens and celestial palaces,
and filled with variegated trees bent low with blossoms, he roamed together with his beloved like a virtuous man in the Nandana grove.
There he took delight in the sounds of singing interwoven with the sweet tones of musical instruments, in dances characterized by graceful movements of the limbs and clever gestures,
in the beauty of the women's playful charms enhanced by intoxication, and in the loveliness of that forest.
While he was staying there, a certain brahmin who recited elegant sayings approached him;
having performed the customary courtesies and honors, his mind captivated by the beauty of the prince’s form, he sat down there.

Thus, that Great Being, while experiencing the methods of play brought about by the power of the abundance of his merit in accordance with his youth, felt a great respect arise within him upon the arrival of that man.

While that brahmin was thus listening to the well-spoken words and had not yet attained the fruit of his arrival, he suddenly heard a tumultuous uproar that interrupted the sounds of singing and instrumental music,

destroyed the joy produced by the occasion of play, and gave rise to fear and despondency among the women; hearing this, he respectfully commanded the attendants of the inner apartments, "Let it be found out what this is."

Then his doorkeepers, their faces pale with fear and despondency, approached him in great haste and reported: "Your Majesty, here comes that man-eater Kalmāṣapāda, the son of Sudāsa, like Death himself in person; through his long practice of slaughtering hundreds of men, his mind has become more cruel than even a Rākṣasa’s, and he is arrogant in his superhuman strength and heroism. He approaches with a form as terrifying and fierce as a demon, truly causing terror to the world."
"Our army has fled, its courage seized by terror; with chariots, horses, and elephants wandering in confusion, the warriors are utterly disarrayed.
Therefore, let Your Majesty devise a remedy, or consider what course of action is appropriate for the present moment."
Then Sutasoma, although he already knew, said to them: "Sirs, who is this so-called Saudāsa?
They replied to him: "Is it not known to Your Majesty how there was once a king named Sudāsa?
Having gone out on a hunt, he was carried off by his horse and entered a dense forest, where he had sexual union with a lioness."
That lioness became pregnant,
and after some time she gave birth to a boy.
He was captured by forest-dwellers and brought before Sudāsa.
Thinking, "I am sonless," he was raised by Sudāsa;
and when his father had departed for the city of the gods, he obtained his own kingdom.
Due to a defect inherited from his mother, however, he became addicted to sensual pleasures.
Thinking, "This is this very best of flavors, human flesh," he tasted human flesh and began to kill and eat his own citizens again and again.
Then the citizens made an effort to put him to death.

Frightened by this, Saudāsa made a vow to the *bhūtas* who feed on the blood and flesh of human offerings: "Once I am released from this peril, I shall perform a sacrifice to the *bhūtas* with a hundred princes."
Thus, having been released from that peril,
he has repeatedly carried off princes;
now he has come to carry off even Your Majesty.

Having heard that the king was the authority, the Bodhisattva— already aware of the transgression of Saudāsa’s character and conduct— out of compassion directed his mind toward healing him; and anticipating his own capacity to pacify that corruption of character, he felt joy at the report of Saudāsa’s approach, as if it were pleasant news.
Experiencing this, he spoke with certainty:
"When he has been fallen from his kingdom, being dependent and as if driven by madness due to greed for human flesh— "
While he followed that wretched state, having abandoned his own dharma and having his merit and fame destroyed.
What scope for valor is there here for me, or for such panic-stricken fear?
With effortless and impetuous prowess, I shall violently strike down this evil-doer.
"He who was indeed to be pitied by me has come of his own accord to my domain even after I had gone to him;
therefore, it is right for me to offer him hospitality, for such is the conduct of the virtuous toward guests."
"Thus, sirs, remain attentive here according to your respective duties.

Having thus instructed those attendants of the inner apartments, and having turned back the young women— who were struggling with eyes wide with profound despair, throats choked with sobbing, and intent on blocking the path— with words of consolation, he proceeded toward the source of that clamor.

And upon seeing the son of Sudāsa—his body girt with a tightly bound garment of soiled cloth, his waist secured by a band of bark-fiber, his long, disheveled hair coarse with dust, his face shrouded in darkness by a dense growth of beard, his fierce eyes rolling in a fit of angry fury, and brandishing a sword and shield as he pursued the fleeing royal army—he, free from fear or trepidation, challenged him: "Ho! Here am I, Sutasoma!"
"Turn back from this very place!
What is the use of this preoccupation with causing the slaughter of wretched people?
But Saudāsa, his pride inflamed by the sound of that challenge, turned away from there like a lion.

Beholding the Bodhisattva alone, armed with no weapon other than his unobstructed [wisdom] and possessing a naturally serene appearance, he said, "I too am hunting for you," and having spoken thus, he rushed forward suddenly and with great impetuosity; without hesitation, he seized him, placed him upon his shoulder, and fled.

The Bodhisattva, perceiving that the king’s mind was puffed up with the arrogance of fury and pride, that his intellect was agitated by agitation, and that he was filled with excessive joy and insolence due to the routing of the royal army, yet remained full of apprehension, realized: "This is not the time for instruction."
Thus he remained indifferent.
Saudāsa, too, having attained as it were a supreme gain through the accomplishment of his desired object, entered his own dwelling-fort with a joyful mind—
a place crowded with the corpses of slain men and its fierce ground drenched in blood.
He threatened the man, as it were, with the inauspicious howls of jackals that sounded like crackling fires.

It was strewn with trees whose leaves were harsh and reddish from being the perches of vultures and crows, and discolored by the smoke of many funeral pyres; it was a place of unappeased horror where *rakṣasas* and *pretas* danced, seen from afar by the eyes of merchants rendered numb with terror.
Having caused the Bodhisattva to descend there, he rested, his eyes fixed intently upon him as he was captivated by the perfection of his form.

Then, recollecting the Brahmin who had approached with well-spoken words and skillful means—whom he had failed to honor, who was now waiting for the Bodhisattva’s departure from the park, and whose heart was bound by hope—a thought arose within him:
"Alas, how painful!"
"He has come from afar with the intention of employing both speech and gifts;
upon hearing that I have been carried off, what indeed will that brahmin do?"
With his mind enveloped by the fire of frustrated hope and exhausted by the intense toil of the sacrificial rites,
he will either sigh deeply after lamenting for me, or he will fall into self-reproach for his own misfortune.

As the Great Being reflected thus, his mind tormented by the other's suffering, tears flowed from him due to his long-standing habituation to compassion. Then Saudāsa, beholding the Bodhisattva with tearful eyes, laughed aloud and said: "O sir!
You are indeed renowned as a wise man because of those many various virtues of yours."
And yet, having fallen under our power, even you shed tears.
Truly, this is well said:
"In times of calamity, fortitude is fruitless; in grief, learning is useless. For there exists no living being that, when struck, does not tremble. (Jm 31.14)
Thus it is said. Now tell me the truth of this:
was it out of grief for your dear life, or your wealth which is the means of happiness, or your kinsmen, or your sovereignty as a lord of men;
or was it by remembering your father who loved his son, or your sons with tearful faces, that you have come to this state of shedding tears?
The Bodhisattva said:
"This outpouring of tears of mine is not because I am remembering my life, nor my parents, nor my children, nor my kinsmen, nor my wife, nor even the pleasures of sovereignty."
"But that brahmin, full of hope, having approached with well-spoken words and hearing that I have been carried off,
will surely burn with despair"— remembering this, I stood there with tearful eyes.
Therefore, you ought to grant him leave, before the heart of this twice-born man is crushed by the frustration of his hopes;
for I shall refresh it with the sprinkling of the water of honor, and I shall offer him the honey of well-spoken words.
Having thus attained freedom from my debt to the divine one, I shall go on to achieve freedom from my debt to you as well,
being gazed upon by your eyes whose moment of joy was created by my arrival here.
Do not let your mind be agitated by the suspicion that this conduct of his is improper;
for the path of those like me, O King, is one thing, while that followed by other people is quite another.
Saudāsa said:
"This which you speak with such earnestness can by no means be believed.
For who, having been released from the mouth of death and standing safe and sound, would ever return to it again?"
Having transcended the fear of death so difficult to overcome, you abide in happiness within your own glorious palace;
what indeed could be the reason that you have come here to me once again?
The Bodhisattva said: "How is it that your reverence does not understand even this great reason for my coming?
Have I not already undertaken to come?
Therefore, enough of suspecting me in such a manner, as if I were equal to a base person."
"I am indeed Sutasoma.
Out of greed and out of fear of death, some people abandon truth as if it were a blade of grass;
but for the virtuous, truth is their wealth and their very life, and therefore they do not forsake it even in the face of hardship. (Jm 31.22)
Neither life nor worldly pleasure protects one who has fallen from truth from the miserable states of existence;
why then would anyone abandon truth for the sake of praise, fame, or happiness—those very things you yourself have performed?

"In one whose path shows visible inconsistency, or whose virtuous prowess remains unseen, goodness does not inspire confidence; and so, having observed this, why do you harbor doubt even toward me? (Jm 31.24)
If indeed I had feared you, or if my mind were attached to pleasures or devoid of compassion, then surely,
considering myself a hero despite your notorious cruelty, I would have approached you with weapons raised and armor on.

This very praise of you would be my greatest desire; having rendered that twice-born man’s labor fruitful, I shall come back to your presence myself once more, for those like us do not utter words that prove false.
Then the son of Sudāsa, unable to endure those words of the Bodhisattva as if they were mere pretension, fell into reflection: "Truly, he boasts indeed of his truthfulness and his righteousness.
Let me first observe his devotion to truth and his love for dharma.
Moreover, what would it matter to me even if he were lost?"
"I indeed possess a hundred kṣatriya princes brought under my control by the majesty of the heroism of my own arms;
having reflected that I shall perform a sacrifice to the spirits according to their request, he said to the Bodhisattva: 'In that case, go!
You shall see both your truthfulness to your promise and your righteousness.'"
"Having gone and fulfilled whatever that brahmin desires,
return quickly so that I may prepare your funeral pyre."
Then the Bodhisattva, having promised him "So be it," returned to his own palace; being greeted with joy by his own people, he summoned that brahmin and heard from him those four verses.

Having heard them, the Great Being’s mind was gladdened by the well-spoken words; showing his favor with kind speech and respectful honors, he composed a thousand-verse poem and rewarded that brahmin with the object he desired.

Then his father, whose mind was intent on restraining him from spending beyond his means, spoke to him with conciliation as the occasion arose: "My son, you ought to know the proper measure in honoring well-spoken words;
for indeed, a great multitude of people must be supported by you, and royal prosperity depends upon the wealth of the treasury."
Therefore, I say this to you:
to honor a sublime utterance with even a hundred [gifts] is the supreme measure; nothing more than that is appropriate.
For how long, indeed, can even the splendor of the Lord of Wealth remain for one who gives excessively?
For wealth is the supreme means for accomplishing one's purpose; therefore, one should not pursue what is pleasant in a way that contradicts it.
Prosperity does not look upon a king devoid of the excellence of a treasury, just as a courtesan does not look upon a man who is destitute.
The Bodhisattva said:
"O King, if it were possible to determine the measure of the value of well-spoken words,
it is evident that even by offering you your entire kingdom as their price, you would not reach the end of the path of what can be said."
If merely hearing its name causes the mind to attain clarity, devotion to the highest good, and steadfastness,
and if through the increase of wisdom it leads to the state of being free from darkness— surely that [Dharma] ought to be purchased even with one's own flesh.
Learning is a lamp that dispels the darkness of delusion; it is the supreme wealth, which cannot be stolen by thieves and the like;
it is a weapon for crushing the enemy of infatuation; and it is the supreme counselor who teaches the way of right conduct.
A friend who remains unchanging even when one has fallen into calamity; a remedy that does not cause pain for the affliction of grief;
a great strength that crushes the power of faults; it is the supreme treasury of both fame and prosperity.
He was one for whom association with the virtuous was a constant offering of gifts; who delighted the learned in assemblies;
who was a sun to the brilliance of the arguments of opponents; and who stripped away the pride and fame of his rivals.
With the colors of their faces and eyes brightened by a natural, unadorned, and intense joy,
and with the tips of their hands busily engaged in acts of conciliation, they proclaimed his extraordinary sequence of deeds.

It was like a collection of unsoiled garlands, because its meaning and reasons were clearly demonstrated, it was refined by various scriptures and traditions, and it was captivating due to its sweetness and polish.

Through the practice of the glory of sacred learning, there arises a clarity of meaning that leads to a serene understanding; this is the specific cause of excellence in eloquence— which is disciplined, radiant, and brilliant, and which forcibly awakens fame.
And having heard the path of the threefold way, which is free from the faults of contradiction, they take refuge in it;
with practice based on following what they have heard as their essence, they cross over the difficult passage of birth without hardship.
How could I, having heard of these things renowned for their many virtues and received like a gift, not honor them? Or how could I ever transgress your command?
"I shall go into the presence of Saudāsa; I have no need for this kingdom or its toils, which is attainable only by following the path of vice and by violating the virtues of one's pledged word."

Then his father, overcome with affection and rising up in agitation, spoke to him respectfully: "My son, it was indeed for your own benefit that I spoke thus. Therefore, enough of yielding to the power of anger in this matter;
your enemies shall meet the fate of Saudāsa."
Furthermore, although you have promised to go into his presence and, out of devotion to truth, desire to fulfill it, I will not permit that either.
For the path of untruth is ordained by the Vedas as being without sin when it is for the purpose of protecting one's own life or for the sake of one's elders.
Therefore, what is the point of your exertion in avoiding that?
Furthermore, those skilled in political science declare that for kings, an adherence to dharma that is seen to conflict with wealth and pleasure is a form of misconduct and a source of calamity.

Therefore, enough of this persistence of yours, which causes us mental anguish and is indifferent to its own welfare. Furthermore, O noble one, since your mind—because it is unaccustomed to it—does not resolve upon breaking your vow, as that would be disgraceful and contrary to the Dharma, even so, our army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry stands ready and prepared for the sake of your liberation; it is well-equipped, devoted, composed of heroic men skilled in weapons, and has been consecrated in the waters of many battles.
A great force, formidable like a mighty torrent—
surrounded by this, go forth against him, bring him under your control,
or deliver him into the power of Death.
"In this way, my vow would be rendered non-futile and my own protection accomplished.

The Bodhisattva said: "O King, I am not able to act otherwise than as I have vowed; nor can I bring myself to strike those who are pitiable, those sunk in the mire of calamity, those facing hell, or those such as these who are friendless and abandoned by kinsmen and friends."
Moreover,
that man-eater committed a cruel yet noble act toward me;
for, trusting my words, he released me even though I had fallen into his power.
"O father, it is because of him that I have obtained this well-spoken teaching;
since he has been especially helpful to me, he deserves my compassion. (Jm 31.42)
"There is no need for Your Majesty to fear my death;
for what power does he have to harm me when I have come here in this manner?
Having thus consoled his father and turned back those well-wishers who were striving to prevent him, the Great-souled One [departed].
And he, alone with his army, free from fear and dejection, devoted to truth, and desiring to discipline Saudāsa for the sake of the world’s welfare, went to that man’s dwelling.

Seeing the Great Being from afar, Saudāsa—though his mind was stained by cruelty rooted in long-standing habit—was filled with extreme wonder, and with his respect and faith greatly increased, clearly fell into this thought:
"Oh, the marvel of marvels! Oh, the wonder of wonders!"
This truthfulness and magnanimity of the king surpasses both humans and gods.
"Alas! This Death, whose very nature is ferocity, has come to me of his own accord, having subdued all fear and agitation; well indeed is it with my fortitude and truthfulness! Jm_31.44.
"It is indeed fitting that his fame for truthfulness is renowned, since he has renounced both his life and his own kingdom for the sake of truth. (Jm 31.45)

Then the Bodhisattva, approaching him whose mind was overcome with wonder and great respect, said: "The wealth of well-spoken words has been obtained, the seeker has been fully honored, and your heart has been brought to joy through your power. Therefore, O King, I have arrived; grant me my desired flesh for the sacrifice, or else prescribe for me the vow of becoming a sacrificial animal."
Saudāsa said:
"The time has not yet passed for me to devour you, for this funeral pyre is still enveloped in smoke.
Let us first listen to these well-spoken words, which are savory when cooked without smoke and served while still warm."
The Bodhisattva said: "What purpose do you have in hearing well-spoken words when you have come to such a state?
You have reached this condition for the sake of your belly, having abandoned all compassion for living beings;
yet these verses proclaim the Dharma, for from that which is contrary to the Dharma, no true Dharma arises."
For you, whose conduct is as distorted as that of a Rākṣasa and who have abandoned the path of the noble, there is no truth; whence could there be dharma? What will you do with sacred learning?
(Vaidya 226) Then Saudāsa, unable to endure that reproach, replied:
"Hold! Tell me, who is that king who does not slay the mates of forest deer in the pleasure grove when his weapons are raised?"
If I were to kill human beings here for the sake of livelihood, then indeed I would be unrighteous; but those who kill deer are not like you.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Indeed, even those who do not bend their bows toward deer that have fled in fear are established in righteousness;
yet the man-eater is most blameworthy even among them, for men are exalted by birth and are certainly not to be devoured."

Then Saudāsa, although addressed by the Bodhisattva in words that were exceedingly harsh, found his own fierce nature overwhelmed by the power of the Bodhisattva’s virtue of loving-kindness; feeling only comforted, he spoke with a smile:
"O Sutasoma, you have indeed been released by me and have returned home, which is delightful with the splendor of sovereignty on all sides."
Since you have come back to me again, it is clear that you are not skilled in the path of political wisdom.
The Bodhisattva said: "This is not so.
Rather, it is I who am skilled in the path of policy, for which reason I do not wish to carry this out—this course by following which there would be an absolute fall from the Dharma."
But there is no attainment of happiness; what indeed can be called skill in that?
Furthermore:
"Moreover, those who are steadfast in practicing the path of policy generally fall into states of woe after death;
having abandoned those crooked paths of policy, I have returned, being devoted to truth."
Therefore, I alone am skilled in policy, for I have abandoned falsehood and delight in truth.
For those who seek fame and pleasure do not call that good policy which is followed by nothing but the binding of further consequences.
Saudāsa said:
"Having abandoned my dear life-breaths, my weeping kinsmen, and the kingdom-based pleasures that captivate the great mind,"
Do you perceive the accomplishment of your purpose in truthful speech, since you have come to me even for the sake of protecting it?
The Bodhisattva said: "There are many excellent qualities based on truthful speech;
however, hear the summary:
truth surpasses all fragrances in its heart-pleasing nature and all flavors in its sweetness."
Apart from toil, through the renown of his meritorious qualities, he performed austerities and undertook the labors of visiting sacred fords.
It is the path for fame that has already seized the opportunity to pervade the world;
it is truly the gateway for entering the abode of the gods, and a bridge for crossing over the difficult fortress of saṃsāra.

Then Saudāsa, saying "Well said, well reasoned," bowed to him and, looking at him with wonder, spoke again: "Other kings do not come under my control when their fortitude is destroyed by fear upon being offered humiliation;
yet you are being abandoned by the splendor of your fortitude—I believe, O lord of men, that you have no fear of death."
The Bodhisattva said:
"When something cannot be avoided even with great effort,
what is the use of fear and dejection, which are incapable of providing a remedy?"
Thus, even those who understand the conditions of worldly existence become base men when they repent due to their addiction to sin and have failed to exert themselves in virtuous deeds;
fearing the suffering of the next world, they become paralyzed by the terror of death.
I do not recall doing anything that would cause remorse in my mind;
since I have made white deeds my very nature, what person established in dharma would fear death?
"And I do not recall any arrival of a petitioner that did not result in great joy for me or for those seeking my help.
Thus, one who has attained contentment through such acts of giving and is established in the Dharma— such a person, who would fear death?
Even after reflecting for a long time, I do not recall making even a footstep of my mind toward evil;
having thus cleared the path to heaven, why should I succumb to fear of death?

Among Brahmins, kinsmen, friends, and those who sought my shelter, as well as among the poor and those who adorned the hermitage, I bestowed much wealth upon each according to their merit; and whatever duty was required for anyone, that was performed by me.
Hundreds of glorious monuments have been established—sacrificial grounds, hermitages, assembly halls, and water-stations.
Since I have attained contentment through these, I have no fear of death; therefore, prepare for a sacrifice or simply devour me.

Upon hearing this, Saudāsa, his eyes filled with tears of grace, his body covered in bristling horripilation, and the darkness of his sinful nature forgotten, looked upon the Bodhisattva with great reverence and said:
"May your evil be stilled!
Truly, today he would rather swallow poison, or a most deadly *hāhahala* venom, or a provoked poisonous snake, or even glowing iron, were he to know [of such a gift]."
O bull among kings, the head and even the heart of one who would wish evil upon such a person as you would shatter into a hundred pieces.
Therefore, you ought to speak those well-spoken words to me as well.
For by this rain of flowers of your speech, my mind has been gladdened, and my curiosity regarding them has increased most excellently. Moreover, O sir:
having seen the ugliness of the shadow of my conduct in the mirror of Dharma, [I am filled with shame].
"Perhaps my mind, eager for the Dharma, might not yet have reached its full momentum."

Then the Bodhisattva, perceiving that his disposition had become humble and his mind was inclined toward hearing the Dharma, said to him: "Therefore, it is fitting for one who seeks the Dharma to listen to it with the excellence of conduct appropriate to that end. Behold:
by sitting on a lower seat, one awakens the splendor of discipline."
With eyes offered in affection, he sat there tasting the honey of her speech.
With a mind made pure, serene, one-pointed, and inclined by reverence,
one should listen to the Dharma with respect, just as a patient listens to the words of a physician.
Then Saudāsa, having spread his own upper garment upon a high rocky surface and having seated the Bodhisattva there,
sat down himself upon the bare ground before the Bodhisattva, intent on gazing up at him with eyes fixed in watchful observation.
He said to the Great Being, "Speak now, friend!
Then the Bodhisattva, with a deep and pervasive voice as sweet as the thundering of a fresh rain-cloud, as if filling that entire forest, spoke:
"Even by mere chance, a single encounter with a virtuous person is brought about."
It becomes utterly immovable; it does not depend on the sequence of practice.
Having heard this, Saudāsa, nodding his head and gesturing with his fingers, said to the Bodhisattva, "Excellent! Excellent! What happened next?
Then the Bodhisattva recited the second verse:
"One should never behave ill toward a virtuous person; one who follows the path of discipline should honor the good."
For the pollen-dust of his virtues, spreading abroad, touches those who are near him without any effort.
Saudāsa said:
"O virtuous one, you who honor well-spoken words with your whole soul have indeed applied your purpose to the proper place; truly, your exertion has not been directed toward the improper."
"And then what?
The Bodhisattva said:
"The chariots of kings, adorned with jewels and gold, proceed [on their way], yet their bodies fall into the deformity of old age."
But for the virtuous, the law does not age; for the good are firm in their affection for virtues.
This is truly a rain of nectar!
Oh, we have been thoroughly satiated!
What follows next?
The Bodhisattva said:
"The sky is far from the surface of the earth, and the further shore is distant from the near shore of the great ocean;
even more distant than the mountain of setting from the mountain of rising is the Dharma for the virtuous and for the wicked."
Then Saudāsa, his affection and great respect aroused by both faith and wonder, said to the Bodhisattva:
"Having heard these sweet verses of yours, whose meanings are radiant with the excellence of their wonderful expressions," (Vaidya 230)
Delighted, for the sake of honoring him in return, I grant you four boons.
"Therefore, choose whatever you desire from me.
Then the Bodhisattva, with wonder and great respect, said to him: "Who are you to grant a boon, you who have no mastery even over yourself, being overcome by passion for what ought not to be done?"
What boon will you grant to another, since your own state has turned away from the pursuit of virtue?

If I were to say, "Give me this boon," and your mind were inclined toward the desire to give it, what compassionate person would consent to such a transgression? For us, even this much is quite enough.
Then Saudāsa, his face slightly bowed with shame, said to the Bodhisattva: "Enough, let not your lordship suspect me thus;
even at the cost of my own life, I shall grant these boons. Therefore, O King, choose confidently whatever you desire."
The Bodhisattva said:

"In that case, be true to your vow; abandon the harming of living beings and release all these people who have been taken captive. And today, O hero among men, do not eat human flesh; instead, grant me these four excellent and most desirable boons."
Saudāsa said:
"I grant you three prior boons; choose a fourth boon other than that.
Do you not realize this, how I am the master who cannot desist from human flesh?"
The Bodhisattva said: "Alas, this has come to pass for you!
Did I not ask, 'Who are you to grant a boon? Moreover, sir, how can you maintain both your vow of truthfulness and your non-violence?"
O King, for one who does not renounce the eating of human flesh.
He said:
"Was it not previously stated by you, 'I shall grant these boons'?"
Even by sacrificing one's life, this very thing is brought about otherwise.
And how can there be non-violence for you while you kill men for the sake of their flesh?
This being so, which three boons could possibly have been granted by you?
Saudāsa said:
"I have abandoned my kingdom and endured suffering in the forest for his sake;
yet dharma has been destroyed and my fame wounded—how then shall I abandon him?"

The Bodhisattva said: "For this very reason, your lordship ought to abandon it. How can you not abandon such a source of misfortune, for whose sake you have fallen away from dharma, wealth, happiness, and fame?"
This ingratitude exists among people ruined by a lack of nobility;
how indeed could such baseness overcome even you?
Therefore, enough of leading you further toward sin;
you ought to realize your true self.
For your honor is indeed Saudāsa.

There are meats inspected by physicians and prepared by skilled cooks—those from domestic animals, those from marshy regions, those born in water, and those from the wilderness. Satisfy your heart with these; desist, for the sake of virtue, from the contemptible flesh of human beings.

Having abandoned the deep resonance of musical instruments like the thundering of water-laden clouds, the sound of song at night, and all those various pleasures of sovereignty— along with your kinsmen, sons, and agreeable attendants— how indeed can you find delight here in this solitary forest?
O Lord of Men, you ought not to go under the sway of the mind; follow the path that does not obstruct Dharma and Artha.
Having conquered all the armies of kings in battle, do not be timid in the undertaking of the war against the mind.
O lord of men, surely the world beyond must also be considered; therefore, one should not indulge in that which is pleasant yet harmful.
But whatever is agreeable to the mind and does not obstruct one's fame—though it may be unpleasant—embrace that like medicine.
(Vaidya 232) Then Saudāsa, his eyes filled with tears of devotion and his throat choked with emotion, approached the Bodhisattva, embraced his feet, and said:
"By the pollen of the flowers of your virtues, this entire world is everywhere perfumed with the fragrance of merit; today it is strewn with the causes of your glory."
While he thus reflects upon his evil deeds and the fierce conduct of the messengers of Death, who else indeed but you could be so compassionate toward me?
"You are my teacher, my preceptor, and indeed my very deity; with my head bowed, I honor these words of yours.
O Sutasoma, I shall certainly not eat human flesh, and I will do exactly as you tell me."

"Come, let us release them as well— those for whose sake the prince was brought by me, who were oppressed by the misery of their bonds, robbed of their luster, and whose minds were overwhelmed with grief."
Then the Bodhisattva, having promised him "So be it," went straight to the place where those princes were imprisoned.
As soon as they saw Sutasoma, those princes rejoiced exceedingly, thinking, "Ah, we are liberated!
At the sight of Sutasoma, those sons of the king shone with the beauty of radiant smiles.
Like beds of night-lotuses blooming at the onset of autumn, augmented by the rays of the moon.

Then the Bodhisattva, having approached them, comforted them and greeted them with kind words; he made them swear an oath not to harm Saudāsa, released them from their bonds, and, followed by Saudāsa and those princes, returned to his own kingdom.
There, having had the necessary rites performed for them, he established those princes and Saudāsa each in their respective kingdoms.
Thus, since association with the virtuous arrives in whatever way it may for the sake of the highest good (*śreyas*), one who seeks the highest good must take refuge in the company of the noble.
Likewise, this should also be stated in the praise of the Tathāgata: "The Blessed Buddha is thus, because even in previous lives when he was not yet known, he was intent on benefiting others.
Similarly, this should also be stated regarding the hearing of the True Dharma (*saddharma*): "Hearing the True Dharma leads to the removal of faults and the cultivation of virtues."
This should also be stated when praising learning: "Thus, learning possesses manifold benefits.

It should also be stated when discussing truth: "Thus, truthful speech is cherished by the virtuous and is a source of merit and fame; thus, noble persons, regardless of their own life, pleasure, or power, protect the truth.
This may likewise be applied when praising truth and when describing compassion.
Thus ends the thirty-first Jātaka, the Sutasoma-jātaka.
32. The Story of the Iron House (*Ayogṛhajātaka*).
Even royal splendor does not obstruct the path to the highest good for those whose minds are filled with spiritual urgency; therefore, one should cultivate familiarity with such urgency.
As it is heard—when the Blessed One was still a bodhisattva, having beheld the world afflicted by hundreds of calamities such as disease, old age, death, and separation from the beloved;

seeing it as suffering, helpless, without protection, without refuge, and without a guide, he was impelled by compassion. With his mind resolved upon its deliverance and possessing an exceedingly noble nature, he accomplished various deeds for its sake.

For the benefit and extraordinary happiness of the world, even though it was averse and unacquainted with him, he once took birth in a certain royal family— a family whose great fortune was manifested by its prosperity, which was never faltering due to its favorable disposition toward the affection of the subjects, and by which its proud vassals were humbled, and which was celebrated for its discipline.

Even as he was being born, he endowed that royal family and that preeminent city—which shared his joys and sorrows—with the supreme splendor of prosperity. There, the Brahmins were delighted and busy with receiving gifts; the servants wore bright attire and were arrogant with pride;
and the city resounded with the cries of many musical instruments, filled with joyful dancing and the absence of any improper conduct.
The sound of singing, weeping, and laughter mingled together; joy was increased by mutual embraces;
and the king’s prosperity was invoked by men satisfied with the gifts of pleasant tidings.
With its gates thrown open and its fastenings released, with its crossroads adorned by uplifted banners,
and with its ground sprinkled with crushed flowers and fragrant liquors, the city bore the lovely splendor of a festival.
Then, with showers of gold, garments, ornaments, and other riches being scattered from great mansions,
Fortune— as if striving to pervade the world— assumed the graceful, meandering course of the intoxicated Gaṅgā.
And at that time, every son born to that king used to die.

Thinking that this was caused by non-human beings, he prepared for the protection of his infant son a magnificent birth-chamber made entirely of iron, yet adorned with various designs of jewels, gold, and silver; therein he established protective rites and counter-measures against malevolent spirits according to the procedures observed in the science of spirits (*bhūtavidyā*) and prescribed in the Vedas.
Having performed the rites for averting evil through appropriate auspicious ceremonies and blessings, he caused the performance of the birth-rites and other sacramental procedures,
as well as the child’s upbringing. Furthermore,
because of that Great Being’s excellence of character, the power of his accumulated merit, and the thoroughness of the protective measures taken, non-human beings could not overpower him.

In the course of time, having received the sacraments and performed the prescribed rites, he acquired various branches of knowledge from teachers who were distinguished by their learning, noble lineage, and conduct; who had attained renown and honor among the wise;

and who were won over by his own virtues of tranquility, humility, and intelligence. Day by day, his person being filled with the splendor of youth and his natural devotion to discipline, he became an object of supreme affection for both his kinsmen and the public.
People follow a virtuous person with the affection of a friend, even if that person is a stranger, unrelated, or far away; in such cases, the beauty of their virtues is the cause.
What connection could there possibly be between the world and the moon, which, having become the laughter of the sky, wanders through the autumnal firmament with its rays?

Then that Great Being, though being entertained by many celestial objects of sense brought forth by the power of his merit and providing him with pleasure, and being looked upon by his father— who was kind-faced with affection and great respect— with trust and without hesitation, once desired to behold the splendor of the Kaumudī festival, which had arrived in due course and displayed a vast and beautiful magnificence within his excellent city; having thus received permission, he set out.

Having mounted his excellent chariot—which was adorned with ornaments variegated with patterns of gold, jewels, and silver; which bore aloft bright flags and banners of various colors fluttering in the wind; which was drawn by four well-trained, swift horses decorated with golden trappings; and which had a charioteer who was skillful, courteous, expert, pure, humble, and steady—he proceeded through that preeminent city preceded by the sound of delightful musical instruments, accompanied by a retinue wearing bright and colorful attire, weapons, and armor; while the hearts of the people were captivated by the sight of him.

Beholding the splendor of the gathering of city-dwellers and country-folk— whose eyes were restless with curiosity, who were occupied with the performance of hymns, salutations, joining of palms, prostrations, and the utterance of blessings, and whose dress was made even more beautiful by the festive occasion— he regained his memory of former births, despite the opportunity for joy having been found in his mind, because of his long-standing familiarity with the sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
"Alas," he thought, "the condition of the world is wretched, rendered tasteless by its transience."
If this splendor of the Kaumudī festival is to become merely a memory, [then what is the point]?
And in such a course of worldly existence, oh, how great is the fearlessness of people! For, though all paths are presided over by death, they wander about joyfully, free from agitation.
While enemies of irresistible power— disease, old age, and death— stand ready with the intent to slay,
and while the difficult path to the next world must inevitably be traversed, what room is there for joy here for one possessed of consciousness?
As if imitating the roar of the great oceans, having made the waters fierce with their agitation,
the clouds— garlanded with gold flashing with lightning— having come together, once more go to dissolution.
Having uprooted the trees whose roots were firmly bound to their banks by means of waters that have gained momentum,
the rivers gradually become once more like the days, as if afflicted by the heat of grief.
Even after uprooting the peaks of mountains, dispersing masses of clouds with its force,
and churning and tossing the waters of the ocean, the power of the wind comes to an end.
A fire with its blazing, fierce flames and scattering sparks goes out after consuming the dry brushwood;
likewise, the splendors of forest regions arise in succession and then vanish once more.
What union does not end in separation? What prosperity does not turn into calamity?
Thus, while the course of the world is so fickle, people feel joy without even reflecting upon it.

Thus reflecting, that Great-souled One, with a mind whose joy and agitation had turned away through spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), found his intellect unattached even to the beautiful and variegated sights of the people spread out for the decoration of the great city. He saw himself, as it were, already arrived at his own palace. With that spiritual urgency further intensified and indifferent toward the pleasures of the senses, he resolved that the Dharma alone was his refuge. Having determined his mind upon its practice, he approached the King at a suitable opportunity and, with palms joined in reverence, requested permission to depart for the forest of asceticism.
"By taking refuge in the life of a renunciant, I wish to accomplish my own welfare;
may you grant me permission for that, as a path of favor."
Having heard that, the king, whose son was dear to him, was pierced like an elephant by a poisoned arrow;
though he was as deep as the ocean, he trembled, his mind distressed by grief, like the sea shaken by the wind.
Then the king, wishing to dissuade him, embraced him out of affection with a voice choked with tears and said:
"My son, why have you suddenly made up your mind to abandon us?"
"By whom was this Kṛtānta, the cause of his own destruction through your displeasure, brought about?
Whose faces among our kinsmen shall become overwhelmed with tears of grief? (Jm 32.18)
"Furthermore, if you have any suspicion regarding me, or if you have heard anything unpleasant, speak it so that I may desist from it; for I do not perceive anything of the sort within myself."
The Bodhisattva said:
"How could there be any offense against you, whose face is so bright with affection?
And who would be capable of reaching me by means of something unpleasant?"
Then, being addressed by the king with tearful eyes, "Why then do you wish to abandon us?", that Great Being replied to him: "Out of fear of death.
Let Your Majesty behold:
O hero among men, from the very first night that a person enters their dwelling in the womb..."
From that time forth, proceeding without faltering, he approached the vicinity of death every day.
Even one well-versed in policy or established in power cannot transcend death or old age;
since all are thus afflicted by these two, I shall therefore resort to the forest for the sake of Dharma.

"Kings, impetuous with pride, conquer armies arrayed with exalted men, horses, chariots, and elephants; yet they are unable to conquer even a single enemy. Therefore, my mind is resolved to take refuge in the Dharma."
Protected by armies consisting of joyful horses, elephants, infantry, and chariots, kings attain liberation from their enemies;
yet even Manu and others, along with their forces, fell helplessly under the power of the enemy Death, who possesses exceeding strength.
Having crushed the city gates and gate-towers with their mace-like tusks in battle, as well as chariots, men, and elephants,
those rutting elephants do not even drive back Death when he approaches them face-to-face, despite those tusks having achieved victory against ramparts.

Skilled in weapons, they pierce with their arrows even those enemies who stand at a great distance, wearing firm and variegated armor and shields; yet they do not strike that long-standing enemy, Death, in battle.
Having quelled the vital energy of elephants with their claw-tips that act like razors and whose points are buried in the tops of their frontal globes,
and having pierced the ears and minds of their enemies with their roars, the lions, their pride and strength destroyed, meet their death and sleep.
Kings inflict punishment upon other offenders in accordance with their faults;
yet they do not apply themselves to the science of penal policy even when faced with the great offense of the enemy of death.

Kings bring even those who have committed offenses under their control through means such as conciliation; however, Death—whose arrogance is made firm by long-standing habit—is not to be overcome by persuasion or similar methods.
Snakes bite men with sprout-like fangs that contain the terrible fire of poison ignited by the flames of their wrath;
yet, when death is the one to be slain—one who is ever skilled in inflicting harm—they become paralyzed in their effort to bite.
Physicians pacify the poison of those bitten even by serpents impetuous with rage through mantras and medicines;
but this Kṛtānta is a venomous serpent of extreme poison with fatal fangs, whose power cannot be overcome by mantras, medicines, or any other means.
Having scattered from the oceans the waters— resounding with the terrifying thundering of massed clouds and containing schools of fish sportively tossed by the winds of their wings—
the *suparṇas* seize the serpents with their wide-open jaws; yet they do not venture to crush death in such a manner.

Having overtaken even those fleeing in terror by their superior speed and having subdued them with the playful display of a thunderbolt-like paw, tigers drink the blood of deer in the forest; yet they are not so adept at such behavior when it comes to death.
Indeed, even after encountering the tiger’s mouth, terrifying with its fangs, a deer may attain release once more;
but for whom, having entered the mouth of Death—with its wide jaws and the tusks of disease, old age, and suffering—is there ever again any prospect of well-being?
The planets, with their deformed and fierce forms and firm grasp, drink away the vitality and lifespans of men by their power;
yet they become subject to the onset of death itself, their pride and violent arrogance utterly destroyed.

Those who have mastered the sciences subdue the planetary spirits that have approached to harm those devoted to worship by means of the power of austerity, auspicious rites, and medicinal herbs; yet the planetary spirit of Death is indeed impossible to ward off.
Those who know the arts of illusion bewilder the eyes of the people in the great assembly;
yet this is some power of the Ender (Antaka) by which even their own eyes are not deceived by him.

Even Dhanvantari and others, who were the foremost of physicians, having destroyed poisons and pacified the diseases of men through mantras perfected by the power of asceticism, have themselves met their end; therefore, my mind bows toward the Dharma at the edge of the forest.

Vidyādharas, possessing the power and majesty of various mantras, appear and then vanish again; they travel by the path of the wind or enter the earth, yet when they encounter death, their power is utterly destroyed.
The lords of the gods repel even the arrogant asuras, and the asuras repel even the arrogant gods; yet,
by those whose minds are mounted on pride and who have raised vast armies— even when united— death remains truly unconquerable.
Having recognized this irresistible ferocity of my enemy, Death, I have no desire for his abode;
yet, neither out of anger nor from a loss of affection, do I go to the forest, but rather resolved for the sake of Dharma.
The king said: "Then what consolation do you have in the forest, when the fear of death is thus beyond remedy, even while you embrace the dharma?
Will the enemy Death not overtake you in the forest? Have the sages, though established in dharma, not perished in the forest?
Indeed, this sequence is ordained everywhere; what purpose, then, is served by abandoning your home to take refuge in the forest?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Granted that death treats with equal indifference those who dwell in houses or in forests, whether they are virtuous or devoid of merit;
yet for those whose souls are devoted to Dharma, it is not a cause for remorse, and indeed, it is only in the forest that one can truly attain the happiness known as Dharma."
Let Your Majesty behold:
in a household that is the abode of negligence, intoxication, lust, greed, and hatred,
what room can there be for the acceptance of dharma, which is the opposite of those?
Dragged away by many evil deeds, distracted by the acquisition and preservation of possessions,
and with a mind unpeaceful due to the onset of calamities, when will the householder ever find the path of tranquility?
But in the forest, having abandoned the expansion of evil deeds and being free from the affliction of possessions, he is happy;
with tranquility as his sole task and a contented mind, he attains happiness, Dharma, and renown.
Dharma protects a person, not wealth or power; Dharma leads to great happiness, not the attainment of worldly sovereignty.
Death brings joy only to one whose soul is devoted to Dharma, for there is no fear of an evil rebirth for one who is intent upon Dharma.
Just as the specific distinctions of action are established with different characteristics for both merit and sin,
so too is the ripening of the unwholesome a miserable rebirth, while that of manifold dharma is a state of happiness.

Having thus entreated his father, that Great-souled One, having received his father’s permission, cast aside the splendor of sovereignty like a blade of grass and took refuge in a forest of asceticism. There, having produced the immeasurable meditations (*dhyāna*) and established the world therein, he ascended to the Brahma-world.
Thus, even the splendor of royal power does not obstruct the path to the highest good for those whose minds are agitated by spiritual urgency; therefore, one should cultivate such urgency.
The same should also be said regarding the praise of the perception of death: "In this way, the perception of swift death leads to spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Likewise, it should be applied to the praise of the recollection of death and to the discourse on impermanence: "In this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent. Similarly, it should be applied to the perception of non-delight in the entire world: "In this way, the conditioned is not a source of security."
Thus, it should also be said that "this world is without protection and without a companion";
and likewise, it should be inferred that "the Dharma is easy to practice in the forest, not at home.
Thus ends the thirty-second Jātaka, the Ayogṛha-jātaka.
33. The Mahiṣa-jātaka:
"Forgiveness should be exercised when there is something to be forgiven, not otherwise"; thus the virtuous regard even those who do them harm as a great gain.
Thus it is heard: once, in a certain forest region, the Bodhisattva became a wild buffalo bull that traveled on foot; his body was coarse from contact with mud, like a fragment of a dark blue cloud.

Although he existed in that animal realm where the perception of the Dharma is difficult to find and delusion is abundant, because his consciousness was sharp, his mind never ceased its exertion in the practice of the Dharma.
Bound by affection through long-standing devotion, compassion never abandoned him;
yet there was some power, whether of his own karma or of that very [being], by which he became thus.
Therefore, the Blessed One surely spoke of the inconceivability of the process of the ripening of karma,
since even though he was compassionate by nature, he underwent birth in the animal realm and maintained the perception of it as the Dharma.
Without karma there is no continuity of rebirth, nor is there any auspicious result that lacks an undesirable ripening;
yet even he, though possessing the notion of "dharma," remained in various states as he encountered those respective traces of karma.

Then, a certain wicked monkey, perceiving that the Great Being’s natural goodness— which had been latent for some time— was now manifest, and seeing through his compassionate conduct that he was free from the agitation of anger, concluded that there was no danger from him; thus, he tormented that Great Being even more severely with various acts of violence.
A wicked person, provoked by excessive insolence toward those who are compassionate and mild, undergoes a state of extreme agitation, for he perceives no danger from them; yet,
when he is touched even by the slightest suspicion of fear, he changes completely.
There he moves about with humble gait, like one who is disciplined, his agitation stilled.
Sometimes, while that Great Being was sleeping trustfully or nodding off under the influence of drowsiness, it would suddenly fall upon him;
sometimes, having climbed onto him like a tree, it would shake him violently;
and sometimes, even when he was hungry, it would stand blocking his path.
On one occasion, he even struck him on the ears with a piece of wood;
and once, while he was eager to plunge into the water, he climbed onto his head and covered both his eyes with his hands.
He even mounted upon him with a raised staff.
Driving [the horse] by force, he imitated the sport of Yama;
yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, regarding all those unruly actions of his as if they were a favor, endured them without agitation, fury, or anger.
For it is the very nature of the wicked to resort to paths contrary to discipline.
And through practice, forbearance toward them becomes like a service rendered to the virtuous.

Then, it is said, a certain yakṣa—unable to endure that humiliation or wishing to test the disposition of that Great Being—stood in the path of the buffalo bull being driven by that wicked monkey and said this: "Ho there!
Have you been hired for this by this wicked monkey?"
"Have you been defeated at dice? Or do you perhaps fear something from him?
Or is it that you do not perceive the strength residing within yourself, such that you are thus humiliated and driven away by him? Pray tell!"
Driven by your speed, the thunderbolt of your tusks' tips would shatter even a diamond, or like a thunderbolt, crush the lords of mountains;
yet these feet of yours, released from the agitation of anger, would sink into the mountain ridges as if into mud.
And this body of yours— compact and firm like a mountain, possessed of complete splendor through its perfection of strength,
and formidable when beheld due to its natural vigor— would be unassailable even by a lion.
"Having seized him with your hands, or with a razor, or with the tip of your tusk, extract his arrogance!
Why do you endure this suffering from tormenting this monkey, who is as powerless as a net?"
Where and how can a wicked person be treated with a gentle disposition and a character marked by virtue,
when he spreads like a phlegmatic disease that advances toward its cure through pungent, hot, and dry remedies?
Then the Bodhisattva, looking at that yakṣa, spoke with words that were patient, impartial, and gentle: "I know him to be surely fickle and always delighting in misconduct;
for this very reason, is it not indeed proper for me to forgive him?"

What forgiveness can there be for one who is unable to retaliate against a stronger person? Moreover, why should one not forgive those virtuous ones whose character is marked by discipline and good conduct?
Since one who is truly capable endures the lapses of the weak,
it is better to suffer humiliation than the loss of one's virtues.

Indeed, the time for proclaiming one's virtues is when one is treated with disrespect and one's strength is diminished; why then, being fond of virtue, would one exert effort toward breaking one's own fortitude by looking for such an occasion?

Indeed, the time for forgiveness is always difficult to obtain when one is dependent on another; yet, when that very moment is brought about by the other, what reason is there to employ a course of anger?
"He who has set out here as if seeking to purify my own sin, without considering the injury to his own dharma—
if I were not to grant him forgiveness in this matter, alas, what kind of ungrateful person would I be?"

The Yakṣa said: "In that case, you shall certainly not escape from the torment of her hair— what man, without abandoning his patience toward a servant who has not abandoned his own insolence due to a lack of respect for virtues, is able to restrain him?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"That pleasure which results from inflicting pain upon another, or the prevention of the arising of suffering for another, is not fit to be pursued by one who seeks happiness;
for its maturation does not lead to the attainment of happiness."

If he does not understand even when being thus awakened by me through the reality of the matter, relying on patience, then those who are intolerant will restrain him from the wrong path as he pursues this course.
Having encountered such treatment from people of that kind, he will not act in this way even toward one like me;
for once he has experienced the fault [of his own conduct], he will not act thus again, and therefore my liberation will be secured.

Then the yakṣa, his mind overcome with faith, wonder, and great respect for that Great Being, honored him by nodding his head and waving his fingers, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke these kind words:

"Whence comes such a state among the animals, and whence this extensive devotion to virtues? By some extraordinary intelligence you have assumed this body; who are you, sir, practicing austerities here in the penance grove?"
Having thus praised him and shaken that wicked monkey from his back, and having instructed him on the means of protection, he vanished right there.

This being so, since forbearance is possible only when there is something to be endured and not otherwise, the virtuous regard even an injurer as a great gain; this is what should be said in the discourse on forbearance.
Thus is seen the excellence of the discernment of Bodhisattvas who have taken birth among animals.
"What human being, whether a layperson or one who has taken the vow of renunciation, would find it fitting to be deficient in these?
This should also be said regarding the praise of the Tathāgata and the reverent listening to the Dharma.
Thus ends the thirty-third Jātaka, the Mahiṣa-jātaka.
34. In the Śatapatra-jātaka,
even though he was being incited, the virtuous one was not capable of engaging in evil due to a lack of habituation.
As it is heard:
once, in a certain forest region, the Bodhisattva was born as a hundred-petaled lotus with variegated petals, beautifully adorned with various colors.
And because of his long-standing cultivation of compassion, even in that state, he did not follow the way of life of a hundred-petaled lotus, which is defiled by the injury of living beings.
With the young shoots of trees, with honey scented by flowers and fresh from the day,
and with fruits of various tastes, fragrances, and colors, he maintained a life of contentment.
Proclaiming the Dharma to others as was appropriate, rescuing the afflicted according to his power,
and restraining the ignoble from their lack of discipline, he manifested his conduct for the sake of others.

Thus, while being protected by that Great Being in that forest region, the multitude of beings grew happily as if they had a teacher, as if they had kinsmen, as if they possessed knowledge, and as if they lived under a righteous king.
Because he protected them out of the greatness of his compassion,
that multitude of beings likewise attained an increase in virtue while being thus guarded by him.

Then once, while that Great Being was wandering through the depths of the forest out of compassion for living beings, he saw in a certain part of the woods a lion whose mane was disheveled and soiled by contact with dust, writhing in a place like one pierced by a poisoned arrow due to being overwhelmed by intense agony.
Approaching him and impelled by pity, he asked: "What is this, O King of Beasts?"

"Indeed, I see that your body is truly unwell. Whether through an excess of passion for pride while among elephants, or from an addiction to speed among deer, this indisposition of yours has been caused by exhaustion, by the arrow of a hunter, or by some kind of ailment."
Therefore, tell me what is to be said to you, if it is so; or whatever task must be done here, let that be spoken.
Whatever power I possess regarding my friends, by means of that I shall accomplish your happiness, and you shall be happy.
The lion said: "O virtuous one, best of birds, this discomfort born of exhaustion is not due to pain or the shaft of a hunter's arrow;
rather, it is this fragment of bone stuck within my throat that torments me intensely like a splinter."
For I am unable to swallow or even spit this out;
therefore, this is the time for friends:
act now as you know best.
"Thus, please make me happy.

Then the Bodhisattva, having reflected upon the means for extracting the arrow because of his sharp intelligence, took a piece of wood equal in length to the obstruction of that [arrow] and said to the lion: "Open your mouth as wide as you can with all your strength."
He did exactly so.

Then the Bodhisattva, having properly placed that piece of wood between his two rows of teeth and entered [the mouth], seized with the tip of his mouth that fragment of bone which was lodged crosswise at the base of the throat, causing it to become loosened in one place while [remaining firm] in the other.
Having grasped it, he pulled it out from the edge;
even as he was exiting, he caused that wooden wedge which had been blocking his mouth to fall away.
For even a skillful surgeon who has observed the procedure well might not extract the arrow despite his efforts.
That which he extracted by means of an intellect cultivated through hundreds of births, perfected without the need for strenuous effort.
Having extracted both the dart and the pain along with the grief it produced,
he was as joyful from the removal of the dart as the man had been from the extraction of the dart itself.
For this is the nature of the virtuous:
having accomplished the happiness of another or averted their misfortune, even at the cost of his own suffering,
the good man attains that excellence of extraordinary joy which he does not find even in his own easily acquired pleasures.

Thus, that Great Being, having allayed the lion’s suffering, his heart filled with joy, took leave of him; and being greeted by the lion in return, he departed as he pleased. Then, on one occasion, while wandering about—a *śatapatra* crane with most beautiful and variegated plumage—he failed to find any kind of food of that sort anywhere. His body overcome by the fire of hunger, he saw that very same lion enjoying the flesh of a young deer that had recently been killed.
He beheld him like a fragment of an autumn cloud, his face, claws, and the tips of his mane stained with blood, as if anointed by the glow of twilight.
Although he had been rendered a benefactor, he did not venture to speak words made bitter by begging;
for even that confident man was overcome by shame, which at that moment imposed upon him a vow of silence.
Nevertheless, out of regard for his duty, he moved within the range of the man's vision, though devoid of shame;
yet that evil-souled one, even while seeing him, did not offer him an invitation.
It is like a seed sown upon a stone slab, or an oblation poured into a heap of ashes whose heat has subsided;
it is like a flower offered to a thankless person or a reed, both of which yield no fruit when the time for fruition arrives.

Then the Bodhisattva, thinking, "Surely he does not recognize me," approached him with even greater confidence; having offered appropriate blessings in the manner of a petitioner, he requested a share [of his flesh], saying:
"May it be well for the King of Beasts, whose livelihood is earned through valor!
I desire from you the honoring of a petitioner, which is the means for achieving fame and merit."

Even as these sweet words of blessing were being spoken, Siṃha—whose conduct was unbecoming to a noble man due to his long acquaintance with cruelty and envy—looked at the Bodhisattva with a rolling, deep-tawny gaze blazing like the fire of anger, as if wishing to consume him, and said: "Stop for a moment, sir! You who know nothing of the weakness of compassion while devouring leaping deer—"
Having entered my mouth, that you still live is not much.
Yet you treat me with such contempt and approach me with this request;
are you weary of life, or do you wish to see the next world?
Then the Bodhisattva, feeling ashamed by those harsh words of refusal, rose up right there into the sky.
Having effectively told him, "We are birds," by the sound of the flapping of his wings, he departed.
Then a certain forest deity, unable to endure that discourtesy toward him—or perhaps wishing to test the extent of his fortitude—flew up and said to that Great Being: "O best of birds!"
Why do you, having done him a favor, endure this lack of respect from that evil-minded man,
even though you possess the power to do so?
What is the purpose of thus neglecting such an ungrateful person?

"You are capable of crushing even this powerful one with a blow from your mouth during its attack, and you could snatch away its prey even while it remains between its fangs; why then does he tolerate this? Is this his arrogance of strength?"
Then the Bodhisattva, though thus treated with disrespect and even urged on by that forest deity, spoke while demonstrating his innate goodness: "Enough, enough with this course;
this is not the path for those like me.
The engagement of the virtuous toward the afflicted is out of compassion, not out of desire for gain."
Whether he accepts it or not, what cause for anger is there in that?
That is indeed a deception for him, that another does not recognize what has been done;
for who, seeking a return favor, would do more for such a person?
But one who has benefited another through righteousness shall, by necessity, attain union with the fruit thereof in the next world,
and even in this life, with glory and prosperity.
If the duty has been performed, what cause for regret could there be?
On the other hand, if it was done for the sake of a return favor, then it was not a true gift, but merely the repayment of a debt.
He who, thinking "the other knows my kindness but not my injury," nevertheless inflicts harm upon me—
does he not, having purified his body of fame with virtues, adopt the conduct of an elephant?
If a suffering person does not recognize a favor received, he may not be joined with prosperity that is lovely through its virtues;
but for one possessed of consciousness, what course could there be other than to destroy his own exalted reputation?
But this seems to me the most appropriate course here:
from that place where, even when one has behaved with perfect propriety, the duty of a friend is not recognized,
one should depart slowly, without harshness and without agitation.
Then that deity, her mind gladdened by those well-spoken words, praised him repeatedly, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! and spoke these pleasing words:
"Though you lack the toil of wearing matted hair and bark garments, you are a seer (*ṛṣi*), a self-controlled ascetic (*yati*) who understands the further shore.
For it is not mere outward dress that constitutes the perfection of a sage; one who is endowed with virtues is a sage in truth."
Having thus observed and honored him, he vanished right there.
Therefore, it should be stated in praise of the virtuous that even when being incited in this manner, a good person is not capable of engaging in evil due to lack of habituation.
Likewise, this is also to be applied in a discourse on patience: through such familiarity with forbearance, one does not become full of enmity.
"One who is not full of fault is dear to many people and pleasing to the mind.
Thus, it should be stated in the praise of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) that "the wise, being abundant in discernment, protect the splendor of their own virtues.

And in the [sections on] the majesty of the Tathāgata and the praise of the cultivation of a noble nature (*bhadraprakṛti*), it is said: "A noble nature thus cultivated does not cease even for those who have gone to the animal realm."
Thus ends the thirty-fourth Jātaka, the Śatapatra-jātaka.
This is the work of the venerable Āryaśūra.
